prompt: The mean oscillation of a function $f$ on an interval $(a,b)$ is defined to be the average value of $|f(x)-\bar f|$ on $(a,b)$, where $\bar f$ is the average value of $f$ on $(a,b)$. Calculate the mean oscillation of the function $f=\log x$ on the interval $(0,b)$.

solutions.title: Rescale to $(0,1)$
solutions.body:
**Average of $f$.** $\displaystyle\bar f=\frac1b\int_0^b\log x\,dx=\frac1b\big[x\log x-x\big]_0^b=\log b-1$ (the integral is improper but convergent since $x\log x\to0$).

**Mean oscillation.** Substitute $x=bt$, $t\in(0,1)$: $\log x-\bar f=\log b+\log t-\log b+1=\log t+1$. Hence
$$\frac1b\int_0^b|\log x-\bar f|\,dx=\int_0^1|\log t+1|\,dt .$$
The integrand changes sign at $t=1/e$, and $\frac{d}{dt}(t\log t)=\log t+1$, so
$$\int_0^1|\log t+1|\,dt=-\big[t\log t\big]_0^{1/e}+\big[t\log t\big]_{1/e}^{1}=\frac1e+\frac1e=\frac2e .$$
In particular the answer does not depend on $b$ (as expected from scaling: $\log(bx)$ differs from $\log x$ by a constant).

**Answer: $\dfrac{2}{e}\approx0.736$**

solutions.title: Use $\int |h| = 2\int h^+$
solutions.body:
For any integrable $h$ with $\int_0^1 h=0$ we have $\int_0^1|h|=2\int_0^1 h^+$. With $h(t)=\log t+1$ (mean zero on $(0,1)$, by the first solution's computation of $\bar f$ after rescaling), $h>0$ exactly on $(1/e,1)$, so
$$\int_0^1|h|=2\int_{1/e}^1(\log t+1)\,dt=2\big[t\log t\big]_{1/e}^{1}=2\cdot\frac1e=\frac2e .$$
A numerical check with $b=3.7$ gives $0.73576\ldots=2/e$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{2}{e}$**

prompt:
Let $I$ be an open interval, and let $f:I\to\mathbb R$ be a differentiable function. Assume that $f'(x)\ge0$ for all $x\in I$, and that all zeroes of $f'$ are isolated (this means that if $f'(x_0)=0$ for some $x_0\in I$, then there is some $\epsilon>0$ such that $f'(x)\ne0$ for all $x\in I$ such that $0<|x-x_0|<\epsilon$).

Without using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, show that $f$ is strictly increasing on $I$ (the latter means that $f(x_1)<f(x_2)$ for all $x_1<x_2$ in $I$).

Do not assume that $f'$ is continuous.
answer: By the mean value theorem $f$ is weakly increasing. If $f(x_1)=f(x_2)$ with $x_1<x_2$, then $f$ is constant on $[x_1,x_2]$, so $f'=0$ on all of $(x_1,x_2)$, contradicting that zeros of $f'$ are isolated.

solutions.title: Mean value theorem twice
solutions.body:
**Weakly increasing.** Let $x_1<x_2$ in $I$. $f$ is differentiable, hence continuous, on $[x_1,x_2]\subset I$, so by the mean value theorem there is $c\in(x_1,x_2)$ with
$$f(x_2)-f(x_1)=f'(c)(x_2-x_1)\ge0 .$$
So $f(x_1)\le f(x_2)$.

**Strictly increasing.** Suppose $x_1<x_2$ and $f(x_1)=f(x_2)$. For $x\in[x_1,x_2]$, monotonicity gives $f(x_1)\le f(x)\le f(x_2)=f(x_1)$, so $f$ is constant on $[x_1,x_2]$. Hence $f'(x)=0$ for every $x\in(x_1,x_2)$ (the difference quotients at such $x$ are $0$ for small increments). Take $x_0=\frac{x_1+x_2}2$: $f'(x_0)=0$ but every point of $(x_1,x_2)$ near $x_0$ is also a zero of $f'$, so $x_0$ is not an isolated zero. Contradiction.

Therefore $f(x_1)<f(x_2)$ whenever $x_1<x_2$. ∎

(No continuity of $f'$ and no integration were used, only the mean value theorem.)

prompt:
Suppose that $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is a continuous function from the reals to the reals, and let $X\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a subset of the real numbers. For each of the following statements either prove it is always true or give an example to show it can be false.

(a) If $X$ is open then $f(X)$ is open.

(b) If $X$ is closed then $f(X)$ is closed.

(c) If $X$ is open then $f^{-1}(X)$ is open.

(d) If $X$ is closed then $f^{-1}(X)$ is closed.
answer: (a) False: $f(x)=x^2$, $f((-1,1))=[0,1)$. (b) False: $f(x)=\frac1{1+x^2}$, $f(\mathbb R)=(0,1]$. (c) True (from the $\varepsilon$–$\delta$ definition). (d) True (take complements in (c)).

solutions.title: Counterexamples and the $\varepsilon$–$\delta$ argument
solutions.body:
**(a) False.** $f(x)=x^2$, $X=(-1,1)$ open, but $f(X)=[0,1)$ is not open (no interval around $0$ is contained in it).

**(b) False.** $f(x)=\dfrac1{1+x^2}$, $X=\mathbb R$ closed, but $f(X)=(0,1]$ is not closed ($1/(1+n^2)\to0\notin f(X)$).

**(c) True.** Let $X$ be open and $x_0\in f^{-1}(X)$. Since $f(x_0)\in X$ and $X$ is open, there is $\varepsilon>0$ with $(f(x_0)-\varepsilon,f(x_0)+\varepsilon)\subseteq X$. By continuity at $x_0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that $|x-x_0|<\delta$ implies $|f(x)-f(x_0)|<\varepsilon$, hence $f(x)\in X$. So $(x_0-\delta,x_0+\delta)\subseteq f^{-1}(X)$, and $f^{-1}(X)$ is open.

**(d) True.** If $X$ is closed, $\mathbb R\setminus X$ is open, so by (c) $f^{-1}(\mathbb R\setminus X)=\mathbb R\setminus f^{-1}(X)$ is open; hence $f^{-1}(X)$ is closed. ∎

prompt: How many zeros does the function $4z^{10}+e^z$ have in the open unit disc $\{z:|z|<1\}$ of the complex plane? Prove that it has no multiple zeros.
answer: $10$ zeros (Rouché: $|e^z|\le e<4=|4z^{10}|$ on $|z|=1$). A multiple zero would satisfy $4z^{10}=-e^z=40z^9$, forcing $z=0$ or $z=10$, neither of which is a zero.

solutions.title: Rouché's theorem
solutions.body:
Let $F(z)=4z^{10}+e^z$, $p(z)=4z^{10}$. On $|z|=1$,
$$|e^z|=e^{\mathrm{Re}\,z}\le e<4=|p(z)| .$$
By Rouché's theorem, $F=p+e^z$ and $p$ have the same number of zeros, counted with multiplicity, in $|z|<1$. Since $p$ has a zero of order $10$ at $0$, $F$ has $10$ zeros in the disc counted with multiplicity (and none on $|z|=1$, since there $|F|\ge 4-e>0$).

**No multiple zeros.** A multiple zero satisfies $F(z)=F'(z)=0$, i.e.
$$4z^{10}=-e^z\quad\text{and}\quad 40z^9=-e^z .$$
Then $4z^{10}=40z^9$, i.e. $4z^9(z-10)=0$, so $z=0$ or $z=10$. But $F(0)=1\ne0$ and $F(10)=4\cdot10^{10}+e^{10}>0$. So $F$ has no multiple zeros at all, and its $10$ zeros in the disc are distinct.

**Answer: 10 zeros, all simple.** ∎

(A numerical evaluation of the argument-principle integral $\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_{|z|=1}F'/F\,dz$ indeed gives $10$.)

prompt:
Let $f$ be an analytic function on the real line, and define $g$ by
$$g(s)=\int_0^1 f(t)\,t^s\,dt\qquad\text{for } s>0.$$
Prove that $g$ can be extended to a meromorphic function on the whole complex plane. (Hint: first do the case $f(t)=t^n$.) Where would you expect to find the poles of $g$?
answer: For $f=t^k$, $g(s)=\frac1{s+k+1}$. In general write $f=\sum_{k\le N}a_kt^k+t^{N+1}h_N(t)$ with $h_N$ bounded on $(0,1]$: $g(s)=\sum_{k\le N}\frac{a_k}{s+k+1}+\int_0^1t^{s+N+1}h_N\,dt$, meromorphic for $\mathrm{Re}\,s>-N-2$. Poles can only be simple poles at $s=-1,-2,-3,\dots$; $s=-k-1$ is a pole (residue $f^{(k)}(0)/k!$) iff $f^{(k)}(0)\ne0$.

solutions.title: Peel off Taylor polynomials
solutions.body:
**Monomials.** For $f(t)=t^k$ and $\mathrm{Re}\,s>-k-1$, $\int_0^1t^{s+k}\,dt=\dfrac1{s+k+1}$, which is meromorphic on $\mathbb C$ with a single simple pole at $s=-k-1$.

**A holomorphy lemma.** If $h$ is continuous and bounded on $(0,1]$, $|h|\le M$, and $m\ge0$, then
$$H(s)=\int_0^1t^{s+m}h(t)\,dt$$
is holomorphic on $\{\mathrm{Re}\,s>-m-1\}$. Indeed, on a half-plane $\mathrm{Re}\,s\ge\sigma_0>-m-1$ the integrand is bounded by $M\,t^{\sigma_0+m}$, which is integrable on $(0,1)$; so $H$ is continuous there (dominated convergence), and for any closed triangle $\Delta$ in the half-plane, Fubini and Cauchy's theorem for $s\mapsto t^{s+m}=e^{(s+m)\log t}$ give $\oint_{\partial\Delta}H(s)\,ds=\int_0^1h(t)\oint_{\partial\Delta}t^{s+m}\,ds\,dt=0$. By Morera's theorem $H$ is holomorphic.

**Continuation.** Let $a_k=f^{(k)}(0)/k!$. Since $f$ is analytic (in particular $C^\infty$) on $\mathbb R$, Taylor's theorem with Lagrange remainder gives, for each $N\ge0$,
$$f(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{N}a_kt^k+t^{N+1}h_N(t),\qquad |h_N(t)|\le\frac{\max_{[0,1]}|f^{(N+1)}|}{(N+1)!}\ \ (0<t\le1),$$
with $h_N(t)=\big(f(t)-\sum_{k\le N}a_kt^k\big)/t^{N+1}$ continuous on $(0,1]$. Hence for $s>0$
$$g(s)=\sum_{k=0}^{N}\frac{a_k}{s+k+1}+\int_0^1t^{s+N+1}h_N(t)\,dt=:G_N(s).$$
By the lemma (with $m=N+1$), $G_N$ is meromorphic on $U_N=\{\mathrm{Re}\,s>-N-2\}$, with at most simple poles at $-1,-2,\dots,-N-1$. For $N<N'$, $G_N$ and $G_{N'}$ agree on $(0,\infty)$, hence on the connected set $U_N$ minus the poles, by the identity theorem. So the $G_N$ fit together into one meromorphic function on $\bigcup_NU_N=\mathbb C$ extending $g$.

**Poles.** On $U_N$ the only possible poles are at $s=-k-1$, $0\le k\le N$, coming from $\frac{a_k}{s+k+1}$; the residue there is $a_k$. So $g$ has (at most simple) poles only at $s=-1,-2,-3,\dots$, and $s=-k-1$ is actually a pole exactly when $f^{(k)}(0)\ne0$, with residue $f^{(k)}(0)/k!$. ∎

(Only smoothness of $f$ on $[0,1]$ was used; analyticity is more than enough.)

prompt: Prove that the function taking $A$ to $S=(I-A)(I+A)^{-1}$ is a bijection from orthogonal real matrices $A$ whose eigenvalues are all different from $-1$ to skew-symmetric real matrices $S$.
answer: (Cayley transform.) $S^T=(I+A^{-1})^{-1}(I-A^{-1})=(A+I)^{-1}(A-I)=-S$. Conversely for skew $S$, $I+S$ is invertible ($x^T(I+S)x=|x|^2$) and $A=(I-S)(I+S)^{-1}$ is orthogonal with $I+A=2(I+S)^{-1}$ invertible; the two maps are mutually inverse.

solutions.title: Explicit inverse map
solutions.body:
Throughout, note that $I-A$, $I+A$ and $(I+A)^{-1}$ commute with each other (all are rational functions of $A$); similarly for $S$.

**$S$ is well defined and skew.** $-1$ is not an eigenvalue of $A$, so $I+A$ is invertible. Using $A^T=A^{-1}$,
$$S^T=\big((I+A)^{-1}\big)^T(I-A)^T=(I+A^{-1})^{-1}(I-A^{-1}).$$
Now $I+A^{-1}=A^{-1}(A+I)$ and $I-A^{-1}=A^{-1}(A-I)$, so
$$S^T=(A+I)^{-1}A\cdot A^{-1}(A-I)=(I+A)^{-1}(A-I)=-(I-A)(I+A)^{-1}=-S .$$

**The inverse map.** Let $S$ be real skew-symmetric. For real $x$, $x^TSx=0$ (it equals its own negative), so $x^T(I+S)x=|x|^2>0$ for $x\ne0$; hence $I+S$ is invertible (same for $I-S$). Define $A=(I-S)(I+S)^{-1}$.
- *Orthogonal:* $A^T=(I+S^T)^{-1}(I-S^T)=(I-S)^{-1}(I+S)$, so $A^TA=(I-S)^{-1}(I+S)(I-S)(I+S)^{-1}=I$ (the factors commute).
- *No eigenvalue $-1$:* $I+A=\big((I+S)+(I-S)\big)(I+S)^{-1}=2(I+S)^{-1}$ is invertible.

**Mutually inverse.** Starting from $A$ with $S=(I-A)(I+A)^{-1}$:
$$I+S=2(I+A)^{-1},\qquad I-S=2A(I+A)^{-1},$$
so $(I-S)(I+S)^{-1}=2A(I+A)^{-1}\cdot\tfrac12(I+A)=A$. The same computation with the roles of $A$ and $S$ exchanged (the formulas are symmetric) shows that starting from $S$ and forming $A=(I-S)(I+S)^{-1}$, we get $(I-A)(I+A)^{-1}=S$.

Hence $A\mapsto S$ is a bijection between the two sets, with inverse $S\mapsto(I-S)(I+S)^{-1}$. ∎

prompt: Let $V$ be the vector space of $n$ by $n$ matrices over a field, let $A$ be an element of $V$, and let $T$ be the linear transformation of $V$ taking $X$ to $AX$. Compute the determinant and trace of $T$ in terms of the determinant and trace of $A$.
answer: $\operatorname{tr}T=n\operatorname{tr}A$ and $\det T=(\det A)^n$ ($T$ acts as $A$ on each of the $n$ columns, so its matrix is $A\oplus\cdots\oplus A$).

solutions.title: Act column by column
solutions.body:
Write $X=[x_1|\cdots|x_n]$ in columns. Then $AX=[Ax_1|\cdots|Ax_n]$, so under the isomorphism $V\cong F^n\oplus\cdots\oplus F^n$ ($n$ copies, one per column), $T$ acts as $A$ on each summand. In the basis $E_{11},E_{21},\dots,E_{n1},E_{12},\dots,E_{nn}$ (ordered column by column) the matrix of $T$ is block diagonal:
$$[T]=\begin{pmatrix}A&&\\&\ddots&\\&&A\end{pmatrix}\quad(n\text{ blocks}).$$
Hence
$$\operatorname{tr}T=n\operatorname{tr}A,\qquad \det T=(\det A)^n. \ ∎$$

solutions.title: Matrix units and multiplicativity
solutions.body:
**Trace.** $T(E_{ij})=AE_{ij}=\sum_k a_{ki}E_{kj}$, whose $E_{ij}$-coefficient is $a_{ii}$. Summing over all $i,j$: $\operatorname{tr}T=\sum_{j}\sum_i a_{ii}=n\operatorname{tr}A$.

**Determinant.** Write $L_A(X)=AX$. Since $L_{AB}=L_AL_B$, the map $A\mapsto\det L_A$ is multiplicative. Every matrix is a product of elementary matrices and one diagonal matrix $\mathrm{diag}(d,1,\dots,1)$ (row reduction), so it suffices to check these. For a diagonal $D=\mathrm{diag}(d,1,\dots,1)$, $L_D$ scales the $n$ matrix units $E_{1j}$ by $d$ and fixes the others: $\det L_D=d^n=(\det D)^n$. For an elementary matrix $E=I+cE_{kl}$ ($k\ne l$), $L_E$ is unipotent (it is $I+cL_{E_{kl}}$ with $L_{E_{kl}}^2=L_{E_{kl}^2}=0$), so $\det L_E=1=(\det E)^n$. Hence $\det L_A=(\det A)^n$ for all $A$. ∎

prompt: Prove that any group of order $18$ is a semidirect product of a normal subgroup of order $9$ by a group of order $2$, and use this to classify these groups.
answer: Sylow: $N$ of order $9$ is normal (index 2), and $G=N\rtimes\langle t\rangle$. Actions are involutions in $\mathrm{Aut}(N)$ up to conjugacy: for $N=\mathbb Z_9$, $\pm1$; for $N=\mathbb Z_3^2$, $I$, $\mathrm{diag}(1,-1)$, $-I$. Exactly $5$ groups: $\mathbb Z_{18}$, $\mathbb Z_3\times\mathbb Z_6$, $D_9$, $\mathbb Z_3\times S_3$, $(\mathbb Z_3\times\mathbb Z_3)\rtimes\mathbb Z_2$ (inversion).

solutions.title: Sylow theory and involutions in $\mathrm{Aut}(N)$
solutions.body:
**Semidirect product.** Let $|G|=18=2\cdot3^2$. By Sylow's theorem there is a subgroup $N$ of order $9$; it has index $2$, hence is normal. By Cauchy's theorem there is an element $t$ of order $2$; $H=\langle t\rangle$ satisfies $N\cap H=1$ (orders $9$ and $2$ are coprime) and $|NH|=18$, so $G=NH$. Therefore $G\cong N\rtimes_\theta\mathbb Z_2$ where $\theta(t)=a\in\mathrm{Aut}(N)$, $a(n)=tnt^{-1}$, satisfies $a^2=1$.

A standard fact: if $a'=\psi a\psi^{-1}$ for some $\psi\in\mathrm{Aut}(N)$, then $(n,t^\varepsilon)\mapsto(\psi(n),t^\varepsilon)$ is an isomorphism $N\rtimes_a\mathbb Z_2\to N\rtimes_{a'}\mathbb Z_2$. So we need the conjugacy classes of elements $a$ with $a^2=1$ in $\mathrm{Aut}(N)$. Groups of order $p^2$ are abelian, so $N\cong\mathbb Z_9$ or $\mathbb Z_3\times\mathbb Z_3$.

**Case $N=\mathbb Z_9$.** $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb Z_9)\cong(\mathbb Z/9)^\times\cong\mathbb Z_6$ is cyclic, so its only elements with $a^2=1$ are $x\mapsto x$ and $x\mapsto-x$. These give
- $\mathbb Z_9\times\mathbb Z_2\cong\mathbb Z_{18}$,
- the dihedral group $D_9=\langle r,s\mid r^9=s^2=1,\ srs^{-1}=r^{-1}\rangle$.

**Case $N=\mathbb Z_3^2=\mathbb F_3^2$.** $\mathrm{Aut}(N)=GL_2(\mathbb F_3)$. If $a^2=I$ then, since $x^2-1=(x-1)(x+1)$ has distinct roots in characteristic $3$, $a$ is diagonalizable with eigenvalues $\pm1$; so $a$ is conjugate to exactly one of $I$, $\mathrm{diag}(1,-1)$, $-I$ (determined by the dimensions of the two eigenspaces, which sum to $2$). These give
- $\mathbb Z_3\times\mathbb Z_3\times\mathbb Z_2\cong\mathbb Z_3\times\mathbb Z_6$,
- $\mathbb Z_3\times(\mathbb Z_3\rtimes\mathbb Z_2)\cong\mathbb Z_3\times S_3$,
- the generalized dihedral group $(\mathbb Z_3\times\mathbb Z_3)\rtimes\mathbb Z_2$, with $t$ acting by $n\mapsto n^{-1}$.

**They are pairwise non-isomorphic.** $\mathbb Z_{18}$ and $\mathbb Z_3\times\mathbb Z_6$ are the abelian ones, distinguished by having/not having an element of order $9$. Among the non-abelian ones, $N$ is the unique Sylow $3$-subgroup (it is normal), so $G$ has an element of order $9$ iff $N$ is cyclic: this singles out $D_9$. Finally $Z(\mathbb Z_3\times S_3)\supseteq\mathbb Z_3\times1$ is nontrivial, while the generalized dihedral group has trivial center: an element $n\in N$ is central iff $n=tnt^{-1}=n^{-1}$ iff $n=1$, and an element $nt$ is not central because it acts on $N$ by inversion, which is nontrivial.

**Conclusion:** there are exactly **5** groups of order $18$: $\mathbb Z_{18}$, $\mathbb Z_3\times\mathbb Z_6$, $D_9$, $\mathbb Z_3\times S_3$, and $(\mathbb Z_3\times\mathbb Z_3)\rtimes\mathbb Z_2$. ∎

prompt: Let $G$ be a finite group and $H$ a subgroup not equal to $G$. Prove that there is an element of $G$ not in any conjugate $xHx^{-1}$ of $H$.
answer: There are $[G:N_G(H)]\le[G:H]$ conjugates, all containing $1$, so their union has at most $[G:H](|H|-1)+1=|G|-[G:H]+1<|G|$ elements when $[G:H]\ge2$.

solutions.title: Count the union of the conjugates
solutions.body:
The conjugates of $H$ correspond to cosets of the normalizer $N_G(H)\supseteq H$, so their number is
$$k=[G:N_G(H)]\le[G:H]=:m .$$
Each conjugate has $|H|$ elements, one of which is the identity, shared by all of them. Hence
$$\Big|\bigcup_{x\in G}xHx^{-1}\Big|\le k(|H|-1)+1\le m(|H|-1)+1=|G|-m+1 .$$
Since $H\ne G$, $m\ge2$, so the union has at most $|G|-1<|G|$ elements. Therefore some element of $G$ lies in no conjugate of $H$. ∎

(The finiteness of $G$ is essential: e.g. in $GL_n(\mathbb C)$ every element is conjugate into the proper subgroup of upper triangular matrices.)

prompt:
Find continuous bounded functions $f_n$ on the reals (for $n\ge0$) such that all integrals and sums below are well defined and finite, but
$$\int_{x=0}^{\infty}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}f_n(x)\,dx\ne\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\int_{x=0}^{\infty}f_n(x)\,dx .$$
answer: Take a continuous bump $g\ge0$ supported in $[0,1]$ with $\int g=1$ and $f_n(x)=g(x-n)-g(x-n-1)$: each $\int_0^\infty f_n=0$, but $\sum_nf_n=g$ (telescoping), whose integral is $1$.

solutions.title: Telescoping bumps
solutions.body:
Let $g$ be continuous, vanishing outside $[0,1]$, with $\int_0^1 g=1$; e.g. $g(x)=4\min(x,1-x)$ for $x\in[0,1]$ and $g=0$ elsewhere. Define
$$f_n(x)=g(x-n)-g(x-n-1),\qquad n\ge0 .$$
Each $f_n$ is continuous, bounded, and vanishes outside $[n,n+2]$.

- **Each integral:** $\displaystyle\int_0^\infty f_n=\int_n^{n+1}g(x-n)\,dx-\int_{n+1}^{n+2}g(x-n-1)\,dx=1-1=0$, so $\sum_n\int_0^\infty f_n=0$.
- **The sum:** for fixed $x$, $\sum_{n=0}^{N}f_n(x)=g(x)-g(x-N-1)$, and $g(x-N-1)=0$ as soon as $N+1>x$. So $\sum_{n=0}^\infty f_n(x)=g(x)$ (only finitely many nonzero terms at each $x$), and $\int_0^\infty\sum_nf_n=\int_0^\infty g=1$.

Thus $1\ne0$. (Interchange fails because $\sum_n\int|f_n|=\sum_n2=\infty$, so Fubini/dominated convergence does not apply.) ∎

prompt: Show that it is possible to find an uncountable set of subsets of the positive integers that is totally ordered by inclusion. ("Totally ordered by inclusion" means that given two of these subsets $M,N$ either $M\subseteq N$ or $N\subseteq M$. For example, the subsets $\{1\}\subseteq\{1,2\}\subseteq\{1,2,3\}\subseteq\cdots$ are totally ordered by inclusion, but are only a countable set of subsets.)
answer: Transport Dedekind cuts: fix a bijection $q:\mathbb Z_{>0}\to\mathbb Q$ and let $M_\alpha=\{n:q(n)<\alpha\}$ for $\alpha\in\mathbb R$. Then $\alpha<\beta\Rightarrow M_\alpha\subsetneq M_\beta$, giving an uncountable chain.

solutions.title: Dedekind cuts
solutions.body:
Since $\mathbb Q$ is countably infinite, fix a bijection $q:\mathbb Z_{>0}\to\mathbb Q$. For each real $\alpha$ let
$$M_\alpha=\{n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}: q(n)<\alpha\}.$$
- **Totally ordered:** if $\alpha\le\beta$ then $q(n)<\alpha$ implies $q(n)<\beta$, so $M_\alpha\subseteq M_\beta$. Any two reals are comparable, hence so are any two of the sets.
- **Distinct:** if $\alpha<\beta$, pick a rational $r$ with $\alpha<r<\beta$ (density of $\mathbb Q$); then $q^{-1}(r)\in M_\beta\setminus M_\alpha$. So $\alpha\mapsto M_\alpha$ is injective.

Hence $\{M_\alpha:\alpha\in\mathbb R\}$ is an uncountable family (it is in bijection with $\mathbb R$) of subsets of the positive integers, totally ordered by inclusion. ∎

prompt: Suppose that the functions $g,f_0,f_1,f_2,\dots$ are smooth real valued functions on $\mathbb R$ such that they all vanish at $0$ and $\lim_{n\to\infty}f_n'(x)=g'(x)$ for all $x$. (Here $g'$ means the derivative of $g$.) Either prove or give a counter-example to the claim that $\lim_{n\to\infty}f_n(x)=g(x)$ for all $x$.
answer: False. Let $\phi$ be smooth with $\phi=0$ on $(-\infty,0]$ and $\phi=1$ on $[1,\infty)$, $f_n(x)=\phi(nx)$, $g=0$: $f_n'(x)=n\phi'(nx)=0$ once $n>1/x$ (and for $x\le0$), so $f_n'\to0=g'$ pointwise, but $f_n(x)\to1$ for $x>0$.

solutions.title: A smooth step that steepens
solutions.body:
**The claim is false.**

Let $\psi(x)=e^{-1/x}$ for $x>0$ and $\psi(x)=0$ for $x\le0$; $\psi$ is smooth. Put
$$\phi(x)=\frac{\psi(x)}{\psi(x)+\psi(1-x)},$$
which is smooth (the denominator never vanishes), with $\phi=0$ on $(-\infty,0]$, $\phi=1$ on $[1,\infty)$, so $\phi'=0$ outside $[0,1]$. Let
$$f_n(x)=\phi(nx)\quad(n\ge1),\qquad f_0=0,\qquad g=0 .$$
All are smooth and vanish at $0$.

- **Derivatives converge to $g'=0$ pointwise:** $f_n'(x)=n\phi'(nx)$. If $x\le0$ then $nx\le0$ and $f_n'(x)=0$. If $x>0$ then for $n>1/x$ we have $nx>1$ and $f_n'(x)=0$. So $f_n'(x)\to0=g'(x)$ for every $x$.
- **But the functions do not converge to $g$:** for $x>0$ and $n>1/x$, $f_n(x)=\phi(nx)=1$, so $f_n(x)\to1\ne0=g(x)$.

So pointwise convergence of derivatives (even with a common value at $0$) does not imply convergence of the functions; one needs e.g. uniform convergence of $f_n'$ on intervals. ∎

*Remark.* The official solution uses the step function ($0$ for $x\le0$, $1$ for $x>1/n$), which is not smooth (not even continuous as written); the smoothed version above fixes this.

prompt: Let $f:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ be an entire function, and suppose that $f(z)/z\to0$ as $|z|\to\infty$. Prove that $f$ is constant.
answer: Cauchy's estimate on $|z|=R$ gives $|f'(a)|\le\sup_{|z-a|=R}|f(z)|/R\to0$; or apply Liouville to the entire function $(f(z)-f(0))/z$, which tends to $0$ at $\infty$.

solutions.title: Cauchy's estimate for $f'$
solutions.body:
Fix $a\in\mathbb C$. By Cauchy's formula on the circle $|z-a|=R$,
$$f'(a)=\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_{|z-a|=R}\frac{f(z)}{(z-a)^2}\,dz,\qquad\text{so}\qquad |f'(a)|\le\frac{\max_{|z-a|=R}|f(z)|}{R}.$$
Let $\varepsilon>0$. By hypothesis there is $R_\varepsilon$ with $|f(z)|\le\varepsilon|z|$ for $|z|\ge R_\varepsilon$. For $R\ge R_\varepsilon+|a|$, every $z$ with $|z-a|=R$ has $|z|\ge R_\varepsilon$ and $|z|\le R+|a|$, so
$$|f'(a)|\le\frac{\varepsilon(R+|a|)}{R}\xrightarrow[R\to\infty]{}\varepsilon .$$
Hence $|f'(a)|\le\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, i.e. $f'(a)=0$. As $a$ was arbitrary, $f'\equiv0$ and $f$ is constant. ∎

solutions.title: Liouville's theorem
solutions.body: Let $h(z)=\dfrac{f(z)-f(0)}{z}$ for $z\ne0$ and $h(0)=f'(0)$. Then $h$ is entire (removable singularity at $0$). As $|z|\to\infty$, $h(z)=\frac{f(z)}{z}-\frac{f(0)}{z}\to0$. So $h$ is bounded outside some disc, and continuous on the disc, hence bounded on $\mathbb C$; by Liouville, $h$ is constant, and the constant is $\lim_{z\to\infty}h=0$. Thus $f(z)=f(0)$ for all $z$. ∎

prompt:
Let $a>0$ be a constant $\ne3$. Let $C_a$ denote the positively oriented circle of radius $a$ centered on the origin. Evaluate
$$\int_{C_a}\frac{z^3+\sin z}{z^3(z-3)}\,dz .$$
(Your answer should be a function of $a$.)
answer: $-\dfrac{2\pi i}{9}$ for $0<a<3$, and $\dfrac{2\pi i\,(24+\sin3)}{27}$ for $a>3$ (residues $-\tfrac19$ at $0$ and $1+\tfrac{\sin3}{27}$ at $3$).

solutions.title: Residues at $0$ and $3$
solutions.body:
Let $g(z)=\dfrac{z^3+\sin z}{z^3(z-3)}=\dfrac1{z-3}+\dfrac{\sin z}{z^3(z-3)}$. It is holomorphic except at $z=0$ and $z=3$.

**At $z=3$:** a simple pole with residue $\dfrac{3^3+\sin3}{3^3}=1+\dfrac{\sin3}{27}$.

**At $z=0$:** $\frac1{z-3}$ is holomorphic there. For the second term,
$$\frac{\sin z}{z^3}=\frac1{z^2}-\frac16+O(z^2),\qquad \frac1{z-3}=-\frac13\cdot\frac{1}{1-z/3}=-\frac13\Big(1+\frac z3+\frac{z^2}9+\cdots\Big).$$
The coefficient of $z^{-1}$ in the product comes only from $\frac1{z^2}\cdot\big(-\frac13\cdot\frac z3\big)$, so
$$\operatorname{Res}_{z=0}g=-\frac19 .$$

**Residue theorem.**
- $0<a<3$: only $z=0$ is inside, so the integral is $2\pi i\cdot\big(-\frac19\big)=-\dfrac{2\pi i}{9}$.
- $a>3$: both poles are inside: $2\pi i\Big(-\dfrac19+1+\dfrac{\sin3}{27}\Big)=\dfrac{2\pi i\,(24+\sin3)}{27}$.

**Answer:** $-\dfrac{2\pi i}{9}$ if $0<a<3$; $\ \dfrac{2\pi i(24+\sin 3)}{27}$ if $a>3$.

solutions.title: Partial fractions check
solutions.body:
Partial fractions give
$$\frac1{z^3(z-3)}=-\frac1{3z^3}-\frac1{9z^2}-\frac1{27z}+\frac1{27(z-3)} .$$
Multiplying by $\sin z=z-\frac{z^3}6+\cdots$, the $z^{-1}$ coefficient at $0$ comes only from $-\frac1{9z^2}\cdot z$ (the terms $-\frac{\sin z}{3z^3}$ and $-\frac{\sin z}{27z}$ contain only even powers of $z$, and the last term is holomorphic at $0$): residue $-\frac19$, as before. The residue at $3$ is $\frac{\sin3}{27}$ from this part plus $1$ from $\frac1{z-3}$.

A direct numerical evaluation of the contour integral gives $-0.69813\,i=-2\pi i/9$ for $a=1$ and $5.61789\,i=2\pi i(24+\sin3)/27$ for $a=5$.

reviewNote: The official solution gives 2πi/9 (a<3) and 2πi(30+sin 3)/27 (a>3), but its expansion uses 1/(1-z/3) = 1 - z/3 + ..., a sign error; the residue at 0 is -1/9 (confirmed by partial fractions and numerical integration), so the corrected values -2πi/9 and 2πi(24+sin 3)/27 are used.

prompt: Let $A$ be the $n$ by $n$ complex matrix whose diagonal entries are all $a$ and whose non-diagonal entries are all $b$. Find the eigenvalues of $A$ and their multiplicities.
answer: $a+(n-1)b$ with multiplicity $1$ (eigenvector $(1,\dots,1)$) and $a-b$ with multiplicity $n-1$ (eigenspace $x_1+\dots+x_n=0$); if $b=0$ these merge into $a$ with multiplicity $n$.

solutions.title: Write $A=(a-b)I+bJ$
solutions.body:
Let $J$ be the all-ones matrix, so $A=(a-b)I+bJ$. $J$ has rank $1$: $J\mathbf 1=n\mathbf 1$ for $\mathbf 1=(1,\dots,1)^T$, and $Jx=0$ for every $x$ in the $(n-1)$-dimensional subspace $W=\{x:\ x_1+\cdots+x_n=0\}$. Since $\mathbb C^n=\mathbb C\mathbf 1\oplus W$, $J$ is diagonalizable with eigenvalues $n$ (multiplicity $1$) and $0$ (multiplicity $n-1$).

Adding $(a-b)I$ shifts every eigenvalue by $a-b$ with the same eigenvectors:
- $A\mathbf 1=\big(a+(n-1)b\big)\mathbf 1$: eigenvalue $a+(n-1)b$, multiplicity $1$;
- $Ax=(a-b)x$ for $x\in W$: eigenvalue $a-b$, multiplicity $n-1$.

(Algebraic and geometric multiplicities agree since $A$ is diagonalizable. If $b=0$ the two values coincide and $A=aI$ has the single eigenvalue $a$ with multiplicity $n$.) ∎

solutions.title: Characteristic polynomial
solutions.body:
$\det(A-\lambda I)$: add all rows to the first row; every entry of the first row becomes $a+(n-1)b-\lambda$. Factor this out, then subtract $b$ times the new first row (all ones) from each other row, leaving an upper triangular matrix with diagonal $1,a-b-\lambda,\dots,a-b-\lambda$. Hence
$$\det(A-\lambda I)=\big(a+(n-1)b-\lambda\big)(a-b-\lambda)^{n-1},$$
confirming the eigenvalues $a+(n-1)b$ (multiplicity $1$) and $a-b$ (multiplicity $n-1$). ∎

prompt: Prove that if $A$ is a real $n$ by $n$ matrix then the series $\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}A^m/m!$ converges. (This means for each $i,j$, the sum of $(i,j)$th entries converges.)
answer: With the operator norm, $\|A^m\|\le\|A\|^m$ and $|(A^m)_{ij}|\le\|A^m\|$, so each entry series is dominated by $\sum\|A\|^m/m!=e^{\|A\|}$ and converges absolutely.

solutions.title: Compare with the scalar exponential
solutions.body:
Use the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^n$ and the operator norm $\|M\|=\sup_{|v|=1}|Mv|$ on matrices. It is submultiplicative, $\|MN\|\le\|M\|\,\|N\|$, so $\|A^m\|\le\|A\|^m$. Each entry is bounded by the norm: $|M_{ij}|=|e_i\cdot Me_j|\le|Me_j|\le\|M\|$.

Hence for each fixed $i,j$,
$$\sum_{m=0}^\infty\left|\frac{(A^m)_{ij}}{m!}\right|\le\sum_{m=0}^\infty\frac{\|A\|^m}{m!}=e^{\|A\|}<\infty,$$
so the series of $(i,j)$ entries converges absolutely, hence converges. ∎

solutions.title: Elementary entry bound
solutions.body: Let $c=\max_{i,j}|a_{ij}|$. By induction, every entry of $A^m$ has absolute value at most $n^{m-1}c^m\le (nc)^m$ for $m\ge1$: indeed $|(A^{m+1})_{ij}|=\big|\sum_k(A^m)_{ik}a_{kj}\big|\le n\cdot n^{m-1}c^m\cdot c$. So the $(i,j)$ entry series is dominated by $\sum_m(nc)^m/m!=e^{nc}$ and converges absolutely. ∎

prompt: Prove that $\sqrt3+\sqrt[3]2$ is irrational.
answer: If $r=\sqrt3+\sqrt[3]2\in\mathbb Q$, then $(r-\sqrt3)^3=2$ gives $\sqrt3=\dfrac{r^3+9r-2}{3r^2+3}\in\mathbb Q$, a contradiction. (Or: $\sqrt3\in\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]2)$ is impossible since $2\nmid3$.)

solutions.title: Field degrees (official approach)
solutions.body:
$x^2-3$ and $x^3-2$ are irreducible over $\mathbb Q$ (Eisenstein at $3$ and at $2$), so $[\mathbb Q(\sqrt3):\mathbb Q]=2$ and $[\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]2):\mathbb Q]=3$.

Suppose $r=\sqrt3+\sqrt[3]2\in\mathbb Q$. Then $\sqrt3=r-\sqrt[3]2\in\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]2)$, so $\mathbb Q(\sqrt3)\subseteq\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]2)$ and by the tower law $2=[\mathbb Q(\sqrt3):\mathbb Q]$ divides $3=[\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]2):\mathbb Q]$. Contradiction. ∎

solutions.title: Cube and isolate $\sqrt3$
solutions.body:
Suppose $r=\sqrt3+\sqrt[3]2$ is rational. Then $\sqrt[3]2=r-\sqrt3$, and cubing,
$$2=r^3-3\sqrt3\,r^2+9r-3\sqrt3=(r^3+9r)-\sqrt3\,(3r^2+3).$$
Since $3r^2+3>0$,
$$\sqrt3=\frac{r^3+9r-2}{3r^2+3}\in\mathbb Q,$$
contradicting the irrationality of $\sqrt3$ (if $\sqrt3=p/q$ in lowest terms then $p^2=3q^2$ forces $3\mid p$, then $3\mid q$). ∎

prompt:
Let $G$ be a finite abelian group, written additively. Assume that for each positive integer $n$ the set $\{a\in G: na=0\}$ has at most $n$ elements.

(a) Prove that $G$ is cyclic.

(b) Deduce from this that the multiplicative group of every finite field is cyclic.
answer: (a) If $G\cong\mathbb Z_{n_1}\times\cdots\times\mathbb Z_{n_s}$ with $1<n_1\mid\cdots\mid n_s$ and $s\ge2$, then $n_1a=0$ has $n_1^s>n_1$ solutions. (Or: an element of maximal order $m$ has $mG=0$, so $|G|\le m$.) (b) In a field $x^n=1$ has at most $n$ roots, so $F^\times$ satisfies (a).

solutions.title: Structure theorem (official approach)
solutions.body:
**(a)** Suppose $G$ is not cyclic (in particular $G\ne0$). By the structure theorem for finite abelian groups, $G\cong\mathbb Z/n_1\times\cdots\times\mathbb Z/n_s$ with $1<n_1\mid n_2\mid\cdots\mid n_s$, and $s\ge2$ because $G$ is not cyclic. In each factor $\mathbb Z/n_i$ (where $n_1\mid n_i$) the equation $n_1x=0$ has exactly $n_1$ solutions, so $\{a\in G: n_1a=0\}$ has $n_1^s>n_1$ elements, violating the hypothesis with $n=n_1$. Hence $G$ is cyclic.

**(b)** Let $F$ be a finite field and $G=F^\times$ (written multiplicatively). For each $n\ge1$, the elements with $a^n=1$ are roots of $x^n-1$, a nonzero polynomial of degree $n$ over a field, so there are at most $n$ of them. By (a), $F^\times$ is cyclic. ∎

solutions.title: Element of maximal order
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $g\in G$ have maximal order $m$.

*Lemma.* In a finite abelian group, the order of every element divides the maximal order $m$. Proof: suppose $h$ has order $k\nmid m$. Then some prime $p$ has $p^\beta\,\|\,k$, $p^\alpha\,\|\,m$ with $\beta>\alpha$. The element $p^\alpha g$ has order $m/p^\alpha$ (coprime to $p$) and $(k/p^\beta)h$ has order $p^\beta$; in an abelian group, elements of coprime orders $u,v$ have a sum of order $uv$. So $G$ has an element of order $p^\beta m/p^\alpha>m$, a contradiction.

Hence $ma=0$ for all $a\in G$, so $\{a: ma=0\}=G$ and the hypothesis gives $|G|\le m$. But $\langle g\rangle$ already has $m$ elements, so $G=\langle g\rangle$ is cyclic.

**(b)** As in the first solution: $x^n-1$ has at most $n$ roots in a field. ∎

prompt:
Prove that for each integer $n\ge0$ there is a polynomial $T_n(z)$ with integer coefficients such that the identity
$$2\cos nx=T_n(2\cos x)$$
holds for all $x$.
answer: Induction using $2\cos(n+1)x=(2\cos x)(2\cos nx)-2\cos(n-1)x$: $T_0=2$, $T_1=z$, $T_{n+1}=zT_n-T_{n-1}$.

solutions.title: Three-term recurrence
solutions.body:
From $\cos(n+1)x+\cos(n-1)x=2\cos nx\cos x$ we get
$$2\cos(n+1)x=(2\cos x)(2\cos nx)-2\cos(n-1)x\qquad(n\ge1).$$
Define $T_0(z)=2$, $T_1(z)=z$, and $T_{n+1}(z)=zT_n(z)-T_{n-1}(z)$ for $n\ge1$. Each $T_n$ has integer coefficients, by induction. Also $2\cos0x=2=T_0(2\cos x)$ and $2\cos x=T_1(2\cos x)$, and if $2\cos kx=T_k(2\cos x)$ for $k=n-1,n$, then
$$2\cos(n+1)x=(2\cos x)T_n(2\cos x)-T_{n-1}(2\cos x)=T_{n+1}(2\cos x).$$
So the identity holds for all $n\ge0$ by strong induction. (E.g. $T_2=z^2-2$, $T_3=z^3-3z$.) ∎

solutions.title: Symmetric functions of $t$ and $1/t$
solutions.body:
Let $t=e^{ix}$, so $2\cos nx=t^n+t^{-n}$ and $z=2\cos x=t+t^{-1}$. We show by strong induction that $t^n+t^{-n}$ is an integer polynomial in $t+t^{-1}$. For $n=0,1$ this is clear. For $n\ge2$, by the binomial theorem
$$(t+t^{-1})^n=\sum_{j=0}^n\binom nj t^{n-2j}=(t^n+t^{-n})+\sum_{1\le j<n/2}\binom nj\bigl(t^{n-2j}+t^{-(n-2j)}\bigr)+\Bigl[\tbinom{n}{n/2}\text{ if }n\text{ even}\Bigr].$$
Every term on the right except $t^n+t^{-n}$ is an integer combination of $t^m+t^{-m}$ with $m<n$ (and constants), hence an integer polynomial in $z$ by induction. Solving for $t^n+t^{-n}$ shows it is too. ∎

prompt:
Let $\{f_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ be a uniformly bounded pointwise equicontinuous sequence of real-valued functions on the compact metric space $(X,d)$. Define the functions $g_n:X\to\mathbb R$, for $n\in\mathbb N$, by
$$g_n(x)=\max\{f_1(x),\dots,f_n(x)\}.$$
Prove that the sequence $\{g_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ converges uniformly. Show that this can be false if the condition about equicontinuity is omitted.
answer: $g_n\uparrow g=\sup_nf_n$. For each $x$, pick $N_x$ with $g(x)-g_{N_x}(x)<\epsilon$ and a neighbourhood $U_x$ where all $|f_m(y)-f_m(x)|<\epsilon$; then $0\le g-g_n<3\epsilon$ on $U_x$ for $n\ge N_x$; finitely many $U_x$ cover $X$. Counterexample: $f_n(x)=\min(1,nx)$ on $[0,1]$.

solutions.title: Local control plus compactness
solutions.body:
Let $|f_n|\le K$ for all $n$. For each $x$, $g_n(x)$ is nondecreasing in $n$ and bounded by $K$, so $g_n(x)\uparrow g(x):=\sup_nf_n(x)$.

Let $\epsilon>0$. For each $x\in X$:
- choose $N_x$ with $g(x)-g_{N_x}(x)<\epsilon$;
- by equicontinuity at $x$, choose an open neighbourhood $U_x$ of $x$ with $|f_m(y)-f_m(x)|<\epsilon$ for all $m$ and all $y\in U_x$.

For $y\in U_x$: each $f_m(y)<f_m(x)+\epsilon\le g(x)+\epsilon$, so $g(y)\le g(x)+\epsilon$. And for $n\ge N_x$, $g_n(y)\ge g_{N_x}(y)\ge g_{N_x}(x)-\epsilon>g(x)-2\epsilon$ (as $g_{N_x}$ is a max of finitely many functions each moving by less than $\epsilon$). Hence
$$0\le g(y)-g_n(y)<3\epsilon\qquad(y\in U_x,\ n\ge N_x).$$
By compactness, $X=U_{x_1}\cup\dots\cup U_{x_r}$. With $N=\max_iN_{x_i}$ we get $0\le g-g_n<3\epsilon$ on all of $X$ for $n\ge N$. So $g_n\to g$ uniformly.

**Without equicontinuity.** On $X=[0,1]$ let $f_n(x)=\min(1,nx)$. These are continuous, bounded by $1$, and increasing in $n$, so $g_n=f_n$. Pointwise, $g_n(0)=0$ and $g_n(x)\to1$ for $x>0$. The limit is discontinuous at $0$, while each $g_n$ is continuous, so the convergence is not uniform (a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous). Indeed $g_n(1/(2n))=\tfrac12$, so $\sup|g-g_n|\ge\frac12$. ∎

prompt:
Consider the solution curve $(x(t),y(t))$ to the equations
$$\frac{dx}{dt}=1+\tfrac12x^2\sin y,\qquad\frac{dy}{dt}=3-x^2$$
with initial conditions $x(0)=0$ and $y(0)=0$. Prove that the solution must cross the line $x=1$ in the $xy$ plane by the time $t=2$.
answer: While $|x|\le1$, $x'\ge1-\frac12=\frac12$; so $x$ increases from $0$ at rate at least $\frac12$ until it reaches $1$, which must happen by $t=2$.

solutions.title: A lower bound on $dx/dt$
solutions.body:
The right-hand side is smooth, so a unique solution exists on a maximal interval $[0,T^*)$. Whenever $|x(t)|\le1$,
$$x'(t)=1+\tfrac12x^2\sin y\ge1-\tfrac12=\tfrac12 .$$

Let
$$\tau=\sup\{t\in[0,T^*):\ |x(s)|\le1\text{ for all }s\in[0,t]\}>0 .$$
On $[0,\tau)$ we have $x'\ge\frac12$, hence $x(t)\ge\frac t2\ge0$.

*Case $\tau=T^*$.* Then $|x|\le1$ on $[0,T^*)$, so $|y'|=|3-x^2|\le3$ and the solution stays bounded on bounded time intervals; a solution of a smooth autonomous system that stays bounded can be continued, so $T^*=\infty$. But then $x(t)\ge t/2>1$ for $t=3$, contradicting $|x|\le1$. So this case is impossible.

*Case $\tau<T^*$.* By continuity and maximality of $\tau$, $|x(\tau)|=1$, and $x(\tau)\ge\tau/2\ge0$, so $x(\tau)=1$. Since $1=x(\tau)\ge\tau/2$, we get $\tau\le2$.

So $x$ reaches the value $1$ at a time $\tau\le2$, and $x'(\tau)\ge\frac12>0$ there, so the curve genuinely crosses the line $x=1$ (from $x<1$ to $x>1$) by time $t=2$. ∎

prompt:
Show that the differential equation
$$f''(z)=zf(z),\qquad f(0)=1,\quad f'(0)=1$$
has a unique entire solution in the complex plane.
answer: An entire solution $f=\sum a_kz^k$ must satisfy $a_0=a_1=1$, $a_2=0$, $k(k-1)a_k=a_{k-3}$, which determines all $a_k$ (uniqueness); the resulting coefficients satisfy $0\le a_k\le1/\lfloor k/3\rfloor!$, so the series has infinite radius of convergence (existence).

solutions.title: Power series
solutions.body:
**Uniqueness.** An entire $f$ equals its Maclaurin series $\sum_{k\ge0}a_kz^k$ on $\mathbb C$, and the series may be differentiated termwise. Then $f''(z)=\sum_{k\ge2}k(k-1)a_kz^{k-2}$ and $zf(z)=\sum_{k\ge3}a_{k-3}z^{k-2}$. Comparing coefficients:
$$a_0=f(0)=1,\quad a_1=f'(0)=1,\quad 2a_2=0,\quad k(k-1)a_k=a_{k-3}\ (k\ge3).$$
These determine every $a_k$, so there is at most one entire solution.

**Existence.** Define $a_k$ by these relations; then $a_{3m+2}=0$ and
$$a_{3m}=\prod_{j=1}^m\frac1{3j(3j-1)},\qquad a_{3m+1}=\prod_{j=1}^m\frac{1}{3j(3j+1)} .$$
By induction $0\le a_k\le1/\lfloor k/3\rfloor!$ (each step multiplies by at most $\frac1{6j^2}\le\frac1j$), so $|a_k|^{1/k}\to0$ and the series $f(z)=\sum a_kz^k$ has infinite radius of convergence. It defines an entire function; termwise differentiation shows $f''=zf$ because the coefficients satisfy the recurrence, and $f(0)=a_0=1$, $f'(0)=a_1=1$. ∎

prompt: Let $f$ be an entire function such that $\operatorname{Re}f(z)\ge0$ for all $z\in\mathbb C$. Show that $f$ is constant.
answer: $e^{-f}$ is entire with $|e^{-f}|=e^{-\operatorname{Re}f}\le1$, so it is constant by Liouville; hence $f'e^{-f}=0$, so $f'=0$.

solutions.title: Liouville applied to $e^{-f}$
solutions.body: Let $g=e^{-f}$, an entire function with $|g(z)|=e^{-\operatorname{Re}f(z)}\le1$. By Liouville's theorem $g$ is constant, so $0=g'=-f'e^{-f}$, and since $e^{-f}$ never vanishes, $f'\equiv0$. Thus $f$ is constant. ∎

solutions.title: A Möbius transformation
solutions.body: The map $\phi(w)=\dfrac{w-1}{w+1}$ sends the closed right half-plane $\operatorname{Re}w\ge0$ into the closed unit disc (since $|w-1|\le|w+1|$ there) and is holomorphic there ($w\neq -1$). Then $\phi\circ f$ is entire and bounded by $1$, so it is constant by Liouville. As $\phi$ is injective, $f$ is constant. ∎

prompt:
Let $\mathbb R[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ be the polynomial ring over the real field $\mathbb R$ in the $n$ variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$. Let the matrix $A$ be the $n\times n$ matrix whose $i$th row is $(1,x_i,x_i^2,\dots,x_i^{n-1})$, $i=1,\dots,n$. Show that
$$\det A=\prod_{i>j}(x_i-x_j).$$
answer: $\det A$ vanishes when $x_i=x_j$, so it is divisible by each $x_i-x_j$, hence by their product $V$; both have total degree $\binom n2$, so $\det A=cV$, and comparing the coefficient of $x_2x_3^2\cdots x_n^{n-1}$ gives $c=1$.

solutions.title: Divisibility and degree count
solutions.body:
Let $D=\det A\in\mathbb R[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ and $V=\prod_{i>j}(x_i-x_j)$.

**Divisibility.** Fix $i>j$. View $D$ as a polynomial in $x_i$ over $\mathbb R[x_k:k\neq  i]$. Substituting $x_i=x_j$ makes rows $i$ and $j$ equal, so $D|_{x_i=x_j}=0$; by the factor theorem, $(x_i-x_j)\mid D$. The linear polynomials $x_i-x_j$ ($i>j$) are pairwise non-associate irreducibles in the UFD $\mathbb R[x_1,\dots,x_n]$, so their product $V$ divides $D$.

**Degrees.** Each term of the Leibniz expansion of $D$ is $\pm\prod_ix_i^{\sigma(i)-1}$, homogeneous of degree $0+1+\dots+(n-1)=\binom n2$. And $V$ is homogeneous of degree $\binom n2$ too. So $D=cV$ for a constant $c$.

**Constant.** The monomial $x_1^0x_2^1x_3^2\cdots x_n^{n-1}$ occurs in $D$ only from the diagonal (identity permutation), with coefficient $1$. In $V=\prod_{i>j}(x_i-x_j)$, to get exponent $n-1$ on $x_n$ we must pick $x_n$ from all $n-1$ factors $x_n-x_j$; then exponent $n-2$ on $x_{n-1}$ forces picking $x_{n-1}$ from all factors $x_{n-1}-x_j$, $j<n-1$; and so on. So this monomial arises in exactly one way, with coefficient $+1$. Hence $c=1$. ∎

solutions.title: Row reduction and induction
solutions.body:
Induct on $n$ ($n=1$: $\det(1)=1$, empty product). Subtract $x_1$ times column $k$ from column $k+1$, for $k=n-1,n-2,\dots,1$ (in that order). Row $i$ becomes $(1,\ x_i-x_1,\ x_i(x_i-x_1),\dots,x_i^{n-2}(x_i-x_1))$, and row 1 becomes $(1,0,\dots,0)$. Expanding along row 1 and pulling out the factor $x_i-x_1$ from each row $i\ge2$,
$$\det A=\prod_{i\ge2}(x_i-x_1)\cdot\det\bigl(x_i^{k}\bigr)_{2\le i\le n,\ 0\le k\le n-2}=\prod_{i\ge2}(x_i-x_1)\prod_{i>j\ge2}(x_i-x_j)$$
by the induction hypothesis, which is $\prod_{i>j}(x_i-x_j)$. ∎

prompt: Show that if $A$ and $B$ are unitary matrices of the same size, then all eigenvalues of $A+B$ have absolute value at most 2.
answer: If $(A+B)v=\lambda v$ with $v\neq 0$ then $|\lambda|\|v\|\le\|Av\|+\|Bv\|=2\|v\|$.

solutions.title: Norm estimate
solutions.body:
Unitary matrices preserve the Euclidean norm. If $(A+B)v=\lambda v$ with $v\neq 0$, then
$$|\lambda|\,\|v\|=\|(A+B)v\|\le\|Av\|+\|Bv\|=2\|v\|,$$
so $|\lambda|\le2$. ∎

prompt: Given a finite group $G$, let $e(G)$ be the least common multiple of the orders of the group's elements. Prove that if the group is abelian, then it contains an element of order $e(G)$, and give a counter-example to this statement for non-abelian groups.
answer: For each prime power $p^r\,\|\,e(G)$ some element has order divisible by $p^r$, so a power of it has order exactly $p^r$; in an abelian group, a product of commuting elements of coprime orders has order equal to the product. Counterexample: $S_3$ has $e=6$ but no element of order 6.

solutions.title: Combine elements of prime-power order
solutions.body:
**Lemma.** If $x,y$ commute and have coprime orders $m,n$, then $xy$ has order $mn$.

*Proof.* $(xy)^{mn}=x^{mn}y^{mn}=1$. If $(xy)^k=1$ then $x^k=y^{-k}\in\langle x\rangle\cap\langle y\rangle$, a subgroup whose order divides $\gcd(m,n)=1$; so $x^k=y^k=1$, hence $m\mid k$ and $n\mid k$, so $mn\mid k$. $\square$

**Abelian case.** Write $e(G)=p_1^{r_1}\cdots p_s^{r_s}$. Since $e(G)$ is the lcm of element orders, for each $i$ some element $g_i$ has order $o_i$ with $p_i^{r_i}\mid o_i$. Then $h_i=g_i^{o_i/p_i^{r_i}}$ has order exactly $p_i^{r_i}$. The $h_i$ commute and have pairwise coprime orders, so by the lemma (and induction) $h=h_1h_2\cdots h_s$ has order $p_1^{r_1}\cdots p_s^{r_s}=e(G)$.

**Non-abelian counterexample.** In $S_3$ the element orders are $1,2,2,2,3,3$, so $e(S_3)=\operatorname{lcm}(1,2,3)=6$, but $S_3$ has no element of order $6$ (it is not cyclic). ∎

prompt:
(a) Give an example (with proof) of an irreducible polynomial $f$ of degree 100 over the rationals $\mathbb Q$ such that $f$ splits into linear factors over the field $\mathbb Q[x]/f(x)$.

(b) Give an example (with proof) of an irreducible polynomial $g$ of degree 100 over the rationals $\mathbb Q$ such that $g$ does not split into linear factors over the field $\mathbb Q[x]/g(x)$.
answer: (a) $f=\Phi_{101}=\frac{x^{101}-1}{x-1}$: $\mathbb Q[x]/f\cong\mathbb Q(\zeta_{101})$ contains all the roots $\zeta^k$. (b) $g=x^{100}-2$ (Eisenstein): $\mathbb Q[x]/g\cong\mathbb Q(\sqrt[100]2)\subset\mathbb R$, but $g$ has non-real roots.

solutions.title: Cyclotomic versus pure radical
solutions.body:
Recall that for irreducible $h$, $\mathbb Q[x]/(h)$ is a field isomorphic to $\mathbb Q(\alpha)$ for any root $\alpha$ of $h$ (via $x\mapsto\alpha$).

**(a)** Let $f(x)=\dfrac{x^{101}-1}{x-1}=x^{100}+x^{99}+\dots+1$. It is irreducible because $101$ is prime: $f(x+1)=\dfrac{(x+1)^{101}-1}{x}=\sum_{k=1}^{101}\binom{101}kx^{k-1}$ is Eisenstein at $101$ (all non-leading coefficients $\binom{101}{k}$, $1\le k\le100$, are divisible by $101$, and the constant term $101$ is not divisible by $101^2$). Its roots are $\zeta^k$, $1\le k\le100$, with $\zeta=e^{2\pi i/101}$. Hence $\mathbb Q[x]/(f)\cong\mathbb Q(\zeta)$ contains every root $\zeta^k$, so $f=\prod_{k=1}^{100}(x-\zeta^k)$ splits there.

**(b)** Let $g(x)=x^{100}-2$, irreducible by Eisenstein at $2$. Then $\mathbb Q[x]/(g)\cong\mathbb Q(\alpha)$ with $\alpha=\sqrt[100]2\in\mathbb R$, so this field embeds in $\mathbb R$. If $g$ split into linear factors over it, all roots of $g$ (in $\mathbb C$) would be the images of elements of this field under the embedding, hence real. But $g$ has the non-real root $\alpha e^{2\pi i/100}$. So $g$ does not split over $\mathbb Q[x]/(g)$. (In fact only the roots $\pm\alpha$ lie there.) ∎

prompt: Prove that the polynomial $p(z)=z^5-6z+3$ has exactly three real roots.
answer: Sign changes $p(-2)<0<p(0)$, $p(1)<0<p(2)$ give at least three real roots; $p'(z)=5z^4-6$ has only two real roots, so by Rolle $p$ has at most three.

solutions.title: Intermediate value theorem and Rolle
solutions.body:
**At least three.** $p(-2)=-32+12+3=-17<0$, $p(0)=3>0$, $p(1)=1-6+3=-2<0$, $p(2)=32-12+3=23>0$. By the intermediate value theorem $p$ has a real root in each of $(-2,0)$, $(0,1)$, $(1,2)$.

**At most three.** $p'(z)=5z^4-6$ has exactly two real roots, $\pm(6/5)^{1/4}$. If $p$ had four (or more) distinct real roots, Rolle's theorem would give three distinct real roots of $p'$ between consecutive ones, a contradiction. A repeated real root $r$ would also be a root of $p'$, so $r^4=6/5$ and $p(r)=r\cdot\frac65-6r+3=3-\frac{24}{5}r$, which vanishes only for $r=\frac58$, but $(5/8)^4\neq \frac65$. So the real roots are simple and there are exactly three. ∎

prompt:
Suppose that $f$ is a nondecreasing real valued function on $[0,1]$. Find functions $g$ and $h_n$ such that
$$f(x)=g(x)+\sum_nh_n(x)$$
where $g$ is continuous, and each of the finite or countable number of functions $h_n$ has one point where it is not continuous, and is zero below this point and constant above it.
answer: Let $x_n$ be the (countably many) discontinuities of $f$, with one-sided limits $l_n=f(x_n^-)$, $r_n=f(x_n^+)$ (use $f(0)$, $f(1)$ at the endpoints). Put $h_n=0$ on $[0,x_n)$, $h_n(x_n)=f(x_n)-l_n$, $h_n=r_n-l_n$ on $(x_n,1]$, and $g=f-\sum h_n$; the series converges uniformly and $g$ is continuous.

solutions.title: Remove the jumps
solutions.body:
**The jumps.** A nondecreasing $f$ has one-sided limits $f(x^\pm)$ everywhere (set $f(0^-)=f(0)$, $f(1^+)=f(1)$), with $f(x^-)\le f(x)\le f(x^+)$, and $f$ is discontinuous at $x$ iff the jump $J(x)=f(x^+)-f(x^-)>0$. For distinct points $y_1<\dots<y_m$ the intervals $(f(y_i^-),f(y_i^+))$ are disjoint subintervals of $[f(0),f(1)]$, so $\sum_iJ(y_i)\le f(1)-f(0)$. Hence for each $k$ there are fewer than $k(f(1)-f(0))+1$ points with $J>1/k$, and the set of discontinuities $\{x_n\}$ is finite or countable, with $\sum_nJ(x_n)\le f(1)-f(0)$.

**The functions $h_n$.** With $l_n=f(x_n^-)$, $r_n=f(x_n^+)$, define
$$h_n(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x<x_n,\\ f(x_n)-l_n,&x=x_n,\\ r_n-l_n,&x>x_n.\end{cases}$$
Each $h_n$ is zero below $x_n$, constant above it, and discontinuous only at $x_n$ (since $J(x_n)>0$). As $0\le h_n\le J(x_n)$ and $\sum J(x_n)<\infty$, the series $H=\sum h_n$ converges uniformly on $[0,1]$ (Weierstrass M-test). Put $g=f-H$.

**$g$ is continuous.** By uniform convergence, one-sided limits can be taken termwise: for any $x\in[0,1]$,
$$H(x^+)-H(x)=\sum_n\bigl(h_n(x^+)-h_n(x)\bigr),$$
and $h_n(x^+)-h_n(x)=0$ unless $x=x_n$, in which case it equals $r_n-f(x_n)$. So $H(x^+)-H(x)=f(x^+)-f(x)$ (both are $0$ if $x$ is not a discontinuity), i.e. $g(x^+)=g(x)$. Similarly $H(x)-H(x^-)=f(x)-f(x^-)$, so $g(x^-)=g(x)$. Hence $g$ is continuous on $[0,1]$, and $f=g+\sum_nh_n$. (Moreover $g$ is nondecreasing.) ∎

prompt:
Let $\varphi(s)$ be a $C^2$ function on $[1,2]$ with $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ vanishing at $s=1,2$. Prove that there is a constant $C>0$ such that for any $\lambda>1$,
$$\left|\int_1^2e^{i\lambda x}\varphi(x)\,dx\right|\le\frac{C}{\lambda^2}.$$
answer: Integrate by parts twice (boundary terms vanish): $\int_1^2e^{i\lambda x}\varphi\,dx=-\frac1{\lambda^2}\int_1^2e^{i\lambda x}\varphi''\,dx$, so $C=\int_1^2|\varphi''|$ (or any positive number at least that) works.

solutions.title: Integration by parts twice
solutions.body:
Since $\frac{d}{dx}\frac{e^{i\lambda x}}{i\lambda}=e^{i\lambda x}$ and $\varphi(1)=\varphi(2)=0$,
$$\int_1^2e^{i\lambda x}\varphi(x)\,dx=\Bigl[\frac{e^{i\lambda x}}{i\lambda}\varphi\Bigr]_1^2-\frac1{i\lambda}\int_1^2e^{i\lambda x}\varphi'(x)\,dx=-\frac1{i\lambda}\int_1^2e^{i\lambda x}\varphi'(x)\,dx .$$
Integrating by parts again, using $\varphi'(1)=\varphi'(2)=0$ and that $\varphi'$ is $C^1$,
$$\int_1^2e^{i\lambda x}\varphi'(x)\,dx=-\frac1{i\lambda}\int_1^2e^{i\lambda x}\varphi''(x)\,dx .$$
Therefore
$$\left|\int_1^2e^{i\lambda x}\varphi(x)\,dx\right|=\frac{1}{\lambda^2}\left|\int_1^2e^{i\lambda x}\varphi''(x)\,dx\right|\le\frac{1}{\lambda^2}\int_1^2|\varphi''(x)|\,dx,$$
so $C=\max\bigl(1,\int_1^2|\varphi''|\bigr)$ works (it is finite because $\varphi''$ is continuous on $[1,2]$). ∎

prompt: Let the points $a$, $b$, and $c$ lie on the unit circle of the complex plane and satisfy $a+b+c=0$. Prove that $a$, $b$, and $c$ form the vertices of an equilateral triangle.
answer: $|a+b|^2=|c|^2=1$ gives $2+2\operatorname{Re}(a\bar b)=1$, so $|a-b|^2=2-2\operatorname{Re}(a\bar b)=3$; by symmetry all three sides have length $\sqrt3$.

solutions.title: Compute the side lengths
solutions.body:
Since $|a|=|b|=1$, $|a\pm b|^2=2\pm2\operatorname{Re}(a\bar b)$. From $a+b=-c$ we get $|a+b|^2=1$, so $\operatorname{Re}(a\bar b)=-\frac12$ and
$$|a-b|^2=2+1=3 .$$
The hypotheses are symmetric in $a,b,c$, so likewise $|b-c|=|c-a|=\sqrt3$. In particular the three points are distinct, and the triangle with vertices $a,b,c$ has all sides equal to $\sqrt3$: it is equilateral. ∎

solutions.title: Rotate so that $a=1$
solutions.body: Multiplying by $\bar a$ (a rotation) preserves all hypotheses and the shape of the triangle, so assume $a=1$. Then $b+c=-1$: $\operatorname{Im}b=-\operatorname{Im}c$ and $\operatorname{Re}b+\operatorname{Re}c=-1$. Points on the unit circle with opposite imaginary parts have equal or opposite real parts; opposite real parts would sum to $0\neq -1$, so $\operatorname{Re}b=\operatorname{Re}c=-\frac12$. Hence $\{b,c\}=\{-\frac12\pm\frac{\sqrt3}2i\}=\{e^{\pm2\pi i/3}\}$, and $1,e^{2\pi i/3},e^{-2\pi i/3}$ are the vertices of an equilateral triangle. ∎

prompt:
Let $\rho>0$. Show that for $n$ large enough, all the zeros of
$$f_n(z)=1+\frac1z+\frac1{2!z^2}+\dots+\frac1{n!z^n}$$
lie in the circle $|z|<\rho$.
answer: With $w=1/z$, $f_n(z)=P_n(w)=\sum_{k\le n}w^k/k!\to e^w$ uniformly on $|w|\le1/\rho$, where $|e^w|\ge e^{-1/\rho}>0$; so for large $n$, $f_n$ has no zeros in $|z|\ge\rho$.

solutions.title: Uniform convergence to $e^{1/z}$
solutions.body:
For $|z|\ge\rho$ put $w=1/z$, so $|w|\le1/\rho$ and $f_n(z)=P_n(w)$ with $P_n(w)=\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{w^k}{k!}$, the partial sums of $e^w$. On the compact disc $|w|\le1/\rho$ the partial sums converge uniformly to $e^w$, and
$$|e^w|=e^{\operatorname{Re}w}\ge e^{-1/\rho}=:m>0 .$$
Choose $N$ with $|P_n(w)-e^w|<m$ for all $n\ge N$ and $|w|\le1/\rho$. Then for $n\ge N$ and $|z|\ge\rho$,
$$|f_n(z)|\ge|e^{1/z}|-|f_n(z)-e^{1/z}|>m-m=0 .$$
So for $n\ge N$, every zero of $f_n$ satisfies $|z|<\rho$. ∎

prompt:
Let
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$$
be a real matrix with $a,b,c,d>0$. Show that $A$ has an eigenvector $\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb R^2$ with $x,y>0$.
answer: The larger eigenvalue $\lambda=\frac{a+d+\sqrt{(a-d)^2+4bc}}2$ is real and $>\max(a,d)$; the eigenvector $(b,\lambda-a)$ has both entries positive. (Or: $A$ maps the closed first quadrant into itself; apply the intermediate value theorem to the induced map on angles $[0,\pi/2]$.)

solutions.title: Explicit eigenvector
solutions.body:
The characteristic polynomial is $t^2-(a+d)t+(ad-bc)$, with discriminant $(a+d)^2-4(ad-bc)=(a-d)^2+4bc>0$. So
$$\lambda=\frac{a+d+\sqrt{(a-d)^2+4bc}}{2}$$
is a real eigenvalue, and since $\sqrt{(a-d)^2+4bc}>|a-d|$, we get $\lambda>\frac{a+d+|a-d|}2=\max(a,d)\ge a$.

The vector $v=\begin{pmatrix}b\\\lambda-a\end{pmatrix}$ satisfies the first row of $(A-\lambda I)v=0$: $(a-\lambda)b+b(\lambda-a)=0$. Since $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue, $A-\lambda I$ is singular and nonzero (its off-diagonal entry $b\neq 0$), so its rows are proportional and $v$, which is nonzero, lies in its kernel. Both coordinates $b>0$ and $\lambda-a>0$ are positive. ∎

solutions.title: Fixed point on the space of directions
solutions.body: For $\theta\in[0,\pi/2]$ let $u(\theta)=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$. Since all entries of $A$ are positive, $Au(\theta)$ has both coordinates $\ge0$ and is nonzero, so it has a direction $\phi(\theta)\in[0,\pi/2]$, depending continuously on $\theta$. Because $b,c>0$, $Au(0)=(a,c)$ and $Au(\pi/2)=(b,d)$ have both coordinates positive, so $\phi(0)>0$ and $\phi(\pi/2)<\pi/2$. The continuous function $\phi(\theta)-\theta$ is positive at $0$ and negative at $\pi/2$, so it vanishes at some $\theta_0\in(0,\pi/2)$. Then $Au(\theta_0)$ is a positive multiple of $u(\theta_0)$, an eigenvector with both coordinates positive. ∎

prompt:
Let $\mathbb F_q$ be a finite field with $q$ elements and let $V$ be an $n$-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb F_q$.

1. Determine the number of elements in $V$.
2. Let $GL_n(\mathbb F_q)$ denote the group of all $n\times n$ nonsingular matrices $A$ over $\mathbb F_q$. Determine the order of $GL_n(\mathbb F_q)$.
3. Let $SL_n(\mathbb F_q)$ denote the subgroup of $GL_n(\mathbb F_q)$ consisting of matrices with determinant 1. Find the order of $SL_n(\mathbb F_q)$.
answer: 1. $q^n$. 2. $|GL_n(\mathbb F_q)|=\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(q^n-q^i)$. 3. $|SL_n(\mathbb F_q)|=\dfrac{1}{q-1}\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(q^n-q^i)$.

solutions.title: Count ordered bases
solutions.body:
**1.** Choosing a basis, $V\cong\mathbb F_q^n$, so $|V|=q^n$.

**2.** An $n\times n$ matrix is nonsingular iff its columns $v_1,\dots,v_n$ are linearly independent. Choose them in order: $v_1$ can be any nonzero vector ($q^n-1$ choices); given independent $v_1,\dots,v_i$, the next column must avoid their span, which has $q^i$ elements, leaving $q^n-q^i$ choices. Hence
$$|GL_n(\mathbb F_q)|=(q^n-1)(q^n-q)(q^n-q^2)\cdots(q^n-q^{n-1}) .$$

**3.** $\det:GL_n(\mathbb F_q)\to\mathbb F_q^\times$ is a homomorphism, surjective since $\operatorname{diag}(t,1,\dots,1)$ has determinant $t$. Its kernel is $SL_n(\mathbb F_q)$, so
$$|SL_n(\mathbb F_q)|=\frac{|GL_n(\mathbb F_q)|}{q-1}=\frac{(q^n-1)(q^n-q)\cdots(q^n-q^{n-1})}{q-1}. $$ ∎

reviewNote: The official solution lists '1. q^n - 1' for the number of elements of V, which appears to be a misprint (|V| = q^n; q^n - 1 is the number of nonzero vectors). The solution here gives q^n.

prompt: If $H$ is a subgroup of a group $G$ of index 5, prove that $H$ contains a normal subgroup of $G$ of index at most 120. Give an example of a group $G$ and a subgroup $H$ of index 5 such that $H$ does not contain a normal subgroup of $G$ of index less than 120.
answer: $G$ acts on the 5 cosets of $H$, giving $\pi:G\to S_5$; $\ker\pi\subseteq H$ is normal of index $|\pi(G)|\le120$. Example: $G=S_5$, $H=S_4$ (the normal subgroups of $S_5$ are $1,A_5,S_5$, and only $1$ lies in $S_4$).

solutions.title: Action on cosets
solutions.body:
**Existence.** $G$ acts by left multiplication on the set $G/H$ of $5$ left cosets, giving a homomorphism $\pi:G\to\operatorname{Sym}(G/H)\cong S_5$. Its kernel $K=\bigcap_{g\in G}gHg^{-1}$ is normal in $G$, and $K\subseteq H$ (an element fixing the coset $H$ lies in $H$). By the first isomorphism theorem $[G:K]=|\pi(G)|\le|S_5|=120$.

**Sharpness.** Let $G=S_5$ and $H=\{\sigma\in S_5:\sigma(5)=5\}\cong S_4$, of index $5$. The normal subgroups of $S_5$ are $1$, $A_5$, $S_5$ (a normal subgroup $N$ meets the simple group $A_5$ in $1$ or $A_5$; if $N\cap A_5=1$ then $|N|\le2$, and a normal subgroup of order $2$ would be central, but $Z(S_5)=1$). Neither $A_5$ (order $60>24$) nor $S_5$ lies in $H$. So the only normal subgroup of $G$ contained in $H$ is $\{1\}$, of index $120$. ∎

prompt: Show that the group $\mathbb Q$ of rational numbers under addition has no subgroups of finite index greater than 1.
answer: If $[\mathbb Q:H]=n$ then $n\cdot x\in H$ for all $x$ (Lagrange in $\mathbb Q/H$), but $n\mathbb Q=\mathbb Q$, so $H=\mathbb Q$.

solutions.title: Multiply by the index
solutions.body: Let $H\le\mathbb Q$ have finite index $n$. The quotient $\mathbb Q/H$ is a group of order $n$, so by Lagrange's theorem $n(x+H)=H$, i.e. $nx\in H$, for every $x\in\mathbb Q$. Given any $y\in\mathbb Q$, apply this to $x=y/n$: $y=n\cdot\frac yn\in H$. So $H=\mathbb Q$ and the index is $1$. ∎

solutions.title: Divisible groups
solutions.body: $\mathbb Q$ is divisible: for every $y$ and $m\ge1$ there is $x$ with $mx=y$. Quotients of divisible groups are divisible. A nontrivial finite group $F$ of order $n$ is not divisible: for $y\neq 0$, every $x$ has $nx=0\neq  y$. So every finite quotient $\mathbb Q/H$ is trivial, i.e. $H=\mathbb Q$. ∎

prompt:
Evaluate the infinite product
$$\prod_{n=3}^{\infty}\frac{n^2-4}{n^2-1}.$$

solutions.title: Telescoping partial products
solutions.body:
Factor each term: $\dfrac{n^2-4}{n^2-1}=\dfrac{n-2}{n-1}\cdot\dfrac{n+2}{n+1}$. For $k\ge 3$ the partial product splits into two telescoping products:
$$\prod_{n=3}^{k}\frac{n-2}{n-1}=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{2}{3}\cdots\frac{k-2}{k-1}=\frac{1}{k-1},\qquad \prod_{n=3}^{k}\frac{n+2}{n+1}=\frac{5}{4}\cdot\frac{6}{5}\cdots\frac{k+2}{k+1}=\frac{k+2}{4}.$$
Hence
$$\prod_{n=3}^{k}\frac{n^2-4}{n^2-1}=\frac{k+2}{4(k-1)}\xrightarrow[k\to\infty]{}\frac14 .$$
(In factorial form this is the official $\frac{1!\,3!}{0!\,4!}\cdot\frac{k!\,(k+4)!}{(k+1)!\,(k+3)!}$ shifted appropriately; either way the limit is $1/4$.)

**Answer: $\tfrac14$**

solutions.title: Split into two convergent products
solutions.body:
Write the term as $\dfrac{1-4/n^2}{1-1/n^2}$. Both $\prod_{n\ge3}(1-4/n^2)$ and $\prod_{n\ge3}(1-1/n^2)$ converge to nonzero limits (since $\sum 1/n^2<\infty$), so the product is their quotient.

- $\prod_{n=3}^k\Big(1-\dfrac4{n^2}\Big)=\prod_{n=3}^k\dfrac{n-2}{n}\cdot\prod_{n=3}^k\dfrac{n+2}{n}=\dfrac{2}{k(k-1)}\cdot\dfrac{(k+1)(k+2)}{12}\to\dfrac16$.
- $\prod_{n=3}^k\Big(1-\dfrac1{n^2}\Big)=\prod_{n=3}^k\dfrac{n-1}{n}\cdot\prod_{n=3}^k\dfrac{n+1}{n}=\dfrac{2}{k}\cdot\dfrac{k+1}{3}\to\dfrac23$.

Hence the product is $\dfrac{1/6}{2/3}=\dfrac14$. (Numerically, the partial product up to $n=10^6$ is $0.2500007\ldots$.)

**Answer: $\tfrac14$**

prompt:
Let $f:[0,1]\times[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ be a continuous function, and let $g:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ be the function
$$g(x)=\min_{0\le y\le 1} f(x,y).$$
Show in detail that $g$ is continuous on $(0,1)$. (It is also continuous at the endpoints, but don't worry about them.)
answer: $f$ is uniformly continuous on the compact square; if $|x_0-x_1|<\delta$ then $g(x_1)\le f(x_1,y_0)<f(x_0,y_0)+\varepsilon=g(x_0)+\varepsilon$ where $y_0$ attains the minimum at $x_0$, and symmetrically, so $|g(x_0)-g(x_1)|<\varepsilon$.

solutions.title: Uniform continuity
solutions.body:
First, $g$ is well defined: for fixed $x$, $y\mapsto f(x,y)$ is continuous on the compact set $[0,1]$, so it attains its minimum.

Since $[0,1]^2$ is compact, $f$ is uniformly continuous. Let $\varepsilon>0$ and choose $\delta>0$ such that $|f(x_0,y_0)-f(x_1,y_1)|<\varepsilon$ whenever $\|(x_0,y_0)-(x_1,y_1)\|<\delta$.

Let $x_0,x_1\in[0,1]$ with $|x_0-x_1|<\delta$. Choose $y_0$ with $g(x_0)=f(x_0,y_0)$. Since $\|(x_1,y_0)-(x_0,y_0)\|=|x_1-x_0|<\delta$,
$$g(x_1)\le f(x_1,y_0)<f(x_0,y_0)+\varepsilon=g(x_0)+\varepsilon .$$
Exchanging the roles of $x_0$ and $x_1$ (choose $y_1$ with $g(x_1)=f(x_1,y_1)$) gives $g(x_0)<g(x_1)+\varepsilon$. Hence $|g(x_0)-g(x_1)|<\varepsilon$.

So $g$ is (uniformly) continuous on $[0,1]$, in particular on $(0,1)$. ∎

prompt:
Prove Taylor's theorem with the remainder in the form of Peano: If a real-valued function on the number line has a well-defined $n$th derivative at $x=0$, then the error of approximating the function near $x=0$ by its degree-$n$ Taylor polynomial is $o(x^n)$. (A function $f$ is $o(x^n)$ at a point if $f/x^n$ tends to $0$ at this point.)

[Do not assume continuity or even existence of the $n$th derivative in any neighborhood of $x=0$.]
answer: Let $g=f-T_n$, so $g(0)=g'(0)=\dots=g^{(n)}(0)=0$. Induct on $n$: $n=1$ is the definition of $g'(0)$; for $n\ge2$, $g'(x)=o(x^{n-1})$ by induction and the mean value theorem gives $|g(x)|=|x\,g'(\xi)|=o(x^n)$. (Equivalently: $n-1$ applications of L'Hôpital.)

solutions.title: Induction with the mean value theorem
solutions.body:
Take $n\ge 1$ (for $n=0$ the statement would require continuity at $0$, which is not given). Saying $f^{(n)}(0)$ exists means that $f,f',\dots,f^{(n-1)}$ exist on some interval $(-r,r)$ and $f^{(n-1)}$ is differentiable at $0$. Let
$$g(x)=f(x)-\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{f^{(k)}(0)}{k!}x^k .$$
Then $g$ has the same differentiability as $f$, and $g^{(k)}(0)=0$ for $k=0,1,\dots,n$.

**Claim.** If $g$ has an $n$th derivative at $0$ and $g(0)=g'(0)=\dots=g^{(n)}(0)=0$, then $g(x)/x^n\to0$ as $x\to0$.

*Proof by induction on $n$.* For $n=1$: $g(x)/x=(g(x)-g(0))/x\to g'(0)=0$ by the definition of the derivative.

For $n\ge2$: $g'$ exists on $(-r,r)$, has an $(n-1)$st derivative at $0$, and $g'(0)=\dots=(g')^{(n-1)}(0)=0$. By induction, $g'(x)/x^{n-1}\to 0$. Let $\varepsilon>0$ and pick $0<\delta<r$ with $|g'(t)|\le\varepsilon|t|^{n-1}$ for $|t|<\delta$. For $0<|x|<\delta$, $g$ is differentiable on the interval between $0$ and $x$, so the mean value theorem gives $\xi$ strictly between $0$ and $x$ with
$$|g(x)|=|g(x)-g(0)|=|x|\,|g'(\xi)|\le |x|\,\varepsilon|\xi|^{n-1}\le\varepsilon|x|^{n}.$$
Hence $|g(x)/x^n|\le\varepsilon$ for $0<|x|<\delta$, i.e. $g(x)=o(x^n)$. ∎

Applying the claim to $g=f-T_nf$ proves Peano's form of Taylor's theorem. Note that only the existence of $f^{(n-1)}$ near $0$ and of $f^{(n)}(0)$ was used. ∎

solutions.title: L'Hôpital's rule (official approach)
solutions.body:
With $g$ as above, $g,g',\dots,g^{(n-1)}$ exist near $0$, vanish at $0$, and are continuous at $0$ (each $g^{(k)}$, $k\le n-1$, is differentiable at $0$). Consider $g(x)/x^n$. Differentiating numerator and denominator $n-1$ times gives
$$\frac{g^{(n-1)}(x)}{n!\,x}=\frac1{n!}\cdot\frac{g^{(n-1)}(x)-g^{(n-1)}(0)}{x}\xrightarrow[x\to0]{}\frac{g^{(n)}(0)}{n!}=0$$
by the *definition* of $g^{(n)}(0)$ (no continuity of $g^{(n)}$ is needed). At each intermediate stage $g^{(k)}(x)/(c_kx^{n-k})$, $0\le k\le n-2$, numerator and denominator are differentiable near $0$ and tend to $0$, and the denominator's derivative is nonzero for $x\ne0$; so L'Hôpital's rule applies $n-1$ times in reverse, and $\lim_{x\to0}g(x)/x^n=0$. ∎

prompt:
Suppose that $f$ is a complex polynomial all of whose roots have real part at most $0$. Show that if $r>0$ then $|f(r)|\ge|f(-r)|$.

Give an example to show that this can be false if the condition that $f$ is a polynomial is replaced by the condition that $f$ is entire.
answer: Write $f=a\prod(z-b_j)$; each factor satisfies $|r-b|^2-|-r-b|^2=-4r\,\mathrm{Re}\,b\ge0$. Counterexample: $f(z)=e^{-z}$ (no zeros) has $|f(r)|=e^{-r}<e^{r}=|f(-r)|$.

solutions.title: Factor into linear factors
solutions.body:
If $f$ is the zero polynomial, both sides are $0$. Otherwise write $f(z)=a\prod_{j=1}^{d}(z-b_j)$ with $a\ne0$ and $\mathrm{Re}\,b_j\le 0$ (if $d=0$, $f$ is constant and there is nothing to prove).

For a single root $b=u+iv$ with $u\le0$ and $r>0$:
$$|r-b|^2-|-r-b|^2=\big((r-u)^2+v^2\big)-\big((r+u)^2+v^2\big)=-4ru\ge 0 .$$
So $|r-b_j|\ge|-r-b_j|$ for every $j$ (geometrically: $b_j$ lies in the closed left half-plane, which is closer to $-r$ than to $r$). Multiplying,
$$|f(r)|=|a|\prod_j|r-b_j|\ge|a|\prod_j|-r-b_j|=|f(-r)| .$$

**Entire counterexample.** $f(z)=e^{-z}$ is entire and has no zeros, so the condition on the roots holds vacuously. But for $r>0$, $|f(r)|=e^{-r}<e^{r}=|f(-r)|$. ∎

prompt:
Evaluate the contour integral
$$\lim_{R\to+\infty}\int_{c-iR}^{c+iR}\frac{1}{z}\,dz$$
where $c$ is a nonzero real number. (Warning: the answer depends on c.)
answer: $\pi i$ if $c>0$, and $-\pi i$ if $c<0$.

solutions.title: Use a branch of the logarithm
solutions.body:
The segment from $c-iR$ to $c+iR$ lies in the half-plane $\{\mathrm{Re}\,z>0\}$ if $c>0$, or $\{\mathrm{Re}\,z<0\}$ if $c<0$. On either half-plane, $1/z$ has a holomorphic primitive $\log z=\ln|z|+i\arg z$ with a continuous choice of argument: $\arg z\in(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$ for $c>0$, and $\arg z\in(\pi/2,3\pi/2)$ for $c<0$. Hence
$$\int_{c-iR}^{c+iR}\frac{dz}{z}=\log(c+iR)-\log(c-iR)=i\big(\arg(c+iR)-\arg(c-iR)\big),$$
since $|c+iR|=|c-iR|$.

- $c>0$: $\arg(c\pm iR)=\pm\arctan(R/c)\to\pm\pi/2$, so the limit is $i\pi$.
- $c<0$: $\arg(c+iR)\to\pi/2$ and $\arg(c-iR)\to 3\pi/2$ (the points approach $\pm i\infty$ from the left half-plane), so the limit is $i(\pi/2-3\pi/2)=-i\pi$.

**Answer: $\pi i$ for $c>0$ and $-\pi i$ for $c<0$.**

solutions.title: Parametrize directly
solutions.body:
Put $z=c+it$, $dz=i\,dt$, $t\in[-R,R]$:
$$\int_{-R}^{R}\frac{i\,dt}{c+it}=\int_{-R}^{R}\frac{i(c-it)}{c^2+t^2}\,dt=\int_{-R}^{R}\frac{t\,dt}{c^2+t^2}+i\int_{-R}^{R}\frac{c\,dt}{c^2+t^2}.$$
The first integrand is odd, so that integral is $0$. The second is $2ic\cdot\frac1{|c|}\arctan\frac{R}{|c|}\to i\pi\,\mathrm{sgn}(c)$.

**Answer: $\pi i\,\mathrm{sgn}(c)$.**

prompt: A plane passing through the origin in $\mathbb R^3$ intersects the ellipsoid $x^2/4+y^2/9+z^2/16=1$ in an ellipse. Determine how many such sections are circles and find their radii.
answer: Exactly $2$ circular sections, both of radius $3$: the planes $z=\pm\sqrt{20/7}\,x$ through the middle axis (the $y$-axis).

solutions.title: Distance extremes in a section
solutions.body:
Write $Q(v)=x^2/4+y^2/9+z^2/16$, so the ellipsoid is $\{Q=1\}$. A plane $\Pi$ through $0$ meets it in an ellipse with semi-axes $a\ge b>0$, which are the maximum and minimum of $|v|$ over the section.

**Every section contains a point at distance $\ge3$ and one at distance $\le 3$.**
$\Pi$ meets the plane $z=0$ in at least a line $\ell$. On the ellipse $\{z=0,\ x^2/4+y^2/9=1\}$ we have $x^2+y^2=9-\tfrac54x^2\le 9$, with equality only at $(0,\pm3,0)$. So the points of the section on $\ell$ have distance $\le3$ from $0$: $b\le 3$, and $b=3$ forces $\ell$ to be the $y$-axis, i.e. $\Pi\supseteq y$-axis. Likewise $\Pi$ meets the plane $x=0$ in a line, and on $\{x=0,\ y^2/9+z^2/16=1\}$ we have $y^2+z^2=9+\tfrac{7}{16}z^2\ge 9$; so $a\ge3$.

**Circles.** A circular section has $a=b$, so $a=b=3$, the radius is $3$, and $\Pi$ contains the $y$-axis. Such a plane is $\Pi_\theta=\mathrm{span}\{e_2,(\cos\theta,0,\sin\theta)\}$. A point $s e_2+t(\cos\theta,0,\sin\theta)$ lies on the ellipsoid iff
$$\frac{s^2}{9}+t^2\Big(\frac{\cos^2\theta}{4}+\frac{\sin^2\theta}{16}\Big)=1,$$
which is a circle of radius $3$ in the orthonormal coordinates $(s,t)$ exactly when $\frac{\cos^2\theta}{4}+\frac{\sin^2\theta}{16}=\frac19$, i.e. $\frac{\cos^2\theta}4+\frac{1-\cos^2\theta}{16}=\frac19$, so $\cos^2\theta=\frac{7}{27}$, $\sin^2\theta=\frac{20}{27}$, $\tan^2\theta=\frac{20}{7}$. There are two such planes, $z=\pm\sqrt{20/7}\,x$.

(Equivalently: the trace ellipse $x^2/4+z^2/16=1$ in the plane $y=0$ meets the circle $x^2+z^2=9$ in two pairs of antipodal points, and each pair together with the $y$-axis spans a circular section.)

**Answer: exactly 2 circular sections, each of radius 3** (the planes $z=\pm\sqrt{20/7}\,x$). ∎

prompt: Suppose that the square complex matrix $A$ is similar to $A^n$ for some integer $n>1$. Prove all eigenvalues of $A$ are either zero or roots of unity.
answer: If $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue, so is $\lambda^n$ (eigenvalue of $A^n\sim A$), hence $\lambda,\lambda^n,\lambda^{n^2},\dots$ are all eigenvalues; finiteness forces $\lambda^{n^i}=\lambda^{n^j}$ with $i<j$, so $\lambda=0$ or $\lambda^{n^j-n^i}=1$.

solutions.title: Iterate the map $\lambda\mapsto\lambda^n$ on the spectrum
solutions.body:
If $Av=\lambda v$ with $v\ne0$, then $A^nv=\lambda^nv$, so $\lambda^n$ is an eigenvalue of $A^n$. Similar matrices have the same eigenvalues, so $\lambda^n$ is an eigenvalue of $A$. Repeating, $\lambda^{n^k}$ is an eigenvalue of $A$ for all $k\ge0$.

$A$ has finitely many eigenvalues, so there are $0\le i<j$ with $\lambda^{n^i}=\lambda^{n^j}$, i.e. $\lambda^{n^i}\big(\lambda^{n^j-n^i}-1\big)=0$. Since $n>1$, $m=n^j-n^i\ge1$. Thus either $\lambda=0$ or $\lambda^m=1$, i.e. $\lambda$ is a root of unity. ∎

solutions.title: Look at the spectrum as a multiset
solutions.body: Let $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_d$ be the eigenvalues of $A$ with algebraic multiplicity. By triangularizing $A=PTP^{-1}$ we see $A^n=PT^nP^{-1}$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_1^n,\dots,\lambda_d^n$. Since $A\sim A^n$, the map $\sigma:\lambda\mapsto\lambda^n$ permutes the multiset $\{\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_d\}$; so some power $\sigma^k$ ($k=d!$ works) fixes each $\lambda_i$: $\lambda_i^{n^k}=\lambda_i$. Hence $\lambda_i=0$ or $\lambda_i^{n^k-1}=1$. ∎

prompt:
Let $\alpha:G\to G_1$ and $\beta:G\to G_2$ be group homomorphisms.

(a) Show that if $\ker\alpha\subseteq\ker\beta$ and $\alpha$ is surjective (onto) then there is a well-defined group homomorphism $\varphi:G_1\to G_2$ such that $\beta=\varphi\circ\alpha$.

(b) Show that if $\ker\alpha\not\subseteq\ker\beta$ then there is no such homomorphism $\varphi$.
answer: (a) Define $\varphi(\alpha(x))=\beta(x)$; it is well defined because $\alpha(x)=\alpha(x')$ implies $x^{-1}x'\in\ker\alpha\subseteq\ker\beta$, and it is a homomorphism because $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are. (b) If $\beta=\varphi\circ\alpha$ then $x\in\ker\alpha\Rightarrow\beta(x)=\varphi(e)=e$, so $\ker\alpha\subseteq\ker\beta$.

solutions.title: Define $\varphi$ on preimages
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $y\in G_1$. Since $\alpha$ is onto, choose $x\in G$ with $\alpha(x)=y$, and set $\varphi(y)=\beta(x)$.

*Well defined:* if also $\alpha(x')=y$, then $\alpha(x^{-1}x')=\alpha(x)^{-1}\alpha(x')=e$, so $x^{-1}x'\in\ker\alpha\subseteq\ker\beta$. Hence $e=\beta(x^{-1}x')=\beta(x)^{-1}\beta(x')$, i.e. $\beta(x')=\beta(x)$.

*Homomorphism:* if $\alpha(x_1)=y_1$, $\alpha(x_2)=y_2$, then $\alpha(x_1x_2)=y_1y_2$, so
$$\varphi(y_1y_2)=\beta(x_1x_2)=\beta(x_1)\beta(x_2)=\varphi(y_1)\varphi(y_2).$$
*Factorization:* for $x\in G$, $\varphi(\alpha(x))=\beta(x)$ by definition (choosing $x$ itself as the preimage), so $\beta=\varphi\circ\alpha$.

**(b)** Contrapositive: suppose some homomorphism $\varphi$ satisfies $\beta=\varphi\circ\alpha$. If $x\in\ker\alpha$ then $\beta(x)=\varphi(\alpha(x))=\varphi(e)=e$, so $x\in\ker\beta$. Thus $\ker\alpha\subseteq\ker\beta$. Hence if $\ker\alpha\not\subseteq\ker\beta$, no such $\varphi$ exists (this part does not need $\alpha$ surjective). ∎

solutions.title: Via the first isomorphism theorem
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $K=\ker\alpha$. By the first isomorphism theorem, $\alpha$ induces an isomorphism $\bar\alpha:G/K\to G_1$ (onto because $\alpha$ is). Since $K\subseteq\ker\beta$, $\beta$ factors through the quotient: $\bar\beta:G/K\to G_2$, $\bar\beta(xK)=\beta(x)$ is well defined ($xK=x'K\Rightarrow x^{-1}x'\in K\subseteq\ker\beta$) and a homomorphism. Put $\varphi=\bar\beta\circ\bar\alpha^{-1}$. Then $\varphi(\alpha(x))=\bar\beta(\bar\alpha^{-1}(\bar\alpha(xK)))=\beta(x)$.

**(b)** As before, $\ker\alpha\subseteq\ker(\varphi\circ\alpha)=\ker\beta$ for any homomorphism $\varphi$. ∎

prompt:
Recall that $S_5$ and $A_5$ are the symmetric group and alternating group on 5 letters, respectively.

Prove or give a counterexample: For every $\sigma\in A_5$ there is a $\tau\in S_5$ such that $\tau^2=\sigma$.
answer: True. Elements of odd order $2k+1$ are squares: $\sigma=(\sigma^{k+1})^2$. The only elements of $A_5$ of even order are double transpositions, and $(a\,b)(c\,d)=(a\,c\,b\,d)^2$.

solutions.title: Case analysis by cycle type
solutions.body:
The cycle types of even permutations in $S_5$ are: the identity, $3$-cycles, $5$-cycles, and products of two disjoint transpositions $(a\,b)(c\,d)$.

**Odd order.** If $\sigma$ has odd order $2k+1$ (identity, $3$-cycles, $5$-cycles), take $\tau=\sigma^{k+1}$: then $\tau^2=\sigma^{2k+2}=\sigma^{2k+1}\sigma=\sigma$. (Equivalently the official $\tau=\sigma^{-k}$.)

**Double transpositions.** For $\sigma=(a\,b)(c\,d)$ take the $4$-cycle $\tau=(a\,c\,b\,d)$. Then $\tau^2$ sends $a\mapsto b$, $b\mapsto a$, $c\mapsto d$, $d\mapsto c$, so $\tau^2=(a\,b)(c\,d)=\sigma$. (Here $\tau\notin A_5$, which is why we need $S_5$.)

Hence every $\sigma\in A_5$ is a square in $S_5$: **the statement is true.** ∎

prompt: Let $f:(a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be a function. Assume that $f$ is strictly increasing on $(a,b)$. (This means that $f(x_1)<f(x_2)$ for all $x_1<x_2$ in $(a,b)$.) Assume also that $f$ is continuous from the left at $b$. Then show that $f$ is strictly increasing on $(a,b]$.
answer: It remains to show $f(x_1)<f(b)$ for $x_1\in(a,b)$: pick $x'\in(x_1,b)$; then $f(x)>f(x')$ for $x\in(x',b)$, so $f(b)=\lim_{x\to b^-}f(x)\ge f(x')>f(x_1)$.

solutions.title: Insert an intermediate point
solutions.body:
Pairs $x_1<x_2$ with both in $(a,b)$ are handled by hypothesis, so it suffices to show $f(x_1)<f(b)$ for every $x_1\in(a,b)$.

Fix such $x_1$ and pick $x'\in(x_1,b)$. For every $x\in(x',b)$ we have $f(x)>f(x')$. Since $f$ is continuous from the left at $b$, $f(b)=\lim_{x\to b^-}f(x)$, and limits preserve non-strict inequalities, so $f(b)\ge f(x')$. Therefore
$$f(x_1)<f(x')\le f(b).$$
Hence $f$ is strictly increasing on $(a,b]$. ∎

(The intermediate point is needed: passing to the limit directly in $f(x_1)<f(x)$ would only give $f(x_1)\le f(b)$.)

prompt: By definition, the unit cube in the space $C[0,1]$ of continuous real-valued functions on the closed interval $[0,1]$ consists of those functions whose norm $\|f\|:=\max_{0\le t\le1}|f(t)|$ doesn't exceed $1$. Find a linear map $\mathbb R^3\to C[0,1]$ such that the inverse image of the unit cube is the unit ball in $\mathbb R^3$.
answer: $(a,b,c)\mapsto a\gamma_1+b\gamma_2+c\gamma_3$ where $\gamma=(\gamma_1,\gamma_2,\gamma_3):[0,1]\to S^2$ is a continuous surjection onto the unit sphere (a Peano curve onto the square followed by spherical coordinates); then $\|L(v)\|=\max_t|v\cdot\gamma(t)|=|v|$.

solutions.title: A space-filling curve onto the sphere
solutions.body:
Any linear map has the form $L(a,b,c)=a\gamma_1+b\gamma_2+c\gamma_3$ with $\gamma_i\in C[0,1]$; write $\gamma(t)=(\gamma_1(t),\gamma_2(t),\gamma_3(t))$, a continuous curve in $\mathbb R^3$. Then for $v=(a,b,c)$,
$$\|L(v)\|=\max_{0\le t\le1}|v\cdot\gamma(t)| .$$

**Choice of $\gamma$.** Let $P:[0,1]\to[0,1]^2$ be a continuous surjection (a Peano space-filling curve), and let
$$\Phi(u,w)=\big(\cos(2\pi u)\sin(\pi w),\ \sin(2\pi u)\sin(\pi w),\ \cos(\pi w)\big),$$
a continuous surjection $[0,1]^2\to S^2$ (spherical coordinates). Put $\gamma=\Phi\circ P$; it is a continuous map of $[0,1]$ **onto** the unit sphere $S^2$.

**Verification.** For every $v\in\mathbb R^3$,
$$\|L(v)\|=\max_{s\in S^2}|v\cdot s|=|v|,$$
by Cauchy–Schwarz ($|v\cdot s|\le|v|$) with equality at $s=v/|v|$ (or trivially if $v=0$). Hence $L(v)$ lies in the unit cube iff $|v|\le1$: the inverse image of the unit cube is exactly the closed unit ball. (In fact $L$ is an isometric embedding of Euclidean $\mathbb R^3$ into $C[0,1]$.)

**Answer:** $L(a,b,c)=a\gamma_1+b\gamma_2+c\gamma_3$ with $\gamma=\Phi\circ P:[0,1]\twoheadrightarrow S^2$. ∎

prompt: Show that the recursive sequence $x_{n+1}=x_n/2+1/x_n$ with the initial value $x_0=1.5$ converges to $\sqrt2$, and that $x_{10}$ has at least $1000$ correct decimal digits.
answer: With $\varepsilon_n=x_n-\sqrt2$: $\varepsilon_{n+1}=\dfrac{\varepsilon_n^2}{2x_n}$, so $0<\varepsilon_{n+1}<\varepsilon_n^2$ and $\varepsilon_{10}<\varepsilon_0^{2^{10}}<10^{-1024}$ (as $\varepsilon_0<0.1$).

solutions.title: Quadratic convergence of Newton's method
solutions.body:
This is Newton's method for $x^2-2$. All $x_n>0$ by induction. Let $\varepsilon_n=x_n-\sqrt2$. Then
$$x_{n+1}-\sqrt2=\frac{x_n^2+2-2\sqrt2\,x_n}{2x_n}=\frac{(x_n-\sqrt2)^2}{2x_n},\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \varepsilon_{n+1}=\frac{\varepsilon_n^2}{2x_n}\ge0 .$$
Now $\varepsilon_0=1.5-\sqrt2\in(0,0.09)$ since $1.41<\sqrt2<1.42$. Inductively $\varepsilon_n\ge0$, so $x_n\ge\sqrt2>1$ and $2x_n>2$, giving
$$0\le\varepsilon_{n+1}<\tfrac12\varepsilon_n^2\le\varepsilon_n^2 .$$
Hence $\varepsilon_n\le\varepsilon_0^{2^n}$, which tends to $0$ since $\varepsilon_0<1$: $x_n\to\sqrt2$. (Indeed $\varepsilon_n>0$ for all $n$, since $\varepsilon_0>0$ and $\varepsilon_{n+1}=0$ would force $\varepsilon_n=0$.)

For $n=10$: $\varepsilon_{10}\le\varepsilon_0^{1024}<(10^{-1})^{1024}=10^{-1024}$. So $0<x_{10}-\sqrt2<10^{-1024}$, so $x_{10}$ approximates $\sqrt2$ with error less than $10^{-1000}$: at least $1000$ correct decimal digits. ∎

*Check:* a direct 1200-digit computation shows $x_{10}-\sqrt2<10^{-1199}$.

prompt: Show that there is a function holomorphic on the open unit disc that is a bijection from the open unit disc to the vertical strip $0<\mathrm{Re}\,z<1$, where $\mathrm{Re}\,z$ is the real part of $z$. You may not use the Riemann mapping theorem.
answer: $F(z)=\dfrac12-\dfrac{i}{\pi}\,\mathrm{Log}\dfrac{1+z}{1-z}$: the Möbius map sends the disc onto the right half-plane, the principal logarithm sends that onto the strip $|\mathrm{Im}\,w|<\pi/2$, and $w\mapsto\frac12-\frac{i}{\pi}w$ sends that onto $0<\mathrm{Re}<1$.

solutions.title: Compose explicit conformal maps
solutions.body:
Let $\mathbb D$ be the unit disc, $H=\{\mathrm{Re}\,w>0\}$, $\Sigma=\{|\mathrm{Im}\,\zeta|<\pi/2\}$, $S=\{0<\mathrm{Re}\,z<1\}$.

1. $M(z)=\dfrac{1+z}{1-z}$ is a bijection $\mathbb D\to H$, holomorphic on $\mathbb D$. Indeed $\mathrm{Re}\,M(z)=\dfrac{1-|z|^2}{|1-z|^2}$, which is $>0$ iff $|z|<1$; and $M$ is a Möbius transformation with inverse $w\mapsto\frac{w-1}{w+1}$, which maps $H$ into $\mathbb D$ (for $\mathrm{Re}\,w>0$, $|w-1|<|w+1|$).
2. The principal logarithm $\mathrm{Log}\,w=\ln|w|+i\arg w$, $\arg w\in(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$, is holomorphic on $H$ and a bijection $H\to\Sigma$, with inverse $\exp$: every $w\in H$ is uniquely $re^{i\theta}$ with $r>0$, $|\theta|<\pi/2$.
3. $A(\zeta)=\dfrac12-\dfrac{i}{\pi}\zeta$ is an affine bijection $\Sigma\to S$: $\mathrm{Re}\,A(\zeta)=\frac12+\frac{\mathrm{Im}\,\zeta}{\pi}\in(0,1)$ iff $|\mathrm{Im}\,\zeta|<\pi/2$.

Hence
$$F(z)=\frac12-\frac{i}{\pi}\,\mathrm{Log}\frac{1+z}{1-z}$$
is holomorphic on $\mathbb D$ and a bijection $\mathbb D\to S$, being a composition of holomorphic bijections. ∎

prompt: Find the radius of convergence of the Taylor series of $1/(e^x+e^{-x})$ at the point $x=1$.
answer: sqrt(1+pi^2/4)

solutions.title: Distance to the nearest complex singularity
solutions.body:
$h(z)=\dfrac{1}{e^z+e^{-z}}=\dfrac{1}{2\cosh z}$ is meromorphic on $\mathbb C$, with poles exactly at the zeros of $\cosh z$, i.e. where $e^{2z}=-1$: $z=i\big(\tfrac\pi2+k\pi\big)$, $k\in\mathbb Z$. These are genuine (simple) poles since $\cosh'(z)=\sinh z=\pm i\ne0$ there.

The radius of convergence of the Taylor series at $1$ of a function meromorphic on $\mathbb C$ equals the distance from $1$ to the nearest pole (the series converges on the largest disc on which the function is holomorphic, and cannot converge beyond a pole, where $|h|\to\infty$). The nearest poles are $\pm i\pi/2$, at distance
$$\sqrt{1+\pi^2/4}.$$

**Answer: $\sqrt{1+\pi^2/4}=\tfrac12\sqrt{4+\pi^2}\approx1.862$**

prompt: Prove that if two real square matrices are similar by conjugation by a complex matrix, then they are similar by conjugation by a real matrix.
answer: If $B=CAC^{-1}$ with $C=D+iE$ ($D,E$ real), then $DA=BD$ and $EA=BE$; $p(t)=\det(D+tE)$ is a real polynomial with $p(i)\ne0$, so $p(t_0)\ne0$ for some real $t_0$, and $B=(D+t_0E)A(D+t_0E)^{-1}$.

solutions.title: Real and imaginary parts of the conjugator
solutions.body:
Suppose $A,B\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ and $B=CAC^{-1}$ with $C\in GL_n(\mathbb C)$. Write $C=D+iE$ with $D,E\in M_n(\mathbb R)$. From $CA=BC$ and the fact that $A,B$ are real, comparing real and imaginary parts gives
$$DA=BD,\qquad EA=BE .$$
Hence $(D+tE)A=B(D+tE)$ for every $t\in\mathbb C$.
