prompt: How many rectangles in the plane are there with sides parallel to the coordinate axes such that all coordinates of all corners are single-digit integers $0, 1, 2, \dots, 9$?

solutions.title: Choose the sides independently
solutions.body:
A rectangle with sides parallel to the axes is $[x_1,x_2]\times[y_1,y_2]$ with $x_1<x_2$ and $y_1<y_2$, and it is determined by the two-element sets $\{x_1,x_2\}$ and $\{y_1,y_2\}$. With coordinates from $\{0,\dots,9\}$ there are $\binom{10}2=45$ choices for each, so the number of rectangles is
$$45^2=2025 .$$
(Degenerate "rectangles" with $x_1=x_2$ or $y_1=y_2$ are not counted.)

**Answer: 2025**

prompt: Prove that there is no infinitely differentiable function on the real number line all of whose derivatives are $0$ at $0$ and positive everywhere else. (Hint: show that if $n$ is a positive integer then $f^{(n)}(1)\ge n!\,f(1)$.)
answer: Taylor at $0$ gives $f(1)=f^{(n)}(\xi_n)/n!<f^{(n)}(1)/n!$; Taylor at $1$ then gives $f(2)>\sum_{k<n}f^{(k)}(1)/k!\ge n f(1)$ for every $n$, impossible since $f(1)>0$.

solutions.title: Taylor's formula twice
solutions.body:
Suppose $f$ is $C^\infty$ with $f^{(k)}(0)=0$ for all $k\ge0$ and $f^{(k)}(x)>0$ for all $k\ge0$ and $x\ne0$.

**Monotonicity.** For each $k$, $f^{(k+1)}>0$ on $(0,\infty)$, so $f^{(k)}$ is strictly increasing on $[0,\infty)$.

**The hint.** Taylor's formula with Lagrange remainder at $a=0$, $b=1$, of order $n\ge1$:
$$f(1)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{f^{(k)}(0)}{k!}+\frac{f^{(n)}(\xi_n)}{n!}=\frac{f^{(n)}(\xi_n)}{n!}\qquad\text{for some }\xi_n\in(0,1).$$
Since $f^{(n)}$ is increasing, $f^{(n)}(1)>f^{(n)}(\xi_n)=n!\,f(1)$. (For $n=0$ the inequality $f^{(0)}(1)\ge0!\,f(1)$ is an equality.)

**Contradiction.** Taylor's formula at $a=1$, $b=2$ of order $n$:
$$f(2)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{f^{(k)}(1)}{k!}+\frac{f^{(n)}(\eta_n)}{n!}>\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{f^{(k)}(1)}{k!}\ge\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{k!\,f(1)}{k!}=n\,f(1),$$
using $f^{(n)}(\eta_n)>0$. So $f(2)>nf(1)$ for every $n\ge1$. Since $f(1)>0$, letting $n\to\infty$ is impossible. Hence no such function exists. ∎

(Only the behaviour on $[0,\infty)$ was used. Note the classical function $e^{-1/x^2}$ has all derivatives $0$ at $0$, but not all of its derivatives are positive.)

prompt: Let $b_n$ be the fractional part of $(1+\sqrt3)^{2n+1}$. Prove that $\lim_{n\to\infty}b_n=0$.
answer: $(1+\sqrt3)^{m}+(1-\sqrt3)^{m}$ is an integer and $-1<(1-\sqrt3)^{2n+1}<0$, so $b_n=(\sqrt3-1)^{2n+1}\to0$.

solutions.title: Conjugate
solutions.body:
Let $\alpha=1+\sqrt3$, $\beta=1-\sqrt3$, and $S_m=\alpha^m+\beta^m$.

**$S_m$ is an integer.** By the binomial theorem, $S_m=\sum_k\binom mk\bigl((\sqrt3)^k+(-\sqrt3)^k\bigr)$, in which the odd-$k$ terms cancel and the even-$k$ terms are integers. (Alternatively, $\alpha,\beta$ are the roots of $x^2-2x-2$, so $S_{m+2}=2S_{m+1}+2S_m$ with $S_0=2$, $S_1=2$.)

**Fractional part.** Since $\sqrt3-1\in(0,1)$, for odd $m=2n+1$ we have $\beta^m=-(\sqrt3-1)^m\in(-1,0)$. Hence
$$\alpha^{m}=S_m-\beta^m=S_m+(\sqrt3-1)^{m},\qquad 0<(\sqrt3-1)^m<1,$$
so the integer part of $\alpha^m$ is $S_m$ and
$$b_n=(\sqrt3-1)^{2n+1}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}0 .$$
∎

prompt:
Find the Fourier transform
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{-2\pi ixy}\,dx}{\cosh(\pi x)}$$
of $1/\cosh(\pi x)$.
answer: $\dfrac{1}{\cosh(\pi y)}$: the function is its own Fourier transform.

solutions.title: Rectangle contour of height $i$
solutions.body:
Let $\Phi(y)=\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{e^{-2\pi ixy}}{\cosh\pi x}dx$ (absolutely convergent) and $g(z)=\dfrac{e^{-2\pi izy}}{\cosh\pi z}$. Since $\cosh(\pi(z+i))=-\cosh(\pi z)$, integrate $g$ around the rectangle with vertices $-R,\ R,\ R+i,\ -R+i$.

- **Bottom side:** $\int_{-R}^Rg(x)\,dx\to\Phi(y)$.
- **Top side** (traversed from right to left): $g(x+i)=\dfrac{e^{-2\pi ixy}e^{2\pi y}}{-\cosh\pi x}$, so it contributes $-\int_{-R}^Rg(x+i)dx\to e^{2\pi y}\Phi(y)$.
- **Vertical sides:** $|\cosh(\pi(\pm R+is))|\ge\sinh(\pi R)$ and $|e^{-2\pi i(\pm R+is)y}|=e^{2\pi sy}\le e^{2\pi|y|}$, so they contribute at most $e^{2\pi|y|}/\sinh(\pi R)\to0$.
- **Pole:** inside the rectangle, $\cosh\pi z=0$ only at $z=\frac i2$, a simple zero with $\frac{d}{dz}\cosh\pi z=\pi\sinh\frac{\pi i}2=\pi i$. So
$$\operatorname{Res}_{z=i/2}g=\frac{e^{-2\pi i(i/2)y}}{\pi i}=\frac{e^{\pi y}}{\pi i}.$$

By the residue theorem, $(1+e^{2\pi y})\Phi(y)=2\pi i\cdot\dfrac{e^{\pi y}}{\pi i}=2e^{\pi y}$, so
$$\Phi(y)=\frac{2e^{\pi y}}{1+e^{2\pi y}}=\frac{2}{e^{-\pi y}+e^{\pi y}}=\frac1{\cosh(\pi y)} .$$

**Answer:** $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{e^{-2\pi ixy}}{\cosh\pi x}dx=\frac1{\cosh\pi y}$.

solutions.title: Sum of residues (official approach)
solutions.body:
$\Phi$ is even in $y$, so take $y<0$; then $|e^{-2\pi izy}|=e^{2\pi y\operatorname{Im}z}$ decays in the upper half plane. Close the contour with large semicircles $|z|=N$ ($N$ an integer, so the arcs stay away from the poles, where $|\cosh\pi z|$ is bounded below). The poles in the upper half plane are $z_k=(k+\frac12)i$, $k\ge0$, with $\frac{d}{dz}\cosh\pi z=\pi\sinh(\pi z_k)=\pi i(-1)^k$, so
$$\Phi(y)=2\pi i\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{e^{2\pi(k+\frac12)y}}{\pi i(-1)^k}=2\sum_{k\ge0}(-1)^ke^{(2k+1)\pi y}=\frac{2e^{\pi y}}{1+e^{2\pi y}}=\frac{1}{\cosh\pi y}.$$
(Numerically, at $y=0.7$ both sides equal $0.21911$.)

prompt:
Let $a_n$ be defined by
$$1-x^2+x^4-x^6+\cdots=\sum_{n\ge0}a_n(x+2)^n .$$
Find $\limsup_{n\to\infty}|a_n|^{1/n}$.
answer: 1/sqrt(5)

solutions.title: Radius of convergence
solutions.body:
The left side is $\dfrac1{1+x^2}$, so the $a_n$ are the Taylor coefficients of $h(x)=\dfrac1{1+x^2}$ at $x=-2$ (the two power series agree on the overlap of their discs of convergence, and the identity theorem determines the $a_n$).

As a function of a complex variable, $h$ is analytic except for poles at $\pm i$. The Taylor series at $-2$ therefore converges on the largest disc centered at $-2$ avoiding $\pm i$, and not beyond (near a pole the function is unbounded). Its radius is
$$R=|-2-i|=\sqrt5 .$$
By the Cauchy–Hadamard formula, $\limsup|a_n|^{1/n}=1/R$.

**Answer:** $\dfrac1{\sqrt5}$.

solutions.title: Explicit coefficients
solutions.body:
For real $x$, $\dfrac1{1+x^2}=\operatorname{Im}\dfrac1{x-i}$. With $w=x+2$ and $\zeta=2+i$,
$$\frac1{x-i}=\frac1{w-\zeta}=-\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{w^n}{\zeta^{n+1}},\qquad\text{so}\qquad a_n=-\operatorname{Im}\,\zeta^{-(n+1)}=\frac{\sin((n+1)\theta)}{5^{(n+1)/2}},$$
where $\theta=\arg(2+i)$, $0<\theta<\frac\pi2$ (check: $a_0=\frac15$). Thus $|a_n|\le5^{-(n+1)/2}$. Conversely, $\sin((n+2)\theta)=\sin((n+1)\theta)\cos\theta+\cos((n+1)\theta)\sin\theta$ shows that $|\sin((n+1)\theta)|$ and $|\sin((n+2)\theta)|$ cannot both be smaller than $c=\frac{\sin\theta}{2}$, so $|a_n|\ge c\,5^{-(n+1)/2}$ for infinitely many $n$. Hence $\limsup|a_n|^{1/n}=5^{-1/2}$.

prompt: For a block-matrix $\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}$ of size $n\times n$ such that $D^{-1}$ exists, prove that its determinant is equal to $\det(A-BD^{-1}C)\det D$.
answer: $\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\-D^{-1}C&I\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}A-BD^{-1}C&B\\0&D\end{pmatrix}$; take determinants of both sides.

solutions.title: Block elimination
solutions.body:
Let $A$ be $k\times k$ and $D$ be $(n-k)\times(n-k)$. Multiplying out blocks,
$$\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\-D^{-1}C&I\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}A-BD^{-1}C&B\\C-DD^{-1}C&D\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}A-BD^{-1}C&B\\0&D\end{pmatrix}.$$

**Block-triangular determinants.** For square $X$ (size $k$) and $D$ (size $n-k$),
$$\begin{pmatrix}X&Y\\0&D\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}I&Y\\0&D\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}X&0\\0&I\end{pmatrix}.$$
Expanding along the last $n-k$ rows (Laplace), $\det\begin{pmatrix}X&0\\0&I\end{pmatrix}=\det X$; expanding along the first $k$ columns, $\det\begin{pmatrix}I&Y\\0&D\end{pmatrix}=\det D$. So $\det\begin{pmatrix}X&Y\\0&D\end{pmatrix}=\det X\det D$. Similarly the lower unitriangular matrix $\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\-D^{-1}C&I\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant $1$ (it is triangular with $1$'s on the diagonal).

**Conclusion.** Taking determinants of the first identity,
$$\det\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}=\det(A-BD^{-1}C)\,\det D .$$
∎

prompt: Suppose that $k$ is a field of characteristic $p$ ($0$ or a prime). Show that there are $n$ by $n$ matrices $A$ and $B$ with coefficients in $k$ such that $AB-BA=I$ if and only if $n$ is divisible by the characteristic of $k$. ($I$ is the identity matrix.)
answer: Necessity: $\operatorname{tr}(AB-BA)=0$ but $\operatorname{tr}I=n$. Sufficiency ($p\mid n$): on $k[x]/(x^n)$, differentiation $D$ and multiplication by $x$ are well defined and satisfy $Dx-xD=I$.

solutions.title: Trace, and the Weyl algebra
solutions.body:
(Here $n\ge1$; "divisible by $0$" is impossible, so in characteristic $0$ the claim is that no such matrices exist.)

**Necessity.** $\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)$, so $\operatorname{tr}(AB-BA)=0$. If $AB-BA=I$ then $n\cdot1=\operatorname{tr}I=0$ in $k$, i.e. the characteristic $p$ divides $n$ (in particular $p\ne0$).

**Sufficiency.** Suppose $p>0$ and $p\mid n$. On $k[x]$ let $D=\frac{d}{dx}$ (formal derivative) and $X$ = multiplication by $x$. For every polynomial $g$,
$$(DX-XD)g=(xg)'-xg'=g,$$
so $DX-XD=\mathrm{id}$. The ideal $(x^n)$ is preserved by $X$, and also by $D$ because $n=0$ in $k$:
$$D(x^ng)=nx^{n-1}g+x^ng'=x^ng'\in(x^n).$$
Hence $D$ and $X$ induce linear operators on the $n$-dimensional space $V=k[x]/(x^n)$ (basis $1,x,\dots,x^{n-1}$), still satisfying $DX-XD=I$. Their matrices $A=[D]$, $B=[X]$ work: explicitly $Ax^j=jx^{j-1}$, $Bx^j=x^{j+1}$ for $j<n-1$ and $Bx^{n-1}=0$.

Check on the last basis vector, where the truncation matters: $(AB-BA)x^{n-1}=A(0)-B\bigl((n-1)x^{n-2}\bigr)=-(n-1)x^{n-1}=x^{n-1}$ since $n=0$. ∎

prompt: Prove that the conjugacy class in $S_n$ of an even permutation does not remain a single conjugacy class in the alternating group $A_n$ if and only if in the cycle decomposition of that permutation all cycles have distinct odd lengths.
answer: The $S_n$-class of $\sigma$ splits in $A_n$ iff the centralizer $C_{S_n}(\sigma)$ contains no odd permutation; an even cycle or two equal odd-length cycles give an odd element of the centralizer, while for distinct odd lengths (fixed points counted as $1$-cycles) the centralizer consists of products of powers of the cycles, all even.

solutions.title: Centralizers and orbit counting
solutions.body:
Throughout, fixed points count as cycles of length $1$. Let $\sigma\in A_n$ with $S_n$-conjugacy class $K$ (contained in $A_n$, since $A_n$ is normal).

**Step 1: $K$ splits iff $C_{S_n}(\sigma)\subseteq A_n$.** By orbit–stabilizer, $|K|=n!/|C_{S_n}(\sigma)|$ and the $A_n$-class of $\sigma$ has size $|A_n|/|C_{A_n}(\sigma)|$, where $C_{A_n}(\sigma)=C_{S_n}(\sigma)\cap A_n$ has index $1$ or $2$ in $C_{S_n}(\sigma)$.

- If $C_{S_n}(\sigma)$ contains an odd permutation, the index is $2$ and the $A_n$-class has size $\frac{n!/2}{|C_{S_n}(\sigma)|/2}=|K|$: $K$ is a single $A_n$-class.
- If $C_{S_n}(\sigma)\subseteq A_n$, the $A_n$-class of $\sigma$ has size $|K|/2$, so $K$ is not a single $A_n$-class. (In fact it splits into exactly two: conjugation by any odd permutation maps $A_n$-classes inside $K$ bijectively onto $A_n$-classes, and $K$ is the union of the $A_n$-classes of $\sigma$ and of $\tau\sigma\tau^{-1}$ for a fixed odd $\tau$.)

**Step 2: if some cycle has even length, or two cycles have the same odd length, the centralizer contains an odd permutation.**

- If $c$ is a cycle of $\sigma$ of even length $L$, then $c$ commutes with $\sigma$ (disjoint cycles commute, and $c$ commutes with itself), and $c$ is a product of $L-1$ transpositions, so it is odd.
- If $(a_1\,a_2\dots a_L)$ and $(b_1\,b_2\dots b_L)$ are two cycles of $\sigma$ of the same odd length $L$, let $\lambda=(a_1\,b_1)(a_2\,b_2)\cdots(a_L\,b_L)$. Then $\sigma\lambda\sigma^{-1}=(\sigma a_1\,\sigma b_1)\cdots(\sigma a_L\,\sigma b_L)=(a_2\,b_2)\cdots(a_L\,b_L)(a_1\,b_1)=\lambda$, so $\lambda$ commutes with $\sigma$; it is a product of $L$ (odd) disjoint transpositions, hence odd.

**Step 3: if all cycles have distinct odd lengths, the centralizer is even.** Let $\sigma=c_1\cdots c_r$ with cycle lengths $L_1,\dots,L_r$ distinct and odd, and let $\tau$ commute with $\sigma$. Then $\tau\sigma\tau^{-1}=\sigma$ means $\tau$ maps each cycle $(a\ \sigma a\ \sigma^2a\dots)$ of $\sigma$ to the cycle $(\tau a\ \sigma\tau a\ \sigma^2\tau a\dots)$ of $\sigma$ of the same length. Lengths are distinct, so $\tau$ maps the support of each $c_i$ to itself. If $a$ is in the support of $c_i$ and $\tau(a)=\sigma^{k_i}(a)$, then $\tau(\sigma^ja)=\sigma^j\tau(a)=\sigma^{k_i}(\sigma^ja)$, so $\tau=c_i^{k_i}$ on that support. Hence $\tau=c_1^{k_1}\cdots c_r^{k_r}$. Each $c_i$ is a cycle of odd length, hence an even permutation, so $\tau$ is even.

**Conclusion.** By Steps 2 and 3, $C_{S_n}(\sigma)\subseteq A_n$ iff all cycles of $\sigma$ have distinct odd lengths; by Step 1, this is exactly when the $S_n$-class of $\sigma$ does not remain a single $A_n$-class. ∎

prompt: How many maximal ideals are in the ring $\mathbb R[x]/(x^{12}+6x^2+5)$?

solutions.title: Distinct irreducible factors
solutions.body:
Maximal ideals of $\mathbb R[x]/(f)$ correspond to maximal ideals $(q)$ of $\mathbb R[x]$ containing $f$, i.e. to the distinct monic irreducible factors $q$ of $f=x^{12}+6x^2+5$.

**Factor $g(y)=y^6+6y+5$** (so $f(x)=g(x^2)$):
$$g(y)=(y+1)^2\,(y^4-2y^3+3y^2-4y+5),$$
as one checks by expanding. Call the quartic $q(y)$.

- $q$ has no real roots: $q(y)=(y^2-y)^2+2(y-1)^2+3>0$.
- $q$ has $4$ distinct roots, none equal to $-1$: $g'=6(y^5+1)$ and $g-\frac y6g'=5(y+1)$, so $\gcd(g,g')$ divides $y+1$; thus $-1$ is the only repeated root of $g$, and it is a root of $(y+1)^2$ only, as $q(-1)=15\ne0$.

So the roots of $q$ are two conjugate pairs $w,\bar w,v,\bar v$ of distinct non-real numbers.

**Factor $f$.** $f(x)=(x^2+1)^2q(x^2)$. The roots of $q(x^2)$ are $\pm\sqrt w,\pm\sqrt{\bar w},\pm\sqrt v,\pm\sqrt{\bar v}$: eight distinct non-real numbers (if $x$ were real, $x^2$ would be a real root of $q$), different from $\pm i$ (since $q(-1)\ne0$). Non-real roots of a real polynomial come in conjugate pairs, so $q(x^2)$ is a product of $4$ distinct irreducible real quadratics, none equal to $x^2+1$.

Hence $f=(x^2+1)^2q_1q_2q_3q_4$ with $5$ distinct irreducible factors, and by the Chinese remainder theorem
$$\mathbb R[x]/(f)\cong\mathbb R[x]/\bigl((x^2+1)^2\bigr)\times\prod_{j=1}^4\mathbb R[x]/(q_j)\cong\mathbb R[x]/\bigl((x^2+1)^2\bigr)\times\mathbb C^4,$$
which has exactly $5$ maximal ideals.

**Answer: 5**

prompt:
Suppose that $f_n(x)$ is a sequence of continuous functions on the closed unit interval. For each of the following statements, either prove it or give a counterexample.

(a) If $f_n$ converges pointwise to a function $f$ then the sequence $\int_0^1f_n(x)\,dx$ has limit $\int_0^1f(x)\,dx$.

(b) If $f_n$ converges uniformly to a function $f$ then the sequence $\int_0^1f_n(x)\,dx$ has limit $\int_0^1f(x)\,dx$.
answer: (a) False: tents of height $2n$ on $[0,1/n]$ converge pointwise to $0$ but have integral $1$. (b) True: $\left|\int f_n-\int f\right|\le\sup|f_n-f|\to0$.

solutions.title: Moving spike; uniform estimate
solutions.body:
**(a) False.** Let $f_n$ be the "tent" with $f_n(0)=0$, rising linearly to $f_n\bigl(\frac1{2n}\bigr)=2n$, back down to $f_n\bigl(\frac1n\bigr)=0$, and $f_n=0$ on $[\frac1n,1]$. Each $f_n$ is continuous with $\int_0^1f_n=\frac12\cdot\frac1n\cdot2n=1$. For every $x$: $f_n(0)=0$, and if $x>0$ then $f_n(x)=0$ as soon as $\frac1n<x$. So $f_n\to f\equiv0$ pointwise, but $\int_0^1f_n=1\not\to0=\int_0^1f$.

**(b) True.** A uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous, so $f$ is integrable. For $\varepsilon>0$ choose $N$ with $\sup_{[0,1]}|f_n-f|<\varepsilon$ for $n\ge N$; then
$$\left|\int_0^1f_n-\int_0^1f\right|\le\int_0^1|f_n-f|\le\varepsilon\qquad(n\ge N).$$
Hence $\int_0^1f_n\to\int_0^1f$. ∎

prompt:
Find the limit
$$\lim_{\epsilon\to0}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\epsilon\,e^{-x^2}\,dx}{x^2+\epsilon^2}$$
where the limit is taken for positive values of $\epsilon$.
answer: pi

solutions.title: Rescale and use dominated convergence
solutions.body:
Substitute $x=\epsilon u$, $dx=\epsilon\,du$:
$$\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{\epsilon e^{-x^2}}{x^2+\epsilon^2}dx=\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{e^{-\epsilon^2u^2}}{u^2+1}du .$$
The integrand tends to $\frac1{1+u^2}$ pointwise as $\epsilon\to0^+$ and is dominated by the integrable function $\frac1{1+u^2}$, so by dominated convergence the limit is
$$\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{du}{1+u^2}=\pi .$$

**Answer:** $\pi$.

solutions.title: Approximate identity (official idea)
solutions.body:
$P_\epsilon(x)=\frac{\epsilon}{x^2+\epsilon^2}$ satisfies $\int P_\epsilon=\pi$ and concentrates at $0$: for any $\delta>0$, $\int_{|x|>\delta}P_\epsilon\,dx=2\bigl(\frac\pi2-\arctan\frac\delta\epsilon\bigr)\to0$. Hence, with $\phi(x)=e^{-x^2}$ (bounded by $1$ and continuous at $0$),
$$\Bigl|\int P_\epsilon\phi-\pi\phi(0)\Bigr|\le\pi\sup_{|x|\le\delta}|\phi(x)-\phi(0)|+2\int_{|x|>\delta}P_\epsilon\to\pi\sup_{|x|\le\delta}|\phi(x)-1|,$$
which is arbitrarily small. So the limit is $\pi\phi(0)=\pi$.

prompt:
A complex function is holomorphic for $|z|>2$ and in this region has derivative
$$\frac{e^z(z-a)}{z^2-z}$$
where $a$ is a complex number. Find $a$.

solutions.title: Residues must cancel
solutions.body:
Let $f$ be the function and $g(z)=f'(z)=\dfrac{e^z(z-a)}{z(z-1)}$. Since $g$ has a primitive ($f$) on $|z|>2$, its integral over the closed curve $|z|=3$ is $0$.

On the other hand, $g$ is meromorphic on $\mathbb C$ with poles only at $0$ and $1$, both inside $|z|=3$, so by the residue theorem
$$0=\oint_{|z|=3}g\,dz=2\pi i\bigl(\operatorname{Res}_0g+\operatorname{Res}_1g\bigr).$$
Now $\operatorname{Res}_0g=\dfrac{e^0(0-a)}{0-1}=a$ and $\operatorname{Res}_1g=\dfrac{e(1-a)}{1}=e(1-a)$. So $a+e-ea=0$, i.e.
$$a=\frac{e}{e-1}.$$
Conversely, for this $a$ the integral of $g$ over every closed curve in $|z|>2$ is (winding number about $0$) $\times\oint_{|z|=3}g=0$, so $g$ has a primitive there.

**Answer:** $a=\dfrac{e}{e-1}$.

prompt: Suppose that $f(t)$ is an infinitely differentiable function of the real variable $t$, which vanishes for $t\ge1$. Prove that $\int_0^1f(t)\,t^s\,dt$ extends to a meromorphic function for all complex $s$, and find the possible values of $s$ that can be poles.
answer: Integrating by parts $k$ times, $F(s)=\dfrac{(-1)^k}{(s+1)\cdots(s+k)}\int_0^1f^{(k)}(t)t^{s+k}dt$ for $\operatorname{Re}s>-k-1$; the possible poles are $s=-1,-2,-3,\dots$ (simple, residue $f^{(m-1)}(0)/(m-1)!$ at $s=-m$).

solutions.title: Repeated integration by parts
solutions.body:
Let $F(s)=\int_0^1f(t)t^s\,dt$. For $\operatorname{Re}s>-1$ the integral converges absolutely and locally uniformly in $s$, so $F$ is holomorphic there.

Since $f\equiv0$ on $[1,\infty)$ and $f$ is smooth, $f^{(j)}(1)=0$ for all $j\ge0$ (the one-sided derivatives from the right vanish). For $\operatorname{Re}s>-1$, integrating by parts,
$$F(s)=\Bigl[f(t)\frac{t^{s+1}}{s+1}\Bigr]_0^1-\frac1{s+1}\int_0^1f'(t)t^{s+1}dt=-\frac1{s+1}\int_0^1f'(t)t^{s+1}dt,$$
because $f(1)=0$ and $t^{s+1}\to0$ as $t\to0^+$. Repeating $k$ times,
$$F(s)=\frac{(-1)^k}{(s+1)(s+2)\cdots(s+k)}\int_0^1f^{(k)}(t)\,t^{s+k}\,dt\qquad(\operatorname{Re}s>-1).$$
The right-hand side is meromorphic on $\operatorname{Re}s>-k-1$ (the integral is holomorphic there), with possible poles only at $-1,\dots,-k$. These extensions for different $k$ agree on their common domain by the identity theorem, so together they define a meromorphic continuation of $F$ to all of $\mathbb C$, whose only possible poles are
$$s=-1,-2,-3,\dots,$$
all at most simple.

**Each can occur.** For $s$ near $-m$, split $f(t)=\sum_{j<m}\frac{f^{(j)}(0)}{j!}t^j+t^mr(t)$ on $[0,1]$ with $r$ continuous; then
$$F(s)=\sum_{j<m}\frac{f^{(j)}(0)}{j!}\cdot\frac1{s+j+1}+\int_0^1r(t)t^{s+m}dt,$$
where the last integral is holomorphic for $\operatorname{Re}s>-m-1$. So the residue at $s=-m$ is $f^{(m-1)}(0)/(m-1)!$, nonzero e.g. when $f(t)=t^{m-1}$ near $0$. ∎

prompt:
Let $P(k)$ be a polynomial. Show that
$$S(n)=\sum_{k=0}^nP(k)$$
is a polynomial.
answer: Write $P$ in the binomial basis $\binom kj$ and use $\sum_{k=0}^n\binom kj=\binom{n+1}{j+1}$; or note that the difference operator maps polynomials of degree $<N$ onto polynomials of degree $<N-1$.

solutions.title: Difference operator (official approach)
solutions.body:
For a polynomial $T$, let $(\Delta T)(n)=T(n)-T(n-1)$. If $\deg T=d\ge1$, the leading terms cancel, so $\deg\Delta T=d-1$; and $\Delta$ kills constants. Let $V_N$ be the space of polynomials of degree $<N$ (dimension $N$). Then $\Delta:V_N\to V_{N-1}$ is linear, and its kernel is exactly the constants: if $T(n)=T(n-1)$ for all $n$, then $T-T(0)$ vanishes at all integers, hence is $0$. By rank–nullity, $\dim\Delta(V_N)=N-1=\dim V_{N-1}$, so $\Delta$ is surjective.

Take $N=\deg P+2$ and choose $T\in V_N$ with $\Delta T=P$. Telescoping,
$$S(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n\bigl(T(k)-T(k-1)\bigr)=T(n)-T(-1),$$
which is a polynomial in $n$ (of degree $\deg P+1$). ∎

solutions.title: Binomial basis and the hockey-stick identity
solutions.body:
The polynomials $\binom kj=\frac{k(k-1)\cdots(k-j+1)}{j!}$, $j=0,1,2,\dots$, have degree $j$ in $k$, so they form a basis of the polynomials: $P(k)=\sum_{j=0}^dc_j\binom kj$. By the hockey-stick identity (induction on $n$ using Pascal's rule $\binom{n+1}{j+1}+\binom{n+1}{j}=\binom{n+2}{j+1}$),
$$\sum_{k=0}^n\binom kj=\binom{n+1}{j+1}.$$
Hence $S(n)=\sum_{j=0}^dc_j\binom{n+1}{j+1}$, a polynomial in $n$. ∎

prompt: Find the number of conjugacy classes of $4\times4$ complex matrices $A$ with $A^4=I$ (the $4\times4$ identity matrix).

solutions.title: Diagonalizable with fourth roots of unity
solutions.body:
$A^4=I$ means the minimal polynomial of $A$ divides $x^4-1=(x-1)(x+1)(x-i)(x+i)$, which has distinct roots. So $A$ is diagonalizable with eigenvalues in $\{1,-1,i,-i\}$, and its conjugacy class is determined by the multiplicities $(a,b,c,d)$ of these eigenvalues, with $a+b+c+d=4$. Every such tuple occurs (take the diagonal matrix). The number of solutions in non-negative integers is, by stars and bars,
$$\binom{4+3}{3}=\binom73=35 .$$

**Answer: 35**

prompt: Find integers $m, n$ with $0<m<n$ such that $x^m\equiv x^n \pmod{2025}$ for all integers $x$. What is the smallest possible value of $n$?

solutions.title: Work modulo $3^4$ and $5^2$
solutions.body:
$2025=3^4\cdot5^2$.

**Lower bound.** Take $x=3$: $3^m(3^{n-m}-1)\equiv0\pmod{81}$, and $3^{n-m}-1$ is prime to $3$, so $81\mid3^m$, i.e. $m\ge4$. Take $x=2$: $2^m(2^{n-m}-1)\equiv0\pmod{2025}$, so $2^{n-m}\equiv1\pmod{2025}$. The order of $2$ mod $81$ is $54$ ($2$ has order $6$ mod $9$, i.e. is a primitive root mod $9$, hence a primitive root mod every power of $3$) and the order of $2$ mod $25$ is $20$ ($2^4=16\ne1$ and $2^{10}=1024\equiv-1$). So $\operatorname{lcm}(54,20)=540\mid n-m$, and
$$n\ge m+540\ge544 .$$

**$m=4$, $n=544$ works.** Modulo $81$: if $3\mid x$, then $x^4\equiv0\equiv x^{544}$; otherwise $x^{54}\equiv1$ by Euler ($\varphi(81)=54$) and $540=10\cdot54$, so $x^{544}=x^4(x^{54})^{10}\equiv x^4$. Modulo $25$: if $5\mid x$, then $25\mid x^2$, so both sides are $0$; otherwise $x^{20}\equiv1$ and $20\mid540$. By the Chinese remainder theorem $x^{544}\equiv x^4\pmod{2025}$ for all $x$. (A brute-force search confirms that $(m,n)=(4,544)$ is the first pair that works.)

**Answer:** $m=4$, $n=544$; the smallest possible $n$ is $544$.

prompt:
Prove that the number of orbits of a finite group acting on a set is the average number of fixed points of elements of the group.

In how many ways up to symmetry can one color the $4$ corners of a square with $10$ colors?
answer: Count pairs $(g,x)$ with $gx=x$ in two ways (Burnside's lemma). Under the $8$ symmetries of the square: $\frac{10^4+2\cdot10+10^2+2\cdot10^3+2\cdot10^2}{8}=1540$ colorings.

solutions.title: Double counting, then Burnside

prompt:
Let $f \in C([0,1])$ be continuous. Suppose
$$\int_0^1 f(x)\,x^n\,dx = 0$$
for every integer $n \ge 0$. Prove that $f \equiv 0$ on $[0,1]$.

You may use without proof that polynomials are uniformly dense in $C([0,1])$.
answer: $\int_0^1 fp=0$ for every polynomial $p$; approximating $f$ uniformly by polynomials gives $\int_0^1 f^2=0$, so $f\equiv 0$.

solutions.title: Approximate $f$ by polynomials
solutions.body:
By linearity, the hypothesis gives $\int_0^1 f(x)p(x)\,dx=0$ for every polynomial $p$.

By the Weierstrass approximation theorem choose polynomials $p_k$ with $\|f-p_k\|_\infty\to 0$. Then
$$\int_0^1 f(x)^2\,dx=\int_0^1 f(x)\bigl(f(x)-p_k(x)\bigr)\,dx+\underbrace{\int_0^1 f(x)p_k(x)\,dx}_{=0}\le \|f\|_\infty\,\|f-p_k\|_\infty\xrightarrow[k\to\infty]{}0 .$$
Hence $\int_0^1 f^2\,dx=0$. (Equivalently: the functional $L(g)=\int_0^1 fg$ is continuous on $C([0,1])$ with the sup norm, vanishes on the dense subspace of polynomials, hence vanishes identically; take $g=f$.)

Finally, $f^2$ is continuous and $\ge 0$. If $f(x_0)\ne 0$ for some $x_0$, then by continuity $f^2>\tfrac12 f(x_0)^2$ on some interval $I\subseteq[0,1]$ of positive length $|I|$, giving $\int_0^1 f^2\ge \tfrac12 f(x_0)^2|I|>0$, a contradiction. So $f\equiv 0$ on $[0,1]$. ∎

prompt:
Let $(f_n)$ be a sequence of differentiable functions on $[0,1]$ with $f_n(0)=0$ for all $n$. Suppose that $(f_n')$ converges uniformly on $[0,1]$ to a continuous function $g$.

1. Prove that $(f_n)$ converges uniformly on $[0,1]$ to a function $f$.
2. Show that $f$ is $C^1$ on $[0,1]$, that $f(0)=0$, and that $f'=g$.
answer: The limit is $f(x)=\int_0^x g(t)\,dt$: by the mean value theorem $\sup|f_n-f|\le\sup|f_n'-g|\to0$, and $f$ is $C^1$ with $f(0)=0$, $f'=g$ by the fundamental theorem of calculus.

solutions.title: Compare with the antiderivative of $g$
solutions.body:
Define
$$F(x)=\int_0^x g(t)\,dt,\qquad x\in[0,1].$$
Since $g$ is continuous, the fundamental theorem of calculus shows that $F$ is differentiable with $F'=g$; so $F$ is $C^1$ and $F(0)=0$.

**Uniform convergence.** Fix $n$ and put $h_n=f_n-F$. It is differentiable on $[0,1]$ with $h_n(0)=0$ and $h_n'=f_n'-g$. For $x\in(0,1]$, the mean value theorem gives some $\xi\in(0,x)$ with
$$|f_n(x)-F(x)|=|h_n(x)-h_n(0)|=x\,|f_n'(\xi)-g(\xi)|\le \sup_{u\in[0,1]}|f_n'(u)-g(u)| ,$$
and the bound holds trivially at $x=0$. Since $f_n'\to g$ uniformly, the right-hand side tends to $0$, so $f_n\to F$ uniformly on $[0,1]$. This proves part 1 with $f=F$.

**Part 2.** The limit is $f=F$, which we saw is $C^1$ with $f(0)=0$ and $f'=g$. ∎

*Remark.* The official solution writes $f_n(x)=\int_0^x f_n'(t)\,dt$; that uses integrability of $f_n'$, which is not part of the hypotheses (a derivative need not be Riemann integrable). The mean value theorem argument above avoids this.

prompt:
Let $f$ be an entire function such that
$$|f(z)| \le A + B|z|^m$$
for some constants $A, B \ge 0$ and a nonnegative integer $m$.

1. Show that $f$ is a polynomial of degree at most $m$.
2. Deduce that if $|f(z)| \le C(1+|z|^{1/2})$ for some $C>0$, then $f$ is constant.
answer: Cauchy's estimates give $|f^{(k)}(0)|\le k!(A+BR^m)/R^k\to 0$ for $k>m$. For part 2, part 1 with $m=1$ gives $f=a+bz$, and $|b|\le C(1+R^{1/2})/R\to0$.

solutions.title: Cauchy estimates
solutions.body:
**Part 1.** Since $f$ is entire, $f(z)=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{f^{(k)}(0)}{k!}z^k$ for all $z$. By Cauchy's integral formula, for every $R>0$,
$$f^{(k)}(0)=\frac{k!}{2\pi i}\oint_{|z|=R}\frac{f(z)}{z^{k+1}}\,dz ,\qquad\text{so}\qquad |f^{(k)}(0)|\le \frac{k!}{2\pi}\cdot 2\pi R\cdot\frac{A+BR^m}{R^{k+1}}=k!\Bigl(\frac{A}{R^k}+\frac{B}{R^{k-m}}\Bigr).$$
If $k>m$, the right-hand side tends to $0$ as $R\to\infty$, so $f^{(k)}(0)=0$. Hence the Taylor series stops at degree $m$: $f$ is a polynomial of degree at most $m$.

**Part 2.** Since $|z|^{1/2}\le 1+|z|$, we get $|f(z)|\le 2C+C|z|$, so by part 1 (with $m=1$) $f(z)=a+bz$. Applying the Cauchy estimate to $f'(0)=b$ with the original bound,
$$|b|=|f'(0)|\le \frac{\max_{|z|=R}|f(z)|}{R}\le \frac{C(1+R^{1/2})}{R}\xrightarrow[R\to\infty]{}0 .$$
So $b=0$ and $f$ is constant. ∎

(Equivalently: the proof of part 1 works for any real exponent $m\ge0$ and shows $f^{(k)}(0)=0$ for every integer $k>m$; with $m=\tfrac12$ this means $k\ge1$.)

prompt:
Let $0<\alpha<1$. Evaluate
$$I(\alpha) := \int_0^\infty \frac{x^{\alpha-1}}{1+x}\,dx$$
using contour integration (do not use Beta/Gamma function identities).
answer: $I(\alpha)=\dfrac{\pi}{\sin(\pi\alpha)}$ (keyhole contour around the positive real axis, residue at $z=-1$).

solutions.title: Keyhole contour
solutions.body:
Let $f(z)=\dfrac{z^{\alpha-1}}{1+z}$ on $\mathbb C\setminus[0,\infty)$, with the branch
$$z^{\alpha-1}=\exp\bigl((\alpha-1)\log z\bigr),\qquad \log z=\ln|z|+i\arg z,\quad \arg z\in(0,2\pi).$$
Its only singularity off the cut is a simple pole at $z=-1=e^{i\pi}$, with
$$\operatorname{Res}_{z=-1}f=(-1)^{\alpha-1}=e^{i\pi(\alpha-1)}=-e^{i\pi\alpha}.$$

Take the keyhole contour $\Gamma$ (for $0<\varepsilon<1<R$): the upper bank of the cut from $\varepsilon$ to $R$, the circle $|z|=R$ counterclockwise, the lower bank from $R$ back to $\varepsilon$, and the circle $|z|=\varepsilon$ clockwise. It encloses $-1$ once, so $\oint_\Gamma f=2\pi i\cdot(-e^{i\pi\alpha})$.

- On the upper bank $\arg z\to0$, so $z^{\alpha-1}=x^{\alpha-1}$; the contribution is $\int_\varepsilon^R\frac{x^{\alpha-1}}{1+x}dx$.
- On the lower bank $\arg z\to2\pi$, so $z^{\alpha-1}=x^{\alpha-1}e^{2\pi i(\alpha-1)}=x^{\alpha-1}e^{2\pi i\alpha}$; traversed from $R$ to $\varepsilon$ the contribution is $-e^{2\pi i\alpha}\int_\varepsilon^R\frac{x^{\alpha-1}}{1+x}dx$.
- On $|z|=R$ (with $R\ge2$): $|f|\le \frac{R^{\alpha-1}}{R-1}\le \frac{2R^{\alpha-1}}{R}$, so the integral is at most $2\pi R\cdot 2R^{\alpha-2}=4\pi R^{\alpha-1}\to0$ since $\alpha<1$.
- On $|z|=\varepsilon$ (with $\varepsilon\le\frac12$): $|f|\le 2\varepsilon^{\alpha-1}$, so the integral is at most $4\pi\varepsilon^{\alpha}\to0$ since $\alpha>0$.

Letting $\varepsilon\to0^+$, $R\to\infty$ (the improper integral converges: the integrand is $\sim x^{\alpha-1}$ at $0$ and $\sim x^{\alpha-2}$ at $\infty$):
$$(1-e^{2\pi i\alpha})\,I(\alpha)=-2\pi i\,e^{i\pi\alpha}.$$
Multiplying numerator and denominator by $e^{-i\pi\alpha}$,
$$I(\alpha)=\frac{-2\pi i}{e^{-i\pi\alpha}-e^{i\pi\alpha}}=\frac{-2\pi i}{-2i\sin(\pi\alpha)}=\frac{\pi}{\sin(\pi\alpha)} .$$

**Answer:** $I(\alpha)=\dfrac{\pi}{\sin \pi\alpha}$.

solutions.title: Check with a special value
solutions.body: For $\alpha=\tfrac12$ substitute $x=u^2$: $\int_0^\infty\frac{x^{-1/2}}{1+x}dx=\int_0^\infty\frac{2\,du}{1+u^2}=\pi$, which agrees with $\pi/\sin(\pi/2)=\pi$. Also $I(\alpha)=I(1-\alpha)$ (substitute $x\mapsto1/x$), consistent with $\sin(\pi\alpha)=\sin(\pi(1-\alpha))$.

prompt: Let $A$ be a real $n\times n$ matrix such that $A^3=A$. Describe all possible Jordan canonical forms of $A$.
answer: $A$ is diagonalizable (its minimal polynomial divides $x(x-1)(x+1)$, which has distinct roots); its Jordan form is $\operatorname{diag}(-1,\dots,-1,0,\dots,0,1,\dots,1)$ with any multiplicities $p+q+r=n$.

solutions.title: Minimal polynomial
solutions.body:
**Eigenvalues.** If $Av=\lambda v$ with $v\ne0$ (over $\mathbb C$), then $\lambda^3v=A^3v=Av=\lambda v$, so $\lambda^3=\lambda$, i.e. $\lambda\in\{-1,0,1\}$.

**Diagonalizability.** $A$ is annihilated by $x^3-x=x(x-1)(x+1)$, so its minimal polynomial divides this product of *distinct* linear factors over $\mathbb R$. A matrix whose minimal polynomial splits into distinct linear factors is diagonalizable (equivalently: a Jordan block $J_k(\lambda)$ with $k\ge2$ has minimal polynomial $(x-\lambda)^k$, which does not divide $x^3-x$). Hence every Jordan block has size $1$.

**Conclusion.** The Jordan canonical form of $A$ is diagonal with entries in $\{-1,0,1\}$; up to the order of the blocks,
$$A\sim \operatorname{diag}(\underbrace{-1,\dots,-1}_{p},\underbrace{0,\dots,0}_{q},\underbrace{1,\dots,1}_{r}),\qquad p,q,r\ge0,\ p+q+r=n .$$
Every such choice occurs, since that real diagonal matrix itself satisfies $A^3=A$. (So there are $\binom{n+2}{2}$ possible forms.) ∎

prompt:
Orthogonally diagonalize the symmetric matrix
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&1\\1&2&1\\1&1&2\end{pmatrix}.$$
Specifically:

1. Find the eigenvalues and eigenspaces of $A$.
2. Within the eigenspace of the repeated eigenvalue, use the Gram–Schmidt process to produce an orthonormal basis.
3. Form an orthogonal matrix $Q$ from your orthonormal eigenvectors and verify that $Q^\top AQ$ is diagonal. Give $Q$ and $Q^\top AQ$ explicitly.
answer: Eigenvalues $4$ (eigenvector $(1,1,1)$) and $1$ (twice, eigenspace $x_1+x_2+x_3=0$); e.g. $Q=\begin{pmatrix}\frac1{\sqrt2}&\frac1{\sqrt6}&\frac1{\sqrt3}\\-\frac1{\sqrt2}&\frac1{\sqrt6}&\frac1{\sqrt3}\\0&-\frac2{\sqrt6}&\frac1{\sqrt3}\end{pmatrix}$, $Q^\top AQ=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,4)$.

solutions.title: Write $A=I+J$
solutions.body:
**1. Eigenvalues and eigenspaces.** $A=I+J$ where $J$ is the all-ones $3\times3$ matrix. $J$ has rank $1$ with $J(1,1,1)^\top=3(1,1,1)^\top$ and $Jx=0$ for $x\perp(1,1,1)$. Hence $A$ has eigenvalues
$$\lambda=4\ \text{(simple)},\qquad \lambda=1\ \text{(multiplicity 2)},$$
with $E_4=\operatorname{span}\{(1,1,1)^\top\}$ and $E_1=\{x: x_1+x_2+x_3=0\}=\operatorname{span}\{u_1,u_2\}$, $u_1=(1,-1,0)^\top$, $u_2=(1,0,-1)^\top$. (Check: $\operatorname{tr}A=6=4+1+1$.)

**2. Gram–Schmidt in $E_1$.**
$$e_1=\frac{u_1}{\|u_1\|}=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(1,-1,0)^\top,\qquad w_2=u_2-\langle u_2,e_1\rangle e_1=(1,0,-1)^\top-\tfrac12(1,-1,0)^\top=\bigl(\tfrac12,\tfrac12,-1\bigr)^\top,$$
$\|w_2\|^2=\tfrac32$, so $e_2=\tfrac1{\sqrt6}(1,1,-2)^\top$. Normalizing the other eigenvector: $e_3=\tfrac1{\sqrt3}(1,1,1)^\top$. Eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix for different eigenvalues are orthogonal, so $\{e_1,e_2,e_3\}$ is an orthonormal eigenbasis.

**3. The orthogonal matrix.**
$$Q=\begin{pmatrix}\frac1{\sqrt2}&\frac1{\sqrt6}&\frac1{\sqrt3}\\[2pt]-\frac1{\sqrt2}&\frac1{\sqrt6}&\frac1{\sqrt3}\\[2pt]0&-\frac2{\sqrt6}&\frac1{\sqrt3}\end{pmatrix},\qquad Q^\top Q=I .$$
Verification: $Ae_1=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(2-1,\,1-2,\,1-1)^\top=e_1$, $Ae_2=\tfrac1{\sqrt6}(2+1-2,\,1+2-2,\,1+1-4)^\top=e_2$, $Ae_3=\tfrac1{\sqrt3}(4,4,4)^\top=4e_3$. So $AQ=Q\operatorname{diag}(1,1,4)$ and
$$Q^\top AQ=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,4),\qquad A=Q\operatorname{diag}(1,1,4)Q^\top .$$

prompt:
Let $G$ be a finite $p$-group, i.e. $|G|=p^n$ for some prime $p$ and integer $n\ge1$.

1. Show that the center $Z(G)$ of $G$ is nontrivial.
2. Deduce that $G$ has a normal subgroup of order $p$.
answer: Class equation: $|G|=|Z(G)|+\sum[G:C_G(x_i)]$ with every index a nontrivial power of $p$, so $p\mid |Z(G)|$. Then a central element of order $p$ generates a normal subgroup of order $p$.

solutions.title: Class equation
solutions.body:
**1.** Let $G$ act on itself by conjugation. The orbit of $x$ is its conjugacy class, of size $[G:C_G(x)]$, which divides $|G|=p^n$ and so is a power of $p$; it equals $1$ exactly when $x\in Z(G)$. Choosing representatives $x_1,\dots,x_k$ of the conjugacy classes of size $>1$, the class equation reads
$$p^n=|G|=|Z(G)|+\sum_{i=1}^k [G:C_G(x_i)] .$$
Each $[G:C_G(x_i)]$ is a power of $p$ greater than $1$, hence divisible by $p$; and $p\mid |G|$ since $n\ge1$. Therefore $p\mid |Z(G)|$. As $e\in Z(G)$, $|Z(G)|\ge1$, so $|Z(G)|\ge p$: the center is nontrivial.

**2.** Pick $z\in Z(G)$, $z\ne e$. Its order is $p^k$ for some $k\ge1$ (Lagrange), so $y=z^{p^{k-1}}$ has order exactly $p$. Then $N=\langle y\rangle$ has order $p$, and since $y$ is central, $gy^jg^{-1}=y^j$ for all $g\in G$, so $N$ is normal. ∎

prompt:
1. Let $R$ be a finite integral domain (a finite commutative ring with $1$ and no zero divisors). Prove that $R$ is a field.
2. Show that if $p$ is the characteristic of $R$ then the Frobenius map $F:R\to R$, $F(x)=x^p$ is an automorphism (and in particular is bijective).
answer: Multiplication by $a\ne0$ is injective, hence bijective on the finite set $R$, so $a$ has an inverse. $F$ is a ring homomorphism ($\binom pk\equiv0$ for $0<k<p$), injective because $R$ has no nilpotents, hence bijective.

solutions.title: Injective self-maps of a finite set
solutions.body:
**1.** Fix $a\in R$, $a\ne0$, and let $m_a:R\to R$, $m_a(x)=ax$. If $ax=ay$ then $a(x-y)=0$, so $x=y$ since $R$ has no zero divisors. Thus $m_a$ is injective, and an injective map from a finite set to itself is surjective. So $ab=1$ for some $b$, i.e. every nonzero element is invertible and $R$ is a field. (Here $1\ne0$ is part of the definition of an integral domain.)

**2.** *The characteristic is a prime.* $R$ is finite, so the additive order of $1$ is some $p\ge2$. If $p=ab$ with $1<a,b<p$, then $(a\cdot1)(b\cdot1)=p\cdot1=0$ with both factors nonzero, impossible. So $p$ is prime.

*$F$ is a ring homomorphism.* Clearly $F(1)=1$ and $F(xy)=x^py^p=F(x)F(y)$ ($R$ is commutative). By the binomial theorem
$$(x+y)^p=x^p+y^p+\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\binom pk x^ky^{p-k},$$
and for $1\le k\le p-1$ the prime $p$ divides $\binom pk=\frac{p!}{k!(p-k)!}$ (it divides the numerator but not the denominator), so these terms are $0$ in characteristic $p$. Hence $F(x+y)=F(x)+F(y)$.

*$F$ is bijective.* If $F(x)=x^p=0$ then $x=0$, since $R$ has no zero divisors; so $\ker F=0$ and $F$ is injective. (Alternatively: $\ker F$ is an ideal of the field $R$ not containing $1$, hence $0$.) As $R$ is finite, $F$ is also surjective. So $F$ is an automorphism of $R$. ∎

prompt: Let $c_n$ be the number of ways of giving $n$ cents change using coins of values $1, 5, 10, 25$ cents. Find $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty} c_n/n^3$.

solutions.title: Partial fractions of the generating function
solutions.body:
The generating function is
$$\sum_{n\ge0}c_nz^n=G(z)=\frac{1}{(1-z)(1-z^5)(1-z^{10})(1-z^{25})} .$$
$G$ is a rational function whose poles are roots of unity. At $z=1$ every factor vanishes, so the pole has order $4$. Any other root of unity $\zeta\ne1$ is a root of at most the three factors $1-z^5,1-z^{10},1-z^{25}$, so it is a pole of order at most $3$.

In the partial fraction decomposition, a term $\dfrac{1}{(1-z/\zeta)^j}$ contributes $\binom{n+j-1}{j-1}\zeta^{-n}=O(n^{j-1})$ to the $n$th coefficient. So all terms except the $(1-z)^{-4}$ term contribute $O(n^2)$. Near $z=1$, writing $1-z^k=(1-z)(1+z+\dots+z^{k-1})$,
$$G(z)=\frac{1}{(1-z)^4}\cdot\frac{1}{(1+\dots+z^4)(1+\dots+z^9)(1+\dots+z^{24})},$$
and the second factor equals $\frac1{5\cdot10\cdot25}=\frac1{1250}$ at $z=1$. So the coefficient of $(1-z)^{-4}$ is $\frac1{1250}$, and
$$c_n=\frac1{1250}\binom{n+3}{3}+O(n^2)=\frac{n^3}{1250\cdot 6}+O(n^2).$$

**Answer:** $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{c_n}{n^3}=\frac{1}{7500}$.

solutions.title: Count lattice points in a tetrahedron
solutions.body:
Once the numbers $b,c,d\ge0$ of nickels, dimes and quarters are chosen with $5b+10c+25d\le n$, the pennies are determined. So $c_n$ is the number of lattice points in the tetrahedron
$$T_n=\{(b,c,d)\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^3:\ 5b+10c+25d\le n\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}(T_n)=\frac16\cdot\frac n5\cdot\frac n{10}\cdot\frac n{25}=\frac{n^3}{7500}.$$
Assign to each lattice point $q=(b,c,d)\in T_n$ the unit cube $q+[0,1)^3$; these $c_n$ cubes are disjoint, and their union $U$ satisfies $T_n\subseteq U\subseteq T_{n+40}$. Indeed, a point $p\in T_n$ lies in the cube of its integer part $\lfloor p\rfloor\in T_n$; and a point of the cube of $q$ exceeds $q$ in the linear form $5b+10c+25d$ by less than $5+10+25=40$. Comparing volumes,
$$\frac{n^3}{7500}\le c_n\le\frac{(n+40)^3}{7500},$$
and $c_n/n^3\to\frac1{7500}$. (A direct computation gives $c_{20000}/20000^3\approx1.338\times10^{-4}$, close to $1/7500\approx1.333\times10^{-4}$.)

prompt: The Catalan numbers $1, 1, 2, 5, 14, \dots$ satisfy $C_n=0$ if $n<0$, $C_0=1$, $C_n=\sum_i C_iC_{n-1-i}$. Find the function $f(x)=\sum_n C_nx^n$, and use this to calculate $C_n$ as the quotient of a binomial coefficient by a linear function.
answer: $f(x)=\dfrac{1-\sqrt{1-4x}}{2x}$ (from $xf^2-f+1=0$), and $C_n=\dfrac{1}{n+1}\dbinom{2n}{n}$.

solutions.title: Quadratic equation for the generating function
solutions.body:
**Functional equation.** Since $C_n=0$ for $n<0$, $f(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}C_nx^n$. The recurrence says that for $k\ge0$, $C_{k+1}=\sum_{i=0}^kC_iC_{k-i}$, which is the coefficient of $x^k$ in $f(x)^2$. Hence
$$f(x)^2=\sum_{k\ge0}C_{k+1}x^k=\frac{f(x)-C_0}{x}=\frac{f(x)-1}{x},\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad xf(x)^2-f(x)+1=0 .$$
(The coefficients satisfy $C_n\le 4^n$ by induction, so all series converge for $|x|<\tfrac14$.)

**Solve.** $f(x)=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt{1-4x}}{2x}$. With the plus sign, $f(x)\sim 1/x$ as $x\to0$, which is not a power series; with the minus sign, $\sqrt{1-4x}=1-2x+O(x^2)$ gives $f(0)=1$. So
$$f(x)=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4x}}{2x}.$$

**Coefficients.** By the binomial series, $\sqrt{1-4x}=\sum_{k\ge0}\binom{1/2}{k}(-4x)^k$, so
$$f(x)=-\frac1{2x}\sum_{k\ge1}\binom{1/2}{k}(-4)^kx^k\quad\Longrightarrow\quad C_n=-\frac12\binom{1/2}{n+1}(-4)^{n+1}.$$
Now
$$\binom{1/2}{n+1}=\frac{\frac12\left(-\frac12\right)\left(-\frac32\right)\cdots\left(\frac12-n\right)}{(n+1)!}=\frac{(-1)^n\,1\cdot3\cdot5\cdots(2n-1)}{2^{n+1}(n+1)!},$$
so
$$C_n=-\frac12\cdot\frac{(-1)^n(2n-1)!!}{2^{n+1}(n+1)!}\cdot(-1)^{n+1}4^{n+1}=\frac{2^n\,(2n-1)!!}{(n+1)!}.$$
Using $(2n-1)!!=\dfrac{(2n)!}{2^n n!}$,
$$C_n=\frac{(2n)!}{n!\,(n+1)!}=\frac1{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}.$$
Check: $C_0,\dots,C_4=1,1,2,5,14$. ∎

prompt:
Evaluate the integral
$$I=\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{d\theta}{5-4\cos\theta}.$$
(Hint: Use the substitution $z=e^{i\theta}$.)

solutions.title: Residues on the unit circle
solutions.body:
Put $z=e^{i\theta}$, so $d\theta=\frac{dz}{iz}$ and $\cos\theta=\frac12\left(z+\frac1z\right)$. Then
$$5-4\cos\theta=\frac{5z-2z^2-2}{z}=-\frac{(2z-1)(z-2)}{z},\qquad I=\oint_{|z|=1}\frac{dz}{i\,(-2z^2+5z-2)}=\oint_{|z|=1}\frac{i\,dz}{(2z-1)(z-2)} .$$
The poles are $z=\frac12$ (inside the unit circle) and $z=2$ (outside). The residue at $z=\frac12$ is
$$\frac{i}{2\,(\frac12-2)}=-\frac{i}{3}.$$
By the residue theorem, $I=2\pi i\cdot\left(-\frac i3\right)=\frac{2\pi}3$.

**Answer:** $I=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.

solutions.title: Poisson kernel / geometric series
solutions.body:
For $0<r<1$ the geometric series give
$$\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}r^{|n|}e^{in\theta}=\frac{1-r^2}{1-2r\cos\theta+r^2}.$$
With $r=\frac12$: $\dfrac{3/4}{5/4-\cos\theta}=\dfrac{3}{5-4\cos\theta}$. So $\dfrac1{5-4\cos\theta}=\dfrac13\sum_{n}2^{-|n|}e^{in\theta}$, uniformly convergent. Integrating term by term, only $n=0$ survives: $I=\frac13\cdot2\pi=\frac{2\pi}{3}$. (This matches the general formula $\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{d\theta}{a-b\cos\theta}=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{a^2-b^2}}$ for $a>|b|$.)

prompt:
Let $f$ be analytic on the disk $D=\{z:|z|<1\}$ and suppose that $|f(z)|\le1$ for all $z\in D$, and that $f(0)=0$.

1. Show that $|f'(0)|\le1$.
2. Find all functions $f$ for which equality holds.
answer: Schwarz lemma: $g(z)=f(z)/z$ extends analytically with $|g|\le1$, so $|f'(0)|=|g(0)|\le1$; equality holds exactly for the rotations $f(z)=e^{i\theta}z$.

solutions.title: Schwarz lemma
solutions.body:
**1.** Since $f(0)=0$, the function
$$g(z)=\begin{cases}f(z)/z,&z\ne0,\\ f'(0),&z=0\end{cases}$$
is analytic on $D$ (the singularity at $0$ is removable: $f(z)=\sum_{k\ge1}a_kz^k$, so $g(z)=\sum_{k\ge1}a_kz^{k-1}$). Fix $0<r<1$. On $|z|=r$ we have $|g(z)|\le 1/r$, so by the maximum modulus principle $|g(z)|\le1/r$ for $|z|\le r$. Fixing $z$ and letting $r\to1^-$ gives $|g(z)|\le1$ on all of $D$. In particular $|f'(0)|=|g(0)|\le1$.

**2.** If $|f'(0)|=1$, then $|g|$ attains its maximum $1$ at the interior point $0$, so by the maximum modulus principle $g$ is constant, $g\equiv c$ with $|c|=1$. Thus $f(z)=cz=e^{i\theta}z$. Conversely every rotation $f(z)=e^{i\theta}z$ maps $D$ into $D$, fixes $0$, and has $|f'(0)|=1$.

**Answer:** $|f'(0)|\le1$, with equality exactly for $f(z)=e^{i\theta}z$, $\theta\in\mathbb R$. ∎

prompt: Let $M=(m_{i,j})$, $0\le i,j<n$ be an $n\times n$ complex matrix with $m_{i,j}=m_{i+j}$ for constants $m_i$ satisfying $m_i=m_{n+i}$. Find the eigenvalues of $M$.
answer: With $\omega=e^{2\pi i/n}$ and $\mu_r=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}m_k\omega^{kr}$: $\mu_0=\sum m_k$; if $n$ is even, $\mu_{n/2}=\sum(-1)^km_k$; and $\pm\sqrt{\mu_r\mu_{n-r}}$ for each $1\le r<n/2$.

solutions.title: Fourier vectors
solutions.body:
Let $\omega=e^{2\pi i/n}$, let $v_r=(1,\omega^r,\omega^{2r},\dots,\omega^{(n-1)r})^\top$ for $r\in\mathbb Z/n$, and put $\mu_r=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}m_k\omega^{kr}$. Indices of $m$ are taken mod $n$, as the periodicity $m_i=m_{n+i}$ allows.

**$M$ swaps $v_r$ and $v_{-r}$.** Substituting $k=i+j$ (mod $n$),
$$(Mv_r)_i=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}m_{i+j}\omega^{jr}=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}m_k\omega^{(k-i)r}=\mu_r\,\omega^{-ir}=\mu_r\,(v_{n-r})_i ,$$
so $Mv_r=\mu_r v_{n-r}$.

**Block decomposition.** The vectors $v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}$ form a basis of $\mathbb C^n$ (they are the columns of the invertible Vandermonde/DFT matrix). Group them as follows:

- $r=0$: $Mv_0=\mu_0v_0$, eigenvalue $\mu_0=\sum_k m_k$.
- $r=n/2$ (only if $n$ is even): $v_{n/2}=v_{n-n/2}$, so $Mv_{n/2}=\mu_{n/2}v_{n/2}$, eigenvalue $\mu_{n/2}=\sum_k(-1)^km_k$.
- $1\le r<n/2$: the plane $\operatorname{span}\{v_r,v_{n-r}\}$ is $M$-invariant, and in the basis $(v_r,v_{n-r})$, $M$ acts by $\begin{pmatrix}0&\mu_{n-r}\\ \mu_r&0\end{pmatrix}$, whose characteristic polynomial is $\lambda^2-\mu_r\mu_{n-r}$.

Since $\mathbb C^n$ is the direct sum of these invariant subspaces, the characteristic polynomial of $M$ is the product of theirs:
$$\det(\lambda I-M)=(\lambda-\mu_0)\,(\lambda-\mu_{n/2})^{[n\text{ even}]}\prod_{1\le r<n/2}\bigl(\lambda^2-\mu_r\mu_{n-r}\bigr).$$

**Answer:** the eigenvalues (with multiplicity) are $\sum_km_k$; $\sum_k(-1)^km_k$ if $n$ is even; and $\pm\sqrt{\mu_r\mu_{n-r}}$ for $r=1,\dots,\lfloor\frac{n-1}2\rfloor$, where $\mu_r=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}m_k\omega^{kr}$.

solutions.title: Relation to circulant matrices
solutions.body: Let $P$ be the permutation matrix with $(Pv)_i=v_{-i}$ (indices mod $n$). Then $C=MP$ has entries $C_{i,j}=m_{i-j}$, a circulant matrix, whose eigenvectors are the $v_r$ with eigenvalues $\sum_k m_k\omega^{-kr}=\mu_{-r}$. Since $P^2=I$ and $Pv_r=v_{-r}$, we recover $Mv_r=CPv_r=Cv_{-r}=\mu_rv_{-r}$, the same $2\times2$ block structure as above. (A quick numerical check with random $m_k$ and $n=6$ confirms the eigenvalues $\mu_0,\ \mu_3,\ \pm\sqrt{\mu_1\mu_5},\ \pm\sqrt{\mu_2\mu_4}$.)

prompt:
For complex square matrices $A_i$, put
$$F_n(A_1,\dots,A_n)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sign}(\sigma)A_{\sigma(1)}A_{\sigma(2)}\cdots A_{\sigma(n)}.$$
The sum is over the symmetric group $S_n$, and $\operatorname{sign}(\sigma)$ is $1$ or $-1$ if $\sigma$ is an even or odd permutation.

Show that $F_n$ vanishes if all its arguments are $m\times m$ matrices and $n>m^2$. (Hint: first show $F_n$ vanishes if two arguments are equal.)
answer: $F_n$ is multilinear and alternating (it vanishes when two arguments are equal), hence vanishes on linearly dependent arguments; any $n>m^2=\dim M_m(\mathbb C)$ matrices are linearly dependent.

solutions.title: Multilinear and alternating
solutions.body:
**$F_n$ is multilinear.** Each term $A_{\sigma(1)}\cdots A_{\sigma(n)}$ contains every argument exactly once as a factor, so it is linear in each $A_k$ separately; hence so is $F_n$.

**$F_n$ vanishes when two arguments coincide.** Suppose $A_k=A_l$ with $k\ne l$, and let $\tau=(k\ l)$. For each $\sigma$, the permutation $\tau\sigma$ satisfies $A_{\tau\sigma(i)}=A_{\sigma(i)}$ for all $i$ (as $\tau$ only swaps the indices $k,l$ of two equal matrices), so the terms for $\sigma$ and $\tau\sigma$ have the same product and opposite signs. Since $\sigma\mapsto\tau\sigma$ is an involution of $S_n$ without fixed points, the terms cancel in pairs and $F_n(A_1,\dots,A_n)=0$.

**$F_n$ vanishes on linearly dependent arguments.** If, say, $A_j=\sum_{i\ne j}c_iA_i$, then by multilinearity in the $j$th slot
$$F_n(A_1,\dots,A_n)=\sum_{i\ne j}c_i\,F_n(A_1,\dots,\underbrace{A_i}_{\text{slot }j},\dots,A_n),$$
and each term has $A_i$ in two slots, so it is $0$.

**Conclusion.** The space of complex $m\times m$ matrices has dimension $m^2$, so if $n>m^2$, any $A_1,\dots,A_n$ are linearly dependent and $F_n(A_1,\dots,A_n)=0$. ∎

(Remark from the official solution: in fact $F_{2m}$ already vanishes on $m\times m$ matrices — the Amitsur–Levitzki theorem — but that is much harder.)

prompt:
1. Let $G$ be a finite group and $\phi: G\to GL_n(\mathbb C)$ a group homomorphism. Show that $\ker(\phi)=\{g\in G \mid \operatorname{tr}(\phi(g))=n\}$.
2. Show that this fails for infinite $G$.
answer: $\phi(g)$ has finite order, so it is diagonalizable with root-of-unity eigenvalues; $n$ numbers of modulus $1$ summing to $n$ all equal $1$, so $\phi(g)=I$. For $G=\mathbb Z$, $k\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}1&k\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ has trace $2$ everywhere but trivial kernel.

solutions.title: Diagonalize elements of finite order
solutions.body:
**1.** If $g\in\ker\phi$ then $\phi(g)=I_n$ has trace $n$. Conversely suppose $\operatorname{tr}\phi(g)=n$. Since $G$ is finite, $g^k=e$ for some $k\ge1$, so $X=\phi(g)$ satisfies $X^k=I$. The polynomial $x^k-1$ has $k$ distinct roots in $\mathbb C$, so the minimal polynomial of $X$ has distinct roots and $X$ is diagonalizable, $X=P\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)P^{-1}$, with $\lambda_i^k=1$, hence $|\lambda_i|=1$. Now
$$n=|\operatorname{tr}X|=|\lambda_1+\dots+\lambda_n|\le|\lambda_1|+\dots+|\lambda_n|=n,$$
and $\operatorname{Re}\lambda_i\le1$ with $\sum_i\operatorname{Re}\lambda_i=n$ forces $\operatorname{Re}\lambda_i=1$, i.e. $\lambda_i=1$ for all $i$. So $X=PIP^{-1}=I$ and $g\in\ker\phi$. Therefore $\ker\phi=\{g:\operatorname{tr}\phi(g)=n\}$.

**2.** Let $G=\mathbb Z$ and $\phi:\mathbb Z\to GL_2(\mathbb C)$, $\phi(k)=\begin{pmatrix}1&k\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$. This is a homomorphism ($\phi(k)\phi(l)=\phi(k+l)$), every $\phi(k)$ has trace $2$, but $\ker\phi=\{0\}\ne\mathbb Z$. ∎

solutions.title: Unitary trick
solutions.body: Averaging any Hermitian inner product over the finite group, $\langle x,y\rangle'=\frac1{|G|}\sum_{h\in G}\langle\phi(h)x,\phi(h)y\rangle$, gives a Hermitian inner product for which every $\phi(g)$ is unitary. Unitary matrices are diagonalizable (spectral theorem) with eigenvalues of modulus $1$, and as above $\operatorname{tr}\phi(g)=n$ forces all eigenvalues to be $1$, hence $\phi(g)=I$. The example in part 2 shows what goes wrong for infinite groups: $\phi(k)$ is unipotent but not diagonalizable.

prompt: Prove that if all elements of a group satisfy $g^2=1$ then the group is abelian. Give an example of a group such that $g^3=1$ for all elements but the group is not abelian.
answer: Every element is its own inverse, so $ab=(ab)^{-1}=b^{-1}a^{-1}=ba$. Example: the Heisenberg group of upper unitriangular $3\times3$ matrices over $\mathbb F_3$ (order 27).

solutions.title: Inverses, then the Heisenberg group
solutions.body:
**Exponent 2 implies abelian.** If $g^2=1$ for all $g$, then $g^{-1}=g$ for all $g$. For $a,b\in G$,
$$ab=(ab)^{-1}=b^{-1}a^{-1}=ba .$$
So $G$ is abelian.

**A non-abelian group of exponent 3.** Let
$$G=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}1&a&c\\0&1&b\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}: a,b,c\in\mathbb F_3\right\},$$
a group of order $27$ under matrix multiplication (products and inverses of upper unitriangular matrices are upper unitriangular).

- *Every element has $X^3=I$.* Write $X=I+N$ with $N$ strictly upper triangular, so $N^3=0$. Since $I$ and $N$ commute, $(I+N)^3=I+3N+3N^2+N^3=I$, because $3=0$ in $\mathbb F_3$.
- *$G$ is not abelian.* For $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$, $B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&1\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$:
$$AB=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1\\0&1&1\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}\ne\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\0&1&1\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}=BA .$$

So $G$ is a non-abelian group in which $g^3=1$ for every element. ∎

prompt: Let $p$ and $q$ be distinct primes and suppose $G$ is a finite group having precisely $p+1$ Sylow $p$-subgroups and $q+1$ Sylow $q$-subgroups. Prove that there exist $P \in \mathrm{Syl}_p(G)$ and $Q \in \mathrm{Syl}_q(G)$ such that the subgroup of $G$ generated by $P$ and $Q$ is $PQ = P \times Q$.
answer: With $p<q$: $q\nmid p+1=|G:N_G(P)|$ (unless $\{p,q\}=\{2,3\}$), so $N_G(P)$ contains a Sylow $q$-subgroup $Q$; in $H=PQ$ the number of Sylow $q$-subgroups is $1$ or $q+1$ and divides $|P|$, and $q+1=p^b$ is impossible for odd $p$, so $Q\trianglelefteq H$ and $H=P\times Q$. The statement fails when $p=2$ and $q=2^b-1$ is a Mersenne prime (e.g. $\mathrm{Sym}_4$).

solutions.title: Normalizers and counting Sylow subgroups
solutions.body:
Without loss of generality $p<q$. Fix $P\in\mathrm{Syl}_p(G)$ and put $N=N_G(P)$, so $|G:N|=p+1$.

**Step 1: $N$ contains a Sylow $q$-subgroup.** If $q\mid p+1$ then $q\le p+1$, and $q>p$ forces $q=p+1$, i.e. $\{p,q\}=\{2,3\}$. Excluding this case, $q\nmid |G:N|$, so the full power of $q$ dividing $|G|$ divides $|N|$, and $N$ contains some $Q\in\mathrm{Syl}_q(G)$.

**Step 2: the subgroup $H=PQ$.** Since $P\trianglelefteq N$ and $Q\le N$, $H=PQ$ is a subgroup with $P\trianglelefteq H$, $P\cap Q=1$ and $|H|=|P||Q|$. The Sylow $q$-subgroups of $H$ are Sylow $q$-subgroups of $G$ (same order), so $n_q(H)\le q+1$; by Sylow, $n_q(H)\equiv 1\pmod q$, hence $n_q(H)\in\{1,q+1\}$. Also $n_q(H)$ divides $|H:Q|=|P|$, a power of $p$.

**Step 3.** If $n_q(H)=q+1$ then $q+1=p^b$. When $p$ is odd this is impossible: $q>p\ge 3$ is odd, so $q+1$ is even while $p^b$ is odd. Hence (for $p$ odd, or more generally whenever $q+1$ is not a power of $p$) $n_q(H)=1$ and $Q\trianglelefteq H$.

Now $P,Q\trianglelefteq H$ with $P\cap Q=1$, so $[P,Q]\subseteq P\cap Q=1$; thus $P$ and $Q$ commute elementwise and $\langle P,Q\rangle=PQ=P\times Q$.

**The exceptional cases.** The argument breaks down exactly when $p=2$ and $q=2^b-1$ is a (Mersenne) prime, and there the statement is actually false. For $q=3$ take $G=\mathrm{Sym}_4$: it has $3$ Sylow $2$-subgroups (dihedral of order 8) and $4$ Sylow $3$-subgroups, but no $3$-cycle centralizes a Sylow $2$-subgroup (each contains the Klein four-group $V$, on which a $3$-cycle acts nontrivially). In general $G=\mathrm{AGL}(1,2^b)\times\mathrm{Sym}_3$ has $1\cdot 3=3$ Sylow $2$-subgroups and $2^b=q+1$ Sylow $q$-subgroups, while every Sylow $2$-subgroup contains the translation group, on which a Sylow $q$-subgroup acts fixed-point-freely. (The official solution simply assumes $\{p,q\}\ne\{2,3\}$; the case $p=2$, $q=7,31,\dots$ is overlooked there.) So the result holds precisely when the smaller prime is odd or $q+1$ is not a power of $2$. ∎

reviewNote: As stated the problem is false for p=2 and q a Mersenne prime (S_4 for q=3, AGL(1,8)xS_3 for q=7, checked by computer); the official solution only excludes {p,q}={2,3}. Solution proves the corrected statement.

prompt: Let $F \subseteq E$ be an algebraic extension of fields. We say that an element $\alpha$ of $E$ is *abelian* if $F[\alpha]$ is a Galois extension of $F$ with abelian Galois group $\mathrm{Gal}(F[\alpha]/F)$. Prove that the set of abelian elements of $E$ is a subfield of $E$ containing $F$.
answer: If $\alpha,\beta$ are abelian, $F[\alpha,\beta]$ is the compositum of two Galois extensions, hence Galois, and $\mathrm{Gal}(F[\alpha,\beta]/F)$ embeds in $\mathrm{Gal}(F[\alpha]/F)\times\mathrm{Gal}(F[\beta]/F)$, so it is abelian; every intermediate field of an abelian extension is Galois with abelian group, so $\alpha\pm\beta,\alpha\beta,\alpha^{-1}$ are abelian.

solutions.title: Compositum of abelian extensions
solutions.body:
Let $A$ be the set of abelian elements. Every $c\in F$ lies in $A$ since $F[c]=F$ is Galois with trivial group.

Let $\alpha,\beta\in A$. As finite Galois extensions, $F[\alpha]$ and $F[\beta]$ are splitting fields over $F$ of separable polynomials $f,g\in F[x]$. Then $L=F[\alpha,\beta]$ is generated by the roots of $fg$, i.e. it is a splitting field of the separable polynomial $\mathrm{lcm}(f,g)$, so $L/F$ is finite Galois. Let $G=\mathrm{Gal}(L/F)$.

Since $F[\alpha]/F$ and $F[\beta]/F$ are normal, every $\sigma\in G$ maps $F[\alpha]$ and $F[\beta]$ to themselves, giving a homomorphism
$$G\to \mathrm{Gal}(F[\alpha]/F)\times \mathrm{Gal}(F[\beta]/F),\qquad \sigma\mapsto(\sigma|_{F[\alpha]},\sigma|_{F[\beta]}).$$
It is injective: if $\sigma$ fixes $\alpha$ and $\beta$, it fixes $L=F[\alpha,\beta]$. The target is abelian, so $G$ is abelian.

Now let $\gamma\in L$. By the Galois correspondence $F[\gamma]=L^H$ for a subgroup $H\le G$. Since $G$ is abelian, $H\trianglelefteq G$, so $F[\gamma]/F$ is Galois with group $G/H$, which is abelian. Thus $\gamma\in A$.

Applying this to $\gamma=\alpha+\beta,\ \alpha-\beta,\ \alpha\beta$ and (for $\alpha\ne0$) $\alpha^{-1}\in F[\alpha]$ shows that $A$ is closed under the field operations. Hence $A$ is a subfield of $E$ containing $F$. ∎

prompt:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over a field $K$ and let $(\ ,\ )$ be a bilinear form on $V$. Suppose $T\colon V \to V$ is a linear transformation satisfying $(v, Tw) = (Tv, w)$ for all $v, w \in V$. Write $N = \ker(T) = \{ v \in V \mid Tv = 0 \}$.

(i) Assume that the form restricted to $N$ is nondegenerate – that is, if $v \in N$ and $(v, N) = 0$, then $v = 0$. If $T$ is nilpotent, prove that $T = 0$.

(ii) Find a 2-dimensional example with $T$ a nonzero nilpotent transformation and with the form $(\ ,\ )$ nondegenerate on the whole vector space $V$.
answer: (i) If $T^kv=0$ with $k\ge2$ minimal, then $w=T^{k-1}v\in N$ and $(w,n)=(T^{k-2}v,Tn)=0$ for $n\in N$, so $w=0$, a contradiction. (ii) $V=K^2$, $Te_1=e_2$, $Te_2=0$, with $(e_1,e_2)=(e_2,e_1)=1$, $(e_1,e_1)=(e_2,e_2)=0$.

solutions.title: Push vectors into the kernel

prompt:
Let $R$ be a ring with $1$ and let $M$ be a right $R$-module. Suppose
$$0 = M_0 \subset M_1 \subset \cdots \subset M_n = M$$
is a chain of submodules such that, for $i = 1, 2, \ldots, n$, the factors $M_i/M_{i-1}$ are simple and pairwise nonisomorphic. If $X$ and $Y$ are isomorphic submodules of $M$, prove that $X = Y$.
answer: Refine $0\subseteq X\subseteq X+Y\subseteq M$ to a composition series. The factors between $X$ and $X+Y$ are those of $(X+Y)/X\cong Y/(X\cap Y)$, hence factors of $Y\cong X$; by Jordan–Hölder $M$ would have a repeated factor unless $X+Y=X$. Symmetrically $X+Y=Y$.

solutions.title: Jordan–Hölder
solutions.body:
$M$ has a composition series with $n$ pairwise nonisomorphic factors, so by the Jordan–Hölder theorem every composition series of $M$ has exactly these factors, each occurring once.

Every submodule of $M$ has finite length, so the chain $0\subseteq X\subseteq X+Y\subseteq M$ can be refined to a composition series of $M$. Its factors are: the composition factors of $X$, then those of $(X+Y)/X$, then those of $M/(X+Y)$.

By the second isomorphism theorem $(X+Y)/X\cong Y/(X\cap Y)$. A composition series of $Y$ through $X\cap Y$ shows that every composition factor of $Y/(X\cap Y)$ is a composition factor of $Y$, hence (as $Y\cong X$) of $X$.

Suppose $X+Y\ne X$. Then $(X+Y)/X$ has some composition factor $S$, and $S$ is also a composition factor of $X$. Thus $S$ occurs at least twice in our composition series of $M$ (once below $X$, once between $X$ and $X+Y$), contradicting the fact that the factors of $M$ are pairwise nonisomorphic. Hence $X+Y=X$, i.e. $Y\subseteq X$. By symmetry $X\subseteq Y$, so $X=Y$. ∎

prompt: Let $G$ be a finite group having exactly $n$ Sylow $p$-subgroups for some prime $p$. Show that there exists a subgroup $H$ of the symmetric group $\mathrm{Sym}_n$ such that $H$ also has exactly $n$ Sylow $p$-subgroups.
answer: Let $G$ act on its $n$ Sylow $p$-subgroups by conjugation, with kernel $K\subseteq N=N_G(P)$, and take $H=G/K\le\mathrm{Sym}_n$. By the Frattini argument $N_G(PK)=N$, so $\bar G$ has $|G:N|=n$ Sylow $p$-subgroups.

solutions.title: Permutation representation and the Frattini argument
solutions.body:
Let $P\in\mathrm{Syl}_p(G)$ and $N=N_G(P)$, so $|G:N|=n$. The conjugation action of $G$ on the $n$-element set $\mathrm{Syl}_p(G)$ (equivalently, the action on the cosets of $N$) gives a homomorphism $\pi\colon G\to\mathrm{Sym}_n$ whose kernel $K=\bigcap_g N^g$ is contained in $N$. Put $H=\pi(G)\cong G/K$, a subgroup of $\mathrm{Sym}_n$. Write $\bar X=XK/K$.

$\bar P=PK/K$ is a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $\bar G$ (its index $|G:PK|$ divides $|G:P|$, which is prime to $p$). The number of Sylow $p$-subgroups of $\bar G$ is $|\bar G:N_{\bar G}(\bar P)|$. By the correspondence theorem $N_{\bar G}(\bar P)=\bar M$ where $M=N_G(PK)$, and $|\bar G:\bar M|=|G:M|$ since $K\subseteq M$.

We claim $M=N$. Since $K\trianglelefteq G$ and $P\le N$, $N$ normalizes $PK$, so $N\subseteq M$. Conversely $PK\trianglelefteq M$ and $P$ is a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $PK$, so the Frattini argument gives $M=N_M(P)\,PK\subseteq N\cdot PK=N$ (as $P,K\subseteq N$).

Therefore $H=\bar G\le\mathrm{Sym}_n$ has exactly $|G:N|=n$ Sylow $p$-subgroups. ∎

prompt:
Let $R$ be a commutative integral domain and let $R[x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n]$ be the polynomial ring over $R$ in the $n$ variables $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$. If $a = (a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n)$ is an $n$-tuple of elements of $R$, then there is an evaluation homomorphism $\phi_a\colon R[x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n] \to R$ given by $\phi_a(f) = f(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n)$.

(a) If $R$ is the field of complex numbers and if $I$ is a proper ideal of $R[x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n]$, show that there exists an $n$-tuple $a = (a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n)$ with $\phi_a(I) \neq R$.

(b) Now let $R$ be the ring of integers and let $I$ be the ideal of the polynomial ring $R[x]$ in one variable generated by $3$ and $x^2 + 1$. Show that $I$ is a proper ideal of $R[x]$ but that $\phi_a(I) = R$ for all 1-tuples $a = (a)$ with $a \in R$.
answer: (a) Nullstellensatz: a maximal ideal $M\supseteq I$ has $\mathbb C[x]/M=\mathbb C$, so $M=\ker\phi_a$ and $\phi_a(I)=0$. (b) $\mathbb Z[x]/I\cong\mathbb F_3[x]/(x^2+1)=\mathbb F_9\ne0$, but $\phi_a(I)\supseteq 3\mathbb Z$ and $a^2+1\not\equiv0\pmod 3$, so $\phi_a(I)=\mathbb Z$.

solutions.title: Nullstellensatz and reduction mod 3
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $S=\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ and let $M$ be a maximal ideal of $S$ containing the proper ideal $I$. Then $S/M$ is a field which is finitely generated as a $\mathbb C$-algebra, so by Zariski's lemma (the weak Nullstellensatz) it is a finite, hence algebraic, extension of $\mathbb C$; as $\mathbb C$ is algebraically closed, the natural map $\mathbb C\to S/M$ is an isomorphism. Let $a_i\in\mathbb C$ correspond to $x_i+M$. The composite $\phi\colon S\to S/M\cong\mathbb C$ is a $\mathbb C$-algebra homomorphism with $\phi(x_i)=a_i$, so $\phi=\phi_a$. Thus $\ker\phi_a=M\supseteq I$, and $\phi_a(I)=0\ne\mathbb C$.

**(b)** Reduction mod $3$ followed by the quotient map gives a surjective ring homomorphism
$$\mathbb Z[x]\to\mathbb F_3[x]\to\mathbb F_3[x]/(x^2+1)$$
whose kernel contains $3$ and $x^2+1$, hence $I$. The target is nonzero (in fact $x^2+1$ has no root in $\mathbb F_3$, so it is the field $\mathbb F_9$), so $I\ne\mathbb Z[x]$.

Now fix $a\in\mathbb Z$. Since $\phi_a$ is surjective, $\phi_a(I)$ is an ideal of $\mathbb Z$; it contains $\phi_a(3)=3$ and $\phi_a(x^2+1)=a^2+1$. Squares mod $3$ are $0$ and $1$, so $a^2+1\equiv1$ or $2\pmod 3$ and $3\nmid a^2+1$. The ideal $\phi_a(I)\supseteq 3\mathbb Z$ is therefore $3\mathbb Z$ or $\mathbb Z$, and it is not $3\mathbb Z$; hence $\phi_a(I)=\mathbb Z$. ∎

prompt:
Let $F \subseteq E$ be an extension of fields of characteristic $\neq 2$ and assume that the degree $|E : F| = 4$.

(a) Show that $E = F[\alpha]$ for some $\alpha$.

(b) If $E = F[\alpha]$, where $\alpha$ is a root of a polynomial of the form $x^4 + ax^2 + b \in F[x]$, prove that there exists an intermediate field properly between $E$ and $F$.

(c) Now let $E = F[\beta]$ with no assumption on $\beta$ and let $L \supseteq E$ be a splitting field for the minimal polynomial of $\beta$ over F. If $\mathrm{Gal}(L/F)$ is isomorphic to the symmetric group $\mathrm{Sym}_4$, show that there is no intermediate field properly between $E$ and $F$.
answer: (a) Minimal polynomials have degree $1,2,4$, nonzero derivative in characteristic $\ne2$, so $E/F$ is separable; use the primitive element theorem. (b) $F[\alpha^2]$ has degree $2$. (c) $E$ is the fixed field of a subgroup $H$ of order $6$ in $\mathrm{Sym}_4$, which is maximal (the only subgroup of order 12 is $\mathrm{Alt}_4$, which has no subgroup of order 6).

solutions.title: Separability, degrees and the Galois correspondence
solutions.body:
**(a)** For $\gamma\in E$, the minimal polynomial $m_\gamma$ of $\gamma$ over $F$ has degree $d\mid 4$, so $d\in\{1,2,4\}$. Its derivative has leading coefficient $d\cdot1\ne0$ because $\mathrm{char}F\ne2$, so $\gcd(m_\gamma,m_\gamma')=1$ ($m_\gamma$ is irreducible and $m_\gamma'\ne0$ has smaller degree). Hence every element is separable, $E/F$ is a finite separable extension, and the primitive element theorem gives $E=F[\alpha]$.

**(b)** $\alpha^2$ is a root of $y^2+ay+b\in F[y]$, so $|F[\alpha^2]:F|\le2$; and $\alpha$ is a root of $x^2-\alpha^2\in F[\alpha^2][x]$, so $|F[\alpha]:F[\alpha^2]|\le2$. Since the product of these degrees is $|E:F|=4$, both equal $2$, and $F[\alpha^2]$ lies properly between $F$ and $E$.

**(c)** Let $m$ be the minimal polynomial of $\beta$, of degree $4$. Since the extension is separable (by (a)), $L/F$ is Galois, and $|L:F|=|\mathrm{Gal}(L/F)|=24$. By the Galois correspondence, $E=L^H$ for a subgroup $H\le G=\mathrm{Gal}(L/F)\cong\mathrm{Sym}_4$ with $|G:H|=|E:F|=4$, i.e. $|H|=6$, and intermediate fields $F\subsetneq K\subsetneq E$ correspond to subgroups $H\subsetneq J\subsetneq G$.

Such a $J$ would have order $12$ (a proper multiple of $6$ dividing $24$). The only subgroup of order $12$ in $\mathrm{Sym}_4$ is $\mathrm{Alt}_4$ (a subgroup of index 2 contains all squares, in particular all $3$-cycles, which generate $\mathrm{Alt}_4$). But $\mathrm{Alt}_4$ has no subgroup of order $6$: such a subgroup would have index $2$, hence be normal and contain the squares of all elements, i.e. all eight $3$-cycles — too many for a group of order 6. So no $J$ exists and $H$ is maximal; there is no field properly between $F$ and $E$. ∎

prompt: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field of prime characteristic $p$ and let $V$ be an $F$-vector space of dimension precisely $p$. Suppose $A$ and $B$ are linear operators on $V$ such that $AB - BA = B$. If $B$ is nonsingular, prove that $V$ has a basis $\{ v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_p \}$ of eigenvectors of $A$ such that $Bv_i = v_{i+1}$ for $1 \le i \le p - 1$ and $Bv_p = \lambda v_1$ for some $0 \neq \lambda \in F$.
answer: If $Av=\mu v$ then $A(Bv)=(\mu+1)Bv$; so $v_i=B^{i-1}v$ are eigenvectors with the $p$ distinct eigenvalues $\mu,\mu+1,\dots,\mu+p-1$, hence a basis, and $Bv_p$ is an eigenvector for $\mu+p=\mu$, so $Bv_p=\lambda v_1$.

solutions.title: B shifts eigenvalues by 1
solutions.body:
Since $F$ is algebraically closed, $A$ has an eigenvector $v
e0$, $Av=\mu v$. From $AB=BA+B$,
$$A(Bw)=B(Aw)+Bw .$$
So if $Aw=
u w$ with $w
e0$, then $A(Bw)=(
u+1)Bw$, and $Bw
e0$ since $B$ is nonsingular: $Bw$ is an eigenvector of $A$ with eigenvalue $
u+1$.

Set $v_i=B^{i-1}v$ for $i=1,\dots,p$. By induction $v_i$ is an eigenvector of $A$ with eigenvalue $\mu+i-1$. The elements $\mu,\mu+1,\dots,\mu+p-1$ of $F$ are distinct (they differ by $1,\dots,p-1$, nonzero in characteristic $p$), and eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent. Since $\dim V=p$, $\{v_1,\dots,v_p\}$ is a basis of $V$, and $Bv_i=v_{i+1}$ for $i<p$ by construction.

Finally, $Bv_p$ is a nonzero eigenvector of $A$ with eigenvalue $\mu+p=\mu$. In the eigenbasis $v_1,\dots,v_p$ with distinct eigenvalues, the $\mu$-eigenspace is $Fv_1$, so $Bv_p=\lambda v_1$ with $\lambda
e0$ (as $Bv_p
eq0$). ∎

prompt:
Let $G \neq \langle 1 \rangle$ be a possibly infinite group whose subgroups are linearly ordered by inclusion. In other words, if $H$ and $K$ are subgroups of $G$, then either $H \subseteq K$ or $K \subseteq H$.

(a) Prove that $G$ is an abelian group and that the orders of the elements of $G$ are all powers of the same prime $p$.

(b) If $G_n = \{ g \in G \mid g^{p^n} = 1 \}$, prove that $|G_n| \le p^n$.
answer: (a) Comparable cyclic subgroups give commuting elements; $\langle x^2\rangle,\langle x^3\rangle$ are incomparable if $x$ has infinite order; subgroups of distinct prime orders are incomparable. (b) Every finite subgroup of $G_n$ is cyclic of exponent dividing $p^n$, and $G_n$ is the union of its finite subgroups.

solutions.title: Compare cyclic subgroups
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $x,y\in G$. Then $\langle x\rangle\subseteq\langle y\rangle$ or $\langle y\rangle\subseteq\langle x\rangle$; either way one is a power of the other, so $xy=yx$. Hence $G$ is abelian.

If $x$ had infinite order, then $\langle x^2\rangle$ and $\langle x^3\rangle$ would be incomparable: $x^2\in\langle x^3\rangle$ would mean $x^2=x^{3k}$, i.e. $2=3k$, and $x^3\in\langle x^2\rangle$ would mean $3=2k$. So every element has finite order.

Since $G\ne1$, some element has order divisible by a prime $p$. If primes $p\ne q$ divide $o(x)$ and $o(y)$ respectively, then $\langle x\rangle$ contains a subgroup $X$ of order $p$ and $\langle y\rangle$ a subgroup $Y$ of order $q$, and neither of $X,Y$ contains the other (orders $p\nmid q$, $q\nmid p$). Thus only one prime $p$ divides element orders, and all orders are powers of $p$.

**(b)** $G_n$ is a subgroup since $G$ is abelian. Let $H\le G_n$ be finite. By the fundamental theorem of finite abelian groups, $H$ is a direct product of cyclic groups; two nontrivial factors $C_1,C_2$ would be incomparable subgroups ($C_1\cap C_2=1$). So $H$ is cyclic, and since $h^{p^n}=1$ for all $h\in H$, $|H|\le p^n$.

Every finitely generated subgroup of the abelian torsion group $G_n$ is finite, so $G_n$ is the union of its finite subgroups. If $|G_n|>p^n$, pick $p^n+1$ distinct elements; they generate a finite subgroup of order $>p^n$, a contradiction. Hence $|G_n|\le p^n$. ∎

prompt: Let $x$ and $y$ be elements of a finite $p$-group $P$ and let $z = [x, y]$ be the commutator $x^{-1}y^{-1}xy$ of $x$ and $y$. Suppose that $x$ lies in every normal subgroup of $P$ which contains $z$. Prove that $x = 1$.
answer: Induction on $|P|$: pass to $P/Z$ with $Z$ a central subgroup of order $p$; by induction $x\in Z$, so $z=[x,y]=1$, and then $x$ lies in the normal subgroup $1$.

solutions.title: Induction modulo a central subgroup
solutions.body:
Induct on $|P|$; the case $|P|=1$ is trivial. Let $|P|>1$. The center of a nontrivial $p$-group is nontrivial, so $P$ has a central subgroup $Z$ of order $p$. Let $\bar P=P/Z$ and write bars for images; then $\bar z=[\bar x,\bar y]$.

The hypothesis passes to $\bar P$: if $\bar M\trianglelefteq\bar P$ contains $\bar z$, its full preimage $M$ is normal in $P$ and contains $z$, so $x\in M$ and $\bar x\in\bar M$. By induction ($|\bar P|<|P|$), $\bar x=1$, i.e. $x\in Z$.

Now $x$ is central, so $z=[x,y]=1$. The trivial subgroup is normal and contains $z$, so by hypothesis $x\in\langle1\rangle$, i.e. $x=1$. ∎

prompt:
Let $K[x]$ be a polynomial ring over the field $K$ and let $R$ be the subring of $K[x]$ consisting of all polynomials whose $x$-coefficient is equal to $0$. Thus a typical element of $R$ has the form
$$a_0 + a_2x^2 + a_3x^3 + \cdots + a_nx^n$$
with $a_i \in K$. Show that the principal ideal $(x^2) = x^2R$ is a primary ideal of $R$ which is not equal to a power of its radical.
answer: $Q=x^2R$ consists of the elements of $R$ with no $x^3$ term and zero constant term; $\sqrt Q=P=x^2R+x^3R$ (constant term $0$). $P\supsetneq Q\supsetneq P^2$ (since $x^3\in P\setminus Q$, $x^2\in Q\setminus P^2$), and a direct computation with constant terms shows $Q$ is primary.

solutions.title: Explicit description of the ideals
solutions.body:
Note $R=K\oplus x^2K[x]$ and
$$Q=x^2R=\{a_2x^2+a_4x^4+a_5x^5+\cdots\}$$
(elements of $R$ with zero constant term and zero $x^3$-coefficient), since $x^2(c_0+c_2x^2+c_3x^3+\cdots)=c_0x^2+c_2x^4+c_3x^5+\cdots$. Let
$$P=\{f\in R: f(0)=0\}=\{a_2x^2+a_3x^3+\cdots\}.$$
$P$ is the kernel of $R\to K$, $f\mapsto f(0)$, so it is a maximal ideal.

**$\sqrt Q=P$.** If $f\in R$ and $f^k\in Q$, then $f(0)^k=0$, so $f\in P$. Conversely if $f\in P$ then $f^2\in x^4K[x]\subseteq Q$. So $\sqrt Q=P$.

**$Q$ is primary.** Let $g,h\in R$ with $gh\in Q$ and $g\notin P$, i.e. $c_0=g(0)\ne0$. Write $g=c_0+c_2x^2+c_3x^3+\cdots$, $h=d_0+d_2x^2+d_3x^3+\cdots$. Then
$$gh=c_0d_0+(c_0d_2+c_2d_0)x^2+(c_0d_3+c_3d_0)x^3+\cdots .$$
$gh\in Q$ gives $c_0d_0=0$, so $d_0=0$, and then $c_0d_3=0$, so $d_3=0$. Thus $h\in Q$. Hence whenever $gh\in Q$, either $h\in Q$ or $g\in P=\sqrt Q$: $Q$ is primary (with radical $P$).

**$Q$ is not a power of $P$.** $P^1=P\ne Q$ since $x^3\in P\setminus Q$. Every product of two elements of $P$ lies in $x^4K[x]$, so $P^n\subseteq P^2\subseteq x^4K[x]$ for $n\ge2$, while $x^2\in Q\setminus x^4K[x]$. So $Q\neq P^n$ for all $n\ge1$ (and $Q\ne P^0=R$). ∎

prompt:
Let $E$ be a finite degree field extension of the rationals $\mathbb{Q}$ and suppose that $f(x)$ is a monic irreducible polynomial in $E[x]$.

(i) Show that there exists a unique monic irreducible polynomial $g(x) \in \mathbb{Q}[x]$ such that $f(x)$ divides $g(x)$ in $E[x]$.

(ii) Let $g(x)$ be as above. If $E$ is a splitting field over $\mathbb{Q}$ for some polynomial in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$, show that the degree of $f(x)$ divides the degree of $g(x)$.

(iii) Give an example to show that the degree of $f(x)$ need not divide the degree of $g(x)$ in general.
answer: (i) $g$ is the minimal polynomial over $\mathbb Q$ of a root $\alpha$ of $f$. (ii) If $E/\mathbb Q$ is Galois, $g$ is the product of the distinct $\mathrm{Gal}(E/\mathbb Q)$-conjugates of $f$, all of degree $\deg f$. (iii) $E=\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]2)$, $f$ the minimal polynomial of $\omega\sqrt[3]2$ over $E$ (degree 2), $g=x^3-2$.

solutions.title: Minimal polynomials and Galois conjugates
solutions.body:
**(i)** Let $\alpha$ be a root of $f$ in an extension of $E$. Then $|E[\alpha]:\mathbb Q|=|E[\alpha]:E|\,|E:\mathbb Q|<\infty$, so $\alpha$ is algebraic over $\mathbb Q$; let $g$ be its minimal polynomial over $\mathbb Q$. Since $f$ is the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $E$ and $g(\alpha)=0$, $f\mid g$ in $E[x]$.

Uniqueness: if $h\in\mathbb Q[x]$ is monic irreducible with $f\mid h$, then $h(\alpha)=0$, so $g\mid h$ in $\mathbb Q[x]$; irreducibility and monicity of $h$ force $h=g$.

**(ii)** If $E$ is a splitting field over $\mathbb Q$, then $E/\mathbb Q$ is Galois (characteristic $0$); let $G=\mathrm{Gal}(E/\mathbb Q)$ act on $E[x]$ coefficientwise. Each $f^\sigma$ is monic irreducible in $E[x]$ of degree $\deg f$, and $f^\sigma\mid g^\sigma=g$. Let $f=f_1,\dots,f_k$ be the distinct conjugates $f^\sigma$ and $h=f_1\cdots f_k$. $G$ permutes the $f_i$, so $h$ is $G$-invariant and $h\in E^G[x]=\mathbb Q[x]$. The $f_i$ are distinct monic irreducibles dividing $g$, so $h\mid g$; and $h(\alpha)=0$, so $g\mid h$. Both are monic, so $g=h$ and $\deg g=k\deg f$.

**(iii)** Let $E=\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]2)\subset\mathbb R$, which is not normal over $\mathbb Q$. Let $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$ and $\beta=\omega\sqrt[3]2$. Then $E[\beta]=E[\omega]$ has degree $2$ over $E$ ($\omega\notin\mathbb R$, and $\omega^2+\omega+1=0$), so the minimal polynomial $f$ of $\beta$ over $E$ has degree $2$; explicitly $f=(x-\omega\sqrt[3]2)(x-\omega^2\sqrt[3]2)=x^2+\sqrt[3]2\,x+\sqrt[3]4$. The unique $g$ of (i) is the minimal polynomial of $\beta$ over $\mathbb Q$, namely $x^3-2$ (irreducible by Eisenstein at $2$). Indeed $x^3-2=(x-\sqrt[3]2)f(x)$, and $2\nmid3$. ∎

prompt:
Let $V$ be a finite dimensional vector space over a field $K$ and let $B\colon V \times V \to K$ be a bilinear form. Suppose that for all $x, y \in V$ we have $B(x, y) = 0$ if and only if $B(y, x) = 0$.

(i) If $v, w \in V$ with $B(v, v) \neq 0$, prove that $B(v, w) = B(w, v)$.

(ii) Deduce that either $B$ is symmetric or $B(v, v) = 0$ for all $v \in V$.
answer: (i) Apply the hypothesis to $v$ and $u=w-kv$ with $k=B(v,w)/B(v,v)$. (ii) If $B(v,v)\ne0$ for some $v$, write $V=Kv\oplus v^\perp$ and use (i) with $v$ or $v+x$ to get symmetry on $v^\perp$.

solutions.title: Orthogonal projection
solutions.body:
**(i)** Let $k=B(v,w)B(v,v)^{-1}$ and $u=w-kv$. Then $B(v,u)=B(v,w)-kB(v,v)=0$, so by hypothesis $B(u,v)=0$, i.e. $B(w,v)=kB(v,v)=B(v,w)$.

**(ii)** Suppose $B(v,v)\ne0$ for some $v$. Let $W=\{w: B(v,w)=0\}$, which by hypothesis also equals $\{w:B(w,v)=0\}$. $W$ is the kernel of the nonzero functional $w\mapsto B(v,w)$ (nonzero at $v$), so $V=Kv\oplus W$.

Let $x,y\in W$. If $B(x,x)\ne0$, then $B(x,y)=B(y,x)$ by (i). If $B(x,x)=0$, then
$$B(v+x,v+x)=B(v,v)+B(v,x)+B(x,v)+B(x,x)=B(v,v)\ne0,$$
so by (i), using $B(v,y)=B(y,v)=0$,
$$B(x,y)=B(v+x,y)=B(y,v+x)=B(y,x).$$
So $B$ is symmetric on $W$. Also $B(v,w)=B(w,v)=0$ for $w\in W$ and trivially $B(v,v)=B(v,v)$. By bilinearity $B$ is symmetric on $V=Kv\oplus W$.

So if $B$ is not symmetric, $B(v,v)=0$ for every $v$ (and then $B$ is alternating). ∎

prompt:
Let $G$ be the multiplicative group of all $2 \times 2$ matrices over the integers $\mathbb{Z}$ whose determinant is equal to $1$. Notice that $G$ acts by right multiplication on the set $\Omega$ of all 1-dimensional subspaces of the 2-dimensional row space $\mathbb{Q}^2$ over the rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$.

(i) Find all elements of $G$ which act trivially, that is which fix every element of $\Omega$.

(ii) Prove that $G$ acts transitively. In other words, show that $\Omega$ is an orbit under the action of $G$.
answer: (i) Only $\pm I$. (ii) Each line contains a primitive vector $(r,s)$, $\gcd(r,s)=1$; choose $x,y$ with $rx-sy=1$, then $g=\begin{pmatrix}r&s\\y&x\end{pmatrix}\in G$ sends $\mathbb Q(1,0)$ to $\mathbb Q(r,s)$.

solutions.title: Test vectors and Bézout
solutions.body:
**(i)** Let $g=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ act trivially. Then $(1,0)g=(a,b)\in\mathbb Q(1,0)$ gives $b=0$; $(0,1)g=(c,d)\in\mathbb Q(0,1)$ gives $c=0$; and $(1,1)g=(a,d)\in\mathbb Q(1,1)$ gives $a=d$. Then $\det g=a^2=1$, so $g=\pm I$. Conversely $\pm I$ send every vector to $\pm$ itself, so they fix every line. The kernel of the action is $\{\pm I\}$.

**(ii)** We show every line $\ell\in\Omega$ lies in the orbit of $\mathbb Q(1,0)$. Take $0\ne(u,v)\in\ell$; multiplying by a common denominator and dividing by the gcd of the numerators, $\ell$ contains a vector $(r,s)\in\mathbb Z^2$ with $\gcd(r,s)=1$. By Bézout there are integers $x,y$ with $rx-sy=1$. Put
$$g=\begin{pmatrix}r&s\\y&x\end{pmatrix},\qquad \det g=rx-sy=1,$$
so $g\in G$, and $(1,0)g=(r,s)$. Hence $(\mathbb Q(1,0))g=\ell$, and the action is transitive. ∎

prompt:
Let $G$ be a finite group and fix a prime number $p$. Define the function $f$ on the set of subgroups $H \subseteq G$ by
$$f(H) = |\{ P \in \mathrm{Syl}_p(G) \mid P \supseteq H \}|.$$
In other words, $f(H)$ is the number of Sylow $p$-subgroups of $G$ which contain $H$. Prove that if $f(H) > 0$, then $f(H) \equiv 1 \bmod p$.
answer: Downward induction on $|H|$: a Sylow $p$-subgroup $T$ of $N_G(H)$ acts by conjugation on the Sylow subgroups containing $H$; the fixed points are exactly the Sylow subgroups containing $T$, and $T\supsetneq H$ unless $H$ is Sylow. So $f(H)\equiv f(T)\equiv1\pmod p$.

solutions.title: Count fixed points of a p-group action
solutions.body:
If $f(H)>0$ then $H$ is contained in a $p$-group, so $H$ is a $p$-subgroup. We prove $f(H)\equiv1\pmod p$ for every $p$-subgroup $H$ by downward induction on $|H|$. If $|H|$ is the full $p$-part of $|G|$, then $H$ is itself Sylow and $f(H)=1$.
