Now let $H$ be a $p$-subgroup that is not Sylow, and assume the claim for all $p$-subgroups of larger order. Let $\Omega=\{P\in\mathrm{Syl}_p(G):P\supseteq H\}$ and let $T$ be a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $N=N_G(H)$.

*$T\supsetneq H$.* $H$ is a normal $p$-subgroup of $N$, so $H$ lies in every Sylow $p$-subgroup of $N$; in particular $H\subseteq T$. Choose $P\in\Omega$ (Sylow's theorem). Since $H\subsetneq P$ and normalizers grow in $p$-groups, $N_P(H)\supsetneq H$; this is a $p$-subgroup of $N$, so $|T|\ge|N_P(H)|>|H|$.

*$T$ acts on $\Omega$.* For $t\in T\subseteq N_G(H)$ and $P\in\Omega$, $P^t$ is Sylow and contains $H^t=H$. Orbits of the $p$-group $T$ have $p$-power size, so $|\Omega|\equiv|\mathrm{Fix}_T(\Omega)|\pmod p$.

*Fixed points.* If $P\in\Omega$ is normalized by $T$, then $TP$ is a subgroup of order $|T||P|/|T\cap P|$, a power of $p$, so $TP=P$ by maximality of $P$, i.e. $T\subseteq P$. Conversely, every Sylow $P\supseteq T$ contains $H$ and is normalized by $T$. Hence $\mathrm{Fix}_T(\Omega)=\{P\in\mathrm{Syl}_p(G):P\supseteq T\}$, whose size is $f(T)$.

$T$ is a $p$-subgroup with $|T|>|H|$, so by induction $f(T)\equiv1\pmod p$ (note $f(T)>0$ by Sylow). Therefore $f(H)=|\Omega|\equiv f(T)\equiv1\pmod p$. ∎

prompt:
Let $F$ be a field and let $R$ be the ring of all $3 \times 3$ matrices over $F$ with $(3,1)$ and $(3,2)$ entry equal to $0$. Thus,
$$R = \begin{pmatrix} F & F & F \\ F & F & F \\ 0 & 0 & F \end{pmatrix}.$$
Prove that the Jacobson radical of $R$ is a minimal left ideal, but not a minimal right ideal.
answer: $J(R)=J=\{$matrices supported on entries $(1,3),(2,3)\}$: $J^2=0$ and $R/J\cong M_2(F)\times F$ is semisimple. $J\cong F^2$ as a left module over the $M_2(F)$ block, which is simple; but the matrices supported on entry $(1,3)$ form a smaller nonzero right ideal.

solutions.title: Identify the radical
solutions.body:
Write elements of $R$ as $r=\begin{pmatrix}A&u\\0&c\end{pmatrix}$ with $A\in M_2(F)$, $u\in F^2$ (a column) and $c\in F$. Multiplication is
$$\begin{pmatrix}A&u\\0&c\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}A'&u'\\0&c'\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}AA'&Au'+uc'\\0&cc'\end{pmatrix}.$$

**The radical.** Let $J=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}0&u\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\right\}$. By the formula, $\pi\colon r\mapsto(A,c)$ is a surjective ring homomorphism $R\to M_2(F)\times F$ with kernel $J$, so $J$ is an ideal, and $J^2=0$. A nilpotent ideal lies in the Jacobson radical, so $J\subseteq J(R)$. Conversely $R/J\cong M_2(F)\times F$ is semisimple Artinian, so $J(R/J)=0$; since $J(R)$ maps into $J(R/J)$ under a surjection, $J(R)\subseteq J$. Hence $J(R)=J$.

**Minimal left ideal.** For $r\in R$ and $j=\begin{pmatrix}0&u\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, $rj=\begin{pmatrix}0&Au\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$. So the left ideals of $R$ inside $J$ correspond to subspaces of $F^2$ stable under all of $M_2(F)$. If $u\ne0$, then $\{Au:A\in M_2(F)\}=F^2$. Thus $Rj=J$ for every $0\ne j\in J$, so $J$ is a minimal left ideal.

**Not a minimal right ideal.** $jr=\begin{pmatrix}0&uc\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, so every subspace of $J$ is a right ideal. In particular $J'=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}0&u\\0&0\end{pmatrix}:u_2=0\right\}$ (matrices supported on the $(1,3)$ entry) is a right ideal with $0\ne J'\subsetneq J$. ∎

prompt:
Let $F$ be a field and let $f(x) \in F[x]$ be an irreducible polynomial. Suppose $E$ is a splitting field for $f(x)$ over $F$ and assume that there exists an element $\alpha \in E$ such that both $\alpha$ and $\alpha + 1$ are roots of $f(x)$.

(i) Show that the characteristic of $F$ is not zero.

(ii) Prove that there exists a field $L$ between $F$ and $E$ such that the degree $|E : L|$ is equal to the characteristic of $F$.
answer: There is $\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(E/F)$ with $\sigma(\alpha)=\alpha+1$, so $\alpha+k$ is a root for every $k$. (i) Finitely many roots force $\mathrm{char}F=p>0$. (ii) $\sigma$ has order divisible by $p$; take $\tau$ of order $p$ in $\mathrm{Aut}(E/F)$ and $L=E^{\langle\tau\rangle}$, so $|E:L|=p$ by Artin's theorem.

solutions.title: An automorphism translating by 1
solutions.body:
Since $f$ is irreducible with roots $\alpha$ and $\alpha+1$, there is an $F$-isomorphism $F(\alpha)\to F(\alpha+1)$ with $\alpha\mapsto\alpha+1$. $E$ is a splitting field of $f$ over both $F(\alpha)$ and $F(\alpha+1)$, so this isomorphism extends to an automorphism $\sigma$ of $E$ fixing $F$, with $\sigma(\alpha)=\alpha+1$. By induction $\sigma^k(\alpha)=\alpha+k$, and each $\sigma^k(\alpha)$ is a root of $f$ (as $\sigma$ fixes the coefficients).

**(i)** If $\mathrm{char}F=0$, the elements $\alpha+k$ ($k=0,1,2,\dots$) are pairwise distinct roots of $f$, impossible since $f$ has at most $\deg f$ roots. So $\mathrm{char}F=p>0$.

**(ii)** Let $p=\mathrm{char}F$. For $0<k<p$, $\sigma^k(\alpha)=\alpha+k\ne\alpha$, while $\sigma^p(\alpha)=\alpha$. The group $\mathrm{Aut}(E/F)$ is finite (it embeds into the permutations of the roots of $f$, which generate $E$), and the order of $\sigma$ is a multiple of $p$, since $\sigma^m(\alpha)=\alpha$ exactly when $p\mid m$. By Cauchy's theorem $\mathrm{Aut}(E/F)$ contains an element $\tau$ of order $p$; let $L=E^{\langle\tau\rangle}$ be its fixed field, so $F\subseteq L\subseteq E$. By Artin's theorem, for a finite group $H$ of automorphisms of a field $E$, $|E:E^H|=|H|$. Hence $|E:L|=p$. ∎

prompt:
Let $V$ be a finite dimensional complex vector space and suppose $\langle\ ,\ \rangle\colon V \times V \to \mathbb{C}$ is an inner product on $V$, that is, $\langle\ ,\ \rangle$ is a positive definite Hermitian form on $V$.

(i) Suppose $T\colon V \to V$ is a linear transformation such that $\langle Tv, v\rangle = 0$ for all $v \in V$. Prove that $V = 0$. [*Sic*; the intended conclusion is $T = 0$.]

(ii) Does the result of part (i) hold if $V$ is assumed to be a real inner product space? Justify your answer.
answer: (i) $T=0$: polarize, using $v+w$ and $v+iw$, to get $\langle Tv,w\rangle=0$ for all $v,w$. (ii) No: rotation by $90^\circ$ on $\mathbb R^2$ satisfies $\langle Tv,v\rangle=0$ but $T\ne0$.

solutions.title: Polarization
solutions.body:
**(i)** (We prove $T=0$.) Take $\langle\,,\rangle$ linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second. For $v,w\in V$,
$$0=\langle T(v+w),v+w\rangle=\langle Tv,v\rangle+\langle Tv,w\rangle+\langle Tw,v\rangle+\langle Tw,w\rangle=\langle Tv,w\rangle+\langle Tw,v\rangle .$$
Replacing $w$ by $iw$: $\langle Tv,iw\rangle+\langle T(iw),v\rangle=-i\langle Tv,w\rangle+i\langle Tw,v\rangle=0$, i.e. $\langle Tv,w\rangle-\langle Tw,v\rangle=0$. Adding the two relations gives $\langle Tv,w\rangle=0$ for all $v,w$. Taking $w=Tv$ and using positive definiteness, $Tv=0$ for all $v$. So $T=0$.

**(ii)** No. On $V=\mathbb R^2$ with the standard inner product let $T(x,y)=(-y,x)$ (rotation by $90^\circ$). Then $\langle T(x,y),(x,y)\rangle=-yx+xy=0$ for all vectors, but $T\ne0$. The proof of (i) breaks down because the trick $w\mapsto iw$ is unavailable; over $\mathbb R$ the condition only says $\langle Tv,w\rangle=-\langle Tw,v\rangle$, i.e. $T$ is skew-adjoint. ∎

reviewNote: The exam text says 'Prove that V = 0' in part (i); this is clearly a misprint for 'T = 0' (V need not be 0). Solution proves T = 0.

prompt:
Let $\mathbb{Z}$ denote the ring of integers and let $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{C}$ be the rational and complex fields, respectively. If $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n \in \mathbb{C}$, then we let $\mathbb{Z}[\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n]$ denote the ring generated by these elements over $\mathbb{Z}$. In particular, note that $\mathbb{Z}[1/2]$ is the set of all rational numbers with denominator a power of $2$. Now suppose that $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n$ are the roots of the integer polynomial $f(x) = a_0x^n + a_1x^{n-1} + \cdots + a_n \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ with $a_0 = 2$.

(i) Prove that $2\alpha_i$ is an algebraic integer for all $i = 1, 2, \ldots, n$.

(ii) Show that $\mathbb{Z}[\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n] \cap \mathbb{Q} \subseteq \mathbb{Z}[1/2]$.

(iii) If some $a_j$ with $j \ge 1$ is odd, prove that $1/2 \in \mathbb{Z}[\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n] \cap \mathbb{Q}$ and deduce that the latter intersection is equal to $\mathbb{Z}[1/2]$. What happens if all $a_j$ are even?
answer: (i) $2\alpha_i$ is a root of the monic $x^n+a_1x^{n-1}+2a_2x^{n-2}+\dots+2^{n-1}a_n$. (ii) $2^N r$ is an algebraic integer for $r\in\mathbb Z[\alpha]$, so rational $r$ lie in $\mathbb Z[1/2]$. (iii) $a_j/2=\pm e_j(\alpha)\in\mathbb Z[\alpha]$, giving $1/2$; if all $a_j$ are even the $\alpha_i$ are algebraic integers and the intersection is $\mathbb Z$.

solutions.title: Scaling roots and symmetric functions
solutions.body:
Let $A=\mathbb Z[\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n]$.

**(i)** Multiply $f(\alpha_i)=0$ by $2^{n-1}$:
$$(2\alpha_i)^n+a_1(2\alpha_i)^{n-1}+2a_2(2\alpha_i)^{n-2}+\cdots+2^{n-1}a_n=0,$$
a monic integer equation. So $2\alpha_i$ is an algebraic integer.

**(ii)** Every element of $A$ is an integer combination of monomials $\alpha_1^{k_1}\cdots\alpha_n^{k_n}$; if $N$ bounds the total degrees, then $2^N r$ is an integer combination of products of the algebraic integers $2\alpha_i$ (and powers of $2$), hence an algebraic integer. If moreover $r\in\mathbb Q$, then $2^Nr$ is a rational algebraic integer, hence in $\mathbb Z$ ($\mathbb Z$ is integrally closed). So $r\in\mathbb Z[1/2]$.

**(iii)** Since $f=2\prod(x-\alpha_i)$, comparing coefficients gives $a_j=2(-1)^je_j(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)$, so $a_j/2=\pm e_j(\alpha)\in A\cap\mathbb Q$. If $a_j$ is odd, write $a_j=2m+1$; then $\tfrac12=\tfrac{a_j}{2}-m\in A\cap\mathbb Q$. Then $A\cap\mathbb Q$ is a ring containing $\mathbb Z$ and $1/2$, so it contains $\mathbb Z[1/2]$; with (ii), $A\cap\mathbb Q=\mathbb Z[1/2]$.

If all $a_j$ are even, $f=2h$ with $h=x^n+\frac{a_1}{2}x^{n-1}+\dots+\frac{a_n}2\in\mathbb Z[x]$ monic, so every $\alpha_i$ is an algebraic integer and $A$ consists of algebraic integers. Then $A\cap\mathbb Q=\mathbb Z$ (as $\mathbb Z\subseteq A$ and rational algebraic integers are integers). ∎

prompt:
Let $G$ be a group of order $|G| = 504 = 7 \cdot 8 \cdot 9$.

(i) If there exists an element $x \in G$ of order $21$, show that there exists a subgroup $H \subset G$ having index $|G : H| = 8$. *Hint.* Find the possibilities for $n_7$, the number of Sylow 7-subgroups of $G$.

(ii) If $G$ is simple, show that it contains no element of order $21$.
answer: (i) $P=\langle x^3\rangle$ is Sylow with $\langle x\rangle\le N_G(P)$, so $n_7\mid24$ and $n_7\equiv1\ (7)$, i.e. $n_7\in\{1,8\}$; take $H=N_G(P)$ if $n_7=8$, and $H=PQ$ ($Q\in\mathrm{Syl}_3$) if $n_7=1$. (ii) Then $G\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Sym}_8$, which has no element of order 21 (a 7-cycle and a 3-cycle need 10 points).

solutions.title: Sylow counting and a permutation representation
solutions.body:
**(i)** Let $C=\langle x\rangle$, of order $21$, and $P=\langle x^3\rangle$, of order $7$; since $7\,\|\,504$, $P$ is a Sylow $7$-subgroup. $C$ is abelian, so $C\le N_G(P)$ and $n_7=|G:N_G(P)|$ divides $|G:C|=24$. With $n_7\equiv1\pmod 7$, the divisors $1,2,3,4,6,8,12,24$ leave $n_7\in\{1,8\}$.
- If $n_7=8$, then $H=N_G(P)$ has index $8$.
- If $n_7=1$, then $P\trianglelefteq G$; for $Q\in\mathrm{Syl}_3(G)$ (order $9$), $H=PQ$ is a subgroup of order $63$, i.e. of index $8$.

**(ii)** Suppose $G$ is simple and has an element of order $21$. By (i) there is $H$ of index $8$. The action of $G$ on the $8$ cosets of $H$ gives a homomorphism $G\to\mathrm{Sym}_8$ whose kernel is a proper normal subgroup (contained in $H$), hence trivial by simplicity. So $G$ embeds in $\mathrm{Sym}_8$, and $\mathrm{Sym}_8$ would contain an element of order $21$. But the order of a permutation is the lcm of its cycle lengths, so an element of order $21$ needs a cycle of length divisible by $7$ and one of length divisible by $3$ (or one of length $\ge21$), i.e. at least $7+3=10>8$ points. Contradiction. ∎

prompt: Let $R$ be a ring and let $M$ be a right $R$-module which has a composition series. Assume that $M$ has a unique simple submodule $N$ and that $N$ is not isomorphic to any composition factor of $M/N$. Prove that the ring $\mathrm{End}_R(M)$ is a division ring. In other words, prove that every nonzero $R$-endomorphism of $M$ is one-to-one and onto.
answer: Every nonzero submodule contains $N$. If $0\ne\theta$ had kernel $K\ne0$, then $N\subseteq K$ and $L=\theta^{-1}(N)$ satisfies $L/K\cong N$, making $N$ a composition factor of $M/N$. So $\theta$ is injective, and then onto by comparing composition lengths.

solutions.title: Kernel argument with composition factors
solutions.body:
Since $M$ has finite length, every nonzero submodule $X$ contains a simple submodule, which must be $N$; so $N\subseteq X$ for all $X\ne0$.

Let $0\ne\theta\in\mathrm{End}_R(M)$ with kernel $K$. Then $\theta(M)\ne0$, so $N\subseteq\theta(M)$. Let $L=\theta^{-1}(N)$; then $K\subseteq L$ and $\theta$ induces $L/K\cong N$ (surjective since $N\subseteq\theta(M)$), so $K\subsetneq L$.

Suppose $K\ne0$. Then $N\subseteq K\subsetneq L\subseteq M$, and passing to $M/N$ we get $K/N\subsetneq L/N\subseteq M/N$ with $(L/N)/(K/N)\cong L/K\cong N$ simple. Refining $0\subseteq K/N\subset L/N\subseteq M/N$ to a composition series of $M/N$ shows that $N$ is a composition factor of $M/N$ — contrary to hypothesis. Hence $K=0$ and $\theta$ is injective.

Then $\theta(M)\cong M$, so $\theta(M)$ and $M$ have the same composition length. A submodule of a finite-length module with the same length is the whole module, so $\theta(M)=M$. Thus every nonzero endomorphism is bijective, hence invertible in $\mathrm{End}_R(M)$, which is therefore a division ring. ∎

prompt:
Let $K \subseteq E$ be fields and let $f(x) \in K[x]$ be a polynomial of degree $n \ge 2$ having $n$ distinct roots $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ in $E$. Suppose that the field extension $K[a_1, a_2]/K$ has degree $|K[a_1, a_2] : K| = n(n - 1)$.

(i) Find the degrees of the irreducible factors of $f(x)$ over the field $K$ and over the field $K[a_1]$.

(ii) If $g(x)$ is the minimal polynomial of $a_1 + a_2$ over $K$, prove that $a_i + a_j$ is a root of $g(x)$ for all $i \neq j$. *Hint.* First consider the case $i = 1$.
answer: (i) Over $K$, $f$ is irreducible (one factor of degree $n$); over $K[a_1]$, $f=(x-a_1)h(x)$ with $h$ irreducible of degree $n-1$. (ii) The Galois group of $f$ is $2$-transitive on the roots (there are $n(n-1)$ embeddings of $K[a_1,a_2]$), so some automorphism maps $a_1+a_2$ to $a_i+a_j$.

solutions.title: Degrees force irreducibility; double transitivity
solutions.body:
**(i)** Assume $f$ monic (scaling does not matter). $|K[a_1]:K|\le n$ with equality iff $f$ is irreducible over $K$ (the minimal polynomial of $a_1$ divides $f$). Write $f=(x-a_1)h(x)$ in $K[a_1][x]$; $a_2$ is a root of $h$, so $|K[a_1,a_2]:K[a_1]|\le n-1$ with equality iff $h$ is irreducible over $K[a_1]$. Since
$$n(n-1)=|K[a_1,a_2]:K[a_1]|\cdot|K[a_1]:K|,$$
both inequalities are equalities. Hence over $K$, $f$ is irreducible (one factor, degree $n$), and over $K[a_1]$, $f$ has exactly two irreducible factors, of degrees $1$ and $n-1$.

**(ii)** Let $L=K[a_1,\dots,a_n]$, a splitting field of the separable polynomial $f$ (distinct roots), so $L/K$ is Galois with group $G$. The $K$-embeddings $K[a_1,a_2]\to L$ number exactly $|K[a_1,a_2]:K|=n(n-1)$ (separable extension). Each is determined by the pair $(\tau(a_1),\tau(a_2))$, which is a pair of *distinct* roots of $f$; there are only $n(n-1)$ such pairs, so every ordered pair $(a_i,a_j)$, $i\neq j$, occurs. Every embedding extends to an element of $G$ ($L$ is normal over $K$). So for $i\ne j$ there is $\sigma\in G$ with $\sigma(a_1)=a_i$, $\sigma(a_2)=a_j$.

Since $g\in K[x]$ and $g(a_1+a_2)=0$, applying $\sigma$ gives $g(a_i+a_j)=0$.

(The hinted route: $g(x+a_1)\in K[a_1][x]$ has root $a_2$, so it is divisible by the minimal polynomial $h$ of $a_2$ over $K[a_1]$, giving $g(a_1+a_k)=0$ for all $k\ge2$; then use transitivity of $G$ on the roots to move $a_1$ to $a_i$.) ∎

prompt: Let $A$ be an $m \times n$ matrix over the integers $\mathbb{Z}$ and consider the system of homogeneous linear equations $AX = 0$ where $X$ is the column vector of unknowns $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$. Suppose that every integer solution of this system has all $x_i$'s equal. Prove that the same is true for every real solution of this system of equations.
answer: Rational solutions scale to integer solutions, so the rational null space is $0$ or spanned by $(1,\dots,1)^T$; the real null space is spanned by the rational one (row reduction happens over $\mathbb Q$), so every real solution is a multiple of $(1,\dots,1)^T$.

solutions.title: Null space over Q versus R
solutions.body:
**Rational solutions.** Let $Y\in\mathbb Q^n$ with $AY=0$. Choose an integer $m\ne0$ with $mY\in\mathbb Z^n$; then $mY$ is an integer solution, so all its entries are equal, hence so are those of $Y$. Thus the null space $N_{\mathbb Q}=\ker_{\mathbb Q}A$ is contained in $\mathbb Q\,\mathbf 1$, where $\mathbf 1=(1,\dots,1)^T$.

**Passing to $\mathbb R$.** Gaussian elimination of $A$ uses only field operations on its (rational) entries, so the reduced row echelon form $E$ of $A$ is the same over $\mathbb Q$ and over $\mathbb R$, and the standard basis of the solution space read off from $E$ (one vector per free variable) consists of rational vectors. Hence $\dim_{\mathbb R}\ker_{\mathbb R}A=n-\mathrm{rank}A=\dim_{\mathbb Q}N_{\mathbb Q}$, and $\ker_{\mathbb R}A$ is the real span of $N_{\mathbb Q}$.

Since $N_{\mathbb Q}\subseteq\mathbb Q\mathbf 1$, either $N_{\mathbb Q}=0$, in which case $\ker_{\mathbb R}A=0$ and the only real solution is $0$; or $N_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Q\mathbf 1$, in which case $\ker_{\mathbb R}A=\mathbb R\mathbf 1$. In both cases every real solution has all coordinates equal. ∎

prompt:
Let $K = \mathbb{Q}[i]$ be the field generated over the rationals $\mathbb{Q}$ by $i = \sqrt{-1}$ and let $R$ be the subring of $K$ defined by
$$R = \{ a + bi \mid a, b \in \mathbb{Z} \}$$
where $\mathbb{Z}$ is the ring of integers. Suppose $\alpha$ is a complex number which is the root of a monic polynomial in $R[x]$. Prove that the minimal monic polynomial of $\alpha$ over $K$ has all coefficients in $R$.
answer: $R=\mathbb Z[i]$ is a UFD (Euclidean), hence integrally closed in $K$. The roots of the minimal polynomial $g$ of $\alpha$ over $K$ are roots of the given monic polynomial, hence integral over $R$; the coefficients of $g$ are symmetric functions of them, so integral over $R$ and in $K$, hence in $R$.

solutions.title: Integral closure
solutions.body:
**$R$ is integrally closed in $K$.** $\mathbb Z[i]$ is Euclidean for the norm $N(a+bi)=a^2+b^2$, hence a PID and a UFD. A UFD is integrally closed in its fraction field: if $u=r/s$ in lowest terms satisfies $u^k+c_1u^{k-1}+\dots+c_k=0$ with $c_j\in R$, then $r^k=-s(c_1r^{k-1}+\dots+c_ks^{k-1})$, so every prime factor of $s$ divides $r$, forcing $s$ to be a unit. The fraction field of $R$ is $K$.

**The argument.** Let $f\in R[x]$ be monic with $f(\alpha)=0$ and let $g$ be the minimal monic polynomial of $\alpha$ over $K$. Then $g\mid f$ in $K[x]$, so every root $\beta$ of $g$ (in $\mathbb C$) is a root of $f$, hence integral over $R$. Write $g=\prod_k(x-\beta_k)$. Its coefficients are $\pm$ elementary symmetric polynomials in the $\beta_k$, and integral elements form a ring, so each coefficient is integral over $R$. Each coefficient also lies in $K$. Since $R$ is integrally closed in $K$, all coefficients of $g$ lie in $R$. ∎

prompt:
Let $G = A \dot\times B$ be the internal direct product of finite subgroups $A$ and $B$. Suppose $H$ is a subgroup of $G$ with $A \cap H = 1$.

(i) Show that $B$ contains a subgroup isomorphic to $H$, but that $B$ need not contain $H$ in general.

(ii) If $A$ and $B$ have relatively prime orders, prove that $H \subseteq B$.
answer: (i) $B\cong G/A\supseteq HA/A\cong H/(H\cap A)\cong H$; example: $G=\langle a\rangle\times\langle b\rangle$ Klein four, $H=\langle ab\rangle$. (ii) $|H|$ divides $|B|$ and $|H/(H\cap B)|$ divides $|A|$, so $H=H\cap B$.

solutions.title: Isomorphism theorems
solutions.body:
**(i)** Projection onto $B$ along $A$ gives $G/A\cong B$. Then
$$H\cong H/(H\cap A)\cong HA/A\le G/A\cong B,$$
so $B$ has a subgroup isomorphic to $H$. (Concretely, the projection $ab\mapsto b$ is injective on $H$ since its kernel $A$ meets $H$ trivially.)

Example where $H\not\subseteq B$: $A=\langle a\rangle$, $B=\langle b\rangle$ cyclic of order $2$, $G=A\times B$ the Klein four-group, $H=\langle ab\rangle$. Then $H\cap A=1$ but $H\not\subseteq B$ (indeed $H\cap B=1$).

**(ii)** By (i), $|H|$ divides $|B|$. Also $H/(H\cap B)\cong HB/B\le G/B\cong A$, so $|H/(H\cap B)|$ divides $|A|$. But $|H/(H\cap B)|$ divides $|H|$, which divides $|B|$, and $\gcd(|A|,|B|)=1$. Hence $|H/(H\cap B)|=1$, i.e. $H=H\cap B\subseteq B$. ∎

prompt:
Let $K \subseteq E$ be an extension of fields and let $R$ be the subring of the polynomial ring $E[x]$ consisting of all polynomials with constant term in $K$. In other words,
$$R = K + Ex + Ex^2 + Ex^3 + \cdots$$
Now let $I$ be a nonzero ideal of $R$ and let $m$ be the minimal degree of the nonzero elements of $I$. Define
$$I_m = \{ f(x) \in I \mid \deg f(x) = m \} \cup \{ 0 \}$$
so that $I_m$ is clearly a nonzero $K$-subspace of $R$.

(i) If $\dim_K I_m = 1$, prove that $I$ is a principal ideal.

(ii) If $\dim_K I_m > 1$, show that $I_m$ contains a nonzero polynomial with constant term equal to $0$.

(iii) If $I$ is a prime ideal which is not principal, prove that $m = 1$.
answer: (i) $I_m=Kf$ and the division algorithm (using $a^{-1}bx^{n-m}\in R$ for $n>m$) shows $I=fR$. (ii) The $K$-linear map $I_m\to K$, $g\mapsto g(0)$, has a nontrivial kernel. (iii) Such $f\in I_m$ with $f(0)=0$ factors as $f=(ax)\cdot g$ with $g\in R$, $\deg g=m-1$, so $g\notin I$ and $ax\in I$; hence $m\le1$, and $m\ne0$.

solutions.title: Division algorithm in R
solutions.body:
**(i)** Let $I_m=Kf$ with $f=\dots+ax^m$, $a\in E^\times$. We show by induction on $\deg g$ that every $g\in I$ lies in $fR$. If $g=0$ fine; $\deg g<m$ forces $g=0$. If $\deg g=m$ then $g\in I_m=Kf\subseteq fR$. If $\deg g=n>m$ with leading coefficient $b$, then $a^{-1}bx^{n-m}\in Ex^{n-m}\subseteq R$ (as $n-m\ge1$), so $h=g-a^{-1}bx^{n-m}f\in I$ has degree $<n$; by induction $h\in fR$, hence $g\in fR$. Thus $I=fR$ is principal.

**(ii)** The map $I_m\to K$, $g\mapsto g(0)$, is $K$-linear (constant terms of elements of $R$ lie in $K$). Since $\dim_KI_m>1=\dim_KK$, its kernel is nonzero: some $0\ne f\in I_m$ has $f(0)=0$.

**(iii)** Since $I$ is not principal, $\dim_KI_m>1$ by (i), and by (ii) there is $0\ne f\in I_m$ with $f(0)=0$. Note $m\ge1$: if $m=0$, $I$ would contain a nonzero constant of $K$, a unit of $R$, so $I=R$, which is not prime. Write $f=ax^k+\dots+bx^m$ with $1\le k\le m$, $a,b\in E^\times$, and
$$f=(ax)\cdot g,\qquad g=x^{k-1}+\dots+a^{-1}bx^{m-1}.$$
Here $ax\in R$, and $g\in R$ because its constant term is $1\in K$ (if $k=1$) or $0$ (if $k>1$). Since $0\ne g$ has degree $m-1<m$, $g\notin I$. As $I$ is prime and $(ax)g=f\in I$, we get $ax\in I$. So $I$ has a nonzero element of degree $1$, giving $m\le1$; hence $m=1$. ∎

prompt:
Let $\mathbb{Q}$ be the field of rational numbers and let $K = \mathbb{Q}[\sqrt{2}]$. Suppose $f(x) \in \mathbb{Q}[x]$ is a monic irreducible polynomial of odd degree $n \ge 1$ and notice that $f(x + \sqrt{2})$ is a monic polynomial of degree $n$ in $K[x]$.

(i) Show that the coefficient of $x^{n-1}$ in $f(x + \sqrt{2})$ is not rational.

(ii) Show that the polynomial $f(x + \sqrt{2})$ is irreducible in $K[x]$.

(iii) Prove that the polynomial $g(x) = f(x + \sqrt{2})f(x - \sqrt{2})$ is irreducible in the ring $\mathbb{Q}[x]$.
answer: (i) The coefficient is $a+n\sqrt2$ where $a\in\mathbb Q$ is that of $f$. (ii) For a root $\alpha$ of $f$, $|K[\alpha]:\mathbb Q|$ is divisible by $2$ and $n$ (odd), so $|K[\alpha]:K|=n$. (iii) In $K[x]$ the factorization $g=f(x+\sqrt2)f(x-\sqrt2)$ into monic irreducibles is unique, and neither factor is in $\mathbb Q[x]$.

solutions.title: Degrees and unique factorization
solutions.body:
**(i)** Write $f=x^n+ax^{n-1}+\dots$ with $a\in\mathbb Q$. Then $f(x+\sqrt2)=(x+\sqrt2)^n+a(x+\sqrt2)^{n-1}+\dots=x^n+(n\sqrt2+a)x^{n-1}+\cdots$, and $n\sqrt2+a\notin\mathbb Q$ since $n\ne0$ and $\sqrt2$ is irrational.

**(ii)** Let $\alpha\in\mathbb C$ be a root of $f$. Then $|\mathbb Q[\alpha]:\mathbb Q|=n$ and $|K:\mathbb Q|=2$ both divide $|K[\alpha]:\mathbb Q|$; as $n$ is odd, $2n\mid|K[\alpha]:\mathbb Q|$, so $|K[\alpha]:K|\ge n$. Now $\beta=\alpha-\sqrt2$ is a root of $f(x+\sqrt2)$ and $K[\beta]=K[\alpha]$, so $\beta$ has degree $\ge n$ over $K$. Its minimal polynomial over $K$ divides the degree-$n$ polynomial $f(x+\sqrt2)$, so they are equal, and $f(x+\sqrt2)$ is irreducible in $K[x]$.

**(iii)** Let $\sigma$ be the nontrivial automorphism of $K$ ($\sqrt2\mapsto-\sqrt2$), extended to $K[x]$ coefficientwise. It maps $f(x+\sqrt2)$ to $f(x-\sqrt2)$, which is therefore also monic irreducible in $K[x]$, and it fixes $g$, so $g\in\mathbb Q[x]$ (monic of degree $2n$). Suppose $g=hk$ with $h,k\in\mathbb Q[x]$ monic of positive degree. In the UFD $K[x]$, $g$ has the factorization $f(x+\sqrt2)\cdot f(x-\sqrt2)$ into monic irreducibles, so up to order $h=f(x+\sqrt2)$. But $f(x+\sqrt2)\notin\mathbb Q[x]$ by (i) — a contradiction. Hence $g$ is irreducible in $\mathbb Q[x]$. ∎

prompt:
Let $V \neq 0$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over the complex numbers $\mathbb{C}$ and let $X, Y, Z$ be linear operators on $V$ which satisfy
$$XY - YX = Z,\qquad XZ = ZX,\qquad YZ = ZY.$$
If $V$ has no proper subspace invariant under all three operators, prove that $\dim_{\mathbb{C}} V = 1$.
answer: An eigenspace of $Z$ is invariant, so $Z=\lambda I$; taking traces, $n\lambda=\mathrm{tr}(XY-YX)=0$, so $Z=0$. Then $X,Y$ commute and have a common eigenvector $v$, and $\mathbb Cv$ is invariant, so $V=\mathbb Cv$.

solutions.title: Schur-type argument and traces
solutions.body:
Let $\lambda$ be an eigenvalue of $Z$ ($\mathbb C$ is algebraically closed) and $W=\ker(Z-\lambda I)\ne0$. Since $X$ and $Y$ commute with $Z$, they preserve $W$ (if $Zw=\lambda w$ then $Z(Xw)=XZw=\lambda Xw$), and so does $Z$. By hypothesis $W=V$, i.e. $Z=\lambda I$.

Let $n=\dim V\ge1$. Then $n\lambda=\mathrm{tr}Z=\mathrm{tr}(XY)-\mathrm{tr}(YX)=0$, so $\lambda=0$ (characteristic $0$) and $Z=0$. Thus $XY=YX$.

Commuting operators on a nonzero complex space have a common eigenvector: an eigenspace $U$ of $X$ is $Y$-invariant, and $Y|_U$ has an eigenvector $v$. The line $\mathbb Cv$ is invariant under $X$, $Y$ and $Z=0$, so $V=\mathbb Cv$ and $\dim V=1$. ∎

prompt:
Let $V$ be a vector space over the rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$ and let $v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n \in V$. Show that there exist elements $w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_m \in V$ which are linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$ and which satisfy
$$\sum_{i=1}^n v_i\mathbb{Z} = \sum_{j=1}^m w_j\mathbb{Z}$$
where $\mathbb{Z}$ is the ring of integers.
answer: $A=\sum v_i\mathbb Z$ is a finitely generated torsion-free abelian group, hence free: $A=\bigoplus_j w_j\mathbb Z$. A $\mathbb Q$-relation $\sum w_jq_j=0$ can be cleared to an integer relation, which must be trivial.

solutions.title: Structure of finitely generated abelian groups
solutions.body:
Let $A=\sum_{i=1}^n v_i\mathbb Z\subseteq V$, a finitely generated abelian group. It is torsion-free: if $kv=0$ with $0
e k\in\mathbb Z$ and $v\in V$, then $v=k^{-1}(kv)=0$ since $V$ is a $\mathbb Q$-vector space. By the fundamental theorem of finitely generated abelian groups, $A$ is free: $A=w_1\mathbb Z\oplus\dots\oplus w_m\mathbb Z$ for some $w_j
e0$ (with $m=0$ if $A=0$). Then $\sum_iv_i\mathbb Z=\sum_jw_j\mathbb Z$.

Linear independence over $\mathbb Q$: suppose $\sum_jw_jq_j=0$ with $q_j\in\mathbb Q$. Multiply by a common denominator $d
e0$ to get $\sum_jw_j(dq_j)=0$ with $dq_j\in\mathbb Z$. Since the sum $ igoplus w_j\mathbb Z$ is direct, each $w_j(dq_j)=0$; as $w_j
e0$ and $A$ is torsion-free, $dq_j=0$, so $q_j=0$. ∎

prompt:
Let $G$ be a finite group and let $P \in \mathrm{Syl}_p(G)$ for some prime $p$. Suppose $N$ is a normal subgroup of $G$ with $|G : N| = |P| > 1$.

(i) Prove that $N$ is the subset of $G$ consisting of all elements of order not divisible by $p$.

(ii) If the elements of $G$ outside of $N$ all have $p$-power order, prove that $P$ is its own normalizer.
answer: (i) $|N|$ is prime to $p$ and $G/N\cong P$ is a $p$-group, so $p'$-elements map to $1$ in $G/N$. (ii) A Sylow $q$-subgroup $Q$ ($q\ne p$) of $N_G(P)$ lies in $N$, so $[Q,P]\subseteq N\cap P=1$; if $Q\ne1$, $xy$ with $o(x)=q$, $o(y)=p$ has order $pq$ and lies outside $N$. Hence $N_G(P)$ is a $p$-group, equal to $P$.

solutions.title: Normal p-complement arguments
solutions.body:
**(i)** $|N|=|G|/|P|$ is prime to $p$, so by Lagrange every element of $N$ has order prime to $p$, and $N\cap P=1$. Then $|NP|=|N||P|=|G|$, so $G=NP$ and $G/N\cong P/(P\cap N)\cong P$ is a $p$-group. If $g\in G$ has order prime to $p$, its image in $G/N$ has order dividing both $o(g)$ and a power of $p$, so it is trivial: $g\in N$. Hence $N=\{g\in G: p
mid o(g)\}$.

**(ii)** Let $q
e p$ be a prime and $Q$ a Sylow $q$-subgroup of $N_G(P)$. By (i), $Q\subseteq N$. For $x\in Q$, $y\in P$: $[x,y]=x^{-1}(y^{-1}xy)\in N$ because $x\in N	rianglelefteq G$, and $[x,y]=(x^{-1}y^{-1}x)y\in P$ because $x$ normalizes $P$. So $[Q,P]\subseteq N\cap P=1$ and $Q$ centralizes $P$.

If $Q
e1$, pick $x\in Q$ of order $q$ and $y\in P$ of order $p$ (possible as $P
e1$). They commute, so $xy$ has order $pq$; it is not of $p$-power order, so by hypothesis $xy\in N$. But then by (i) its order is prime to $p$ — a contradiction. So every Sylow $q$-subgroup of $N_G(P)$ ($q
e p$) is trivial, i.e. $N_G(P)$ is a $p$-group containing the Sylow $p$-subgroup $P$. Hence $N_G(P)=P$. ∎

prompt:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $P$ be a prime ideal of $R$. If $V$ is a (right) $R$-module, define
$$W = \{ v \in V \mid va = 0 \text{ for some } a \in R \setminus P \}$$
where $R \setminus P$ is the set of elements of $R$ not in $P$.

(i) Show that $W$ is an $R$-submodule of $V$.

(ii) If $R$ is Noetherian and $V$ is a finitely generated $R$-module, prove that $Wb = 0$ for some $b \in R \setminus P$.

(iii) If $V$ is a simple $R$-module and $W = 0$, prove that $P$ is a maximal ideal.
answer: (i) $R\setminus P$ is multiplicatively closed: $v_1a_1=v_2a_2=0\Rightarrow(v_1+v_2)a_1a_2=0$. (ii) $W$ is finitely generated; multiply the annihilating elements of its generators. (iii) $\mathrm{ann}(v)$ is maximal for $0\ne v\in V$ and misses $R\setminus P$, so $\mathrm{ann}(v)\subseteq P$, forcing $P=\mathrm{ann}(v)$.

solutions.title: Use that R \ P is multiplicative
solutions.body:
(We assume $1\in R$, acting as the identity on $V$.) Since $P$ is prime, $S=R\setminus P$ is closed under multiplication and contains $1$.

**(i)** $0\in W$ since $0\cdot1=0$. If $v_1a_1=0=v_2a_2$ with $a_i\in S$, then $(v_1+v_2)a_1a_2=0$ and $a_1a_2\in S$, so $v_1+v_2\in W$. For $r\in R$, $(v_1r)a_1=(v_1a_1)r=0$ (commutativity), so $v_1r\in W$. Thus $W$ is a submodule.

**(ii)** A finitely generated module over a Noetherian ring is Noetherian, so $W=w_1R+\dots+w_nR$. Pick $b_i\in S$ with $w_ib_i=0$ and put $b=b_1\cdots b_n\in S$. Then $w_ib=0$ for all $i$, so $Wb=\sum_i (w_iR)b=\sum_i (w_ib)R=0$.

**(iii)** Fix $0\ne v\in V$. Since $V$ is simple, $r\mapsto vr$ is a surjection $R\to V$ with kernel $M=\mathrm{ann}(v)$, and $R/M\cong V$ simple means $M$ is a maximal ideal. Since $W=0$, $v\notin W$, so no element of $S$ kills $v$: $M\cap S=\emptyset$, i.e. $M\subseteq P$. As $M$ is maximal and $P$ is proper, $P=M$ is maximal. ∎

prompt:
Let $E$ be a splitting field of the polynomial $x^3 - 2$ over the rationals $\mathbb{Q}$, and assume that $E$ is contained in the complex numbers $\mathbb{C}$. Let $F = E \cap \mathbb{R}$ be the real subfield of $E$, and note that $F = \mathbb{Q}[\sqrt[3]{2}]$.

(i) Show that $G = \mathrm{Gal}(E/\mathbb{Q})$ contains an element $\sigma$ with the property that the only elements of $F$ fixed by $\sigma$ are rational.

(ii) Let $a \in F$ and suppose that $a^3 \in \mathbb{Q}$. Show that one of $a$, $a\sqrt[3]{2}$, or $a\sqrt[3]{4}$ is contained in $\mathbb{Q}$.

(iii) Prove that $\sqrt[3]{3} \notin E$.
answer: (i) Take $\sigma$ of order 3, $\sigma(\sqrt[3]2)=\omega\sqrt[3]2$: its fixed field $\mathbb Q(\omega)$ has degree $2$, so it meets $F$ (degree 3) in $\mathbb Q$. (ii) $\sigma(a)=\omega^{-i}a$, so $\sigma$ fixes $a\sqrt[3]2^{\,i}\in F$. (iii) Otherwise $\sqrt[3]3\in F$ and one of $\sqrt[3]3,\sqrt[3]6,\sqrt[3]{12}$ would be rational.

solutions.title: Galois group of x^3 - 2
solutions.body:
**(i)** Let $\theta=\sqrt[3]2$ and $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$. Then $E=\mathbb Q(\theta,\omega)=F(\omega)$, $|F:\mathbb Q|=3$ ($x^3-2$ is Eisenstein) and $|E:F|=2$ ($\omega\notin\mathbb R$), so $|G|=6$ and $G\cong\mathrm{Sym}_3$ acting on the roots $\theta,\omega\theta,\omega^2\theta$. Let $\sigma\in G$ with $\sigma(\theta)=\omega\theta$, $\sigma(\omega)=\omega$ (it exists: $E=\mathbb Q(\omega)(\theta)$ and $x^3-2$ is irreducible over $\mathbb Q(\omega)$ by degrees). Its fixed field $L$ satisfies $|E:L|=3$, so $|L:\mathbb Q|=2$ (in fact $L=\mathbb Q(\omega)$). Then $|F\cap L:\mathbb Q|$ divides $3$ and $2$, so $F\cap L=\mathbb Q$: the only elements of $F$ fixed by $\sigma$ are rational.

**(ii)** Let $a\in F$ with $a^3=c\in\mathbb Q$. If $a=0$ we are done. Otherwise $\sigma(a)$ is a root of $x^3-c$, whose roots are $a,\omega a,\omega^2a$; so $\sigma(a)=\omega^{-i}a$ for some $i\in\{0,1,2\}$. Then
$$\sigma(a\theta^i)=\omega^{-i}a\cdot\omega^i\theta^i=a\theta^i,$$
and $a\theta^i\in F$, so by (i) $a\theta^i\in\mathbb Q$. That is, one of $a$, $a\sqrt[3]2$, $a\sqrt[3]4$ is rational.

**(iii)** If $a=\sqrt[3]3\in E$, then $a\in E\cap\mathbb R=F$ and $a^3=3\in\mathbb Q$. By (ii), one of $\sqrt[3]3$, $\sqrt[3]6$, $\sqrt[3]{12}$ is rational. But $x^3-3$, $x^3-6$, $x^3-12$ are irreducible over $\mathbb Q$ by Eisenstein at $3$ (for $12$: $3\mid12$, $9\nmid12$), so none of these cube roots is rational. Hence $\sqrt[3]3\notin E$. ∎

prompt: Let $A$ be an $n \times n$ matrix over a field $K$ and assume that the characteristic polynomial of $A$ has distinct roots in the algebraic closure of $K$. Prove that any two $n\times n$ $K$-matrices which commute with A must commute with each other.
answer: Over $\bar K$, $A=PDP^{-1}$ with $D$ diagonal with distinct entries; the centralizer of $D$ is the diagonal matrices ($z_{ij}(\lambda_i-\lambda_j)=0$), which commute with each other.

solutions.title: Diagonalize over the algebraic closure
solutions.body:
Work in $M_n(\bar K)\supseteq M_n(K)$. Since the characteristic polynomial has $n$ distinct roots $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$, $A$ is diagonalizable over $\bar K$: $P^{-1}AP=D=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$ with $P\in GL_n(\bar K)$.

If $Z=[z_{ij}]$ commutes with $D$, compare $(i,j)$ entries: $(ZD)_{ij}=z_{ij}\lambda_j$ and $(DZ)_{ij}=\lambda_iz_{ij}$, so $z_{ij}(\lambda_i-\lambda_j)=0$ and $z_{ij}=0$ for $i\ne j$. So the centralizer of $D$ consists of diagonal matrices.

Let $X,Y\in M_n(K)$ commute with $A$. Then $P^{-1}XP$ and $P^{-1}YP$ commute with $D$, hence are diagonal, hence commute with each other; conjugating back, $XY=YX$. ∎

prompt:
Let $S = M_n(F)$ be the ring of $n \times n$ matrices over the field $F$.

(i) If $s \in S$ is nilpotent, prove that the trace of $s$ is zero.

(ii) Suppose $R$ is a ring and that $\theta\colon R \to S$ is a surjective ring homomorphism. Let $I$ be an ideal of $R$ with the property that every element of $I$ is a sum of nilpotent elements of $R$. Show that $\theta(I) = 0$.
answer: (i) All eigenvalues (in $\bar F$) of a nilpotent matrix are $0$, and the trace is their sum. (ii) $\theta(I)$ is an ideal of the simple ring $S$ on which the trace vanishes, so it does not contain $e_{11}$; hence $\theta(I)\ne S$ and $\theta(I)=0$.

solutions.title: Trace and simplicity of matrix rings
solutions.body:
**(i)** If $s^k=0$ and $\lambda\in ar F$ is an eigenvalue of $s$ with eigenvector $v$, then $0=s^kv=\lambda^kv$, so $\lambda=0$. Thus the characteristic polynomial is $x^n$, and $\mathrm{tr}\,s$ (minus the $x^{n-1}$ coefficient, i.e. the sum of the eigenvalues with multiplicity) is $0$.

**(ii)** Since $	heta$ is surjective, $	heta(I)$ is a two-sided ideal of $S$: $	heta(r)	heta(i)=	heta(ri)\in	heta(I)$, and every element of $S$ is some $	heta(r)$. Every $x\in I$ is a sum of nilpotents $y_k$, and each $	heta(y_k)$ is nilpotent, so $\mathrm{tr}\,	heta(x)=\sum_k\mathrm{tr}\,	heta(y_k)=0$ by (i). In particular the matrix unit $e_{11}$, of trace $1$, is not in $	heta(I)$, so $	heta(I)
e S$. But $M_n(F)$ is a simple ring (any nonzero ideal contains some $a
e0$, and $e_{ii}=a_{kl}^{-1}e_{ik}ae_{li}$ for an entry $a_{kl}
e0$, so it contains $\sum e_{ii}=1$). Hence $	heta(I)=0$. ∎

prompt:
A finite group is said to be *perfect* if it has no nontrivial abelian homomorphic image.

(i) Show that a perfect group has no nontrivial solvable homomorphic image.

(ii) Let $H \trianglelefteq G$ with $G/H$ perfect. If $\theta\colon G \to S$ is a homomorphism from $G$ to a solvable group $S$ and if $N = \ker\theta$, prove that $G = NH$ and deduce that $\theta(H) = \theta(G)$.
answer: (i) A nontrivial solvable image $S$ has a nontrivial abelian image $S/S'$. (ii) $G/NH$ is an image of the solvable group $G/N$ and of the perfect group $G/H$, so it is trivial; then $\theta(G)=\theta(NH)=\theta(H)$.

solutions.title: Abelianization
solutions.body:
**(i)** Let $G$ be perfect and $\varphi\colon G	o S$ surjective with $S
e1$ solvable. A nontrivial solvable group satisfies $S'
e S$ (otherwise the derived series would be constant at $S
eq1$). Then $G	o S	o S/S'$ is a surjection onto a nontrivial abelian group, contradicting perfection.

**(ii)** $G/N\cong	heta(G)\le S$ is solvable (subgroups of solvable groups are solvable). $NH$ is a normal subgroup of $G$ (product of normal subgroups), and $G/NH$ is a homomorphic image both of $G/N$ (so it is solvable) and of $G/H$ (which is perfect). By (i), $G/NH=1$, i.e. $G=NH$. Therefore $	heta(G)=	heta(N)	heta(H)=	heta(H)$. ∎

prompt:
Let $R$ be a ring and let $V$ be a right $R$-module. Assume that every simple submodule of $V$ is a direct summand of $V$.

(i) If $W$ is any submodule of $V$, show that any simple submodule of $W$ is a direct summand of $W$.

(ii) If $V$ is an Artinian module, that is if its submodules satisfy the minimal condition, prove that $V$ is a direct sum of finitely many simple submodules.
answer: (i) If $V=X\oplus Y$ then $W=X\oplus(W\cap Y)$ by the modular law. (ii) Take $W$ minimal among submodules that are not finite direct sums of simples; a simple $X\le W$ splits off, $W=X\oplus Y$ with $Y\subsetneq W$, contradiction.

solutions.title: Modular law and minimal counterexample
solutions.body:
**(i)** Let $X\le W$ be simple. By hypothesis $V=X\oplus Y$ for some submodule $Y$. Since $X\subseteq W$, the modular law gives
$$W=W\cap(X+Y)=X+(W\cap Y),$$
and $X\cap(W\cap Y)\subseteq X\cap Y=0$. So $W=X\oplus(W\cap Y)$.

**(ii)** Suppose not. By the minimal condition choose $W\le V$ minimal among submodules that are *not* finite direct sums of simple modules. $W\ne0$ (the empty sum gives $0$). By the minimal condition again, $W$ has a minimal nonzero submodule $X$, which is simple. By (i), $W=X\oplus Y$ for some $Y\le W$, and $Y\ne W$ since $X\ne0$. By minimality of $W$, $Y$ is a finite direct sum of simples, hence so is $W=X\oplus Y$ — a contradiction. ∎

prompt:
Let $\alpha$ be the real positive 16th root of $3$ and consider the field $F = \mathbb{Q}[\alpha]$ generated by $\alpha$ over the rationals $\mathbb{Q}$. Notice that we have the chain of intermediate fields
$$\mathbb{Q} \subseteq \mathbb{Q}[\alpha^8] \subseteq \mathbb{Q}[\alpha^4] \subseteq \mathbb{Q}[\alpha^2] \subseteq \mathbb{Q}[\alpha] = F.$$

(i) Compute the degrees of these five intermediate fields over $\mathbb{Q}$ and conclude that these fields are all distinct.

(ii) Show that every intermediate field between $\mathbb{Q}$ and $F$ is one of the above. *Hint.* If $\mathbb{Q} \subseteq K \subseteq F$, consider the constant term of the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $K$.
answer: (i) Degrees $1,2,4,8,16$ (Eisenstein for $x^{2^k}-3$). (ii) If $|F:K|=n$, the constant term of the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $K$ is $\pm\alpha^n\epsilon$ with $\epsilon$ a real root of unity, so $\alpha^n\in K$ and $K=\mathbb Q[\alpha^n]$ by degrees.

solutions.title: Constant term of the minimal polynomial
solutions.body:
**(i)** For $k=0,1,2,3,4$, $\alpha^{16/2^k}$ is a root of $x^{2^k}-3$, which is irreducible by Eisenstein at $3$. Hence $|\mathbb Q[\alpha^{8}]:\mathbb Q|=2$, $|\mathbb Q[\alpha^4]:\mathbb Q|=4$, $|\mathbb Q[\alpha^2]:\mathbb Q|=8$, $|\mathbb Q[\alpha]:\mathbb Q|=16$ (and $\mathbb Q$ has degree $1$). The degrees are distinct, so the five fields are distinct.

**(ii)** Let $\mathbb Q\subseteq K\subseteq F$. Then $F=K[\alpha]$; let $n=|F:K|$, which divides $16$, and let $f(x)=x^n+\dots+c$ be the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $K$. Since $f$ divides $x^{16}-3=\prod_{\zeta^{16}=1}(x-\zeta\alpha)$, its roots are $\zeta_1\alpha,\dots,\zeta_n\alpha$ for some $16$th roots of unity $\zeta_j$, and
$$c=(-1)^n\prod_j\zeta_j\alpha=\epsilon\,\alpha^n$$
with $\epsilon$ a root of unity. Now $c\in K\subseteq F\subseteq\mathbb R$ and $\alpha^n>0$ is real, so $\epsilon$ is a real root of unity, $\epsilon=\pm1$. Hence $\alpha^n=\pm c\in K$ and $\mathbb Q[\alpha^n]\subseteq K$. By (i), $|\mathbb Q[\alpha^n]:\mathbb Q|=16/n$, so
$$16=|F:K|\,|K:\mathbb Q[\alpha^n]|\,|\mathbb Q[\alpha^n]:\mathbb Q|=n\cdot|K:\mathbb Q[\alpha^n]|\cdot\tfrac{16}{n},$$
giving $K=\mathbb Q[\alpha^n]$ with $n\in\{1,2,4,8,16\}$ — one of the five listed fields. ∎

prompt: Let $X$ be a subspace of $M_n(\mathbb{C})$, the $\mathbb{C}$-vector space of all $n\times n$ complex matrices. Assume that every nonzero matrix in $X$ is invertible. Prove that $\dim_{\mathbb{C}} X \le 1$.
answer: Fix invertible $x\in X$; for $y\in X$ let $k$ be an eigenvalue of $yx^{-1}$. Then $\det(kx-y)=\det(kI-yx^{-1})\det x=0$, so $kx-y=0$ and $X=\mathbb Cx$.

solutions.title: Use an eigenvalue
solutions.body:
If $X=0$ we are done. Otherwise fix $0\ne x\in X$, which is invertible. Let $y\in X$ and let $k\in\mathbb C$ be an eigenvalue of $yx^{-1}$ (it exists since $\mathbb C$ is algebraically closed). Then
$$\det(kx-y)=\det\big((kI-yx^{-1})x\big)=\det(kI-yx^{-1})\det x=0 .$$
So $kx-y\in X$ is not invertible, hence $kx-y=0$ by hypothesis, i.e. $y=kx$. Therefore $X=\mathbb Cx$ and $\dim_{\mathbb C}X=1$. ∎

(Alternative: if $x,y\in X$ were independent, $t\mapsto\det(x+ty)$ would be a polynomial of degree $\le n$ with constant term $\det x\ne0$ and leading coefficient $\det y\ne0$, so it has a root $t_0\in\mathbb C$, and $x+t_0y$ is a nonzero singular element of $X$.)

prompt:
Let $E$ be an algebraic extension of the rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$ and let $\alpha \in E$.

(i) Prove that there exists a nonzero integer $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that $n\alpha$ is an algebraic integer.

(ii) Show that $\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]$ does not contain $\mathbb{Q}$ and hence conclude that $\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]$ is not a field.
answer: (i) If $n$ is the leading coefficient of an integer polynomial killing $\alpha$, multiply the equation by $n^{s-1}$. (ii) For a prime $p\nmid n$, $1/p\in\mathbb Z[\alpha]$ would make $n^t/p$ a rational algebraic integer, i.e. $p\mid n^t$.

solutions.title: Clearing denominators
solutions.body:
**(i)** $\alpha$ satisfies a nonzero polynomial over $\mathbb Q$; clearing denominators,
$$z_0+z_1\alpha+\dots+z_{s-1}\alpha^{s-1}+n\alpha^s=0,\qquad z_i\in\mathbb Z,\ 0\ne n\in\mathbb Z.$$
Multiplying by $n^{s-1}$:
$$(n\alpha)^s+z_{s-1}(n\alpha)^{s-1}+z_{s-2}n(n\alpha)^{s-2}+\dots+z_0n^{s-1}=0,$$
a monic integer equation for $n\alpha$. So $n\alpha$ is an algebraic integer.

**(ii)** With $n$ as in (i), choose a prime $p\nmid n$. Suppose $1/p\in\mathbb Z[\alpha]$, say $1/p=\sum_{i=0}^tc_i\alpha^i$ with $c_i\in\mathbb Z$. Then
$$\frac{n^t}{p}=\sum_{i=0}^tc_in^{t-i}(n\alpha)^i$$
is an algebraic integer (algebraic integers form a ring). It is rational, and $\mathbb Z$ is integrally closed in $\mathbb Q$, so $n^t/p\in\mathbb Z$, i.e. $p\mid n^t$, hence $p\mid n$ — a contradiction. So $1/p\notin\mathbb Z[\alpha]$ and $\mathbb Z[\alpha]\not\supseteq\mathbb Q$.

If $\mathbb Z[\alpha]$ were a field, it would contain the inverses of all nonzero integers and hence $\mathbb Q$. So $\mathbb Z[\alpha]$ is not a field. ∎

prompt:
Let $G$ be a finite group. We say that a subgroup $M$ of $G$ has property $(*)$ if $M$ is abelian, maximal, and not normal in $G$.

(i) If $M$ and $N$ are distinct subgroups of $G$ with property $(*)$, prove that $M \cap N = Z$, where $Z = Z(G)$ is the center of $G$.

(ii) Let $M$ have property $(*)$ and let $S(M)$ denote the set of all noncentral elements of $G$ which are conjugate to elements of $M$. Note that
$$S(M) = \bigcup_{x \in G} (M \setminus Z)^x.$$
Compute the cardinality $|S(M)|$ of $S(M)$ in terms of $|M| = m$, $|Z| = z$, and $|G| = g$. Deduce that $g - z > |S(M)| > (g - z)/2$.

(iii) Show that any two subgroups of $G$ having property $(*)$ must be conjugate in $G$.
answer: (i) $M\supseteq Z$ (else $MZ=G$ and $M\trianglelefteq G$), and $M\cap N$ is centralized by $\langle M,N\rangle=G$. (ii) $N_G(M)=M$, so $M$ has $g/m$ conjugates, pairwise meeting in $Z$: $|S(M)|=(m-z)\,g/m$; then $m\ge2z$ gives the bounds. (iii) Non-conjugate $M,N$ would give disjoint $S(M),S(N)\subseteq G\setminus Z$, each of size $>(g-z)/2$.

solutions.title: Counting conjugates of a self-normalizing abelian subgroup
solutions.body:
**(i)** If $Z\not\subseteq M$ then $MZ\supsetneq M$ is a subgroup, so $MZ=G$ by maximality; but $Z$ is central and $M$ abelian, so $M\trianglelefteq MZ=G$, a contradiction. Hence $Z\subseteq M$, and likewise $Z\subseteq N$, so $Z\subseteq M\cap N$. Conversely, $M$ and $N$ are abelian, so every element of $M$ and of $N$ centralizes $M\cap N$; thus $C_G(M\cap N)\supseteq\langle M,N\rangle=G$ (as $M\ne N$ are maximal, $\langle M,N\rangle\supsetneq M$). So $M\cap N\subseteq Z$.

**(ii)** Every conjugate $M^x$ also has property $(*)$, so by (i) two distinct conjugates intersect exactly in $Z$, and the sets $M^x\setminus Z=(M\setminus Z)^x$ for distinct conjugates are pairwise disjoint. Since $M\subseteq N_G(M)\subsetneq G$ and $M$ is maximal, $N_G(M)=M$, so $M$ has exactly $g/m$ conjugates. Therefore
$$|S(M)|=(m-z)\cdot\frac{g}{m}=g-\frac{zg}{m}.$$
Since $g/m>1$, $|S(M)|<g-z$. Since $Z\subsetneq M$ ($M$ is not normal, $Z$ is) and $z\mid m$, we have $m\ge2z$, so
$$|S(M)|=g\Big(1-\frac zm\Big)\ge\frac g2>\frac{g-z}{2}.$$

**(iii)** Let $M,N$ have property $(*)$ and suppose they are not conjugate. If $s\in S(M)\cap S(N)$, then $s\in M^x\cap N^y$ for some $x,y$; $M^x\ne N^y$ (not conjugate), both have $(*)$, so by (i) $s\in Z$, contradicting $s\notin Z$. Hence $S(M)$, $S(N)$ are disjoint subsets of $G\setminus Z$, and by (ii)
$$g-z\ge|S(M)|+|S(N)|>\frac{g-z}2+\frac{g-z}2=g-z,$$
a contradiction. ∎

prompt:
Let $R$ be a ring. If $V$ and $W$ are right $R$-modules, we write $V \sim W$ when $V$ is isomorphic to a submodule of $W$ and $W$ is isomorphic to a submodule of $V$.

(i) If $V \sim W$ and if $V$ satisfies the minimum condition, prove that $V$ and $W$ are isomorphic.

(ii) Suppose $R = \mathbb{Z}$ is the ring of integers. If $V \sim W$ and if $V$ is finitely generated, prove that $V$ and $W$ are isomorphic.

(iii) Suppose $R$ is a commutative integral domain and let $I$ be a nonzero ideal of $R$. Show that $R \sim I$ when we view $R$ and $I$ as right $R$-modules. Conclude that if $R$ is not a PID, then there exist nonisomorphic $R$-modules $V$ and $W$ with $V \sim W$.
answer: (i) An Artinian module has no proper submodule isomorphic to itself, so the injection $V\to W\to V$ is onto and $W\cong V$. (ii) Rank and torsion subgroup are monotone under embeddings of finitely generated abelian groups, so they agree. (iii) $I\subseteq R$ and $R\cong aR\subseteq I$; a non-principal $I$ is not isomorphic to $R$.

solutions.title: Minimal condition, invariants, ideals
solutions.body:
**(i)** By the minimum condition choose $V_0\le V$ minimal among submodules isomorphic to $V$. Then $V_0$ has no proper submodule isomorphic to $V_0$ (it would be a smaller submodule of $V$ isomorphic to $V$); transporting along $V\cong V_0$, $V$ has no proper submodule isomorphic to $V$. Now let $f\colon V\to W$ and $g\colon W\to V$ be injective. Then $gf(V)\cong V$ is a submodule of $V$, so $gf(V)=V$; as $gf(V)\subseteq g(W)\subseteq V$, $g(W)=V$ and $g$ is an isomorphism $W\cong V$.

**(ii)** Since $W$ embeds in the finitely generated abelian group $V$, $W$ is finitely generated too ($\mathbb Z$ is Noetherian). For a finitely generated abelian group $X$, write $X\cong T(X)\oplus\mathbb Z^{r(X)}$ with $T(X)$ the finite torsion subgroup and $r(X)=\dim_{\mathbb Q}(X\otimes\mathbb Q)$. If $X\hookrightarrow Y$, then $T(X)\hookrightarrow T(Y)$ (torsion maps to torsion), so $|T(X)|\le|T(Y)|$, and $X\otimes\mathbb Q\hookrightarrow Y\otimes\mathbb Q$ ($\mathbb Q$ is flat), so $r(X)\le r(Y)$. Applying this both ways, $r(V)=r(W)$ and $|T(V)|=|T(W)|$; then the injection $T(V)\hookrightarrow T(W)$ between finite groups of equal size is an isomorphism. Hence $V\cong T(V)\oplus\mathbb Z^r\cong T(W)\oplus\mathbb Z^r\cong W$.

**(iii)** $I$ is a submodule of $R$. For $0\ne a\in I$, $r\mapsto ar$ is injective ($R$ is a domain), so $R\cong aR\subseteq I$. Thus $R\sim I$. If $\varphi\colon R\to I$ is an isomorphism, then $I=\varphi(1)R$ is principal. So if $R$ is not a PID, pick a non-principal (necessarily nonzero) ideal $I$: then $R\sim I$ but $R\not\cong I$. ∎

prompt:
Let $E$ be the subfield of the real numbers generated over $\mathbb{Q}$ by $\sqrt{2}$ and $\sqrt[3]{2}$.

(i) Show that $|E : \mathbb{Q}| = 6$.

(ii) If $K$ is a field with $\mathbb{Q} \subseteq K \subseteq E$, show that $K$ is one of the fields $\mathbb{Q}$, $\mathbb{Q}[\sqrt{2}]$, $\mathbb{Q}[\sqrt[3]{2}]$, or $E$.

(iii) Prove that $E = \mathbb{Q}[\sqrt{2} + \sqrt[3]{2}]$.
answer: (i) $2$ and $3$ divide $|E:\mathbb Q|\le6$. (ii) A quadratic $K$ contains $\sqrt2$ (else $K[\sqrt2]$ has degree 4); a cubic $K$ has $E/K$ Galois of degree 2, whose nontrivial automorphism must fix the only real cube root of 2. (iii) $\mathbb Q[\sqrt2+\sqrt[3]2]$ is not contained in $\mathbb Q[\sqrt2]$ or $\mathbb Q[\sqrt[3]2]$, so it is $E$.

solutions.title: Degrees and the lattice of subfields
solutions.body:
Let $F_2=\mathbb Q[\sqrt2]$, $F_3=\mathbb Q[\sqrt[3]2]$; by Eisenstein, $|F_2:\mathbb Q|=2$, $|F_3:\mathbb Q|=3$.

**(i)** $2$ and $3$ divide $|E:\mathbb Q|$, so $6$ does; and $E=F_3[\sqrt2]$ gives $|E:\mathbb Q|\le 2\cdot3=6$. So $|E:\mathbb Q|=6$.

**(ii)** $|K:\mathbb Q|\in\{1,2,3,6\}$; degrees $1$ and $6$ give $K=\mathbb Q$ and $K=E$.
- If $|K:\mathbb Q|=2$, let $L=K[\sqrt2]\subseteq E$. Then $|L:\mathbb Q|\in\{2,4\}$ and divides $6$, so it is $2$ and $L=K$; thus $\sqrt2\in K$, $F_2\subseteq K$, and equal degrees give $K=F_2$.
- If $|K:\mathbb Q|=3$, then $|E:K|=2$, so (characteristic $0$) $E/K$ is Galois with group $\{1,\sigma\}$. $\sigma(\sqrt[3]2)$ is a root of $x^3-2$ lying in $E\subseteq\mathbb R$, and $\sqrt[3]2$ is the only real root, so $\sigma$ fixes $\sqrt[3]2$ and $\sqrt[3]2\in K$. Thus $F_3\subseteq K$ and $K=F_3$.

**(iii)** Let $\gamma=\sqrt2+\sqrt[3]2$ and $L=\mathbb Q[\gamma]$, one of the four fields in (ii). If $L\subseteq F_2$, then $\sqrt[3]2=\gamma-\sqrt2\in F_2$, impossible as $3\nmid2$. If $L\subseteq F_3$, then $\sqrt2=\gamma-\sqrt[3]2\in F_3$, impossible as $2\nmid3$. Hence $L=E$. (Check: the minimal polynomial of $\gamma$ is $x^6-6x^4-4x^3+12x^2-24x-4$, of degree 6.) ∎

prompt:
Let $V$ and $W$ be finite-dimensional vector spaces over an algebraically closed field $F$ and let $A\colon V \to V$ and $B\colon W \to W$ be linear operators. Suppose $T\colon V \to W$ is a nonzero linear transformation such that $T(A(v)) = B(T(v))$ for all $v \in V$, and let $N = \ker T$.

(i) Show that $A(N) \subseteq N$.

(ii) Show that there exists $\lambda \in F$ and a vector $v \in V$ with $v \notin N$ such that $A(v) - \lambda v \in N$.

(iii) If $\lambda$ is as in part (ii), show that $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue for both $A$ and $B$.
answer: (i) $TA(N)=BT(N)=0$. (ii) Take an eigenvector of the induced operator on $V/N\ne0$. (iii) $T(v)\ne0$ is a $\lambda$-eigenvector of $B$; and $A-\lambda I$ is not invertible on $V$, since otherwise it would induce an invertible map on $V/N$.

solutions.title: Induced operator on the quotient
solutions.body:
**(i)** For $n\in N$, $T(A(n))=B(T(n))=B(0)=0$, so $A(n)\in N$.

**(ii)** By (i), $A$ induces $\bar A\colon V/N\to V/N$, $\bar A(v+N)=A(v)+N$. Since $T\ne0$, $N\ne V$, so $V/N\neq0$ and (as $F$ is algebraically closed) $\bar A$ has an eigenvector $\bar v=v+N\ne0$ with $\bar A\bar v=\lambda\bar v$. That is, $v\notin N$ and $A(v)-\lambda v\in N$.

**(iii)** Write $A(v)=\lambda v+n$ with $n\in N$. Then
$$B(T(v))=T(A(v))=\lambda T(v)+T(n)=\lambda T(v),$$
and $T(v)\ne0$ since $v\notin N$. So $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $B$.

For $A$: suppose $A-\lambda I$ were invertible on $V$. It maps $N$ into $N$ (by (i)) injectively, hence onto $N$ ($N$ finite-dimensional). Then the induced map $\bar A-\lambda I$ on $V/N$ is surjective (any $w+N$ equals $(A-\lambda I)u+N$ for some $u$), hence injective — but it kills $\bar v\ne0$. Contradiction. So $A-\lambda I$ is singular and $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A$. ∎

prompt:
Let $S$ be the set of all $2\times2$ complex matrices of the form
$$\begin{pmatrix} a & \bar b \\ b & \bar a \end{pmatrix}$$
with $a, b \in \mathbb{C}$ and where, as usual, $\bar{\ }$ denotes complex conjugation.

(i) Show that $S$ is a subring of the ring $M_2(\mathbb{C})$ of all $2\times2$ matrices over $\mathbb{C}$.

(ii) Determine the center $Z$ of $S$ and show that $Z$ is isomorphic to the real numbers $\mathbb{R}$.

(iii) Prove that
$$I = \left\{ \begin{pmatrix} x & \bar x \\ x & \bar x \end{pmatrix} \;\middle|\; x \in \mathbb{C} \right\}$$
is a minimal right ideal of $S$ and that it is faithful as a right $S$-module.

(iv) Show that $\dim_Z I = 2$ and conclude that $S \cong M_2(\mathbb{R})$.
answer: Writing $(a,b)$ for the matrix: $(a,b)(c,d)=(ac+\bar bd,\ bc+\bar ad)$. (ii) $Z=\{(r,0):r\in\mathbb R\}$, the real scalar matrices. (iii) $(x,x)(c,d)=(xc+\bar xd,\ xc+\bar xd)\in I$, $(x,x)(c,0)=(xc,xc)$ fills $I$ when $x\ne0$, and $I(c,d)=0$ forces $c=d=0$. (iv) $I$ has $\mathbb R$-basis $(1,1),(i,i)$; $S$ ($\dim_{\mathbb R}4$) embeds faithfully in $\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb R}(I)\cong M_2(\mathbb R)$, hence $S\cong M_2(\mathbb R)$.

solutions.title: Compute in coordinates
solutions.body:
Write $(a,b)=\begin{pmatrix}a&\bar b\\b&\bar a\end{pmatrix}$.

**(i)** $(a,b)\pm(c,d)=(a\pm c,b\pm d)$, and
$$\begin{pmatrix}a&\bar b\\b&\bar a\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}c&\bar d\\d&\bar c\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}ac+\bar bd&a\bar d+\bar b\bar c\\bc+\bar ad&b\bar d+\bar a\bar c\end{pmatrix}=(ac+\bar bd,\ bc+\bar ad),$$
since the $(1,2)$ and $(2,2)$ entries are the conjugates of the $(2,1)$ and $(1,1)$ entries. With $1=(1,0)$, $S$ is a subring.

**(ii)** Let $(a,b)\in Z$. Commuting with $(i,0)$: $(i,0)(a,b)=(ia,\ \bar i\,b)=(ia,-ib)$ and $(a,b)(i,0)=(ia,\ ib)$, so $b=0$. Commuting with $(0,1)$: $(a,0)(0,1)=(0,\bar a)$ and $(0,1)(a,0)=(0,a)$, so $a=\bar a\in\mathbb R$. Conversely $(r,0)=rI$ with $r$ real is a scalar matrix, central in $S$. So $Z=\{rI:r\in\mathbb R\}\cong\mathbb R$.

**(iii)** $I=\{(x,x):x\in\mathbb C\}$ is an additive subgroup, and $(x,x)(c,d)=(xc+\bar xd,\ xc+\bar xd)\in I$, so $I$ is a right ideal. If $0\ne(x,x)\in I$, then for any $y\in\mathbb C$, $(x,x)(y/x,0)=(y,y)$; so every nonzero element generates $I$, and $I$ is a minimal right ideal. Faithful: if $I(c,d)=0$, then $(1,1)(c,d)=(c+d,c+d)=0$ and $(i,i)(c,d)=(ic-id,\ \dots)=0$, so $c+d=0=c-d$ and $(c,d)=0$.

**(iv)** As a $Z=\mathbb R$-space, $I\cong\mathbb C$ via $(x,x)\leftrightarrow x$, with basis $(1,1),(i,i)$; so $\dim_ZI=2$. Right multiplication gives a ring homomorphism $\rho\colon S\to\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb R}(I)^{\mathrm{op}}$, $\rho(s)(v)=vs$; it is $\mathbb R$-linear and injective by faithfulness. Now $\dim_{\mathbb R}S=4$ (basis $(1,0),(i,0),(0,1),(0,i)$) and $\dim_{\mathbb R}\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb R}(I)=4$, so $\rho$ is an isomorphism. Hence $S\cong M_2(\mathbb R)^{\mathrm{op}}\cong M_2(\mathbb R)$ (transpose is an anti-automorphism of $M_2(\mathbb R)$). ∎

(Remark: $\det(a,b)=|a|^2-|b|^2$ is indefinite, which is why $S$ is the split algebra $M_2(\mathbb R)$ rather than the quaternions.)

prompt:
Let $P$ be a Sylow $p$-subgroup of a finite group $G$ and let $N = N_G(P)$ be its normalizer.

(i) Show that $N$ is not contained in any proper normal subgroup of $G$.

(ii) If the commutator subgroup $G'$ is abelian, prove that $G' \cap N$ is normal in $G$.
answer: (i) Frattini: if $N\subseteq M\trianglelefteq G$ then $G=MN_G(P)=M$. (ii) $G'\cap N$ is normalized by $N$ and (as $G'$ is abelian) by $G'$; its normalizer contains $G'$, hence is normal, and contains $N$, so it is $G$ by (i).

solutions.title: Frattini argument
solutions.body:
**(i)** Suppose $N\subseteq M\trianglelefteq G$. Then $P\subseteq M$ is a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $M$, so the Frattini argument gives $G=M\,N_G(P)=MN=M$. Hence $M$ is not proper.

**(ii)** Let $D=G'\cap N$ and $L=N_G(D)$. Since $G'\trianglelefteq G$, $D\trianglelefteq N$, so $N\subseteq L$. Since $G'$ is abelian and $D\subseteq G'$, $G'$ normalizes $D$, so $G'\subseteq L$. Any subgroup containing $G'$ is normal ($L/G'$ is a subgroup of the abelian group $G/G'$, hence normal). So $L$ is a normal subgroup containing $N$, and by (i) $L=G$, i.e. $D\trianglelefteq G$. ∎

prompt:
Let $R$ be a commutative Noetherian domain and suppose that $P$ is the unique nonzero prime ideal of $R$.

(i) Show that every element of $R$ not in $P$ is a unit of $R$.

(ii) If $Q$ is a nonzero ideal of $R$, prove that $Q$ is primary and that $Q \supseteq P^n$ for some integer $n \ge 1$.

(iii) If $P = (\pi)$ is principal, prove that every nonzero element of $R$ is a product of a unit and a power of $\pi$.
answer: (i) A nonunit lies in a maximal ideal, which is a nonzero prime, so in $P$. (ii) $\sqrt Q=P$ is maximal, so $Q$ is primary, and $P$ finitely generated gives $P^n\subseteq Q$. (iii) Take $n$ minimal with $\pi^n\in rR$, $\pi^n=rs$; if $s$ is not a unit, $s=\pi t$ and $\pi^{n-1}=rt$ contradicts minimality, so $r=s^{-1}\pi^n$.

solutions.title: Local ring with one nonzero prime
solutions.body:
(We take $Q$ proper in (ii); $R$ itself is excluded from being primary by convention.)

**(i)** Let $r
otin P$. If $r$ were not a unit, $rR$ would be a proper ideal, contained in some maximal ideal $M$. Then $M
eq0$ ($r
e0$ since $0\in P$) and $M$ is prime, so $M=P$ and $r\in P$ — a contradiction.

**(ii)** Let $0
e Q\subsetneq R$. The radical $\sqrt Q$ is the intersection of the primes containing $Q$; the only primes are $0$ and $P$, and $0
ot\supseteq Q$, so $\sqrt Q=P$. An ideal whose radical is a maximal ideal is primary: $R/Q$ has a unique prime ideal $P/Q$, so every element of $R/Q$ is either a unit (outside $P/Q$) or nilpotent (in the nilradical $P/Q$); hence zero divisors of $R/Q$ are nilpotent, which is the definition of $Q$ being primary. ($P$ is maximal by (i).) Finally $P=(p_1,\dots,p_k)$ is finitely generated (Noetherian), and $p_j^{e}\in Q$ for some common $e$; then every product of $n=k(e-1)+1$ elements of $P$ is a sum of monomials in the $p_j$ of degree $n$, each containing some $p_j^{e}$, so $P^n\subseteq Q$.

**(iii)** Let $0
e r\in R$. If $r$ is a unit, $r=r\pi^0$. Otherwise $Q=rR$ is a nonzero proper ideal, so by (ii) $P^n=(\pi^n)\subseteq rR$ for some $n\ge1$; choose $n\ge0$ minimal with $\pi^n\in rR$, say $\pi^n=rs$. If $s$ is a unit, $r=s^{-1}\pi^n$ and we are done. If not, $s\in P$ by (i), so $s=\pi t$, and $\pi^n=r\pi t$; cancelling $\pi
e0$ in the domain $R$ gives $\pi^{n-1}=rt\in rR$, contradicting minimality (note $n\ge1$ here since $\pi^0=1\in rR$ would make $r$ a unit). ∎

prompt:
Let $\mathbb{Q}$ be the field of rational numbers and let $f(x) = x^8 + x^4 + 1$ be a polynomial in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$. Suppose $E$ is a splitting field for $f(x)$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ and set $G = \mathrm{Gal}(E/\mathbb{Q})$.

(i) Find $|E : \mathbb{Q}|$ and determine the Galois group $G$ up to isomorphism.

(ii) If $\Omega \subset E$ is the set of roots of $f(x)$, find the number of orbits for the action of $G$ on $\Omega$.
answer: $f=\Phi_3\Phi_6\Phi_{12}=(x^2+x+1)(x^2-x+1)(x^4-x^2+1)$, so $E=\mathbb Q(\zeta_{12})$: $|E:\mathbb Q|=4$, $G\cong(\mathbb Z/12)^\times\cong\mathbb Z/2\times\mathbb Z/2$; there are $3$ orbits.

solutions.title: Cyclotomic factorization
solutions.body:
Since $(x^4-1)f(x)=x^{12}-1$, the roots of $f$ are the $12$th roots of unity that are not $4$th roots of unity, i.e. those of order $3$, $6$ or $12$. Hence
$$f=\Phi_3\Phi_6\Phi_{12}=(x^2+x+1)(x^2-x+1)(x^4-x^2+1),$$
which one can also check by multiplying out: $(x^2+x+1)(x^2-x+1)=x^4+x^2+1$ and $(x^4+x^2+1)(x^4-x^2+1)=x^8+x^4+1$.

**(i)** $E$ contains a primitive $12$th root of unity $\zeta$ and all roots of $f$ are powers of $\zeta$, so $E=\mathbb Q(\zeta)$. Thus $|E:\mathbb Q|=\varphi(12)=4$ and $G\cong(\mathbb Z/12\mathbb Z)^\times=\{1,5,7,11\}$. Since $5^2\equiv7^2\equiv11^2\equiv1\pmod{12}$, every element has order $\le 2$: $G\cong\mathbb Z/2\times\mathbb Z/2$ (Klein four-group).

**(ii)** The orbits of $G$ on $\Omega$ are the root sets of the distinct irreducible factors of $f$ over $\mathbb Q$ (Galois acts transitively on roots of each irreducible factor, and preserves each factor). Cyclotomic polynomials are irreducible, so there are **3 orbits**, of sizes $2,2,4$ (primitive cube roots, primitive sixth roots, primitive twelfth roots). ∎

prompt: Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix over an algebraically closed field $K$ and let $K[A]$ denote the $K$-linear span of the matrices $I = A^0, A, A^2, A^3, \ldots$. Show that $A$ is diagonalizable if and only if $K[A]$ contains no nonzero nilpotent element.
answer: If $A$ is diagonal, $K[A]$ consists of diagonal matrices. Conversely, if the minimal polynomial $f$ has a repeated root $\alpha$, then $g=f/(x-\alpha)$ gives $0\ne g(A)\in K[A]$ with $g(A)^2=0$ (as $f\mid g^2$); so a reduced $K[A]$ forces $f$ to have distinct roots, i.e. $A$ diagonalizable.

solutions.title: Minimal polynomial
solutions.body:
**($\Rightarrow$)** If $A=PDP^{-1}$ with $D$ diagonal, then every element of $K[A]$ is $P\,p(D)\,P^{-1}$ with $p(D)$ diagonal. A diagonal nilpotent matrix is $0$ (its entries are nilpotent field elements), so $K[A]$ has no nonzero nilpotents.

**($\Leftarrow$)** Let $f$ be the minimal polynomial of $A$; since $K$ is algebraically closed, $f=\prod_{i=1}^k(x-\alpha_i)$. Then $K[A]\cong K[x]/(f)$, so for $g\in K[x]$, $g(A)=0$ iff $f\mid g$. Suppose $f$ has a repeated root, say $\alpha_1=\alpha_2$, and let $g=f/(x-\alpha_1)$. Then $\deg g<\deg f$, so $g(A)\ne0$; and since $(x-\alpha_1)^2\mid f$, $h=f/(x-\alpha_1)^2$ is a polynomial with $g^2=f\cdot h$, so $g(A)^2=0$. Thus $g(A)$ is a nonzero nilpotent element of $K[A]$. Hence, if $K[A]$ has no nonzero nilpotent, $f$ has distinct roots, and a matrix whose minimal polynomial splits with distinct roots is diagonalizable. ∎

prompt:
Let $G$ be a (not necessarily finite) group and denote the operation in $G$ by multiplication. Let $\mathbb{Z}[G]$ denote the group ring of $G$ over the integers $\mathbb{Z}$. Thus, every element of $\mathbb{Z}[G]$ is a finite $\mathbb{Z}$-linear combination of elements of $G$, and the multiplication in $\mathbb{Z}[G]$ is built naturally from the multiplication in $G$. Let $I$ be a right ideal of $\mathbb{Z}[G]$ and define
$$\mathrm{gp}(I) = \{ g \in G \mid 1 - g \in I \}.$$

(i) Prove that $\mathrm{gp}(I)$ is a subgroup of $G$.

(ii) If $I$ is a 2-sided ideal of $\mathbb{Z}[G]$, show that $\mathrm{gp}(I)$ is normal in $G$.

(iii) If $\mathrm{gp}(I) = G$, prove that $I$ is a 2-sided ideal of $\mathbb{Z}[G]$.
answer: (i) $1-gh=(1-g)h+(1-h)$ and $1-g^{-1}=-(1-g)g^{-1}$. (ii) $1-x^{-1}gx=x^{-1}(1-g)x$. (iii) $g\alpha=\alpha-(1-g)\alpha\in I$ for $\alpha\in I$, so $I$ is closed under left multiplication by $G$, hence by $\mathbb Z[G]$.

solutions.title: Identities in the group ring
solutions.body:
**(i)** $1-1=0\in I$, so $1\in\mathrm{gp}(I)$. If $g,h\in\mathrm{gp}(I)$, then, since $I$ is a right ideal,
$$1-gh=(1-g)h+(1-h)\in I,\qquad 1-g^{-1}=-(1-g)g^{-1}\in I .$$
So $gh,g^{-1}\in\mathrm{gp}(I)$, and $\mathrm{gp}(I)$ is a subgroup.

**(ii)** If $I$ is two-sided, $g\in\mathrm{gp}(I)$ and $x\in G$, then $1-x^{-1}gx=x^{-1}(1-g)x\in I$, so $x^{-1}gx\in\mathrm{gp}(I)$.

**(iii)** Let $\alpha\in I$ and $g\in G=\mathrm{gp}(I)$. Then $1-g\in I$, so $(1-g)\alpha\in I$ ($I$ is a right ideal), and $g\alpha=\alpha-(1-g)\alpha\in I$. So $gI\subseteq I$ for all $g\in G$; since every element of $\mathbb Z[G]$ is a $\mathbb Z$-combination of group elements and $I$ is an additive group, $\mathbb Z[G]\,I\subseteq I$. Thus $I$ is a two-sided ideal. ∎

prompt:
We say that a group $G$ has property $(*)$ if every normal abelian subgroup of $G$ is contained in $Z(G)$, the center of $G$.

(a) Suppose that $N$ and $M$ are normal subgroups of a group $G$ and that $G/N$ and $G/M$ have property $(*)$. Prove that $G/(N\cap M)$ has property $(*)$.

(b) Let $N \trianglelefteq G$ and assume that $G/N$ has property $(*)$. If $N$ has no nontrivial abelian normal subgroups, prove that $G$ has property $(*)$.

(c) Show that a finite $p$-group with property $(*)$ must be abelian.
answer: (a), (b): for $A$ normal abelian (mod the relevant subgroup), $(*)$ for $G/N$ gives $[A,G]\subseteq N$. (a) $[A,G]\subseteq N\cap M$. (b) $[A,G]\subseteq A\cap N$ is an abelian normal subgroup of $N$, so it is trivial. (c) If $G\ne Z(G)$, take $A/Z$ of order $p$ central in $G/Z$; $A$ is abelian and normal but not central.

solutions.title: Commutators
solutions.body:
Throughout, for subgroups $X,Y$ write $[X,Y]$ for the subgroup generated by all $[x,y]=x^{-1}y^{-1}xy$. A normal subgroup $A/N$ of $G/N$ is central iff $[A,G]\subseteq N$.

**Key observation.** If $G/N$ has $(*)$ and $A\trianglelefteq G$ is such that $AN/N$ is abelian (e.g. $A$ abelian), then $AN/N$ is a normal abelian subgroup of $G/N$, hence central, so $[A,G]\subseteq[AN,G]\subseteq N$.

**(a)** Let $\bar G=G/(N\cap M)$ and let $A/(N\cap M)$ be a normal abelian subgroup of $\bar G$, with $N\cap M\subseteq A\trianglelefteq G$. Then $AN/N$ is a homomorphic image of $A/(N\cap M)$, hence abelian, and normal in $G/N$. By the key observation $[A,G]\subseteq N$; similarly $[A,G]\subseteq M$. So $[A,G]\subseteq N\cap M$, i.e. $A/(N\cap M)$ is central in $\bar G$. Thus $\bar G$ has $(*)$.

**(b)** Let $A$ be a normal abelian subgroup of $G$. By the key observation, $[A,G]\subseteq N$. Since $A\trianglelefteq G$, every $[a,g]=a^{-1}(g^{-1}ag)\in A$, so $[A,G]\subseteq A$; in particular $[A,G]$ is abelian. Also $[A,G]$ is normal in $G$ (the generating set is invariant under conjugation: $[a,g]^h=[a^h,g^h]$), hence normal in $N$. So $[A,G]$ is an abelian normal subgroup of $N$, and by hypothesis $[A,G]=1$, i.e. $A\subseteq Z(G)$. So $G$ has $(*)$.

**(c)** Let $G$ be a finite $p$-group with $(*)$ and $Z=Z(G)$. Suppose $G\ne Z$. The nontrivial $p$-group $G/Z$ has nontrivial center, so it contains a central subgroup $A/Z$ of order $p$. Then $A\trianglelefteq G$ (central subgroups are normal and $A$ is its preimage). As $A/Z$ is cyclic, say generated by $aZ$, every element of $A$ is $a^kz$ with $z\in Z$, and such elements commute; so $A$ is abelian. By $(*)$, $A\subseteq Z$, contradicting $|A/Z|=p$. Hence $G=Z$ is abelian. ∎

prompt:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$, let $n\ge 2$ be a fixed integer, and suppose that $x^n=x$ for all $x\in R$.

(a) If $P$ is a prime ideal of $R$, show that $R/P$ is a finite field containing at most $n$ elements.

(b) Prove that the intersection of all prime ideals of $R$ is the zero ideal.

(c) If $R$ is a Noetherian ring, conclude that $R$ is finite.
answer: (a) In the domain $R/P$, $\bar x\ne0$ gives $\bar x^{n-1}=1$, so $\bar x$ is a unit; all elements are roots of $t^n-t$, so $|R/P|\le n$. (b) The intersection is the nilradical, and $x^2=0\Rightarrow x=x^n=0$. (c) Finitely many minimal primes $P_1,\dots,P_k$ with $\bigcap P_i=0$, so $R\hookrightarrow\prod R/P_i$, finite.

solutions.title: Reduced ring, finite residue fields
solutions.body:
**(a)** Write $\bar R=R/P$, a nonzero integral domain, and $\bar x$ for the image of $x$. We have $\bar x^n=\bar x$. If $\bar x\ne0$, then $\bar x(\bar x^{n-1}-1)=0$ in a domain gives $\bar x^{n-1}=1$, so $\bar x$ is invertible with inverse $\bar x^{n-2}$ (here $n\ge2$). Hence $\bar R$ is a field. Every element of $\bar R$ is a root of the polynomial $t^n-t\in\bar R[t]$, which has at most $n$ roots in the field $\bar R$. So $|\bar R|\le n$.

**(b)** The intersection of all prime ideals of a commutative ring is its nilradical, the set of nilpotent elements. If $x$ is nilpotent, choose $k$ with $x^k=0$; since $x=x^n=x^{n^2}=\cdots=x^{n^j}$ for all $j$, and $n^j\ge k$ for large $j$, we get $x=0$. So the nilradical, i.e. the intersection of all primes, is $0$.

**(c)** A Noetherian ring has only finitely many minimal prime ideals $P_1,\dots,P_k$, and every prime contains a minimal one. Hence $\bigcap_i P_i=\bigcap_{P\text{ prime}}P=0$ by (b). The map $R\to R/P_1\times\cdots\times R/P_k$, $r\mapsto(r+P_i)_i$, is a ring homomorphism with kernel $\bigcap P_i=0$, so it is injective. By (a) each $R/P_i$ has at most $n$ elements, so $|R|\le n^k<\infty$. ∎

prompt:
Let $f(x)=x^6+3\in\mathbb{Q}[x]$, let $\alpha$ be a root of $f(x)$ in $\mathbb{C}$, and set $E=\mathbb{Q}[\alpha]$.

(a) Show that $E$ contains a primitive $6$th root of unity.

(b) Prove that $E$ is Galois over $\mathbb{Q}$.

(c) Count the number of intermediate fields $F$ with $\mathbb{Q}\subseteq F\subseteq E$ and $|F:\mathbb{Q}|=3$. Justify your answer.
answer: (a) $\alpha^3=\pm\sqrt{-3}$, and $(1\pm\sqrt{-3})/2$ are the primitive 6th roots of unity. (b) $E$ contains all roots $\omega^i\alpha$. (c) $|E:\mathbb{Q}|=6$ (Eisenstein), and $\mathrm{Gal}(E/\mathbb{Q})\cong S_3$ (two distinct involutions $\alpha\mapsto-\alpha$ and complex conjugation), so there are exactly **3** such fields.

solutions.title: Roots of unity and the Galois group
solutions.body:
**(a)** Put $\beta=\alpha^3$. Then $\beta^2=\alpha^6=-3$, so $\beta=\pm\sqrt{-3}\in E$. Since $x^6-1=(x-1)(x+1)(x^2+x+1)(x^2-x+1)$, the primitive 6th roots of unity are the roots of $x^2-x+1$, namely $\frac{1\pm\sqrt{-3}}{2}=\frac{1\pm\beta}{2}\in E$.

**(b)** Let $\omega\in E$ be a primitive 6th root of unity. The six numbers $\omega^i\alpha$ ($0\le i\le5$) are distinct roots of $x^6+3$, hence all of its roots, and they lie in $E$. Since $E=\mathbb{Q}[\alpha]$ is generated by them, $E$ is the splitting field of $x^6+3$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, so $E/\mathbb{Q}$ is normal, and separable as we are in characteristic $0$; hence Galois.

**(c)** $x^6+3$ is irreducible by Eisenstein at $3$, so $|E:\mathbb{Q}|=6$ and $G=\mathrm{Gal}(E/\mathbb{Q})$ has order $6$; thus $G\cong C_6$ or $G\cong S_3$.

Let $\gamma=-\sqrt[3]{3}\in\mathbb{R}$, a root of $x^3+3$. The roots of $f$ are the square roots of the roots of $x^3+3$, and they all lie in $E$ by (b); so $\gamma=\alpha_j^2\in E$ for some root $\alpha_j$, and $\mathbb{Q}(\gamma)\subseteq E$ has degree $3$ ($x^3+3$ is Eisenstein). It is not normal over $\mathbb{Q}$: it is contained in $\mathbb{R}$, but the other two roots $\omega^2\gamma,\omega^4\gamma$ of $x^3+3$ are not real. If $G$ were abelian, every subgroup would be normal and every intermediate field Galois over $\mathbb{Q}$. Hence $G$ is nonabelian, so $G\cong S_3$.

By the Galois correspondence, intermediate fields $F$ with $|F:\mathbb{Q}|=3$ correspond to subgroups $H$ with $|H|=|E:F|=2$. $S_3$ has exactly three subgroups of order $2$ (generated by its three transpositions). Hence there are exactly **three** such fields.

**Answer: 3.** ∎

solutions.title: Listing the cubic subfields
solutions.body:
With $\gamma=-\sqrt[3]{3}$ and $\omega$ a primitive 6th root of unity (so $\omega^2$ is a primitive cube root of unity), the roots of $x^3+3$ are $\gamma,\omega^2\gamma,\omega^4\gamma$; each is the square of a root of $f$, so lies in $E$. The fields $F_1=\mathbb{Q}(\gamma)$, $F_2=\mathbb{Q}(\omega^2\gamma)$, $F_3=\mathbb{Q}(\omega^4\gamma)$ are cubic (Eisenstein) and pairwise distinct: $F_1\subset\mathbb{R}$ while $\omega^2\gamma,\omega^4\gamma\notin\mathbb{R}$; and if two of them coincided, that cubic field would contain two roots, hence their ratio (a primitive cube root of unity, of degree 2), and $2\nmid3$. So there are at least three cubic subfields.

Conversely, $|G|=6$ and $G$ is nonabelian (as $F_1$ is not normal), so $G\cong S_3$ has exactly three subgroups of order $2$, hence $E$ has at most three subfields of degree $3$. So $F_1,F_2,F_3$ are all of them. **Answer: 3.** ∎

prompt:
Let $V$ be a finite dimensional vector space over a field $K$ and let $T\colon V\to V$ be a linear operator. Assume that there exists a nonzero vector $v\in V$ such that $V$ is spanned by the vectors $vT^i$ for $i=0,1,2,\ldots$.

(a) Show that there exists a basis for $V$ with respect to which the matrix of $T$ has the form
$$\begin{pmatrix} 0&1&&&\\ &0&1&&\\ &&\ddots&\ddots&\\ &&&0&1\\ a_0&a_1&\cdots&a_{n-2}&a_{n-1}\end{pmatrix}$$
for suitable $a_i\in K$.

(b) Prove that the minimal polynomial and the characteristic polynomial of $T$ are identical.
answer: (a) With $n$ maximal such that $v,vT,\dots,vT^{n-1}$ are independent, these span a $T$-invariant subspace containing all $vT^k$, hence form a basis, and the matrix (rows = images of basis vectors) is the companion form. (b) No nonzero polynomial of degree $<n$ kills $v$, so the minimal polynomial has degree $n=\deg\chi_T$, and it divides $\chi_T$.

solutions.title: Cyclic vector basis
solutions.body:
Operators act on the right, so the matrix of $T$ in a basis $b_1,\dots,b_n$ has as its $i$-th row the coordinates of $b_iT$.

**(a)** Since $V$ is finite dimensional and $v\ne0$, choose $n\ge1$ maximal such that $v,vT,\dots,vT^{n-1}$ are linearly independent. Then $vT^n$ is a linear combination: $vT^n=a_0v+a_1vT+\cdots+a_{n-1}vT^{n-1}$. Let $W$ be the span of $v,\dots,vT^{n-1}$. Then $WT\subseteq W$ (the images of the spanning vectors are $vT,\dots,vT^{n-1},vT^n\in W$), so by induction $vT^k\in W$ for all $k\ge0$. Since these vectors span $V$, $W=V$, and $\mathcal B=\{v,vT,\dots,vT^{n-1}\}$ is a basis. Now $(vT^i)T=vT^{i+1}$ for $0\le i\le n-2$, giving rows $e_{i+2}$ (a $1$ just right of the diagonal), and $(vT^{n-1})T=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}a_j\,vT^j$, giving the last row $(a_0,\dots,a_{n-1})$. This is the required matrix.

**(b)** Let $\mu$ be the minimal polynomial and $\chi$ the characteristic polynomial; $\deg\chi=n=\dim V$ and $\mu\mid\chi$ by Cayley–Hamilton. If $g(x)=\sum_{i<n}c_ix^i$ is nonzero of degree $<n$, then $vg(T)=\sum c_i\,vT^i\ne0$ by independence of $\mathcal B$, so $g(T)\ne0$. Hence $\deg\mu\ge n$. Being monic of the same degree with $\mu\mid\chi$, we get $\mu=\chi$. ∎

prompt:
The goal of this problem is to prove:

**Theorem.** Let $M_3(F)$ denote the space of $3\times3$ matrices over the field $F$. The following are equivalent.

(i) $F$ has an extension field of degree $3$.

(ii) $M_3(F)$ contains a $3$-dimensional subspace whose nonzero members are all invertible matrices.

(iii) $M_3(F)$ contains a $2$-dimensional subspace whose nonzero members are all invertible matrices.

(a) If $E$ is an extension field of $F$ of degree $3$, show that the ring $M_3(F)$ contains an isomorphic copy of $E$. Deduce that (i) implies (ii).

(b) Let $A$ and $B$ be linearly independent invertible matrices in $M_3(F)$. If the characteristic polynomial of $AB^{-1}$ is not irreducible over $F$, show that some nonzero $F$-linear combination of $A$ and $B$ is not invertible. Deduce that (iii) implies (i).
answer: (a) The regular representation $e\mapsto$ (matrix of multiplication by $e$ on $E\cong F^3$) embeds $E$ in $M_3(F)$; its image is a 3-dimensional subspace of invertible matrices. (b) A reducible cubic has a root $\lambda\in F$, so $\lambda B-A=(\lambda I-AB^{-1})B$ is singular and nonzero. Hence for a basis $A,B$ of the subspace in (iii), $\chi_{AB^{-1}}$ is irreducible and a root generates a cubic extension.

solutions.title: Regular representation and eigenvalues
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $|E:F|=3$ and fix an $F$-basis of $E$, identifying $E\cong F^3$. For $e\in E$ let $T_e\colon E\to E$, $x\mapsto xe$; it is $F$-linear, so it has a matrix $T_e\in M_3(F)$. The map $\theta\colon e\mapsto T_e$ is $F$-linear and multiplicative ($T_{ee'}=T_eT_{e'}$; the order of composition is irrelevant as $E$ is commutative), with $T_1=I$. It is injective since $T_e(1)=e$. So $\theta(E)$ is a subring of $M_3(F)$ isomorphic to $E$, and a 3-dimensional $F$-subspace. If $e\ne0$ then $T_eT_{e^{-1}}=T_1=I$, so every nonzero member of $\theta(E)$ is invertible. This proves (i)$\Rightarrow$(ii); (ii)$\Rightarrow$(iii) is trivial (take any 2-dimensional subspace).

**(b)** The characteristic polynomial $\chi$ of $AB^{-1}$ is a cubic. If it is reducible over $F$, it has a factor of degree $1$, so a root $\lambda\in F$. Then $\lambda I-AB^{-1}$ is singular, hence so is $(\lambda I-AB^{-1})B=\lambda B-A$. Since $A,B$ are linearly independent, $\lambda B-A\neq0$; it is the desired nonzero non-invertible combination.

Now assume (iii): let $V\subseteq M_3(F)$ be 2-dimensional with all nonzero members invertible, and let $A,B$ be a basis. By the above, $\chi_{AB^{-1}}$ must be irreducible over $F$ (otherwise $V$ would contain a nonzero singular matrix). Let $\alpha$ be a root of $\chi$ in some extension; then $E=F[\alpha]$ is a field with $|E:F|=\deg\chi=3$. So (iii)$\Rightarrow$(i), and the three conditions are equivalent. ∎

prompt:
A finite group $G$ is said to have property $*$ if there exists a conjugacy class $K$ of $G$ such that $G$ is generated by the elements of $K$.

(i) If $G$ has property $*$, prove that $G/G'$ is cyclic, where $G'$ is the commutator subgroup of $G$.

(ii) Show that $G$ has property $*$ if and only if $G$ is not the set-theoretic union of its proper normal subgroups.

(iii) Suppose $G=N\times M$ where $N$ is nonabelian simple and $M$ has property $*$. Prove that $G$ has property $*$. (Hint. First show that every normal subgroup of $G$ that does not contain $N$ must be contained in $M$.)
answer: (i) All elements of $K$ have the same image in the abelian group $G/G'$, which that image generates. (ii) $\langle K\rangle$ is normal, so $G=\langle g^G\rangle$ iff $g$ lies in no proper normal subgroup. (iii) A normal $L\not\supseteq N$ has $L\cap N=1$, so $L\subseteq C_G(N)=M$; then $(n,m)$ with $n\neq1$ and $m$ in no proper normal subgroup of $M$ lies in no proper normal subgroup of $G$.

solutions.title: Normal closures
solutions.body:
For $g\in G$ write $g^G$ for its conjugacy class. The subgroup $\langle g^G\rangle$ is normal (its generating set is closed under conjugation) and it is the smallest normal subgroup containing $g$.

**(i)** Let $G=\langle K\rangle$ with $K=g^G$. In $G/G'$ conjugate elements have the same image, since $h^{-1}gh=g[g,h]$. So $G/G'$ is generated by the single element $gG'$, hence cyclic.

**(ii)** If some $g$ lies in no proper normal subgroup, then the normal subgroup $\langle g^G\rangle$ containing $g$ must be $G$, so $G$ has $*$. Conversely, suppose $G=\langle g^G\rangle$ and $g\in N\trianglelefteq G$. Then $g^G\subseteq N$, so $G=\langle g^G\rangle\subseteq N$, i.e. $N=G$.
