So $g$ is not in the union of the proper normal subgroups. Thus $G$ has $*$ iff some element lies outside every proper normal subgroup, i.e. iff $G$ is not the union of its proper normal subgroups.

**(iii)** *Hint.* Let $L\trianglelefteq G$ with $N\not\subseteq L$. Then $L\cap N\trianglelefteq N$ is a proper normal subgroup of the simple group $N$, so $L\cap N=1$. Hence $[L,N]\subseteq L\cap N=1$ (both are normal), so $L\subseteq C_G(N)$. In $G=N\times M$, $C_G(N)=Z(N)\times M=M$ because the nonabelian simple group $N$ has trivial center. So $L\subseteq M$.

By (ii) applied to $M$, pick $m\in M$ lying in no proper normal subgroup of $M$, and pick $1\ne n\in N$. Put $g=nm$ (i.e. $(n,m)$). Let $L\trianglelefteq G$ contain $g$.
- If $N\not\subseteq L$, then $L\subseteq M$ by the hint, but $g\notin M$ since $n\ne1$; impossible.
- If $N\subseteq L$, then $m=n^{-1}g\in L\cap M$. Now $L\cap M$ is normal in $G$, hence in $M$, and contains $m$, so $L\cap M=M$. Thus $L\supseteq NM=G$.

So $g$ lies in no proper normal subgroup of $G$, and by (ii) $G$ has property $*$. ∎

prompt:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ and suppose that $M$ is an ideal of $R$.

(i) If $M$ is both maximal and principal, show that there is no ideal $I$ of $R$ satisfying $M>I>M^2$, where $>$ denotes strict inclusion.

(ii) Give examples to show that neither of the two conditions on $M$ in part (i) can be removed.
answer: (i) If $M=(m)$ and $M^2\subseteq I\subseteq M$, let $J=\{r:rm\in I\}\supseteq M$; then $J=R$ gives $I=M$ and $J=M$ gives $I=Mm=M^2$. (ii) Maximal, not principal: $R=F[x,y]$, $M=(x,y)$, $I=(x,y^2)$. Principal, not maximal: $R=\mathbb{Z}$, $M=(4)$, $I=(8)$.

solutions.title: The colon ideal
solutions.body:
**(i)** Let $M=mR$ be maximal and let $I$ be an ideal with $M^2\subseteq I\subseteq M$. Every element of $I$ has the form $rm$. Put $J=\{r\in R\mid rm\in I\}$, an ideal of $R$. Since $M\cdot m\subseteq M^2\subseteq I$, we have $M\subseteq J$, so $J=M$ or $J=R$ by maximality.
- If $J=R$, then $m\in I$, so $M=mR\subseteq I$ and $I=M$.
- If $J=M$, then $I=\{rm\mid r\in J\}=Mm=M^2$.

So no ideal lies strictly between $M^2$ and $M$.

**(ii)** *Maximal but not principal.* $R=F[x,y]$ ($F$ a field), $M=(x,y)$ (maximal, as $R/M\cong F$), $M^2=(x^2,xy,y^2)$, and $I=(x,y^2)$. Then $I\supsetneq M^2$ since $x\notin M^2$ (every element of $M^2$ has no terms of degree $<2$), and $I\subsetneq M$ since $y\notin I$ (every element of $I$ is $xa+y^2b$, whose linear part is a multiple of $x$).

*Principal but not maximal.* $R=\mathbb{Z}$, $M=(4)$, $M^2=(16)$, $I=(8)$: $(4)\supsetneq(8)\supsetneq(16)$. ∎

prompt:
Let $\mathbb{Q}\subseteq L\subseteq E$ be fields with $\mathbb{Q}$ the rational numbers and with $|E:L|<\infty$. Let $K$ be the subfield of $E$ consisting of all those elements of $E$ which are algebraic over $\mathbb{Q}$, and assume that $K\cap L=\mathbb{Q}$.

(i) If $\alpha\in K$, show that its minimal polynomial over $\mathbb{Q}$ is irreducible over $L$ and deduce that $|\mathbb{Q}[\alpha]:\mathbb{Q}|\le|E:L|$.

(ii) Show that $|K:\mathbb{Q}|\le|E:L|$. (Hint. Start with a subfield $M$ of $K$ maximal with the property that $|M:\mathbb{Q}|\le|E:L|$.)
answer: (i) The coefficients of a monic factor over $L$ are polynomials in roots of $f$, hence algebraic over $\mathbb{Q}$, and lie in $L\subseteq E$, so they lie in $K\cap L=\mathbb{Q}$; thus $|L[\alpha]:L|=\deg f\le|E:L|$. (ii) Take $M\subseteq K$ of maximal degree $\le|E:L|$; for $\alpha\in K$, $M[\alpha]=\mathbb{Q}[\gamma]$ (primitive element) has degree $\le|E:L|$ by (i), so $M[\alpha]=M$; hence $K=M$.

solutions.title: Coefficients are algebraic
solutions.body:
Let $n=|E:L|$ and fix an algebraic closure $\Omega$ of $E$.

**(i)** Let $\alpha\in K$ with minimal polynomial $f\in\mathbb{Q}[x]$. Suppose $f=gh$ in $L[x]$ with $g$ monic. In $\Omega[x]$, $f=\prod(x-\alpha_i)$ with all $\alpha_i$ algebraic over $\mathbb{Q}$, and by unique factorization $g$ is a product of some of the $x-\alpha_i$. Hence the coefficients of $g$ are (elementary symmetric) polynomials in some $\alpha_i$, so they are algebraic over $\mathbb{Q}$. They also lie in $L\subseteq E$, so they lie in $K\cap L=\mathbb{Q}$. Thus $g\in\mathbb{Q}[x]$ divides $f$ in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$, and irreducibility of $f$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ forces $g=1$ or $g=f$. So $f$ is irreducible over $L$, hence is the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $L$, and
$$|\mathbb{Q}[\alpha]:\mathbb{Q}|=\deg f=|L[\alpha]:L|\le|E:L|=n,$$
since $L\subseteq L[\alpha]\subseteq E$.

**(ii)** Among the subfields $M\subseteq K$ with $|M:\mathbb{Q}|\le n$ (e.g. $\mathbb{Q}$), choose one of maximal degree. Let $\alpha\in K$. Then $M[\alpha]\subseteq K$ is a finite extension of $\mathbb{Q}$, and since we are in characteristic $0$ the primitive element theorem gives $M[\alpha]=\mathbb{Q}[\gamma]$ for some $\gamma\in K$. By (i), $|M[\alpha]:\mathbb{Q}|=|\mathbb{Q}[\gamma]:\mathbb{Q}|\le n$. Since $M\subseteq M[\alpha]$ and $M$ has maximal degree among such fields, $|M[\alpha]:\mathbb{Q}|=|M:\mathbb{Q}|$, so $M[\alpha]=M$ and $\alpha\in M$. Hence $K=M$ and $|K:\mathbb{Q}|\le n=|E:L|$. ∎

prompt:
Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $K$ and let $S$ and $T$ be $K$-linear operators on $V$. Suppose that $S$ is one-to-one, that $T(v)=0$ for some $0\neq v\in V$, and that $TS-ST=S$.

(i) For every integer $n\ge0$, prove that $S^n(v)$ is an eigenvector for $T$ and determine the corresponding eigenvalue.

(ii) If $K$ has characteristic $0$, prove that $\dim_K V=\infty$.

(iii) If $K$ has characteristic $p>0$, then $\dim_K V$ can be finite. Give a concrete example of such a finite-dimensional situation when $p=3$.
answer: (i) $TS^n=S^nT+nS^n$, so $T(S^nv)=n\,S^nv$ with $S^nv\ne0$: eigenvalue $n$. (ii) In characteristic $0$ the eigenvalues $0,1,2,\dots$ are distinct, giving infinitely many independent vectors. (iii) $K=\mathbb{F}_3$, $V=K^3$, $S$ the cyclic shift $v_i\mapsto v_{i+1}$ (indices mod 3), $T=\mathrm{diag}(0,1,2)$.

solutions.title: Commutation relation
solutions.body:
**(i)** We claim $TS^n=S^nT+nS^n$ for all $n\ge0$. For $n=0$ it is trivial. If it holds for $n$, then using $TS=ST+S$,
$$TS^{n+1}=(TS)S^n=(ST+S)S^n=S(TS^n)+S^{n+1}=S(S^nT+nS^n)+S^{n+1}=S^{n+1}T+(n+1)S^{n+1}.$$
Applying this to $v$ with $Tv=0$: $T(S^nv)=n\,S^nv$. Since $S$ is injective and $v\ne0$, $S^nv\ne0$. So $S^nv$ is an eigenvector of $T$ with eigenvalue $n\cdot1_K$.

**(ii)** If $\mathrm{char}\,K=0$, the scalars $0,1,2,\dots$ are pairwise distinct. Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent, so $v,Sv,S^2v,\dots$ are linearly independent and $\dim V=\infty$.

**(iii)** Let $K=\mathbb{F}_3$, $V=K^3$ with basis $v_0,v_1,v_2$, and define $S(v_i)=v_{i+1}$ (indices mod 3) and $T(v_i)=i\,v_i$. $S$ permutes a basis, so it is one-to-one, and $T(v_0)=0$ with $v_0\ne0$. Check $TS-ST=S$ on the basis: $(TS-ST)(v_i)=T(v_{i+1})-iS(v_i)=\big((i+1)-i\big)v_{i+1}=v_{i+1}=S(v_i)$ for $i=0,1$, and for $i=2$: $T(v_0)-2v_0=0-2v_0=v_0=S(v_2)$ because $-2=1$ in $\mathbb{F}_3$. In matrices (columns = images): $S=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&1\\1&0&0\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $T=\mathrm{diag}(0,1,2)$. ∎

prompt:
Let $q$ be a prime power and let $F$ be the finite field of size $q$. Let
$$f(x)=\frac{x^5-1}{x-1}=x^4+x^3+x^2+x+1\in F[x].$$

(i) If $f(x)$ has a root in $F$, show that $f(x)$ splits completely over $F$, and prove that this happens precisely when $q\equiv0$ or $1\bmod 5$.

(ii) If $f(x)$ has an irreducible monic factor $g(x)$ of degree $2$, show that $g(x)$ has constant term equal to $1$.

(iii) Factor $f(x)$ explicitly into irreducible quadratic factors when $q=29$.
answer: (i) A root $\zeta\ne1$ has order 5, so $\zeta,\zeta^2,\zeta^3,\zeta^4$ are the roots; $\zeta=1$ forces characteristic 5 and $f=(x-1)^4$. Roots exist iff $5\mid q$ or $5\mid q-1$. (ii) The constant term $c$ is a product of two 5th roots of unity, so $c^5=1$ in $F$, and $F$ has no element of order 5, so $c=1$. (iii) Over $\mathbb{F}_{29}$: $f=(x^2+6x+1)(x^2-5x+1)$.

solutions.title: Roots of unity in finite fields
solutions.body:
Every root $\zeta$ of $f$ (in any extension) satisfies $\zeta^5=1$, since $(x-1)f(x)=x^5-1$.

**(i)** Suppose $\zeta\in F$ is a root. If $\zeta\ne1$, its multiplicative order divides $5$ and is not $1$, so it is $5$; then $\zeta,\zeta^2,\zeta^3,\zeta^4$ are four distinct elements of $F$, each a root of $x^5-1$ different from $1$, hence roots of $f$; so $f=\prod_{i=1}^4(x-\zeta^i)$ splits over $F$. If $\zeta=1$, then $0=f(1)=5$ in $F$, so $\mathrm{char}F=5$ and $f=(x^5-1)/(x-1)=(x-1)^5/(x-1)=(x-1)^4$ splits.

So $f$ has a root in $F$ iff either $\mathrm{char}F=5$ (i.e. $q\equiv0\bmod5$) or $F^\times$ contains an element of order $5$. As $F^\times$ is cyclic of order $q-1$, the latter holds iff $5\mid q-1$. Hence $f$ has a root (equivalently, splits) iff $q\equiv0$ or $1\pmod5$.

**(ii)** If $g$ is an irreducible quadratic factor, then $f$ has no root in $F$ (otherwise it would split into linear factors by (i), and $g$ could not be an irreducible factor). In particular $\mathrm{char}F\neq5$ and $F^\times$ has no element of order $5$. Over a splitting field, $g=(x-\beta)(x-\beta')$ with $\beta^5=\beta'^5=1$, so its constant term $c=\beta\beta'\in F$ satisfies $c^5=1$. Hence $c=1$.

**(iii)** $29\equiv4\pmod5$, so $f$ has no roots in $\mathbb{F}_{29}$; but $29^2\equiv1\pmod5$, so the roots lie in $\mathbb{F}_{29^2}$ and $f$ is a product of two irreducible quadratics, both with constant term $1$ by (ii): $f=(x^2+ax+1)(x^2+bx+1)$. Comparing coefficients: $x^3$: $a+b=1$; $x^2$: $ab+2=1$, so $ab=-1$; $x^1$: $a+b=1$ again. So $a,b$ are the roots of $t^2-t-1$, i.e. $t=(1\pm\sqrt5)/2$. In $\mathbb{F}_{29}$, $11^2=121=4\cdot29+5$, so $\sqrt5=\pm11$ and $t=(1+11)/2=6$ or $t=(1-11)/2=-5$. Check: $6+(-5)=1$, $6\cdot(-5)=-30=-1$. Hence
$$x^4+x^3+x^2+x+1=(x^2+6x+1)(x^2-5x+1)=(x^2+6x+1)(x^2+24x+1)\quad\text{over }\mathbb{F}_{29},$$
and both factors are irreducible since $f$ has no roots in $\mathbb{F}_{29}$. ∎

prompt:
Suppose that $G$ is a finite group that has exactly $50$ Sylow $7$-subgroups. Let $P\in\mathrm{Syl}_7(G)$ and write $N=N_G(P)$.

(a) Show that $N$ is a maximal subgroup of $G$.

(b) If $N$ has a normal Sylow $5$-subgroup $Q$, prove that $Q\trianglelefteq G$.
answer: (a) For $N\le H\le G$, $|H:N|=n_7(H)\equiv1\pmod7$ divides $50$, so it is $1$ or $50$. (b) Take $R\in\mathrm{Syl}_5(G)$ containing $Q$; $R\cap N=Q<R$, so $N_R(Q)>Q$ is not inside $N$, and $G=\langle N,N_R(Q)\rangle$ normalizes $Q$.

solutions.title: Sylow counting and growing normalizers
solutions.body:
**(a)** By Sylow's theorem, $|G:N|=n_7(G)=50$. Let $N\le H\le G$. Then $P\in\mathrm{Syl}_7(H)$ and $N_H(P)=N$, so $|H:N|=n_7(H)\equiv1\pmod7$. Also $|H:N|$ divides $|G:N|=50$. The divisors of $50$ are $1,2,5,10,25,50$, which are $\equiv1,2,5,3,4,1\pmod 7$. So $|H:N|\in\{1,50\}$, i.e. $H=N$ or $H=G$. As $|G:N|=50>1$, $N$ is a maximal subgroup.

**(b)** If $Q=1$ there is nothing to prove, so assume $Q\ne1$. Since $Q\trianglelefteq N$ is a Sylow $5$-subgroup of $N$, it is the unique one, so it contains every $5$-subgroup of $N$. Let $R\in\mathrm{Syl}_5(G)$ with $Q\subseteq R$. Then $R\cap N$ is a $5$-subgroup of $N$ containing $Q$, so $R\cap N=Q$. Since $5\mid50=|G:N|$, the $5$-part of $|G|$ exceeds that of $|N|$, so $Q\subsetneq R$.

In a finite $p$-group, a proper subgroup is properly contained in its normalizer ("normalizers grow"). Hence $N_R(Q)\supsetneq Q$. If $N_R(Q)\subseteq N$ we would have $N_R(Q)\subseteq R\cap N=Q$, a contradiction. So $N_R(Q)\not\subseteq N$, and $\langle N,N_R(Q)\rangle$ properly contains $N$; by (a) it equals $G$. Both $N$ and $N_R(Q)$ normalize $Q$, so $G$ normalizes $Q$, i.e. $Q\trianglelefteq G$. ∎

prompt:
Let $R$ be a commutative domain with $1$.

(a) Let $a,b\in R$ and assume that the principal ideal $(ab)$ is primary. If $a\neq0$ and $b$ is not a unit of $R$, prove that $b^n\in(a)$ for some integer $n\ge1$.

(b) Now assume that every principal ideal of $R$ is primary and let $P$ be any nonzero prime ideal of $R$. Show that $P$ contains every nonunit of $R$. Deduce that $P$ is the unique nonzero prime ideal of $R$.
answer: (a) $ab\in(ab)$ primary gives $a\in(ab)$ (then $b$ is a unit, cancelling $a$) or $b^n\in(ab)\subseteq(a)$. (b) For $0\ne a\in P$ and a nonunit $b$, (a) gives $b^n\in(a)\subseteq P$, so $b\in P$; thus $P$ is exactly the set of nonunits, the same for every nonzero prime.

solutions.title: Use the primary condition on $ab$
solutions.body:
Recall that a proper ideal $I$ is primary if $xy\in I$ and $x\notin I$ imply $y^n\in I$ for some $n\ge1$.

**(a)** Since $ab\in(ab)$ and $(ab)$ is primary, either $a\in(ab)$ or $b^n\in(ab)$ for some $n\ge1$. If $a\in(ab)$, write $a=abr$; then $a(1-br)=0$ with $a\neq0$ in a domain, so $br=1$ and $b$ is a unit — excluded. Hence $b^n\in(ab)\subseteq(a)$.

**(b)** Let $P\ne0$ be prime, fix $0\ne a\in P$, and let $b$ be any nonunit. As $(ab)$ is primary, part (a) gives $b^n\in(a)\subseteq P$ for some $n$, and since $P$ is prime, $b\in P$. So $P$ contains every nonunit. Conversely, $P$ is proper and so contains no unit. Hence $P$ equals the set of nonunits of $R$. This description does not depend on $P$, so any two nonzero primes coincide: $P$ is the unique nonzero prime ideal of $R$. ∎

prompt:
Let $\alpha$ be a nonzero real number and suppose that $\alpha^n\in\mathbb{Q}$, the rational numbers, for some positive integer $n$. Let $g(x)$ be the minimal (monic) polynomial of $\alpha$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, and suppose that $\deg g=m$.

(a) Show that $g(0)=\pm\alpha^m$.

(b) Deduce that $g(x)=x^m-b$ for some rational number $b$.

(c) Prove that $m$ divides $n$.
answer: (a) The roots of $g\mid x^n-\alpha^n$ are $\varepsilon\alpha$ with $\varepsilon^n=1$, so $g(0)=\delta\alpha^m$ with $\delta$ a root of unity, which is real, so $\delta=\pm1$. (b) $\alpha^m\in\mathbb{Q}$, so $g\mid x^m-\alpha^m$ and comparing degrees $g=x^m-\alpha^m$. (c) Writing $n=qm+r$, $\alpha^r\in\mathbb{Q}$, and $r>0$ would give a polynomial of degree $<m$.

solutions.title: Roots are root-of-unity multiples of $\alpha$
solutions.body:
Let $a=\alpha^n\in\mathbb{Q}$. Then $\alpha$ is a root of $x^n-a\in\mathbb{Q}[x]$, so $g\mid x^n-a$.

**(a)** The complex roots of $x^n-a$ are the numbers $\varepsilon\alpha$ with $\varepsilon^n=1$ (they are $n$ distinct roots, as $\alpha\ne0$). So the roots of $g$ are $\varepsilon_1\alpha,\dots,\varepsilon_m\alpha$ with $\varepsilon_i^n=1$, and
$$g(0)=(-1)^m\prod_{i=1}^m\varepsilon_i\alpha=\delta\,\alpha^m,\qquad \delta=(-1)^m\textstyle\prod\varepsilon_i,$$
where $\delta$ is a root of unity. Since $g(0)\in\mathbb{Q}\subset\mathbb{R}$ and $\alpha^m$ is real and nonzero, $\delta$ is real; the only real roots of unity are $\pm1$. So $g(0)=\pm\alpha^m$.

**(b)** By (a), $b:=\alpha^m=\pm g(0)\in\mathbb{Q}$. Then $\alpha$ is a root of $x^m-b\in\mathbb{Q}[x]$, so $g\mid x^m-b$. Both are monic of degree $m$, hence $g(x)=x^m-b$.

**(c)** Write $n=qm+r$ with $0\le r<m$. Then $\alpha^r=\alpha^n/(\alpha^m)^q\in\mathbb{Q}$, say $\alpha^r=c$. If $r\ge1$, $\alpha$ is a root of $x^r-c$, so $g\mid x^r-c$, impossible as $0<r<m=\deg g$. Hence $r=0$ and $m\mid n$. ∎

prompt: Let $V$ be a finite dimensional vector space over an algebraically closed field $K$ and let $T\colon V\to V$ be a linear operator. Also let $I\colon V\to V$ denote the identity operator. Show that $V$ has a basis consisting of eigenvectors of $T$ if and only if the kernel of $(\lambda I-T)^2$ is equal to the kernel of $\lambda I-T$ for all choices of $\lambda\in K$.
answer: ($\Rightarrow$) In an eigenbasis both kernels are spanned by the basis vectors with eigenvalue $\lambda$. ($\Leftarrow$) If the minimal polynomial $f=\prod(x-\lambda_i)$ had a repeated root $\lambda_1$, write $f=(x-\lambda_1)^2g$; then $g(T)V\subseteq\ker(\lambda_1I-T)^2=\ker(\lambda_1I-T)$, so $(x-\lambda_1)g$ kills $T$, contradicting minimality. A split minimal polynomial with distinct roots means $T$ is diagonalizable.

solutions.title: Minimal polynomial
solutions.body:
**($\Rightarrow$)** Let $v_1,\dots,v_n$ be a basis with $Tv_i=\lambda_iv_i$, and let $\lambda\in K$. For $v=\sum k_iv_i$,
$$(\lambda I-T)v=\sum k_i(\lambda-\lambda_i)v_i,\qquad(\lambda I-T)^2v=\sum k_i(\lambda-\lambda_i)^2v_i.$$
By linear independence, each of these is $0$ iff $k_i=0$ for every $i$ with $\lambda_i\ne\lambda$. So both kernels equal the span of $\{v_i:\lambda_i=\lambda\}$.

**($\Leftarrow$)** Since $K$ is algebraically closed, the minimal polynomial splits: $f(x)=\prod_{i=1}^m(x-\lambda_i)$. Suppose it has a repeated root, say $\lambda_1=\lambda_2$, and put $g(x)=\prod_{i=3}^m(x-\lambda_i)$, so $f=(x-\lambda_1)^2g$. Then $(\lambda_1I-T)^2g(T)V=f(T)V=0$, so $g(T)V\subseteq\ker(\lambda_1I-T)^2=\ker(\lambda_1I-T)$. Hence $(T-\lambda_1I)g(T)=0$, so $T$ satisfies $(x-\lambda_1)g(x)$ of degree $m-1$, contradicting minimality. So $f$ has distinct roots.

Finally, a split minimal polynomial with distinct roots gives an eigenbasis: the polynomials $f_i=f/(x-\lambda_i)$ have no common root, so they are coprime and $1=\sum_if_ih_i$ for some $h_i\in K[x]$. Then every $v=\sum_if_i(T)h_i(T)v$, and $(T-\lambda_iI)f_i(T)h_i(T)v=f(T)h_i(T)v=0$, so $V=\sum_iE_{\lambda_i}$ is a sum of eigenspaces. The sum is direct (eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are independent), so the union of bases of the eigenspaces is a basis of eigenvectors. ∎

prompt:
Let $R$ be a ring with $1$ and let $V$ be a right $R$-module. Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are $R$-submodules of $V$ such that $V=X\dotplus Y$, the (internal) direct sum. If $\theta$ is any $R$-homomorphism from $X$ to $Y$, define $W_\theta\subseteq V$ to be the set of elements $x-\theta(x)\in V$ for all $x\in X$.

(a) Show that $W_\theta$ is an $R$-submodule of $V$ and that $V=W_\theta\dotplus Y$.

(b) Conversely, suppose $U$ is an $R$-submodule of $V$ such that $V=U\dotplus Y$. Prove that $U=W_\theta$ for some $R$-homomorphism $\theta\colon X\to Y$.
answer: (a) $W_\theta$ is the image of the homomorphism $x\mapsto x-\theta(x)$; $x=(x-\theta x)+\theta x$ gives $V=W_\theta+Y$, and $x-\theta x\in Y$ forces $x\in X\cap Y=0$. (b) Let $\theta\colon X\to Y$ be the restriction to $X$ of the projection $V=U\dotplus Y\to Y$; then $x-\theta(x)\in U$, so $W_\theta\subseteq U$, and conversely each $u=x-y$ has $y=\theta(x)$.

solutions.title: Graphs of homomorphisms
solutions.body:
**(a)** The map $\phi\colon X\to V$, $\phi(x)=x-\theta(x)$, is an $R$-homomorphism, and $W_\theta=\phi(X)$, so $W_\theta$ is a submodule. For $x\in X$, $x=(x-\theta(x))+\theta(x)\in W_\theta+Y$; so $X\subseteq W_\theta+Y$ and $V=X+Y=W_\theta+Y$. If $w=x-\theta(x)\in W_\theta\cap Y$, then $x=w+\theta(x)\in X\cap Y=0$, so $x=0$ and $w=0$. Hence $V=W_\theta\dotplus Y$.

**(b)** Let $\pi\colon V=U\dotplus Y\to Y$ be the projection along $U$ (an $R$-homomorphism) and $\theta=\pi|_X\colon X\to Y$. For $x\in X$, write $x=u+\theta(x)$ with $u\in U$; then $x-\theta(x)=u\in U$, so $W_\theta\subseteq U$.

Conversely, let $u\in U$ and write $u=x-y$ with $x\in X$, $y\in Y$ (possible since $V=X\dotplus Y$). Then $x=u+y$ is the decomposition of $x$ in $U\dotplus Y$, so $\theta(x)=\pi(x)=y$ and $u=x-\theta(x)\in W_\theta$. Thus $U=W_\theta$. ∎

prompt:
Let $G$ be a finite group having the property that for every choice of two subgroups $X\subseteq G$ and $Y\subseteq G$, either $X\cap Y=1$ or $X\subseteq Y$ or $Y\subseteq X$.

(i) If $H\subseteq G$, show that either $|H|$ is a prime power or else that $|H|$ and $|G:H|$ are relatively prime.

(ii) If $1<N\trianglelefteq G$, prove that $G/N$ is nilpotent.

(iii) If $N\trianglelefteq G$ and $N\neq G$, show that $N$ is nilpotent.
answer:
(i) If $|H|$ is not a prime power, each Sylow $p$-subgroup $P$ of $G$ meeting $H$ in a Sylow subgroup $
e1$ of $H$ must lie in $H$. (ii) Two Sylow subgroups $P/N,Q/N$ for different primes would give incomparable $P,Q$ with $P\cap Q=N
e1$; so $G/N$ is a $p$-group. (iii) For $1
e P\in\mathrm{Syl}_p(N)$, Frattini gives $G=NN_G(P)$, and $N_G(P)\cap N
e1$ forces $N\subseteq N_G(P)$, so every Sylow subgroup of $N$ is normal.

solutions.title: Comparability of subgroups
solutions.body:
**(i)** Suppose $|H|$ is not a prime power, and let $p$ be a prime dividing $|H|$. Let $Q\in\mathrm{Syl}_p(H)$ and choose $P\in\mathrm{Syl}_p(G)$ with $Q\subseteq P$. Then $P\cap H\supseteq Q
e1$, so $P\subseteq H$ or $H\subseteq P$. The latter would make $H$ a $p$-group, contrary to assumption. Hence $P\subseteq H$, so the full $p$-part of $|G|$ divides $|H|$ and $p
mid|G:H|$. As this holds for every prime $p$ dividing $|H|$, $\gcd(|H|,|G:H|)=1$.

**(ii)** We show $G/N$ is a $p$-group for some prime $p$ (or trivial), hence nilpotent. Suppose distinct primes $p,q$ divide $|G/N|$, and take $P,Q$ with $N\subseteq P,Q$, $P/N\in\mathrm{Syl}_p(G/N)$, $Q/N\in\mathrm{Syl}_q(G/N)$, both nontrivial. Then $(P\cap Q)/N\subseteq P/N\cap Q/N=1$, so $P\cap Q=N
e1$. Hence $P\subseteq Q$ or $Q\subseteq P$; but $P\subseteq Q$ would make the nontrivial $p$-group $P/N$ a subgroup of the $q$-group $Q/N$, impossible, and symmetrically. Contradiction.

**(iii)** A finite group is nilpotent iff all its Sylow subgroups are normal. Let $P\in\mathrm{Syl}_p(N)$ with $P
e1$. By the Frattini argument, $G=N\,N_G(P)$. Now $N_G(P)\cap N\supseteq P
e1$, so $N_G(P)\subseteq N$ or $N\subseteq N_G(P)$. In the first case $G=N\,N_G(P)=N$, contradicting $N
e G$. So $N\subseteq N_G(P)$, i.e. $P	rianglelefteq N$. Thus every Sylow subgroup of $N$ is normal and $N$ is nilpotent. ∎

prompt: Let $R$ be a ring, let $V$ be a right $R$-module, and suppose that $V=V_1\dotplus V_2\dotplus V_3\dotplus\cdots$ is the (internal) direct sum of its submodules $V_1,V_2,V_3,\ldots$. Show that $V$ is an Artinian module if and only if each $V_i$ is Artinian and only finitely many of the $V_i$'s are nonzero.
answer: ($\Rightarrow$) Submodules of Artinian modules are Artinian, and the chain $W_i=V_i\dotplus V_{i+1}\dotplus\cdots$ stabilizes, forcing $V_i=0$ for large $i$. ($\Leftarrow$) Induction on the number of nonzero summands, using that an extension of an Artinian module by an Artinian module is Artinian.

solutions.title: Tail chain and extensions
solutions.body:
**($\Rightarrow$)** Submodules of $V_i$ are submodules of $V$, so each $V_i$ inherits the descending chain condition. For $i\ge1$ let $W_i=V_i\dotplus V_{i+1}\dotplus\cdots$. Then $W_1\supseteq W_2\supseteq\cdots$ is a descending chain, so there is $n$ with $W_i=W_{i+1}$ for all $i\ge n$. But $W_i=V_i\dotplus W_{i+1}$ is a direct sum, so $W_i=W_{i+1}$ forces $V_i=V_i\cap W_{i+1}=0$. Hence $V_i=0$ for all $i\ge n$.

**($\Leftarrow$)** We may assume $V=V_1\dotplus\cdots\dotplus V_n$. Recall: if $W\subseteq V$ with $W$ and $V/W$ Artinian, then $V$ is Artinian. (Proof: given $U_1\supseteq U_2\supseteq\cdots$, the chains $U_k\cap W$ and $(U_k+W)/W$ stabilize, say for $k\ge k_0$; then for $k\ge k_0$, $U_{k+1}\subseteq U_k$ with $U_{k+1}\cap W=U_k\cap W$ and $U_{k+1}+W=U_k+W$, and the modular law gives $U_k=U_k\cap(U_{k+1}+W)=U_{k+1}+(U_k\cap W)=U_{k+1}$.)

Induct on $n$; $n=1$ is given. For $n>1$ let $W=V_1\dotplus\cdots\dotplus V_{n-1}$, Artinian by induction. Then $V/W\cong V_n$ is Artinian, so $V$ is Artinian. ∎

prompt:
Let $f(x)\in\mathbb{Q}[x]$ be a polynomial of degree $5$ over the rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$ that is not solvable by radicals, and let $S$ be the splitting field of $f(x)$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ which is contained in the complex numbers.

(i) Show that there exists at most one subfield $E$ of $S$ such that $|E:\mathbb{Q}|=2$.

(ii) If $\alpha,\beta\in S$ are irrational elements which satisfy $\alpha^2\in\mathbb{Q}$ and $\beta^2\in\mathbb{Q}$, prove that $\alpha\beta\in\mathbb{Q}$.
answer: (i) $G=\mathrm{Gal}(S/\mathbb{Q})$ is a nonsolvable subgroup of $S_5$, hence $A_5$ or $S_5$, which have $0$ resp. $1$ subgroups of index 2. (ii) Then $\mathbb{Q}[\alpha]=\mathbb{Q}[\beta]$, so $\beta=a\alpha+b$; squaring forces $b=0$, so $\alpha\beta=a\alpha^2\in\mathbb{Q}$.

solutions.title: Nonsolvable subgroups of $S_5$
solutions.body:
**(i)** $S/\mathbb{Q}$ is Galois with group $G$, which acts faithfully on the $\le5$ roots of $f$, so $G\le S_5$. Since $f$ is not solvable by radicals, $G$ is not solvable (Galois).

*Claim: $G=A_5$ or $G=S_5$.* By Burnside's $p^aq^b$ theorem, $|G|$ is divisible by $2$, $3$ and $5$, so $30\mid|G|$, and $|G|\mid120$; so $|G|\in\{30,60,120\}$. A group of order $30$ is solvable (a group of order $2m$ with $m$ odd has a normal subgroup of index $2$, here of order $15$, which is cyclic). If $|G|=120$, $G=S_5$. If $|G|=60$, $G$ has index $2$ in $S_5$, hence is normal, so $G\cap A_5\trianglelefteq A_5$ with $|A_5:G\cap A_5|\le2$; as $A_5$ is simple and has no subgroup of index $2$, $G\cap A_5=A_5$, so $G=A_5$.

Subfields $E$ with $|E:\mathbb{Q}|=2$ correspond to subgroups $H\le G$ of index $2$. Such $H$ is normal with abelian quotient, so $H\supseteq G'$. For $G=A_5$, $G'=A_5$, so no $H$ exists. For $G=S_5$, $G'=A_5$ has index $2$, so $H=A_5$ is the only one. Hence there is at most one such $E$.

**(ii)** $\mathbb{Q}[\alpha]$ and $\mathbb{Q}[\beta]$ are subfields of $S$ of degree $2$ (as $\alpha,\beta\notin\mathbb{Q}$ have degree-2 minimal polynomials $x^2-\alpha^2$, $x^2-\beta^2$). By (i) they are equal, so $\beta=a\alpha+b$ with $a,b\in\mathbb{Q}$. Then $\beta^2=a^2\alpha^2+b^2+2ab\alpha$, so $2ab\alpha\in\mathbb{Q}$, hence $ab=0$ (as $\alpha\notin\mathbb{Q}$). If $a=0$, $\beta=b\in\mathbb{Q}$, a contradiction. So $b=0$, $\beta=a\alpha$ and $\alpha\beta=a\alpha^2\in\mathbb{Q}$. ∎

prompt:
If $K$ is a field, then the general linear group $G=GL_n(K)$ is the multiplicative group of $n\times n$ invertible matrices over $K$.

(i) If the characteristic of $K$ is not equal to $2$, show that $G$ has precisely $n$ conjugacy classes of elements of order $2$.

(ii) If $\mathrm{char}\,K=2$, show that $G$ has precisely $[n/2]$ (the greatest integer in $n/2$) conjugacy classes of elements of order $2$.
answer: Conjugacy in $GL_n(K)$ is similarity. (i) $X^2=I$ with $x^2-1$ separable: $X\sim\mathrm{diag}(-I_r,I_{n-r})$, $1\le r\le n$, distinguished by $r=\mathrm{rank}(I-X)$. (ii) $(X-I)^2=0$: Jordan form with $r$ blocks $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, $1\le r\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, again $r=\mathrm{rank}(I-X)$.

solutions.title: Canonical forms of involutions
solutions.body:
Two invertible matrices are conjugate in $G$ iff they are similar, so we count similarity classes of $X$ with $X^2=I
e X$. Similar matrices have the same rank of $I-X$.

**(i)** $\mathrm{char}K
e2$. $X$ satisfies $x^2-1=(x-1)(x+1)$, a product of distinct linear factors, so $X$ is diagonalizable over $K$ with eigenvalues in $\{1,-1\}$. Thus $X\sim D_r=\mathrm{diag}(-1,\dots,-1,1,\dots,1)$ with $r$ entries $-1$. Since $X
eq I$, $r\ge1$; and $r=\mathrm{rank}(I-D_r)$, since $I-D_r=\mathrm{diag}(2,\dots,2,0,\dots,0)$ and $2
e0$. So $D_1,\dots,D_n$ are pairwise non-similar, each has order exactly $2$, and every involution is similar to one of them: exactly $n$ classes.

**(ii)** $\mathrm{char}K=2$. Now $X^2-I=(X-I)^2=0$, so the minimal polynomial divides $(x-1)^2$; the characteristic polynomial is $(x-1)^n$, which splits over $K$, so $X$ has a Jordan form over $K$ with eigenvalue $1$ and blocks of size $\le2$. Hence $X\sim D_r=\mathrm{diag}(J,\dots,J,1,\dots,1)$ with $r$ copies of $J= egin{pmatrix}1&1\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, where $2r\le n$; and $X
e I$ forces $r\ge1$. Conversely each $D_r$ ($r\ge1$) has $D_r^2=I$ (as $J^2= egin{pmatrix}1&2\0&1\end{pmatrix}=I$) and $D_r
e I$. Finally $I-D_r$ has exactly $r$ nonzero entries, one in each of $r$ distinct rows and columns, so $\mathrm{rank}(I-D_r)=r$, and different $r$ give non-similar matrices. So there are exactly $\lfloor n/2floor$ classes. ∎

prompt: Let $S$ be a commutative integral domain and let $R$ be a subring of $S$ with the same identity $1$. Suppose that there exist finitely many elements $s_1,s_2,\ldots,s_n\in S$ such that $S=s_1R+s_2R+\cdots+s_nR$. Show that $R$ is a field if and only if $S$ is a field.
answer: $S$ is a finitely generated $R$-module, hence integral over $R$. If $R$ is a field, multiplication by $s\ne0$ is an injective $R$-linear map of the finite-dimensional space $S$, hence surjective. If $S$ is a field and $0\ne r\in R$, an integral equation for $r^{-1}$ multiplied by $r^{n-1}$ shows $r^{-1}\in R$.

solutions.title: Integrality
solutions.body:
Since $S$ is a commutative ring that is a finitely generated $R$-module, every $s\in S$ is integral over $R$ (determinant trick / Cayley–Hamilton).

**$R$ a field $\Rightarrow$ $S$ a field.** $S$ is a finite-dimensional $R$-vector space. Let $0\ne s\in S$. The map $\mu_s\colon S\to S$, $t\mapsto st$, is $R$-linear and injective because $S$ is a domain. An injective linear map of a finite-dimensional space is surjective, so $st=1$ for some $t$. Hence $S$ is a field.

(Alternatively: take a monic relation $s^n+r_{n-1}s^{n-1}+\cdots+r_0=0$ of minimal degree; minimality and $S$ being a domain give $r_0\ne0$, and then $s^{-1}=-r_0^{-1}(s^{n-1}+\cdots+r_1)$.)

**$S$ a field $\Rightarrow$ $R$ a field.** Let $0\ne r\in R$. Then $r^{-1}\in S$ is integral over $R$: $(r^{-1})^n+c_{n-1}(r^{-1})^{n-1}+\cdots+c_0=0$ with $c_i\in R$. Multiplying by $r^{n-1}$:
$$r^{-1}=-(c_{n-1}+c_{n-2}r+\cdots+c_0r^{n-1})\in R.$$
So every nonzero element of $R$ is invertible in $R$, and $R$ is a field. ∎

prompt:
If $G$ is a finite group, we define $\mathrm{soc}(G)$ to be the subgroup generated by all the minimal normal subgroups of $G$.

(a) If $\langle1\rangle\neq N\trianglelefteq G$, show that $N\cap\mathrm{soc}(G)\neq\langle1\rangle$.

(b) Prove that $\mathrm{soc}(\mathrm{soc}(G))=\mathrm{soc}(G)$.

(c) If $\mathrm{soc}(G)=G$, show that every minimal normal subgroup of $G$ is simple.
answer: (a) $N$ contains a minimal normal subgroup of $G$. (b) $S=\mathrm{soc}(G)$ is characteristic, so $\mathrm{soc}(S)\trianglelefteq G$; each minimal normal $N$ of $G$ meets $\mathrm{soc}(S)$ nontrivially by (a) applied in $S$, so $N\subseteq\mathrm{soc}(S)$. (c) For $1\ne H\trianglelefteq M$ ($M$ minimal normal), every other minimal normal $N$ centralizes $M$, so $N_G(H)\supseteq\langle\text{all minimal normals}\rangle=G$ and $H=M$.

solutions.title: Minimal normal subgroups
solutions.body:
**(a)** $G$ is finite and $N\ne1$, so among the nontrivial normal subgroups of $G$ contained in $N$ there is a minimal one, $M$; it is a minimal normal subgroup of $G$, so $M\subseteq\mathrm{soc}(G)$ and $N\cap\mathrm{soc}(G)\supseteq M\ne1$.

**(b)** Let $S=\mathrm{soc}(G)$. Clearly $\mathrm{soc}(S)\subseteq S$. Automorphisms of $G$ permute the minimal normal subgroups of $G$, so $S$ is characteristic in $G$; similarly $\mathrm{soc}(S)$ is characteristic in $S$, hence normal in $G$. Let $N$ be a minimal normal subgroup of $G$. Then $1\ne N\subseteq S$ and $N\trianglelefteq S$, so by (a) applied to the group $S$, $N\cap\mathrm{soc}(S)\ne1$. But $N\cap\mathrm{soc}(S)\trianglelefteq G$ and $N$ is minimal normal in $G$, so $N\cap\mathrm{soc}(S)=N$, i.e. $N\subseteq\mathrm{soc}(S)$. Since $S$ is generated by such $N$, $S\subseteq\mathrm{soc}(S)$. Hence equality.

**(c)** Let $G=\mathrm{soc}(G)$, $M$ a minimal normal subgroup, and $1\ne H\trianglelefteq M$. Let $N$ be any minimal normal subgroup of $G$.
- If $N\ne M$, then $M\cap N$ is normal in $G$ and properly contained in $M$ or $N$, so $M\cap N=1$; hence $[M,N]\subseteq M\cap N=1$, $N$ centralizes $M\supseteq H$, so $N$ normalizes $H$.
- If $N=M$, then $N$ normalizes $H$ because $H\trianglelefteq M$.

Thus $N_G(H)$ contains every minimal normal subgroup, so $N_G(H)\supseteq\mathrm{soc}(G)=G$ and $H\trianglelefteq G$. By minimality of $M$, $H=M$. So $M$ has no normal subgroups other than $1$ and $M$, i.e. $M$ is simple. ∎

(a) Show that each $I_q$ is a nonzero ideal of $R$.

(b) If $M$ is a maximal ideal of $R$, let $R_M=\{a/b\in F\mid a\in R,\ b\in R,\ b\notin M\}$ and recall that $R_M$ is a subring of $F$ that contains $R$. Prove that $R=\bigcap_M R_M$, where the latter intersection is over all maximal ideals $M$ of $R$.

e R$; a generator $\alpha$ would divide both, have norm dividing 4, not 1 or 2, so $\alpha=\pm(1+\sqrt{-3})$ and $\alpha=\pm2$ simultaneously.

**(a)** If $r,s\in I_q$ and $t\in R$, then $(r+s)q=rq+sq\in R$ and $(tr)q=t(rq)\in R$; also $0\in I_q$. So $I_q$ is an ideal. Writing $q=a/b$ with $a,b\in R$, $b
e0$, we get $bq=a\in R$, so $0

**(b)** Each $R_M\supseteq R$, so $R\subseteq igcap_MR_M$. Conversely let $q\in igcap_MR_M$. If $I_q
e R$, it lies in some maximal ideal $M$. As $q\in R_M$, $q=a/b$ with $b

prompt:
Let $F$ be a field and suppose $f(x)\in F[x]$ is an irreducible polynomial. Fix an integer $n$ and let $g(x)=f(x^n)$.

(a) If $h(x)$ is any irreducible factor of $g(x)$ in $F[x]$, show that the degree of $h(x)$ is a multiple of the degree of $f(x)$.

(b) Now suppose that $F$ has characteristic $0$ and that it contains a primitive $n$th root of unity. Show that all irreducible factors of $g(x)$ in $F[x]$ have equal degrees.
answer: (a) For a root $\alpha$ of $h$, $\alpha^n$ is a root of $f$, so $\deg h=|F(\alpha):F(\alpha^n)|\cdot\deg f$. (b) For roots $\alpha,\beta$ of two factors, an $F$-isomorphism $F(\alpha^n)\to F(\beta^n)$ extends to an automorphism $\tau$ of the splitting field $E$ of $g$; $\tau(\alpha)=\varepsilon\beta$ with $\varepsilon\in F$, so $F(\alpha)\cong F(\beta)$ and the degrees agree.

solutions.title: Tower of degrees and extending isomorphisms
solutions.body:
Work inside an algebraic closure of $F$; take $n\ge1$.

**(a)** Let $\alpha$ be a root of $h$. Since $h$ is irreducible, $\deg h=|F(\alpha):F|$. As $h\mid g$, $f(\alpha^n)=g(\alpha)=0$, and $f$ is irreducible, so $\deg f=|F(\alpha^n):F|$. Since $F\subseteq F(\alpha^n)\subseteq F(\alpha)$,
$$\deg h=|F(\alpha):F(\alpha^n)|\cdot|F(\alpha^n):F|=|F(\alpha):F(\alpha^n)|\cdot\deg f.$$

**(b)** Let $E$ be a splitting field of $g$ over $F$, and let $h,k$ be irreducible factors of $g$ with roots $\alpha,\beta\in E$. Then $\alpha^n,\beta^n$ are roots of the irreducible $f$, so there is an $F$-isomorphism $\sigma\colon F(\alpha^n)\to F(\beta^n)$ with $\sigma(\alpha^n)=\beta^n$. $E$ is a splitting field of $g$ over $F(\alpha^n)$ and over $F(\beta^n)$, and $\sigma$ fixes the coefficients of $g\in F[x]$. By uniqueness of splitting fields, $\sigma$ extends to an isomorphism $\tau\colon E\to E$ fixing $F$.

Now $\tau(\alpha)^n=\tau(\alpha^n)=\beta^n$, so $\tau(\alpha)=\varepsilon\beta$ for some $n$th root of unity $\varepsilon$ (all $n$th roots of $\beta^n$ are $\zeta^i\beta$ where $\zeta\in F$ is the given primitive root; if $\beta=0$ then $\tau(\alpha)=0$). So $\varepsilon\in F$ and $F(\tau(\alpha))=F(\varepsilon\beta)=F(\beta)$. Since $\tau$ restricts to an $F$-isomorphism $F(\alpha)\to F(\tau(\alpha))=F(\beta)$,
$$\deg h=|F(\alpha):F|=|F(\beta):F|=\deg k.$$ ∎

prompt:
Let $V$ be a finite dimensional vector space over the field $K$ and let $(\ ,\ )\colon V\times V\to K$ be a symmetric bilinear form. For any subspace $U$ of $V$, we let $U^\perp=\{v\in V\mid(U,v)=0\}$. Thus $U^\perp$ is also a subspace of $V$, and the form is nonsingular precisely when $V^\perp=0$.

(a) Show that $\dim U+\dim U^\perp\ge\dim V$ for any subspace $U$ of $V$.

(b) If the form is nonsingular and if $V=U+X$ is the sum of subspaces $U$ and $X$, prove that $\dim U^\perp+\dim X^\perp\le\dim V$.

(c) If the form is nonsingular, show that $\dim U+\dim U^\perp=\dim V$ for any subspace $U$ of $V$.
answer: (a) $U^\perp$ is the kernel of $v\mapsto((u_i,v))_i\in K^r$. (b) $U^\perp\cap X^\perp=(U+X)^\perp=V^\perp=0$. (c) With $X$ a complement of $U$: $\dim U^\perp\le\dim V-\dim X^\perp\le\dim X$ by (b) and (a), so $\dim U+\dim U^\perp\le\dim V$; combine with (a).

solutions.title: Rank–nullity
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $u_1,\dots,u_r$ be a basis of $U$ and define $T\colon V\to K^r$, $T(v)=((u_1,v),\dots,(u_r,v))$. $T$ is linear and $\ker T=U^\perp$ (a vector orthogonal to a basis of $U$ is orthogonal to $U$). By rank–nullity, $\dim V=\dim\operatorname{im}T+\dim U^\perp\le r+\dim U^\perp$.

**(b)** A vector in $U^\perp\cap X^\perp$ is orthogonal to $U+X=V$, so $U^\perp\cap X^\perp=V^\perp=0$. Hence $U^\perp+X^\perp$ is direct and $\dim U^\perp+\dim X^\perp=\dim(U^\perp\oplus X^\perp)\le\dim V$.

**(c)** Choose a complement $X$ with $V=U\oplus X$. By (b) and (a) (applied to $X$),
$$\dim U^\perp+\dim X^\perp\le\dim V\le\dim X+\dim X^\perp,$$
so $\dim U^\perp\le\dim X$. Thus $\dim U+\dim U^\perp\le\dim U+\dim X=\dim V$, and (a) gives the reverse inequality. ∎

prompt:
Let $A$ be a (not necessarily finite) abelian group and let $B$ be a subgroup of $A$.

(a) If $B$ is a direct factor of $A$, show that $B$ is a direct factor of every subgroup $C$ satisfying $B\subseteq C\subseteq A$.

(b) Conversely, assume that $B$ is a direct factor of every subgroup $C$ such that $B\subseteq C\subseteq A$ and $C/B$ is cyclic. If $|A:B|<\infty$, show that $B$ is a direct factor of $A$.
answer: (a) If $A=B\oplus X$, the modular law gives $C=B\oplus(X\cap C)$. (b) Write the finite group $A/B=\bigoplus\bar C_i$ with $\bar C_i$ cyclic, split $C_i=B\oplus X_i$, and check $A=B\oplus(X_1+\cdots+X_n)$.

solutions.title: Modular law and cyclic decomposition
solutions.body:
Write $A$ additively.

**(a)** Let $A=B\oplus X$ and $B\subseteq C\subseteq A$. By the modular law (valid since $B\subseteq C$), $C=(B+X)\cap C=B+(X\cap C)$, and $B\cap(X\cap C)\subseteq B\cap X=0$. So $C=B\oplus(X\cap C)$.

**(b)** $\bar A=A/B$ is a finite abelian group, so $\bar A=\bar C_1\oplus\cdots\oplus\bar C_n$ with each $\bar C_i$ cyclic. Let $C_i\supseteq B$ be the preimage of $\bar C_i$. By hypothesis $C_i=B\oplus X_i$ for some subgroup $X_i$. Put $X=X_1+\cdots+X_n$.

- $A=B+X$: since $\bar A=\sum\bar C_i$, $A=C_1+\cdots+C_n=\sum(B+X_i)=B+X$.
- $B\cap X=0$: if $a=x_1+\cdots+x_n\in B$ with $x_i\in X_i$, then $0=\bar a=\bar x_1+\cdots+\bar x_n$ with $\bar x_i\in\bar C_i$; as the sum of the $\bar C_i$ is direct, each $\bar x_i=0$, i.e. $x_i\in B\cap X_i=0$. So $a=0$.

Hence $A=B\oplus X$. ∎

prompt:
Fix a prime $p$ and let $G$ be a finite group with the property that every nonidentity $p$-subgroup of $G$ is contained in a unique Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$. Suppose $N\trianglelefteq G$ and $|N|$ is divisible by $p$.

(i) If $P$ and $Q$ are Sylow $p$-subgroups of $G$, show that $Q=P^n$ for some element $n\in N$.

(ii) Prove that $G/N$ has a unique Sylow $p$-subgroup.
answer: (i) $P\cap N,\,Q\cap N\in\mathrm{Syl}_p(N)$, so $Q\cap N=(P\cap N)^n$ with $n\in N$; the nonidentity $p$-group $Q\cap N$ lies in both $Q$ and $P^n$, so $Q=P^n$. (ii) Sylow subgroups of $G/N$ are images $PN/N$, and $P^nN/N=PN/N$.

solutions.title: Sylow in the normal subgroup
solutions.body:
**(i)** Since $N\trianglelefteq G$, $P\cap N$ and $Q\cap N$ are Sylow $p$-subgroups of $N$. By Sylow's theorem in $N$, $Q\cap N=(P\cap N)^n$ for some $n\in N$. Because $p$ divides $|N|$, $Q\cap N\neq1$. Now $Q\supseteq Q\cap N$ and $P^n\supseteq(P\cap N)^n=Q\cap N$, and $P^n$ is a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$. By uniqueness of the Sylow $p$-subgroup containing $Q\cap N$, $Q=P^n$.

**(ii)** Let $\bar{\ }\colon G\to G/N$. Every Sylow $p$-subgroup of $\bar G$ is the image $\bar P$ of some $P\in\mathrm{Syl}_p(G)$. Given two, $\bar P$ and $\bar Q$, (i) gives $Q=P^n$ with $n\in N$, so $\bar Q=\bar P^{\bar n}=\bar P$ since $\bar n=1$. So $G/N$ has a unique Sylow $p$-subgroup. ∎

prompt:
Let $R$ be a commutative domain and write $(a)$ for the principal ideal generated by $a\in R$. Recall that an element of $R$ is said to be irreducible if it is nonzero, not a unit, and has no proper factorization.

(i) Show that $(a)\subseteq(b)$ if and only if $b\mid a$, and that $(a)=(b)$ if and only if $b=au$ for some unit $u\in R$.

(ii) If $R$ is a UFD (unique factorization domain), prove that the set of principal ideals of $R$ satisfies the maximal condition.

(iii) If the set of principal ideals of $R$ satisfies the maximal condition, show that every nonzero, nonunit element of $R$ can be written as a finite product of irreducible elements.
answer: (i) $(a)\subseteq(b)\iff a\in(b)$; mutual divisibility plus cancellation gives a unit. (ii) Choose $(a)$ in the family with the fewest prime factors; a strictly larger $(b)$ would have $b$ a proper divisor with fewer prime factors. (iii) A maximal counterexample $(a)$ factors as $bc$ with $(b),(c)\supsetneq(a)$, which are products of irreducibles.

solutions.title: Counting prime factors
solutions.body:
**(i)** $(a)\subseteq(b)$ iff $a\in(b)$ iff $a=bc$ for some $c$, i.e. $b\mid a$. Hence $(a)=(b)$ iff $a\mid b$ and $b\mid a$. If $b=au$ with $u$ a unit, then $a=bu^{-1}$ and clearly $(a)=(b)$. Conversely, if $b=au$ and $a=bv$, then $a=avu$. If $a=0$ then $b=0$ and $b=a\cdot1$. If $a
e0$, cancellation in the domain gives $vu=1$, so $u$ is a unit.

**(ii)** For $0
eq a\in R$, write $a=up_1\cdots p_k$ ($u$ a unit, $p_i$ prime) and let $\ell(a)=k$, well defined by uniqueness; $\ell(a)=0$ iff $a$ is a unit. For $a=bc$ with $a
e0$, $\ell(a)=\ell(b)+\ell(c)$. Let $\mathcal P$ be a nonempty set of principal ideals. If $\mathcal P=\{0\}$, $0$ is maximal. Otherwise choose $(a)\in\mathcal P$, $a
e0$, with $\ell(a)$ minimal. If $(b)\in\mathcal P$ and $(b)\supseteq(a)$, then $b
eq0$ and $a=bc$, so $\ell(c)=\ell(a)-\ell(b)\le0$ by minimality, i.e. $c$ is a unit and $(a)=(b)$ by (i). So $(a)$ is maximal in $\mathcal P$.

**(iii)** Let $\mathcal C$ be the set of principal ideals $(a)$ with $a$ nonzero, nonunit, and not a finite product of irreducibles (this depends only on $(a)$, since associates of irreducibles are irreducible). Suppose $\mathcal C
e\emptyset$ and let $(a)$ be a maximal member. Then $a$ is not irreducible, so $a=bc$ with $b,c$ nonunits (both nonzero). Then $(b),(c)\supseteq(a)$, and $(b)=(a)$ would give $b=au$, so $a=auc$, $uc=1$, contradicting that $c$ is not a unit; similarly $(c)
e(a)$. By maximality $(b),(c)
otin\mathcal C$, and $b,c$ are nonzero nonunits, so each is a finite product of irreducibles, hence so is $a=bc$ — a contradiction. So $\mathcal C=\emptyset$. ∎

prompt:
Let $p$ be a prime, let $F\subseteq K$ be fields of characteristic $0$, and assume that $F$ contains a primitive $p$th root of unity. Fix $a\in K$.

(i) Prove that there exists a field $E\supseteq K$ such that $E$ contains a $p$th root of $a$ and $|E:K|=1$ or $p$.

(ii) Now assume that $K$ is a finite degree Galois extension of $F$. Show that there exists a field $E\supseteq K$ such that $E$ contains a $p$th root of $a$, $E$ is Galois over $F$, and $|E:K|$ is a power of $p$.
answer: (i) Let $E$ be the splitting field of $x^p-a$ over $K$; any one root generates it (roots differ by $p$th roots of unity in $F$), so all irreducible factors have degree $|E:K|$, which divides $p$. (ii) Adjoin to $K$ the roots of $\prod_{\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)}(x^p-\sigma(a))\in F[x]$ one factor at a time; $E$ is a splitting field over $F$, and each step has degree $1$ or $p$ by (i).

solutions.title: Kummer-type towers
solutions.body:
Work in a fixed algebraic closure of $K$; let $\zeta\in F$ be a primitive $p$th root of unity.

**(i)** Let $f=x^p-a$ and let $E$ be its splitting field over $K$. If $a=0$, $E=K$. Otherwise, if $\beta$ is any root, the roots of $f$ are $\zeta^i\beta$ ($0\le i<p$), so $K[\beta]=E$. Factor $f=g_1\cdots g_r$ into irreducibles in $K[x]$, and let $\beta_j$ be a root of $g_j$. Then $\deg g_j=|K[\beta_j]:K|=|E:K|$ for every $j$, so $p=\deg f=r\,|E:K|$. As $p$ is prime, $|E:K|\in\{1,p\}$. Clearly $E$ contains a $p$th root of $a$.

**(ii)** Let $K$ be the splitting field over $F$ of some $g\in F[x]$, and let $\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)=\{\sigma_1=1,\sigma_2,\dots,\sigma_n\}$. Put $h(x)=\prod_{i=1}^n(x^p-\sigma_i(a))$. Its coefficients are fixed by $\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$ (which permutes the factors), so $h\in F[x]$. Let $E$ be the splitting field of $gh$ over $F$; it contains $K$ and a $p$th root of $a$, and $E/F$ is Galois (a splitting field in characteristic $0$).

For $0\le j\le n$ let $E_j$ be the field generated over $K$ by the roots of $\prod_{i\le j}(x^p-\sigma_i(a))$, so $K=E_0\subseteq E_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq E_n=E$. $E_j$ is the splitting field of $x^p-\sigma_j(a)$ over $E_{j-1}$, and $F\subseteq E_{j-1}$ contains $\zeta$, so by (i) $|E_j:E_{j-1}|\in\{1,p\}$. Therefore $|E:K|=\prod_j|E_j:E_{j-1}|$ is a power of $p$. ∎

prompt:
Let $V$ be a finite dimensional vector space over a field of characteristic $0$. Suppose $T\colon V\to V$ is a linear operator such that the trace $\mathrm{tr}\,T^k=0$ for all integers $k\ge1$.

(i) Show that the constant term of the characteristic polynomial of $T$ is zero, and deduce that $T(V)\neq V$.

(ii) Let $S$ denote the restriction of $T$ to the subspace $T(V)$, so that $S$ is a linear operator on $T(V)$. Prove that $\mathrm{tr}\,S^k=0$ for all integers $k\ge1$.

(iii) Show that $T$ is nilpotent.
answer: (i) Take the trace of Cayley–Hamilton $T^n+a_1T^{n-1}+\cdots+a_nI=0$: $na_n=0$, so $a_n=0$, $\det T=0$. (ii) In a basis extending one of $T(V)$, $T=\begin{pmatrix}A&*\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, so $\mathrm{tr}\,S^k=\mathrm{tr}\,A^k=\mathrm{tr}\,T^k$. (iii) Induction on $\dim V$: $S$ is nilpotent, so $T^{j+1}=S^jT=0$.

solutions.title: Cayley–Hamilton and induction
solutions.body:
Let $n=\dim V$.

**(i)** Let $\chi(x)=x^n+a_1x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_{n-1}x+a_n$ be the characteristic polynomial. By Cayley–Hamilton, $0=T^n+a_1T^{n-1}+\cdots+a_{n-1}T+a_nI$. Taking traces (trace is linear) and using $\mathrm{tr}\,T^k=0$ for $k\ge1$, we get $0=a_n\,\mathrm{tr}\,I=na_n$. In characteristic $0$, $n\neq0$ (for $n\ge1$), so $a_n=0$. Since $\det T=\pm a_n=0$, $T$ is singular, hence not surjective: $T(V)\ne V$.

**(ii)** $T(T(V))\subseteq T(V)$, so $S$ is well defined. Choose a basis of $T(V)$ and extend it to a basis of $V$. Since $T$ maps $V$ into $T(V)$, its matrix (columns = images) is $B=\begin{pmatrix}A&C\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, where $A$ is the matrix of $S$. Then $B^k=\begin{pmatrix}A^k&A^{k-1}C\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, so $\mathrm{tr}\,S^k=\mathrm{tr}\,A^k=\mathrm{tr}\,B^k=\mathrm{tr}\,T^k=0$.

**(iii)** Induct on $n$; for $n=0$ there is nothing to prove. For $n\ge1$, $\dim T(V)<n$ by (i), and $S$ satisfies the hypothesis by (ii), so $S$ is nilpotent by induction: $S^j=0$ for some $j$. Then $T^{j+1}(V)=T^j(T(V))=S^j(T(V))=0$, so $T$ is nilpotent. ∎

prompt:
Let $G$ be a (not necessarily finite) group and let $\theta\colon G\to G$ be a homomorphism such that $\theta^n(G)=\{1\}$ for some integer $n\ge1$.

(i) If the kernel of $\theta$ is finite, prove that the kernel of $\theta^2$ is finite, and deduce that $G$ is finite.

(ii) If $\theta(G)$ has finite index in $G$, prove that $\theta^2(G)$ has finite index in $G$, and deduce that $G$ is finite.
answer: (i) $\theta$ maps $H=\ker\theta^2$ into $\ker\theta$ with kernel $\ker\theta$, so $|H|\le|\ker\theta|^2$; then induct on $n$ using the induced map on $G/\ker\theta$. (ii) $|\theta(G):\theta^2(G)|\le|G:\theta(G)|$; induct on $n$ using the restriction of $\theta$ to $\theta(G)$.

solutions.title: Induction on the nilpotency exponent
solutions.body:
**(i)** Let $H=\ker\theta^2$. Then $\theta(H)\subseteq\ker\theta$, and the restriction $\theta|_H\colon H\to\ker\theta$ has kernel $H\cap\ker\theta=\ker\theta$. So $|H|=|\theta(H)|\cdot|\ker\theta|\le|\ker\theta|^2<\infty$.

Now show $G$ finite by induction on $n$. If $n=1$, $\theta(G)=1$, so $G=\ker\theta$ is finite. For $n\ge2$, let $K=\ker\theta\trianglelefteq G$. Since $\theta(K)=1\subseteq K$, $\theta$ induces a homomorphism $\varphi\colon G/K\to G/K$, $gK\mapsto\theta(g)K$. Its kernel is $\{gK:\theta(g)\in K\}=\ker\theta^2/K$, which is finite by the above. Also $\varphi^{n-1}(G/K)=\theta^{n-1}(G)K/K=K/K$ is trivial, because $\theta(\theta^{n-1}(G))=\theta^n(G)=1$ gives $\theta^{n-1}(G)\subseteq K$. By induction $G/K$ is finite, and $K$ is finite, so $G$ is finite.

**(ii)** $\theta\colon G\to\theta(G)$ is surjective and maps $\theta(G)$ onto $\theta^2(G)$, so it maps each coset $x\theta(G)$ onto the coset $\theta(x)\theta^2(G)$; hence $|\theta(G):\theta^2(G)|\le|G:\theta(G)|$ and $|G:\theta^2(G)|=|G:\theta(G)|\,|\theta(G):\theta^2(G)|<\infty$.

Induct on $n$. If $n=1$, $\theta(G)=1$ has finite index, so $G$ is finite. For $n\ge2$, let $\varphi=\theta|_{\theta(G)}\colon\theta(G)\to\theta(G)$. Then $\varphi^{n-1}(\theta(G))=\theta^n(G)=1$ and $|\theta(G):\varphi(\theta(G))|=|\theta(G):\theta^2(G)|<\infty$. By induction $\theta(G)$ is finite, and since it has finite index, $G$ is finite. ∎

prompt:
Let $G$ be a group and let $K\subseteq H$ be subgroups of $G$ with $K\trianglelefteq H$.

(a) Prove that $H$ normalizes $C_G(K)$.

(b) If $H\trianglelefteq G$ and $C_H(K)=\langle1\rangle$, prove that $H$ centralizes $C_G(K)$.
answer: (a) Conjugating $gk=kg$ by $h\in H$ shows $g^h$ centralizes $K^h=K$. (b) In $\bar G=H\,C_G(K)$ both $H$ and $C_G(K)$ are normal with intersection $C_H(K)=1$, so $[H,C_G(K)]=1$.

solutions.title: Disjoint normal subgroups commute
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $g\in C_G(K)$, $h\in H$. For $k\in K$, $k^{h^{-1}}\in K$ since $K\trianglelefteq H$, so $g$ commutes with $k^{h^{-1}}$; conjugating by $h$, $g^h$ commutes with $k$. Thus $g^h\in C_G(K)$ for all $h\in H$, i.e. $H$ normalizes $C_G(K)$.

**(b)** Let $C=C_G(K)$. By (a), $\bar G=HC$ is a subgroup and $C\trianglelefteq\bar G$ (it is normalized by $H$ and by itself). Since $H\trianglelefteq G$, also $H\trianglelefteq\bar G$. Moreover $H\cap C=C_H(K)=1$. For $h\in H$, $c\in C$, the commutator $[h,c]=h^{-1}(c^{-1}hc)\in H$ and $[h,c]=(h^{-1}c^{-1}h)c\in C$, so $[h,c]\in H\cap C=1$. Hence $H$ centralizes $C_G(K)$. ∎

prompt:
In this problem, the word *ideal* always means *two-sided ideal*. Now let $R$ be a (not necessarily commutative) ring with $1$. An ideal $P$ of $R$ is said to be *prime* if, for all ideals $A$ and $B$ of $R$, the inclusion $AB\subseteq P$ implies that $A\subseteq P$ or $B\subseteq P$.

(a) If an ideal $Q$ is not prime, show that there exist ideals $A>Q$ and $B>Q$ with $AB\subseteq Q$.

(b) Let $I$ and $Q$ be ideals of $R$ and assume that $Q$ is maximal with the property that it contains no power of $I$. Show that $Q$ is prime.

(c) Suppose $I$ is a nonnilpotent ideal of $R$. If $R$ satisfies the ascending chain condition on ideals, prove that there exists a prime ideal of $R$ which does not contain $I$.
answer: (a) Replace the witnesses $A',B'$ by $A'+Q$, $B'+Q$. (b) Otherwise $A\supseteq I^m$, $B\supseteq I^k$ with $AB\subseteq Q$ gives $I^{m+k}\subseteq Q$. (c) ACC gives a maximal ideal $Q$ among those containing no power of $I$ (nonempty: $0$); it is prime by (b) and does not contain $I$.

solutions.title: Maximal counterexample
solutions.body:
**(a)** Since $Q$ is not prime, there are ideals $A',B'$ with $A'B'\subseteq Q$, $A'\not\subseteq Q$, $B'\not\subseteq Q$. Let $A=A'+Q$, $B=B'+Q$; these are ideals properly containing $Q$, and $AB\subseteq A'B'+A'Q+QB'+QQ\subseteq Q$.

**(b)** Note $Q\ne R$ (as $R\supseteq I^1$). Suppose $Q$ is not prime and take $A,B\supsetneq Q$ with $AB\subseteq Q$ as in (a). By maximality of $Q$, $A\supseteq I^m$ and $B\supseteq I^k$ for some $m,k\ge1$. Then $I^{m+k}=I^mI^k\subseteq AB\subseteq Q$, contradicting the choice of $Q$. So $Q$ is prime.

**(c)** Let $\mathcal S$ be the set of ideals containing no power of $I$. As $I$ is not nilpotent, $0\in\mathcal S$. ACC on ideals is equivalent to every nonempty family of ideals having a maximal member, so $\mathcal S$ has a maximal member $Q$. By (b), $Q$ is prime, and $I\not\subseteq Q$ since $Q\in\mathcal S$. ∎

prompt:
Let $K\subseteq L$ be a finite degree extension of fields. Suppose that $E$ and $F$ are intermediate fields, each Galois over $K$, and that $L=EF$ is the field generated by $E$ and $F$. (This means that no proper subfield of $L$ contains both $E$ and $F$.)

(a) Prove that $L$ is Galois over $K$.

(b) If $\mathrm{Gal}(E/K)=G$ and $\mathrm{Gal}(F/K)=H$, show that $\mathrm{Gal}(L/K)$ is isomorphic to a subgroup of $G\times H$.
answer: (a) If $E,F$ split separable $f,g$, then $L$ is generated by the roots of $fg$, so it splits the separable polynomial $\mathrm{lcm}(f,g)$. (b) Restriction $\sigma\mapsto(\sigma|_E,\sigma|_F)$ is an injective homomorphism into $G\times H$.

solutions.title: Splitting fields and restriction
solutions.body:
**(a)** $E$ and $F$ are splitting fields over $K$ of separable polynomials $f,g\in K[x]$. The subfield of $L$ generated over $K$ by the roots of $f$ and $g$ contains $E$ and $F$, hence equals $L$. So $L$ is the splitting field over $K$ of $\mathrm{lcm}(f,g)$, whose irreducible factors each divide $f$ or $g$ and are therefore separable. Hence $L/K$ is normal and separable, i.e. Galois.

**(b)** Let $T=\mathrm{Gal}(L/K)$. As $E/K$ is normal, every $t\in T$ maps $E$ onto itself, so restriction gives a homomorphism $\theta\colon T\to G$; similarly $\varphi\colon T\to H$. Then $\psi(t)=(\theta(t),\varphi(t))$ is a homomorphism $T\to G\times H$. If $\psi(t)=1$, then $t$ fixes $E$ and $F$ pointwise; the fixed field of $t$ is a subfield of $L$ containing $E$ and $F$, so it is $L$ and $t=1$. Thus $\psi$ is injective and $T\cong\psi(T)\le G\times H$. ∎

prompt:
In this problem, all matrices are viewed over the complex numbers.

(a) For which complex numbers $x$, if any, is the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\8&x\end{pmatrix}$ not similar to a diagonal matrix? Explain.

(b) Let $J$ be the $n\times n$ matrix all of whose entries are equal to $1$. Find a diagonal matrix similar to $J$ or prove that none exists.
answer: (a) Exactly $x=9$ and $x=-7$ (the characteristic polynomial $\lambda^2-(x+1)\lambda+(x+16)$ has a double root, and the matrix is not scalar). (b) $J\sim\mathrm{diag}(n,0,\dots,0)$.

solutions.title: Characteristic and minimal polynomials
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $A(x)=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\8&x\end{pmatrix}$. Its characteristic polynomial is
$$\varphi(\lambda)=\lambda^2-(x+1)\lambda+(x+16).$$
If $\varphi$ has distinct roots, $A(x)$ is diagonalizable. It has a double root iff the discriminant vanishes: $(x+1)^2=4(x+16)$, i.e. $x^2-2x-63=(x-9)(x+7)=0$. For $x=9$, $\varphi=(\lambda-5)^2$; for $x=-7$, $\varphi=(\lambda+3)^2$. If $A(x)$ were then diagonalizable it would be similar to the scalar matrix $\mu I$, hence equal to $\mu I$; but $A(x)$ has off-diagonal entries $-2,8\ne0$. So $A(x)$ is **not** diagonalizable exactly for $x=9$ and $x=-7$.

**(b)** $J^2=nJ$ (each entry of $J^2$ is $n$), so $J$ satisfies $\lambda(\lambda-n)$, which has distinct roots $0,n$ (for $n\ge1$). Hence $J$ is diagonalizable with eigenvalues in $\{0,n\}$, say $J\sim D$ with $b$ entries equal to $n$ and the rest $0$. Comparing traces, $n=\mathrm{tr}\,J=bn$, so $b=1$. Thus
$$J\sim D=\mathrm{diag}(n,0,\dots,0).$$
(Equivalently: $\mathrm{rank}\,J=1$, so $D$ has one nonzero entry, which equals $\mathrm{tr}\,J=n$; the vector $(1,\dots,1)$ is an eigenvector for $n$, and the $(n-1)$-dimensional kernel consists of vectors with coordinate sum $0$.) ∎

prompt:
Let $F[x,y]$ be the polynomial ring over the field $F$ in the two indeterminates $x$ and $y$. Suppose $f(x)\in F[x]\subseteq F[x,y]$ and $g(y)\in F[y]\subseteq F[x,y]$ are polynomials of positive degree in the indeterminates $x$ and $y$, respectively. Let $I=(f(x),g(y))$ be the ideal of $F[x,y]$ generated by $f(x)$ and $g(y)$.

(a) Prove that $I\neq F[x,y]$.

(b) If $f(x)=x-\alpha$ and $g(y)=y-\beta$ for some $\alpha,\beta\in F$, show that $I$ is a maximal ideal of $F[x,y]$.
answer: (a) Evaluating at a root $\alpha$ of $f$ and a root $\beta$ of $g$ in $\bar F$ kills $I$ but not $1$. (b) Modulo $I$, $h(x,y)\equiv h(\alpha,\beta)$, so $F[x,y]/I\cong F$, a field.

solutions.title: Dimension count for (a)
solutions.body: For (a) one can also argue: $F[x,y]/(f,g)\cong F[x]/(f)\otimes_FF[y]/(g)$, which has $F$-dimension $\deg f\cdot\deg g>0$; concretely, the monomials $x^iy^j$ with $i<\deg f$, $j<\deg g$ form a basis modulo $I$ (divide by the monic versions of $f$ in $x$ and $g$ in $y$). A nonzero quotient means $I\ne F[x,y]$. For (b), with $\deg f=\deg g=1$ the quotient is $1$-dimensional, spanned by the image of $1$, so $F[x,y]/I\cong F$ is a field and $I$ is maximal. ∎

(i) Show that $p$ does not divide $|A|$.

(ii) Prove that the set $S$ of elements of $G$ not conjugate to any nonidentity element of $A$ has cardinality precisely $p^n$.

(iii) Show that $G$ is not simple.

prompt:
Let $R$ be a ring with $1$, and recall that $R$ is naturally a right $R$-module with respect to right multiplication. We denote this right regular $R$-module by $R_R$.

(i) Prove that $R$ is a division ring if and only if $R_R$ is a simple $R$-module.

(ii) Prove that $R$ is a division ring if and only if every nonzero right $R$-module contains a submodule isomorphic to $R_R$.
answer: (i) Submodules of $R_R$ are right ideals; if $R_R$ is simple each $x\ne0$ has a right inverse $y$, which itself has a right inverse $z$, and $x=z$. (ii) Over a division ring $r\mapsto vr$ is injective for $v\ne0$; conversely $R/M$ ($M$ a maximal right ideal) is simple and contains a copy of $R_R$, so $R_R$ is simple.

prompt:
Let $f(x)\in\mathbb{Q}[x]$ be an irreducible polynomial over the rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$, and let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be roots of $f(x)$ in the complex numbers $\mathbb{C}$. Suppose $\mathbb{Q}\subseteq E\subseteq\mathbb{C}$ where $E$ is a (finite) Galois extension of $\mathbb{Q}$.

(i) Show that $\mathbb{Q}[\alpha]\cap E$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb{Q}[\beta]\cap E$.

(ii) Now assume that $E=\mathbb{Q}[\varepsilon]$ where $\varepsilon$ is a root of unity. Prove that $\mathbb{Q}[\alpha]\cap E=\mathbb{Q}[\beta]\cap E$.
answer: (i) Extend $\alpha\mapsto\beta$ to an automorphism $\tau$ of a Galois field $F\supseteq E(\alpha,\beta)$; $\tau(E)=E$, so $\tau$ maps $\mathbb{Q}[\alpha]\cap E$ onto $\mathbb{Q}[\beta]\cap E$. (ii) $\mathrm{Gal}(E/\mathbb{Q})$ is abelian, so every subfield of $E$ is Galois and $\tau(\mathbb{Q}[\alpha]\cap E)=\mathbb{Q}[\alpha]\cap E$.

solutions.title: Extending the isomorphism $\alpha\mapsto\beta$
solutions.body:
Fact: if $E\subseteq\mathbb{C}$ is finite Galois over $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\tau\colon F\to\mathbb{C}$ is a field embedding of some $F\supseteq E$, then $\tau(E)=E$ (normality).

**(i)** Let $F\subseteq\mathbb{C}$ be the splitting field over $\mathbb{Q}$ of $g=f\cdot h$, where $E$ is the splitting field of $h\in\mathbb{Q}[x]$. Then $\alpha,\beta\in F$ and $E\subseteq F$. Since $f$ is irreducible, there is an isomorphism $\sigma\colon\mathbb{Q}[\alpha]\to\mathbb{Q}[\beta]$ with $\sigma(\alpha)=\beta$. $F$ is a splitting field of $g$ over both $\mathbb{Q}[\alpha]$ and $\mathbb{Q}[\beta]$, so $\sigma$ extends to an automorphism $\tau$ of $F$. Then $\tau(E)=E$ and $\tau(\mathbb{Q}[\alpha])=\mathbb{Q}[\beta]$, so $\tau(\mathbb{Q}[\alpha]\cap E)=\mathbb{Q}[\beta]\cap E$ ($\tau$ is a bijection of $F$). Hence these fields are isomorphic via $\tau$.

**(ii)** If $E=\mathbb{Q}[\varepsilon]$ with $\varepsilon$ a primitive $m$th root of unity, then $\mathrm{Gal}(E/\mathbb{Q})$ embeds in $(\mathbb{Z}/m)^\times$ and is abelian. So every subgroup is normal and every intermediate field of $E/\mathbb{Q}$ is Galois over $\mathbb{Q}$. In particular $D=\mathbb{Q}[\alpha]\cap E$ is Galois over $\mathbb{Q}$, so $\tau(D)=D$ by the fact above. By (i), $\tau(D)=\mathbb{Q}[\beta]\cap E$. Hence $\mathbb{Q}[\alpha]\cap E=\mathbb{Q}[\beta]\cap E$. ∎

prompt:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over an algebraically closed field $F$, and let $S$ and $T$ be commuting linear operators on $V$. Assume that the characteristic polynomial of $S$ has distinct roots.

(i) Show that every eigenvector of $S$ is an eigenvector for $T$.

(ii) If $T$ is nilpotent, prove that $T=0$.
answer: (i) $T$ preserves each eigenspace of $S$, and these are $1$-dimensional. (ii) $T$ is diagonal in the eigenbasis of $S$, with nilpotent hence zero diagonal entries.

solutions.title: One-dimensional eigenspaces
solutions.body:
Let $n=\dim V$ and let $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n$ be the $n$ distinct roots of the characteristic polynomial of $S$ (it splits since $F$ is algebraically closed). Each $\alpha_i$ is an eigenvalue with eigenvector $v_i$; eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are independent, so $v_1,\dots,v_n$ is a basis and each eigenspace $E_{\alpha_i}=Fv_i$ is $1$-dimensional.

**(i)** Let $v$ be an eigenvector of $S$, $Sv=\alpha_iv$, so $v\in E_{\alpha_i}=Fv_i$. Since $ST=TS$, $S(Tv)=T(Sv)=\alpha_iTv$, so $Tv\in E_{\alpha_i}=Fv$, i.e. $Tv=\beta v$ for some $\beta\in F$. Thus $v$ is an eigenvector of $T$.

**(ii)** By (i), $Tv_i=\beta_iv_i$. If $T^k=0$ then $\beta_i^kv_i=0$, so $\beta_i=0$. Hence $T$ kills the basis $v_1,\dots,v_n$, and $T=0$. ∎

prompt:
Let $R$ be a ring with $1$ and let $V$ be a right $R$-module. Assume that $M_1,M_2,\ldots,M_n$ are finitely many $R$-submodules of $V$ with $M_1\cap M_2\cap\cdots\cap M_n=0$, and let $W$ be the (external) direct sum
$$W=V/M_1\oplus V/M_2\oplus\cdots\oplus V/M_n.$$

(i) Show that $V$ is isomorphic to an $R$-submodule of $W$.

(ii) Now suppose in addition that the modules $V/M_i$ are simple and pairwise nonisomorphic. Prove that $V$ is isomorphic to $W$. (Hint. First observe that $W$ has a composition series of length $n$.)
answer: (i) $v\mapsto(v+M_i)_i$ has kernel $\bigcap M_i=0$. (ii) $W$ has length $n$; $V$ embeds in $W$, so has finite length, and each $V/M_i$ is a composition factor of $V$, giving $n$ distinct factors; so $\ell(V)\ge n=\ell(W)$ and the embedding is onto.

solutions.title: Composition length
solutions.body:
**(i)** Let $\theta\colon V\to W$, $\theta(v)=(v+M_1,\dots,v+M_n)$. It is an $R$-homomorphism with $\ker\theta=\bigcap_iM_i=0$, so $V\cong\theta(V)\subseteq W$.

**(ii)** Write $W_i=V/M_i$. The chain $0\subseteq W_1\subseteq W_1\oplus W_2\subseteq\cdots\subseteq W_1\oplus\cdots\oplus W_n=W$ has factors $\cong W_i$, which are simple, so it is a composition series and $W$ has length $n$. Hence $\theta(V)\cong V$ has finite length $\le n$, and so does $W/\theta(V)$, with $\ell(V)+\ell(W/\theta(V))=n$.

For each $i$, the chain $0\subseteq M_i\subseteq V$ refines to a composition series of $V$ whose top factor is the simple module $V/M_i$; by Jordan–Hölder, $V/M_i$ is a composition factor of $V$. The $V/M_i$ are pairwise nonisomorphic, so $V$ has at least $n$ composition factors (counted with multiplicity): $\ell(V)\ge n$. Therefore $\ell(W/\theta(V))=0$, i.e. $\theta(V)=W$, and $V\cong W$. ∎

prompt:
Suppose that a group $G$ is the (internal) direct product of subgroups $S$ and $T$. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$ such that $SH=G=TH$.

(a) Prove that $S\cap H$ and $T\cap H$ are normal subgroups of $G$.

(b) If $S\cap H=1=T\cap H$, prove that $S$ and $T$ are isomorphic.

(c) If $S\cap H=1=T\cap H$ and $H$ is normal in $G$, show that $G$ is abelian.
answer: (a) $S\cap H\trianglelefteq H$, and $T$ centralizes $S$, so $N_G(S\cap H)\supseteq HT=G$. (b) $T\cong G/S=SH/S\cong H$ and likewise $S\cong H$. (c) $[H,S]\subseteq H\cap S=1$ and $[H,T]=1$, so $C_G(S)\supseteq HT=G$ and $C_G(T)\supseteq HS=G$; thus $G=ST$ is central.

solutions.title: Commuting direct factors
solutions.body:
Since $S,T\trianglelefteq G$ and $S\cap T=1$, $[S,T]\subseteq S\cap T=1$, so $S$ and $T$ commute elementwise.

**(a)** As $S\trianglelefteq G$, $S\cap H\trianglelefteq H$. Also $T$ centralizes $S\cap H\subseteq S$, so $T$ normalizes it. Hence $N_G(S\cap H)\supseteq HT=G$, i.e. $S\cap H\trianglelefteq G$. The argument for $T\cap H$ is symmetric (using $G=SH$).

**(b)** By the second isomorphism theorem, $G/S=SH/S\cong H/(S\cap H)\cong H$. Since $G=S\times T$, $G/S\cong T$. So $T\cong H$, and by symmetry $S\cong H$; hence $S\cong T$.

**(c)** With $H\trianglelefteq G$: $[H,S]\subseteq H\cap S=1$ and $[H,T]\subseteq H\cap T=1$. So $H$ centralizes $S$ and $T$. Then $C_G(S)\supseteq HT=G$ and $C_G(T)\supseteq HS=G$, so $S,T\subseteq Z(G)$ and $G=ST\subseteq Z(G)$: $G$ is abelian. ∎

prompt:
Let $K\subseteq E$ be a finite degree extension of fields of characteristic $0$, and let $F_1$ and $F_2$ be intermediate fields. These intermediate fields are said to be linearly disjoint over $K$ if $|\langle F_1,F_2\rangle:K|=|F_1:K|\,|F_2:K|$, where $\langle F_1,F_2\rangle$ is the subfield of $E$ generated by $F_1$ and $F_2$.

(a) Prove that $|\langle F_1,F_2\rangle:F_1|\le|F_2:K|$ for any $F_1$ and $F_2$.

(b) If $|F_1:K|$ and $|F_2:K|$ are relatively prime, prove that $F_1$ and $F_2$ are linearly disjoint over $K$.

(c) Give an example with $|F_1:K|=2=|F_2:K|$ to show that fields can be linearly disjoint without having relatively prime degrees.

(d) If $F_1$ and $F_2$ are linearly disjoint and Galois over $K$, prove that the Galois groups satisfy $\mathrm{Gal}(\langle F_1,F_2\rangle/K)\cong\mathrm{Gal}(F_1/K)\times\mathrm{Gal}(F_2/K)$.
answer: (a) For a $K$-basis $a_1,\dots,a_n$ of $F_2$, $\sum F_1a_k$ is a ring, finite-dimensional over $F_1$ and a domain, hence a field, so it is $\langle F_1,F_2\rangle$. (b) Both degrees divide $|\langle F_1,F_2\rangle:K|\le|F_1:K||F_2:K|$. (c) $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2)$, $\mathbb{Q}(i)$. (d) Restriction gives an injection into the product, and orders agree.

solutions.title: Spanning sets and degree counting
solutions.body:
Let $F=\langle F_1,F_2\rangle$.

**(a)** Let $a_1,\dots,a_n$ be a $K$-basis of $F_2$, $n=|F_2:K|$, and $L=\sum_kF_1a_k$. Each $a_ia_j\in F_2=\sum_kKa_k$, so $L$ is closed under multiplication; it is a subring of $E$ containing $F_1$ and $F_2$, an integral domain, and a finite-dimensional $F_1$-vector space. A finite-dimensional domain over a field is a field (multiplication by a nonzero element is injective, hence surjective). So $L$ is a field containing $F_1,F_2$, contained in $F$; thus $L=F$, and $|F:F_1|\le n$ since $a_1,\dots,a_n$ span.

**(b)** By (a), $|F:K|=|F:F_1|\,|F_1:K|\le|F_2:K|\,|F_1:K|$. Both $|F_1:K|$ and $|F_2:K|$ divide $|F:K|$, and they are coprime, so their product divides $|F:K|$. Hence equality.

**(c)** $K=\mathbb{Q}$, $F_1=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2)$, $F_2=\mathbb{Q}(i)$ inside $E=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2,i)$. Since $F_1\subset\mathbb{R}$, $i\notin F_1$, so $|F:F_1|=|F_1(i):F_1|=2$ and $|F:\mathbb{Q}|=4=2\cdot2$.

**(d)** $F/K$ is Galois (compositum of Galois extensions: splitting field of the product of the defining polynomials). Restriction gives a homomorphism $\theta\colon\mathrm{Gal}(F/K)\to\mathrm{Gal}(F_1/K)\times\mathrm{Gal}(F_2/K)$; if $\sigma\in\ker\theta$, it fixes $F_1$ and $F_2$, hence $F$, so $\theta$ is injective. Orders: $|\mathrm{Gal}(F/K)|=|F:K|=|F_1:K||F_2:K|$, which is the order of the product. So $\theta$ is an isomorphism. ∎

prompt:
Let $V$ be a complex vector space, not necessarily of finite dimension. Suppose that $A,B\colon V\to V$ are nonzero $\mathbb{C}$-linear transformations with $AB=\lambda BA$ for some fixed nonzero complex number $\lambda$. Assume that no proper subspace of $V$ is invariant under both $A$ and $B$. That is, if $W$ is a subspace of $V$ with $AW\subseteq W$ and $BW\subseteq W$, then $W=0$ or $V$.

(a) Show that $A$ and $B$ are both one-to-one and onto.

(b) If $V$ is finite dimensional, prove that $\lambda$ is a root of unity.

(c) Show that a finite-dimensional example exists with $\lambda=-1$.
answer: (a) $\ker A$ and $\operatorname{im}A$ (and likewise for $B$) are invariant under both, so are $0$ resp. $V$. (b) $\det A\det B=\lambda^n\det B\det A$ with nonzero determinants gives $\lambda^n=1$. (c) $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$, $B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ on $\mathbb{C}^2$.

solutions.title: Invariant kernels and images
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $N=\ker A$. Clearly $AN=0\subseteq N$; and for $v\in N$, $A(Bv)=\lambda B(Av)=0$, so $BN\subseteq N$. Hence $N=0$ or $V$; $N=V$ means $A=0$, excluded. So $A$ is injective. Let $I=AV$. Then $AI\subseteq I$ and $B(Av)=\lambda^{-1}A(Bv)\in I$. So $I=0$ or $V$; $I=0$ means $A=0$. So $A$ is onto. Using $BA=\lambda^{-1}AB$, the same arguments show $\ker B$ and $BV$ are invariant under both, so $B$ is one-to-one and onto.

**(b)** Let $n=\dim V$ (finite, and $n\ge1$ since $A\ne0$). Taking determinants in $AB=\lambda BA$ gives $\det A\det B=\lambda^n\det B\det A$. By (a), $\det A,\det B\neq0$, so $\lambda^n=1$.

**(c)** On $V=\mathbb{C}^2$ let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$, $B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Then $AB=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}=-BA$. A proper nonzero invariant subspace would be a line invariant under $A$, hence $\mathbb{C}e_1$ or $\mathbb{C}e_2$ (the eigenspaces of $A$, as its eigenvalues are distinct); but $B$ swaps $e_1$ and $e_2$. So no proper nonzero subspace is invariant under both. ∎

prompt:
Let $R$ be a ring and let $Z$ denote its center. A derivation $D\colon R\to R$ is a map satisfying $D(a+b)=D(a)+D(b)$ and $D(ab)=aD(b)+D(a)b$ for all $a,b\in R$.

(a) If $r\in R$, show that the map $A_r\colon R\to R$ given by $A_r(a)=ar-ra$, for all $a\in R$, is a derivation of $R$.

(b) If $D$ is a derivation of $R$, prove that $D(Z)\subseteq Z$.

(c) If $D$ is a derivation of $R$ and $e\in Z$ is an idempotent, prove that $D(e)=0$. (Hint. You may need to evaluate $(1-2e)^2$.)
answer: (a) Direct computation: $abr-rab=a(br-rb)+(ar-ra)b$. (b) Apply $D$ to $rz=zr$ and use $zD(r)=D(r)z$. (c) $D(e)=D(e^2)=2eD(e)$, so $(1-2e)D(e)=0$; multiply by $1-2e$, using $(1-2e)^2=1$.

solutions.title: Direct computation
solutions.body:
**(a)** $A_r(a+b)=(a+b)r-r(a+b)=A_r(a)+A_r(b)$, and
$$A_r(ab)=abr-rab=a(br-rb)+(ar-ra)b=aA_r(b)+A_r(a)b.$$

**(b)** Let $z\in Z$, $r\in R$. Applying $D$ to $rz=zr$:
$$rD(z)+D(r)z=D(rz)=D(zr)=zD(r)+D(z)r.$$
Since $z$ is central, $D(r)z=zD(r)$, leaving $rD(z)=D(z)r$. So $D(z)\in Z$.

**(c)** (Here $R$ has $1$, as in the hint.) By (b), $D(e)\in Z$, so $e$ and $D(e)$ commute, and
$$D(e)=D(e^2)=eD(e)+D(e)e=2eD(e).$$
Thus $(1-2e)D(e)=0$. Now $(1-2e)^2=1-4e+4e^2=1$, so multiplying on the left by $1-2e$ gives $D(e)=0$. ∎

prompt:
Let $G$ be a group of order $2^4\cdot5^3\cdot11$ and let $H$ be a group of order $5^3\cdot11$.

(a) Show that $H$ has a normal Sylow $11$-subgroup.

(b) If the number of Sylow $5$-subgroups of $G$ is (strictly) less than $16$, prove that $G$ has a proper normal subgroup of order divisible by $5$.

(c) If $G$ has exactly sixteen Sylow $5$-subgroups, show that $G$ has a normal Sylow $11$-subgroup.
answer: (a) $n_{11}(H)\mid125$, $\equiv1\pmod{11}$, so $n_{11}=1$. (b) $n_5\in\{1,11\}$; for $11$, the kernel of the action on the $11$ cosets of $N_G(P)$ is proper and has order divisible by $5$ since $5^3\nmid11!$. (c) $N_G(P)$ has order $5^3\cdot11$, so by (a) contains a normal Sylow 11-subgroup $Q$; $n_{11}(G)\mid16$ and $\equiv1\pmod{11}$, so $Q\trianglelefteq G$.

solutions.title: Sylow counting and permutation action
solutions.body:
$|G|=2^4\cdot5^3\cdot11=22000$.

**(a)** $n_{11}(H)$ divides $5^3$ and is $\equiv1\pmod{11}$. The divisors $1,5,25,125$ are $\equiv1,5,3,4\pmod{11}$, so $n_{11}(H)=1$.

**(b)** $n_5=n_5(G)$ divides $2^4\cdot11=176$ and $n_5\equiv1\pmod5$. The divisors of $176$ below $16$ are $1,2,4,8,11$, of which $1$ and $11$ are $\equiv1\pmod5$. If $n_5=1$, the Sylow $5$-subgroup is normal, proper, of order $125$. If $n_5=11$, let $N=N_G(P)$ for $P\in\mathrm{Syl}_5(G)$, so $|G:N|=11$. $G$ acts on the $11$ right cosets of $N$, giving $\theta\colon G\to S_{11}$ with kernel $K\subseteq N$; in particular $K\ne G$. Since $G/K$ embeds in $S_{11}$ and $5^3\nmid11!$ (the $5$-part of $11!$ is $5^2$), $5\mid|K|$. So $K$ is the required proper normal subgroup.

**(c)** If $n_5=16$, let $N=N_G(P)$; then $|N|=22000/16=1375=5^3\cdot11$. By (a), $N$ has a normal Sylow $11$-subgroup $Q$, which is also a Sylow $11$-subgroup of $G$. Since $N\subseteq N_G(Q)$, $n_{11}(G)=|G:N_G(Q)|$ divides $|G:N|=16$. The divisors $1,2,4,8,16$ are $\equiv1,2,4,8,5\pmod{11}$, so $n_{11}(G)=1$ and $Q\trianglelefteq G$. ∎
