prompt:
Let $L/K$ be a finite degree Galois extension of fields with Galois group given by $\mathrm{Gal}(L/K)=G$, and let $E$ be an intermediate field. Then $E$ is said to be a *2-tower* over $K$ if there exists a chain of fields $K=E_0\subseteq E_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq E_n=E$ such that $|E_i:E_{i-1}|=2$ for all $i=1,2,\ldots,n$.

(a) If $G$ is abelian, prove that $E$ is a 2-tower over $K$ if and only if the degree $|E:K|$ is a power of $2$.

(b) Show by example that the characterization of 2-towers given in part (a) is false if $G$ is allowed to be a nonabelian group.
answer: (a) A tower has degree $2^n$; conversely $E/K$ is Galois with abelian group of order $2^n$, which has a chain of subgroups of index $2$. (b) For a quartic with Galois group $A_4$, e.g. $x^4+8x+12$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, $E=\mathbb{Q}(\theta)$ ($\theta$ a root) has degree $4$, but $A_4$ has no subgroup of order 6 between $A_3$ and $A_4$, so no intermediate quadratic field.

solutions.title: Galois correspondence
solutions.body:
**(a)** If $E$ is a 2-tower, $|E:K|=\prod|E_i:E_{i-1}|=2^n$. Conversely, let $|E:K|=2^n$. By the Galois correspondence $E=L^H$ for some $H\le G$; $G$ abelian implies $H\trianglelefteq G$, so $E/K$ is Galois with group $A=G/H$, an abelian group of order $2^n$. A finite abelian (indeed any) $2$-group has a chain $A=A_0\supseteq A_1\supseteq\cdots\supseteq A_n=1$ with $|A_{i-1}:A_i|=2$ (e.g. a composition series). Put $E_i=E^{A_i}$. Then $K=E_0\subseteq E_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq E_n=E$ and $|E_i:E_{i-1}|=|A_{i-1}:A_i|=2$. So $E$ is a 2-tower.

**(b)** We need a Galois extension with group $A_4$ and an intermediate field of degree $4$ with no intermediate quadratic field. Let $f=x^4+8x+12\in\mathbb{Q}[x]$ and $L$ its splitting field.
- $f$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$: it has no rational root (none of $\pm1,\pm2,\pm3,\pm4,\pm6,\pm12$ is a root, as $f>0$ for $x\ge0$ and one checks the negative ones), and by Gauss's lemma a factorization into quadratics would be $(x^2+ax+b)(x^2-ax+c)$ with integers satisfying $b+c=a^2$, $a(c-b)=8$, $bc=12$; for $a\in\{\pm1,\pm2,\pm4,\pm8\}$ the first two equations give $(b,c)$ non-integral or equal to $(0,4),(4,0),(7,9),(9,7)$, none with $bc=12$.
- Its discriminant is $-27\cdot8^4+256\cdot12^3=331776=576^2$, a square, so $G\le A_4$.
- Its resolvent cubic $x^3-48x-64$ has no rational root (test the divisors of $64$), so it is irreducible and $3\mid|G|$, while $4\mid|G|$ since $f$ is irreducible.

Hence $|G|=12$ and $G=A_4$. Let $\theta$ be a root of $f$ and $E=\mathbb{Q}(\theta)$, so $|E:\mathbb{Q}|=4=2^2$, and $E=L^H$ where $H$ is the stabilizer of $\theta$, of order $3$. If $E$ were a 2-tower, there would be $E_1$ with $|E_1:\mathbb{Q}|=2$, $\mathbb{Q}\subset E_1\subset E$, corresponding to a subgroup $T$ with $H<T<A_4$ and $|T|=6$. But $A_4$ has no subgroup of order $6$. So $E$ is not a 2-tower although its degree is a power of $2$.

(The official example is the same in spirit: $A_4$ acting on $L=F(x_1,\dots,x_4)$ by permuting variables, $K=L^{A_4}$, $E=L^{A_3}$; $A_3$ is a maximal subgroup of $A_4$.) ∎

prompt:
Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix over the complex numbers and assume that the rank of $A$ is equal to $1$.

(a) What are the possible Jordan canonical forms for $A$? Justify your answer.

(b) For each of the forms obtained in part (a), compute the characteristic polynomial of $A$ and the minimal polynomial of $A$.
answer: (a) Either $\mathrm{diag}(\lambda,0,\dots,0)$ with $\lambda=\mathrm{tr}\,A\neq0$, or (when $\mathrm{tr}\,A=0$, $n\ge2$) one block $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ plus zeros. (b) First case: $\chi=x^{n-1}(x-\lambda)$, $m=x(x-\lambda)$. Second case: $\chi=x^n$, $m=x^2$.

solutions.title: Rank of Jordan blocks
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $B$ be the Jordan form of $A$; $\mathrm{rank}\,B=\mathrm{rank}\,A=1$. The rank of a block diagonal matrix is the sum of the ranks of the blocks. A Jordan block $J_k(\mu)$ has rank $k$ if $\mu\ne0$ and rank $k-1$ if $\mu=0$. So exactly one block has rank $1$ and all others have rank $0$, i.e. are $J_1(0)=(0)$. The rank-1 block is either $J_1(\lambda)=(\lambda)$ with $\lambda\ne0$, or $J_2(0)=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$. Hence
$$B=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda,0,\dots,0)\ (\lambda\ne0)\qquad\text{or}\qquad B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\oplus0_{n-2}\ (n\ge2).$$
In both cases $\lambda=\mathrm{tr}\,B=\mathrm{tr}\,A$, so the first occurs iff $\mathrm{tr}\,A\ne0$. Both occur (e.g. $E_{11}$ and $E_{12}$).

**(b)** Similar matrices have the same characteristic and minimal polynomials.
- $B=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda,0,\dots,0)$, $\lambda\ne0$: $\chi_A=x^{n-1}(x-\lambda)$; $B$ is diagonalizable with eigenvalues $\lambda\neq0$ and (if $n\ge2$) $0$, so $m_A=x(x-\lambda)$ for $n\ge2$ (and $m_A=x-\lambda$ when $n=1$).
- $B=J_2(0)\oplus0$: $\chi_A=x^n$, and $m_A=x^2$ (the largest Jordan block has size $2$). ∎

prompt:
Let $R=F[x,y]$ be the polynomial ring over the field $F$ in the two indeterminates $x$ and $y$, and let $I=xR$ be the principal ideal of $R$ generated by $x$. Define $S=F+I$, so that $S$ is a subring of $R$, and observe that $I$ is an ideal of $S$.

(a) Show that $I$ is not finitely generated as an ideal of $S$.

(b) Prove that there are infinitely many ideals of $S$ that are not ideals of $R$.
answer: (a) If $I=a_1S+\cdots+a_kS$, then modulo $I^2=x^2R$ every element of $I$ is an $F$-combination of the $a_i$, so $xy^n$ with $n$ above all $y$-degrees is not reached. (b) The principal $S$-ideals $xy^nS=Fxy^n+x^2y^nR$ ($n\ge0$) are pairwise distinct and none is an $R$-ideal, as $xy^{n+1}\notin xy^nS$. (Alternatively: a strictly ascending chain of $S$-ideals can contain only finitely many $R$-ideals, $R$ being Noetherian.)

solutions.title: Work modulo $x^2$
solutions.body:
**(a)** Suppose $I=a_1S+\cdots+a_kS$ with $a_i\in I=xF[x,y]$. Let $n$ exceed the $y$-degrees of all $a_i$. Then $xy^n\in I$, so
$$xy^n=\sum_ia_i(f_i+b_i),\qquad f_i\in F,\ b_i\in I.$$
Each $a_ib_i\in I^2=x^2R$, so all its monomials are divisible by $x^2$. Hence the terms of $xy^n$ that are not divisible by $x^2$ must come from $\sum f_ia_i$, a polynomial of $y$-degree $<n$. But $xy^n$ is itself not divisible by $x^2$ and has $y$-degree $n$, a contradiction. So $I$ is not finitely generated over $S$.

**(b)** *Argument 1 (Noetherian).* By (a), $S$ is not Noetherian, so there is a strictly ascending chain $J_1\subsetneq J_2\subsetneq\cdots$ of ideals of $S$. $R$ is Noetherian (Hilbert basis theorem). If infinitely many $J_i$ were ideals of $R$, they would form a strictly ascending chain of ideals of $R$, impossible. So all but finitely many $J_i$ are ideals of $S$ that are not ideals of $R$; these are infinitely many distinct ideals.

*Argument 2 (explicit).* For $n\ge0$ let $J_n=xy^nS=Fxy^n+x^2y^nR$, an ideal of $S$. These are distinct for different $n$: the elements of $J_n$ not divisible by $x^2$ have $x$-linear part exactly $c\,xy^n$ with $c\ne0$. And $J_n$ is not an ideal of $R$: $y\cdot xy^n=xy^{n+1}\notin J_n$, since its $x$-linear part is $xy^{n+1}$, not a scalar multiple of $xy^n$. ∎

prompt:
Let $G$ be a finite group of order $504=2^3\cdot3^2\cdot7$.

(a) Show that $G$ cannot be isomorphic to a subgroup of the alternating group $\mathrm{Alt}_7$.

(b) If $G$ is simple, determine the number of Sylow $3$-subgroups of $G$.
answer: (a) Such a subgroup would have index $5$ in the simple group $\mathrm{Alt}_7$ of order $2520>5!$. (b) $n_3\in\{1,4,7,28\}$; $1$ and $4$ contradict simplicity, $7$ embeds $G$ in $\mathrm{Sym}_7$ and then in $\mathrm{Alt}_7$, contradicting (a). So $n_3=28$.

solutions.title: The $n!$ theorem
solutions.body:
We use: if $H\le X$ has index $m$, the action of $X$ on the cosets of $H$ gives a homomorphism $X\to S_m$ whose kernel is a normal subgroup of $X$ contained in $H$.

**(a)** If $G\le A=\mathrm{Alt}_7$, then $|A:G|=2520/504=5$. The kernel $K$ of $A\to S_5$ is normal in $A$ and contained in $G$, so $K\ne A$; as $A$ is simple, $K=1$ and $A$ embeds in $S_5$, impossible since $2520>120$.

**(b)** $n_3\equiv1\pmod3$ and $n_3\mid2^3\cdot7=56$: the divisors $1,2,4,7,8,14,28,56$ give $n_3\in\{1,4,7,28\}$.
- $n_3=1$: the Sylow $3$-subgroup is normal, contradicting simplicity.
- $n_3=4$: $G$ acts on its Sylow $3$-subgroups by conjugation, giving $G\to S_4$ with nontrivial image (transitive action); the kernel is a proper normal subgroup, so it is trivial, and $G$ embeds in $S_4$, impossible as $504>24$.
- $n_3=7$: likewise $G$ embeds in $S_7$. Then $G\cap\mathrm{Alt}_7\trianglelefteq G$ with index $\le2$; $G$ is simple of non-prime order, so it has no normal subgroup of index $2$, and $G\subseteq\mathrm{Alt}_7$, contradicting (a).

Hence $n_3=28$. (This occurs: $PSL_2(8)$ is simple of order $504$.) ∎

prompt:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ and let $M$ be a maximal ideal of $R$.

(a) Show that the ring $R/M^2$ has no idempotents other than $0$ and $1$.

(b) We know that $M/M^2$ is naturally an $R/M$-module. If $R$ is Noetherian, prove that this module is finitely generated.

(c) Finally, assume that $R=K[x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_t]$ is a polynomial ring in finitely many variables over the field $K$. Prove that $\dim_K(R/M^2)<\infty$.
answer: (a) The image of an idempotent $e$ in the field $R/M$ is $0$ or $1$; if $e\in M/M^2$ then $e=e^2=0$, otherwise apply this to $1-e$. (b) Generators of $M$ over $R$ give generators of $M/M^2$ over $R/M$. (c) Nullstellensatz: $\dim_KR/M<\infty$; with (b), $\dim_KR/M^2=\dim_KM/M^2+\dim_KR/M<\infty$.

solutions.title: Local structure at $M$
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $\theta\colon R/M^2\to R/M$ be the natural map; its kernel $M/M^2$ consists of elements with square $0$. Let $e$ be idempotent. In the field $R/M$, $\theta(e)\theta(1-e)=\theta(e-e^2)=0$, so $\theta(e)=0$ or $\theta(1-e)=0$. If $\theta(e)=0$, then $e\in M/M^2$ and $e=e^2=0$. If $\theta(1-e)=0$, the same argument applied to the idempotent $1-e$ gives $1-e=0$, so $e=1$.

**(b)** Since $R$ is Noetherian, $M=m_1R+\cdots+m_kR$. Then $M/M^2=\sum\bar m_iR$, and since $M$ acts as zero on $M/M^2$, the $R$-action factors through $R/M$: $M/M^2=\sum\bar m_i(R/M)$. So $M/M^2$ is a finite-dimensional $R/M$-vector space.

**(c)** By Hilbert's Nullstellensatz (Zariski's lemma), the field $R/M$ is a finite extension of $K$, so $\dim_KR/M<\infty$. By the Hilbert basis theorem $R$ is Noetherian, so by (b) $\dim_{R/M}M/M^2<\infty$, hence $\dim_KM/M^2=\dim_{R/M}(M/M^2)\cdot\dim_K(R/M)<\infty$. The $K$-linear surjection $R/M^2\to R/M$ has kernel $M/M^2$, so
$$\dim_KR/M^2=\dim_KM/M^2+\dim_KR/M<\infty.$$
∎

prompt:
Let $F\subseteq E$ be fields and suppose $0\neq\alpha\in E$ with $E=F[\alpha]$. Assume that some power of $\alpha$ lies in $F$ and let $n$ be the smallest positive integer such that $\alpha^n\in F$.

(a) If $\alpha^m\in F$ with $m>0$, show that $m$ is a multiple of $n$.

(b) If $E$ is a separable extension of $F$, prove that the characteristic of $F$ does not divide $n$.

(c) If every root of unity in $E$ lies in $F$, show that $|E:F|=n$.
answer: (a) Division with remainder: $\alpha^r\in F$ with $0\le r<n$ forces $r=0$. (b) If $n=pt$ then $\beta=\alpha^t\notin F$ has $\beta^p\in F$, so its minimal polynomial divides $(x-\beta)^p$ and is inseparable. (c) The minimal polynomial $f$ of $\alpha$ divides $x^n-\alpha^n$, so its constant term is $\pm\delta\alpha^r$ ($r=\deg f$, $\delta$ a root of unity); then $\delta\in E$, hence $\delta\in F$, so $\alpha^r\in F$ and $r=n$.

solutions.title: Minimal polynomial divides $x^n-\alpha^n$
solutions.body:
**(a)** Write $m=qn+r$ with $0\le r<n$. Then $\alpha^r=\alpha^m(\alpha^n)^{-q}\in F$. By minimality of $n$, $r=0$, so $n\mid m$.

**(b)** Suppose $\mathrm{char}F=p>0$ and $n=pt$. By minimality, $\beta=\alpha^t\notin F$, while $\beta^p=\alpha^n\in F$. So $\beta$ is a root of $x^p-\beta^p=(x-\beta)^p$ in $E[x]$. Its minimal polynomial over $F$ divides $(x-\beta)^p$ and has degree $>1$ (as $\beta\notin F$), so it is $(x-\beta)^k$ with $k\ge2$, which has a repeated root. So $\beta\in E$ is inseparable over $F$, contradicting separability of $E/F$.

**(c)** Let $f$ be the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $F$, $r=\deg f=|E:F|$. Since $\alpha$ is a root of $x^n-\alpha^n\in F[x]$, $f\mid x^n-\alpha^n$; so $r\le n$, and in an algebraic closure every root of $f$ is $\varepsilon\alpha$ with $\varepsilon^n=1$. The product of the $r$ roots of $f$ is $\delta\alpha^r$ for some $n$th root of unity $\delta$, and equals $\pm f(0)\in F$. So $\delta\alpha^r\in F\subseteq E$, and since $0\ne\alpha\in E$, $\delta\in E$. By hypothesis $\delta\in F$, hence $\alpha^r\in F$. By minimality of $n$ and $1\le r\le n$, $r=n$. Thus $|E:F|=n$. ∎

prompt:
Let $A$ be a real $n\times n$ matrix. We say that $A$ is a *difference of two squares* if there exist real $n\times n$ matrices $B$ and $C$ with $BC=CB=0$ and $A=B^2-C^2$.

(a) If $A$ is a diagonal matrix, show that it is a difference of two squares.

(b) If $A$ is a symmetric matrix that is not necessarily diagonal, again show that it is a difference of two squares.

(c) Suppose $A$ is a difference of two squares, with corresponding matrices $B$ and $C$ as above. If $B$ has a nonzero real eigenvalue, prove that $A$ has a positive real eigenvalue.
answer: (a) Split each diagonal entry: $b_i=\sqrt{a_i},c_i=0$ if $a_i>0$, else $b_i=0,c_i=\sqrt{-a_i}$. (b) Diagonalize $A=PDP^{-1}$ (spectral theorem) and conjugate the matrices from (a). (c) If $Bv=\lambda v$, $\lambda\ne0$, then $Cv=\lambda^{-1}CBv=0$, so $Av=\lambda^2v$ with $\lambda^2>0$.

solutions.title: Diagonalize, then split signs
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $A=\mathrm{diag}(a_1,\dots,a_n)$. Define diagonal $B=\mathrm{diag}(b_i)$, $C=\mathrm{diag}(c_i)$ by $b_i=\sqrt{a_i}$, $c_i=0$ if $a_i>0$, and $b_i=0$, $c_i=\sqrt{-a_i}$ if $a_i\le0$. Then $b_ic_i=0$ and $b_i^2-c_i^2=a_i$, so $BC=CB=0$ and $A=B^2-C^2$.

**(b)** By the spectral theorem there is a real invertible (orthogonal) $P$ with $D=P^{-1}AP$ diagonal. By (a), $D=U^2-V^2$ with $UV=VU=0$. Put $B=PUP^{-1}$, $C=PVP^{-1}$ (real). Since $X\mapsto PXP^{-1}$ is a ring automorphism, $BC=CB=0$ and $B^2-C^2=P(U^2-V^2)P^{-1}=A$.

**(c)** Let $\lambda\neq0$ be a real eigenvalue of $B$ with real eigenvector $v\ne0$ ($B-\lambda I$ is a singular real matrix, so it has a real null vector). Then $v=\lambda^{-1}Bv$, so $Cv=\lambda^{-1}CBv=0$. Hence $Av=B^2v-C^2v=\lambda^2v$, and $\lambda^2>0$ is a positive real eigenvalue of $A$. ∎

prompt:
Let $K$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and view the polynomial ring $V=K[x]$ as a $K$-vector space. Let $M\colon V\to V$ be the linear operator given by multiplication by $x$, so that $M(x^n)=x^{n+1}$ for all integers $n\ge0$. In addition, let $D\colon V\to V$ be the linear operator given by differentiation with respect to $x$, so that $D(x^n)=nx^{n-1}$ for all $n\ge0$. Let $\mathcal L$ denote the set of all linear operators of the form $M^iD^j$ with $i,j\ge0$, where $M^0=D^0=I$ is the identity operator on $V$.

(a) Prove that $DM-MD=I$.

(b) Show that $\mathcal L$ is a $K$-linearly independent set.

(c) For all nonnegative integers $t$, prove that $DM^t$ is in the $K$-linear span of the set $\mathcal L$.
answer: (a) $(DM-MD)x^n=(n+1)x^n-nx^n=x^n$. (b) In a nontrivial relation, let $k$ be the least $j$ that occurs; applying it to $x^k$ gives $k!\sum_ia_{ik}x^i=0$, so all $a_{ik}=0$. (c) Induction: $DM^{t+1}=(I+MD)M^t=M^t+M(DM^t)$; in fact $DM^t=M^tD+tM^{t-1}$.

solutions.title: Weyl algebra relations
solutions.body:
**(a)** $DM(x^n)=D(x^{n+1})=(n+1)x^n$ and $MD(x^n)=M(nx^{n-1})=nx^n$, so $(DM-MD)(x^n)=x^n$ for all $n$. Two linear maps agreeing on the basis $\{x^n\}$ are equal: $DM-MD=I$.

**(b)** Suppose a finite relation $\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}M^iD^j=0$ holds with not all $a_{ij}=0$. Let $k$ be the smallest $j$ with $a_{ij}\neq0$ for some $i$. Apply the relation to $x^k$: $D^j(x^k)=0$ for $j>k$, the terms with $j<k$ have zero coefficients, and $D^k(x^k)=k!$. So $0=\sum_ia_{ik}M^i(k!)=k!\sum_ia_{ik}x^i$. Since $\mathrm{char}K=0$, $k!\ne0$, and the $x^i$ are independent, so $a_{ik}=0$ for all $i$ — contradicting the choice of $k$. Hence $\mathcal L$ is linearly independent.

**(c)** Induction on $t$. For $t=0$, $DM^0=D\in\mathcal L$. Assume $DM^t\in\mathrm{span}\,\mathcal L$. By (a), $DM=I+MD$, so
$$DM^{t+1}=(DM)M^t=M^t+M(DM^t).$$
$M^t\in\mathcal L$, and $\mathrm{span}\,\mathcal L$ is closed under left multiplication by $M$ ($M\cdot M^iD^j=M^{i+1}D^j$), so $DM^{t+1}\in\mathrm{span}\,\mathcal L$. (Explicitly, the induction gives $DM^t=M^tD+tM^{t-1}$ for $t\ge1$.) ∎

prompt:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be distinct subgroups of a finite group $G$. We say that $X$ and $Y$ are a *weird pair* if $|X| = |Y|$ and if no subgroup of $G$ other than $X$ and $Y$ has this same order.

(a) If $G$ is a group having a weird pair of subgroups, show that some subgroup of $G$ has a weird pair of normal subgroups.

(b) If $G = A \times B$ is a direct product of solvable groups, show that the subgroups $A \times 1$ and $1 \times B$ cannot be a weird pair.

(c) Show that a solvable group cannot contain a weird pair of subgroups.
answer: (a) In $H=\langle X,Y\rangle$, conjugates of $X$ by $Y$ have order $|X|$ and are not $Y$, so $X,Y\trianglelefteq H$. (b) A nontrivial homomorphism $\theta\colon A\to A/N\cong C_p\hookrightarrow B$ gives a third subgroup $\{(a,\theta(a))\}$ of order $|A|$. (c) Reduce to $G=XY$ with $X,Y\trianglelefteq G$, pass to $G/(X\cap Y)=X/N\times Y/N$ and apply (b).

solutions.title: Normalize, then pass to a direct product
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $H=\langle X,Y\rangle\le G$. Any subgroup of $H$ of order $|X|$ is a subgroup of $G$ of that order, so it is $X$ or $Y$; thus $X,Y$ is a weird pair in $H$. Let $y\in Y$. Then $X^y=y^{-1}Xy\le H$ has order $|X|$, so $X^y\in\{X,Y\}$. If $X^y=Y$ then $X=Y^{y^{-1}}=Y$ (as $y\in Y$), contradicting $X\neq Y$. Hence $X^y=X$, so $Y\le N_H(X)$. Also $X\le N_H(X)$, so $N_H(X)\supseteq\langle X,Y\rangle=H$ and $X\trianglelefteq H$. By symmetry $Y\trianglelefteq H$.

**(b)** Suppose $A\times1$ and $1\times B$ form a weird pair. Then $|A|=|B|$, and $|A|>1$ (otherwise both subgroups are trivial and equal). Since $A\ne1$ is solvable, $A'\ne A$, and the nontrivial abelian group $A/A'$ has a quotient of prime order $p$; so there is $N\trianglelefteq A$ with $A/N\cong C_p$. Since $p\mid|A|=|B|$, Cauchy's theorem gives $P\le B$ with $|P|=p$. Composing $A\to A/N\cong C_p\cong P\hookrightarrow B$ we get a nontrivial homomorphism $\theta\colon A\to B$. Let
$$C=\{(a,\theta(a))\mid a\in A\}\le A\times B .$$
It is a subgroup (the graph of a homomorphism) and $a\mapsto(a,\theta(a))$ is a bijection $A\to C$, so $|C|=|A|$. $C\ne A\times1$ because $\theta\ne1$, and $C\neq1\times B$ because $C$ contains $(a,\theta(a))$ with $a\ne1$. This contradicts the weird-pair property.

**(c)** Let $G$ be solvable and suppose $X,Y$ is a weird pair in $G$. By (a), replacing $G$ by the (solvable) subgroup $\langle X,Y\rangle$, we may assume $X,Y\trianglelefteq G$; then $XY$ is a subgroup containing $X$ and $Y$, so $G=XY$. Let $N=X\cap Y\trianglelefteq G$ and $\bar G=G/N$, $A=X/N$, $B=Y/N$. Then $A,B\trianglelefteq\bar G$, $A\cap B=1$ and $\bar G=AB$, so $\bar G=A\times B$ (internal direct product), with $A,B$ solvable.

$A,B$ is a weird pair in $\bar G$: $|A|=|X|/|N|=|B|$, $A\ne B$, and any subgroup of $\bar G$ of order $|A|$ has the form $Z/N$ with $N\le Z\le G$ and $|Z|=|X|$, hence $Z\in\{X,Y\}$. Under the identification $\bar G=A\times B$ these are $A\times1$ and $1\times B$, contradicting (b). ∎

prompt:
Let $R$ be a ring with $1$. Recall that an ideal $P$ of $R$ is said to be (right) *primitive* if there exists a simple right $R$-module $W$ with $P = \{r \in R \mid Wr = 0\}$. Furthermore, we recall that the Jacobson radical, $\mathrm{Jrad}(R)$, of $R$ is defined to be the intersection of all primitive ideals of $R$.

(a) Let $V$ be a right $R$-module having a composition series of length $n$ and suppose that $R$ acts faithfully on $V$. Show that $J = \mathrm{Jrad}(R)$ is an intersection of $n$ primitive ideals of $R$ and that $J^n = 0$.

(b) Give an example of the situation in part (a) with $n = 2$ and with $\mathrm{Jrad}(R) \neq 0$. Justify your answer.
answer: (a) With composition factors $W_i=V_i/V_{i-1}$ and $P_i=\mathrm{ann}(W_i)$, $I=\bigcap P_i\supseteq J$ satisfies $V_iI\subseteq V_{i-1}$, so $VI^n=0$, $I^n=0$, hence $I\subseteq J$; so $J=I$ and $J^n=0$. (b) $R=\begin{pmatrix}K&K\\0&K\end{pmatrix}$ acting on row vectors $K^2$; $\begin{pmatrix}0&K\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ is a nonzero nilpotent ideal.

solutions.title: Annihilators of composition factors
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $0=V_0\subset V_1\subset\cdots\subset V_n=V$ be a composition series, $W_i=V_i/V_{i-1}$ (simple), and $P_i=\{r\in R\mid W_ir=0\}$, a primitive ideal. Put $I=P_1\cap\cdots\cap P_n$. Since $J$ is the intersection of *all* primitive ideals, $J\subseteq I$.

Since $W_iI=0$ we have $V_iI\subseteq V_{i-1}$ for each $i$; by induction $V_iI^i\subseteq V_0=0$, so $VI^n=V_nI^n=0$. As $R$ acts faithfully on $V$, $I^n=0$.

A nilpotent ideal lies in every primitive ideal: if $W$ is simple and $I^n=0$, then $WI$ is a submodule, so $WI=0$ or $WI=W$; the latter gives $W=WI^n=0$, impossible. So $WI=0$, i.e. $I\subseteq\mathrm{ann}(W)$. Hence $I\subseteq J$, and therefore $J=I=P_1\cap\cdots\cap P_n$ and $J^n=I^n=0$.

**(b)** Let $K$ be a field and
$$R=\begin{pmatrix}K&K\\0&K\end{pmatrix}\subseteq M_2(K),$$
acting by right multiplication on the row space $V=K^2$. The action is faithful ($e_1r$ and $e_2r$ are the rows of $r$). $V_1=(0,K)$ is an $R$-submodule since $(0,c)\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\0&d\end{pmatrix}=(0,cd)$. Any $R$-module of $K$-dimension $1$ is simple (as $R\supseteq K\cdot I$, every $R$-submodule is a $K$-subspace), so $V_1$ and $V/V_1$ are simple and $0\subset V_1\subset V$ is a composition series of length $2$.

Finally $N=\begin{pmatrix}0&K\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ is a two-sided ideal of $R$ (direct check: $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\0&d\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0&x\\0&0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0&ax\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix}0&x\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\0&d\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0&xd\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$) with $N^2=0$. By the argument in (a), nilpotent ideals lie in $\mathrm{Jrad}(R)$, so $\mathrm{Jrad}(R)\supseteq N\ne0$. (In fact $\mathrm{Jrad}(R)=N$.) ∎

prompt:
Let $f(x) \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ be a monic polynomial with integer coefficients and suppose that $f(\alpha) = 0 = f(2\alpha)$ for some complex number $\alpha$.

(a) Show that $f(0)$, the constant term of $f$, is not equal to $1$.

(b) If $f$ is irreducible, prove that $\alpha = 0$.
answer: (a) If $f(0)=1$ then $\alpha\neq0$, and the product of the roots $\alpha\cdot2\alpha\cdot\prod\beta_i=\pm1$ makes $\tfrac12=\pm\alpha^2\prod\beta_i$ an algebraic integer, impossible. (b) Some $\sigma$ in the Galois group maps $\alpha\mapsto2\alpha$; then $\alpha=\sigma^m(\alpha)=2^m\alpha$, so $\alpha=0$.

solutions.title: Algebraic integers and the Galois group
solutions.body:
**(a)** If $\alpha=0$ then $f(0)=0
e1$. So assume $\alpha
eq0$; then $\alpha
e2\alpha$ and over $\mathbb C$ we can write $f(x)=(x-\alpha)(x-2\alpha)\prod_{i=1}^k(x- eta_i)$. The roots of the monic integer polynomial $f$ are algebraic integers, and comparing constant terms, $\alpha\cdot2\alpha\cdot\prod eta_i=\pm f(0)$. If $f(0)=1$, then
$$	frac12=\pm\,\alpha^2\prod_{i=1}^k eta_i ,$$
a product of algebraic integers, hence an algebraic integer. But $\mathbb Z$ is a UFD, hence integrally closed, so the only rational algebraic integers are integers, and $	frac12
otin\mathbb Z$. Contradiction; so $f(0)
eq1$.

**(b)** Let $K\subseteq\mathbb C$ be the splitting field of $f$ over $\mathbb Q$ and $G=\mathrm{Gal}(K/\mathbb Q)$, a finite group. Since $f$ is irreducible, $G$ acts transitively on its roots, so there is $\sigma\in G$ with $\sigma(\alpha)=2\alpha$. By induction $\sigma^n(\alpha)=2^n\alpha$ (as $\sigma$ fixes $2$). If $m\ge1$ is the order of $\sigma$, then $\alpha=\sigma^m(\alpha)=2^m\alpha$, so $(2^m-1)\alpha=0$ and $\alpha=0$ since $2^m-1
