prompt:
Let $A$ be an $n \times n$ matrix over the complex numbers and let $A^*$ denote the conjugate transpose of $A$.

(a) Prove that all eigenvalues of the product matrix $A^*A$ are real and nonnegative.

(b) If $I$ is the $n \times n$ complex identity matrix, show that $\det(I + A^*A)$ is real and positive.
answer: (a) If $A^*Av=\lambda v$, $v\ne0$, then $\lambda=\langle Av,Av\rangle/\langle v,v\rangle\ge0$. (b) The eigenvalues of $I+A^*A$ are $1+\lambda\ge1$, and the determinant is their product.

solutions.title: Rayleigh quotient
solutions.body:
Use the Hermitian inner product $\langle v,w\rangle=v^*w$ on $\mathbb C^n$; $\langle v,v\rangle>0$ for $v\ne0$.

**(a)** Let $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ be an eigenvalue of $A^*A$ with eigenvector $v\neq0$. Then $v^*A^*Av=\lambda v^*v$, i.e. $\langle Av,Av\rangle=\lambda\langle v,v\rangle$. Hence $\lambda=\langle Av,Av\rangle/\langle v,v\rangle$ is real and $\ge0$.

**(b)** If $(I+A^*A)v=\lambda v$ with $v\ne0$, then $A^*Av=(\lambda-1)v$, so $\lambda-1$ is an eigenvalue of $A^*A$ and $\lambda\ge1$ by (a). Over $\mathbb C$ the determinant is the product of the eigenvalues (with algebraic multiplicity), so $\det(I+A^*A)$ is a product of real numbers $\ge1$; hence it is real and $\ge1>0$. ∎

prompt:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over some field $F$ and let $T\colon V \to V$ be a linear operator. Write $F[T]$ to denote the ring of all linear operators on $V$ that can be expressed as polynomials in $T$. Assume that no nonzero proper subspace of $V$ is mapped into itself by $T$.

(a) If $0 \neq S \in F[T]$, show that $\{v \in V \mid vS = 0\}$ is the zero subspace.

(b) Prove that $F[T]$ is a field.

(c) Show that $|F[T] : F| = \dim_F V$.
answer: (a) $\ker S$ is $T$-invariant (as $ST=TS$) and $\ne V$, so it is $0$. (b) Each $0\ne S\in F[T]$ is invertible and Cayley–Hamilton expresses $S^{-1}$ as a polynomial in $S$, hence in $T$. (c) $V$ is a vector space over the field $F[T]$ whose subspaces are $T$-invariant, so $\dim_{F[T]}V=1$ and $V\cong F[T]$ as $F$-spaces.

solutions.title: Kernels are invariant subspaces
solutions.body:
Operators act on the right: $v\mapsto vS$. Assume $V\neq0$.

**(a)** Let $W=\{v\mid vS=0\}$. Since $S\ne0$, $W\ne V$. Since $S$ is a polynomial in $T$, $ST=TS$; so for $v\in W$, $(vT)S=(vS)T=0$, i.e. $WT\subseteq W$. By hypothesis $W=0$.

**(b)** $F[T]$ is a commutative ring with $1$ (and $1\ne0$ as $V\ne0$). Let $0\ne S\in F[T]$. By (a) $S$ is injective, hence invertible. By Cayley–Hamilton, with $r=\dim_FV$, $S^r+a_1S^{r-1}+\cdots+a_{r-1}S+a_rI=0$ with $a_i\in F$, and $a_r=\pm\det S\neq0$. Multiplying by $a_r^{-1}S^{-1}$:
$$S^{-1}=-a_r^{-1}\left(S^{r-1}+a_1S^{r-2}+\cdots+a_{r-1}I\right)\in F[T].$$
Thus every nonzero element of $F[T]$ is invertible in $F[T]$, so $F[T]$ is a field.

**(c)** $V$ is a vector space over the field $E=F[T]$ (via $v\cdot S=vS$), and the $E$-scalars include $F$. Every $E$-subspace of $V$ is $T$-stable, so by hypothesis $V$ has no nonzero proper $E$-subspaces, i.e. $\dim_EV=1$. Pick $0\ne v\in V$; then $S\mapsto vS$ is an isomorphism $E\to V$ of $E$-spaces, in particular of $F$-spaces. Hence $|F[T]:F|=\dim_FE=\dim_FV$. ∎

prompt:
For any finite group $G$ and prime $p$, we let $n_p(G)$ denote the number of Sylow $p$-subgroups of $G$. Now suppose $K \trianglelefteq G$, and let $P$ be a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$.

(a) Show that $n_p(G/K)$ divides $n_p(G)$.

(b) Prove that $n_p(G/K) = n_p(G)$ if and only if $P \trianglelefteq PK$.
answer: With $N=N_G(P)\subseteq M=N_G(PK)$: $n_p(G)=|G:N|$ and $n_p(G/K)=|G:M|$, so $n_p(G)=n_p(G/K)\,|M:N|$. Equality iff $M=N$, iff $P\trianglelefteq PK$ (a normal Sylow subgroup of $PK$ is characteristic).

solutions.title: Compare normalizers
solutions.body:
Let $N=N_G(P)$ and $M=N_G(PK)$. Since $K\trianglelefteq G$, any $g$ normalizing $P$ normalizes $PK$, so $N\subseteq M$. By Sylow, $n_p(G)=|G:N|$.

In $\bar G=G/K$, $\bar P=PK/K$ is a Sylow $p$-subgroup (its index $|G:PK|$ divides $|G:P|$, prime to $p$). By the correspondence theorem, $gK$ normalizes $PK/K$ iff $g$ normalizes $PK$, so $N_{\bar G}(\bar P)=M/K$ and
$$n_p(G/K)=|G/K:M/K|=|G:M|.$$

**(a)** $n_p(G)=|G:N|=|G:M|\,|M:N|=n_p(G/K)\,|M:N|$. So $n_p(G/K)\mid n_p(G)$, with equality iff $M=N$.

**(b)** Suppose $P\trianglelefteq PK$. $P$ is a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $PK$, and a normal Sylow subgroup is the unique one of its order, hence characteristic in $PK$. Since $PK\trianglelefteq M$, $P\trianglelefteq M$, i.e. $M\subseteq N$. So $M=N$ and $n_p(G/K)=n_p(G)$.

Conversely, if $n_p(G/K)=n_p(G)$ then $N=M\supseteq PK$; since $P\trianglelefteq N$, we get $P\trianglelefteq PK$. ∎

prompt:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$, and recall that a proper ideal $I \triangleleft R$ is said to be *primary* if, for all $r, s \in R$, the inclusion $rs \in I$ implies that either $r \in I$ or $s^n \in I$ for some integer $n \geq 1$. Assume now that every proper ideal of $R$ is primary.

(a) If $P$ is a prime ideal of $R$ and if $I \triangleleft R$, prove that either $I \subseteq P$ or $P = IP \subseteq I$.

(b) If $M$ is a maximal ideal of $R$, prove that $M$ is precisely the set of nonunits of $R$.

(c) Show that a proper ideal $J$ of $R$ is prime if and only if, for all $r \in R$, the inclusion $r^2 \in J$ implies that $r \in J$.
answer: (a) Pick $s\in I\setminus P$; for $p\in P$, $ps\in IP$ (primary) and $s^n\notin IP\subseteq P$ force $p\in IP$. (b) A nonunit $r$ gives a proper ideal $rR$ comparable with $M$ by (a), so $rR\subseteq M$. (c) If $r^2\in J\Rightarrow r\in J$, then $s^n\in J\Rightarrow s\in J$ by induction, and primary becomes prime.

solutions.title: Use primariness of the right ideal
solutions.body:
**(a)** Suppose $I\not\subseteq P$ and choose $s\in I\setminus P$. If $IP=R$ then $R=IP\subseteq P$, impossible; so $IP$ is proper, hence primary. Let $p\in P$. Then $ps\in IP$, so either $p\in IP$ or $s^n\in IP$ for some $n\ge1$. The latter gives $s^n\in P$, so $s\in P$ since $P$ is prime — a contradiction. Hence $P\subseteq IP$. Always $IP\subseteq P$ and $IP\subseteq I$, so $P=IP\subseteq I$.

**(b)** Elements of $M$ are nonunits since $M$ is proper. Conversely let $r$ be a nonunit, so $I=rR$ is a proper ideal. $M$ is prime, so by (a) either $I\subseteq M$ or $M\subseteq I$; in the second case maximality and $I\ne R$ give $I=M$. Either way $r\in I\subseteq M$. (So $R$ is local.)

**(c)** If $J$ is prime and $r^2=r\cdot r\in J$, then $r\in J$.

Conversely assume $r^2\in J\Rightarrow r\in J$. First, $s^n\in J\Rightarrow s\in J$ for all $n\ge1$, by induction on $n$: trivial for $n=1$; if $n\ge2$ then $2(n-1)\ge n$, so $(s^{n-1})^2=s^{n-2}\cdot s^n\in J$, hence $s^{n-1}\in J$ and by induction $s\in J$. Now if $rs\in J$, since $J$ is primary either $r\in J$ or $s^n\in J$ for some $n$, i.e. $s\in J$. So $J$ is prime. ∎

prompt:
Let $F$ be a field with algebraic closure $\overline{F}$, let $f(x) \in F[x]$ be a polynomial of degree $n \geq 1$, and let $E \supseteq F$ be the splitting field of $f(x)$ over $F$ with $E \subseteq \overline{F}$. Assume that $f(x)$ has $n$ distinct roots $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n$ in $E$.

(a) Show that there exists an element $\beta \in E$ and $n$ polynomials $p_i(x) \in F[x]$ with $p_i(\beta) = \alpha_i$ for all $i = 1, 2, \ldots, n$.

(b) Continuing with the notation of (a), let $g(x) \in F[x]$ be the minimal polynomial of $\beta$ over $F$. If $\gamma \in \overline{F}$ is any root of $g(x)$, show that $p_1(\gamma), p_2(\gamma), \ldots, p_n(\gamma)$ are equal to $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n$ in some order.

(c) Continuing with the notation of (a) and (b), if $\gamma$ and $\gamma'$ are both roots of $g(x)$ and if $p_i(\gamma) = p_i(\gamma')$ for all $i = 1, 2, \ldots, n$, show that $\gamma = \gamma'$.
answer: (a) $E/F$ is finite separable, so $E=F[\beta]$ (primitive element) and $\alpha_i=p_i(\beta)$. (b) $\beta\mapsto\gamma$ extends to an $F$-automorphism $\sigma$ of the normal extension $E$, and $p_i(\gamma)=\sigma(\alpha_i)$, a permutation of the roots. (c) The automorphism $\tau\colon\gamma\mapsto\gamma'$ fixes every $\alpha_i$, hence fixes $E$, so $\gamma'=\gamma$.

solutions.title: Primitive element and automorphisms
solutions.body:
**(a)** Since $f$ has $n$ distinct roots it is separable, so $E=F[\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n]$ is a finite separable (indeed Galois) extension of $F$. By the primitive element theorem $E=F[\beta]$ for some $\beta\in E$; then each $\alpha_i\in F[\beta]$ can be written $\alpha_i=p_i(\beta)$ with $p_i\in F[x]$.

**(b)** $g$ is irreducible over $F$ with the root $\beta\in E$; since $E/F$ is normal, $g$ splits in $E$, so $\gamma\in E$. As $g$ is irreducible, there is an $F$-isomorphism $\sigma\colon F[\beta]\to F[\gamma]$ with $\sigma(\beta)=\gamma$. Since $[F[\gamma]:F]=\deg g=[E:F]$ and $F[\gamma]\subseteq E$, $F[\gamma]=E$; so $\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(E/F)$. Because $\sigma$ fixes the coefficients of $p_i$,
$$p_i(\gamma)=p_i(\sigma(\beta))=\sigma(p_i(\beta))=\sigma(\alpha_i).$$
$\sigma$ maps roots of $f\in F[x]$ to roots of $f$ and is injective, so it permutes $\{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n\}$. Hence $p_1(\gamma),\dots,p_n(\gamma)$ are $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n$ in some order.

**(c)** As in (b), $F[\gamma]=E=F[\gamma']$ and there is $\tau\in\mathrm{Gal}(E/F)$ with $\tau(\gamma)=\gamma'$ (compose the isomorphisms $F[\beta]\to F[\gamma]$ and $F[\beta]\to F[\gamma']$). By (b), $\{p_i(\gamma)\}=\{\alpha_i\}$, and $\tau(p_i(\gamma))=p_i(\tau(\gamma))=p_i(\gamma')=p_i(\gamma)$. So $\tau$ fixes every $\alpha_i$, hence fixes $E=F[\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n]$ pointwise; thus $\tau=\mathrm{id}$ and $\gamma'=\tau(\gamma)=\gamma$. ∎

prompt:
Let $A$ be an $n \times n$ matrix over an algebraically closed field $K$.

(a) Show that $A = B + C$ where $B$ is a diagonalizable matrix, $C$ is nilpotent with $C^n = 0$, and $BC = CB$.

(b) If $\operatorname{char} K = p > 0$, prove that $A^{p^t}$ is diagonalizable for some integer $t \geq 0$.

(c) If $K$ is the complex number field, prove that the exponential matrix $\exp(A) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} A^k/k!$ exists.
answer: (a) From the Jordan form $P^{-1}AP=D+N$ ($D$ diagonal, $N$ strictly upper triangular blockwise, $DN=ND$) take $B=PDP^{-1}$, $C=PNP^{-1}$. (b) For $p^t\ge n$, $A^{p^t}=B^{p^t}+C^{p^t}=B^{p^t}$. (c) With $\|X\|=\max|x_{ij}|$, $\|A^k\|\le(n\|A\|)^k$, so the series converges entrywise absolutely.

solutions.title: Jordan decomposition
solutions.body:
**(a)** Since $K$ is algebraically closed, there is an invertible $P$ with $P^{-1}AP=\mathrm{diag}(J_1,\dots,J_k)$, where $J_i=\lambda_iI_{k_i}+N_i$ is a Jordan block, $N_i$ having $1$'s on the superdiagonal and $N_i^{k_i}=0$. Let $D=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1I_{k_1},\dots,\lambda_kI_{k_k})$ and $N=\mathrm{diag}(N_1,\dots,N_k)$. Blockwise, $\lambda_iI$ commutes with $N_i$, so $DN=ND$; and $N^n=\mathrm{diag}(N_i^n)=0$ since $k_i\le n$. Set $B=PDP^{-1}$ (diagonalizable), $C=PNP^{-1}$. Then $A=B+C$, $BC=CB$ and $C^n=0$.

**(b)** Choose $t$ with $p^t\ge n$. Since $B,C$ commute, the binomial theorem holds, and in characteristic $p$ the binomial coefficients $\binom{p^t}{j}$, $0<j<p^t$, vanish. Hence $A^{p^t}=B^{p^t}+C^{p^t}=B^{p^t}=PD^{p^t}P^{-1}$, which is diagonalizable.

**(c)** For an $n\times n$ complex matrix $X$ let $\|X\|=\max_{i,j}|x_{ij}|$. Then $|(XY)_{ij}|=|\sum_l x_{il}y_{lj}|\le n\|X\|\|Y\|$, so $\|XY\|\le n\|X\|\|Y\|$, and by induction $\|A^k\|\le n^{k-1}\|A\|^k\le(n\|A\|)^k$ for $k\ge1$. Therefore, for each entry $(i,j)$,
$$\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{|(A^k)_{ij}|}{k!}\le\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{(n\|A\|)^k}{k!}=e^{n\|A\|}<\infty,$$
so each entry series converges absolutely and $\exp(A)$ exists.

*Alternative:* with $A=B+C$ as in (a), $B=PDP^{-1}$ gives $\exp(B)=P\,\mathrm{diag}(e^{\mu_1},\dots,e^{\mu_n})P^{-1}$, and since $BC=CB$, $C^n=0$, the partial sums of $\sum A^k/k!=\sum_k\sum_{i<n}\frac{B^{k-i}}{(k-i)!}\frac{C^i}{i!}$ converge to $\exp(B)\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}C^i/i!$. ∎

prompt:
Let $R$ be a ring with $1$, let $V$ be a right $R$-module, and let $W$ be a submodule of $V$. Suppose that $V = V_1 \dotplus V_2 \dotplus \cdots \dotplus V_n = \sum_i V_i$ is an internal direct sum of the simple (that is, irreducible) submodules $V_1, V_2, \ldots, V_n$. Furthermore, for each subscript $j$, let $V'_j = \sum_{i \neq j} V_i$ be the internal direct sum of those $V_i$ with $i \neq j$, so that $V = V_j \dotplus V'_j$.

(a) If $W \neq 0$, prove that $W$ contains a minimal proper submodule and a maximal proper submodule.

(b) If $W$ is a maximal proper submodule of $V$, prove that there exists a subscript $k$ with $V = W \dotplus V_k$ and hence that $V/W \cong V_k$.

(c) If $W$ is simple, show that there exists a subscript $j$ with $W \cong V_j$ and $W \dotplus V'_j = V$.
answer: (a) $V$ has a composition series of length $n$, so submodules satisfy ACC and DCC. (b) Some $V_k\not\subseteq W$; then $W\cap V_k=0$ and $W+V_k=V$ by maximality. (c) Since $\bigcap_j V'_j=0$, some $V'_j\not\supseteq W$; then $W\cap V'_j=0$, and $V'_j$ is maximal, so $V=W\dotplus V'_j$ and $W\cong V/V'_j\cong V_j$.

solutions.title: Finite length and simplicity
solutions.body:
Here "minimal proper submodule" of $W$ means a minimal nonzero submodule.

**(a)** Let $V^i=V_1\dotplus\cdots\dotplus V_i$. Then $0=V^0\subset V^1\subset\cdots\subset V^n=V$ with $V^i/V^{i-1}\cong V_i$ simple, so $V$ has a composition series of length $n$. By Jordan–Hölder every strictly increasing chain of submodules of $V$ has length $\le n$, so the submodules of $V$ satisfy both the ascending and descending chain conditions, hence every nonempty set of submodules has maximal and minimal elements. Since $W\neq0$, the set of nonzero submodules of $W$ has a minimal element $X$, and the set of proper submodules of $W$ (which contains $0$) has a maximal element $Y$.

**(b)** Since $W\ne V=\sum V_i$, some $V_k\not\subseteq W$. Then $W\cap V_k$ is a proper submodule of the simple module $V_k$, so $W\cap V_k=0$. $W+V_k$ properly contains $W$, so by maximality $W+V_k=V$. Hence $V=W\dotplus V_k$ and $V/W\cong V_k$.

**(c)** Let $\pi_k\colon V\to V_k$ be the projections; $\ker\pi_k=V'_k$ and $\bigcap_k V'_k=\bigcap_k\ker\pi_k=0$. Since $W\ne0$, some $j$ has $W\not\subseteq V'_j$. Then $W\cap V'_j$ is a proper submodule of the simple $W$, so $W\cap V'_j=0$, and $W\dotplus V'_j$ properly contains $V'_j$. Since $V/V'_j\cong V_j$ is simple, $V'_j$ is a maximal submodule, so $W\dotplus V'_j=V$. Consequently $W\cong (W\dotplus V'_j)/V'_j=V/V'_j\cong V_j$. ∎

prompt:
Let $N$ be a normal subgroup of the finite group $G$. A subgroup $H$ of $G$ is said to be a *complement* for $N$ in $G$ if $NH = G$ and $N \cap H = 1$.

(a) Show that all complements for $N$ in $G$ are isomorphic.

(b) If $N$ has a complement in $G$ that is a $p$-group for some prime $p$, prove that every Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$ contains a complement for $N$.

(c) Assume that the center of $N$ is trivial, that is equal to the identity subgroup, and that every automorphism of $N$ is inner. Prove that $N$ has a unique complement $H$ that is normal in G.
answer: (a) Each complement $H\cong NH/N=G/N$. (b) If $H\le S\in\mathrm{Syl}_p(G)$ and $P=S^g$, then $H^g\le P$ is again a complement. (c) $C=C_G(N)$ is a normal complement ($G=NC$ since $N\to\mathrm{Aut}(N)$ is onto, $N\cap C=Z(N)=1$); any normal complement $H$ centralizes $N$, so $H\le C$ and $C=(N\cap C)H=H$.

solutions.title: Conjugation action on N
solutions.body:
**(a)** If $H$ is a complement, then $G/N=NH/N\cong H/(H\cap N)=H/1\cong H$. So every complement is isomorphic to $G/N$.

**(b)** Let $H$ be a complement that is a $p$-group, and let $S\in\mathrm{Syl}_p(G)$ contain $H$. Any Sylow $p$-subgroup has the form $P=S^g=g^{-1}Sg$, so $P\supseteq H^g$. Since $N\trianglelefteq G$: $G=G^g=N^gH^g=NH^g$ and $N\cap H^g=(N\cap H)^g=1$. Thus $H^g\le P$ is a complement for $N$.

**(c)** Conjugation gives a homomorphism $\theta\colon G\to\mathrm{Aut}(N)$ with kernel $C=C_G(N)\trianglelefteq G$. The image $\theta(N)$ is $\mathrm{Inn}(N)=\mathrm{Aut}(N)$ by hypothesis, so for each $g\in G$ there is $n\in N$ with $\theta(g)=\theta(n)$, i.e. $n^{-1}g\in C$; hence $G=NC$. Also $N\cap C=Z(N)=1$. Thus $C$ is a normal complement for $N$.

Uniqueness: let $H$ be any normal complement. Then $N,H\trianglelefteq G$ with $N\cap H=1$, so $[N,H]\subseteq N\cap H=1$ and $H\le C$. By Dedekind's modular law (as $H\le C$),
$$C=C\cap NH=(C\cap N)H=1\cdot H=H.$$
So $H=C_G(N)$ is the unique normal complement. ∎

prompt:
Let $R$ be a commutative integral domain with $1$, and assume that $R$ is integrally closed in its field of fractions. Let $R[x]$ denote the ring of polynomials over $R$ in the variable $x$.

(a) Let $S \supseteq R$, where $S$ is a commutative integral domain with the same $1$, and let $s \in S$ be an element integral over $R$. If $I$ is the ideal of $R[x]$ consisting of all polynomials $f(x)$ with $f(s) = 0$, prove that $I$ is principal.

(b) Let $I$ be a prime ideal of $R[x]$ containing a monic polynomial. If $I \cap R = 0$, prove that $I$ is principal.
answer: (a) The minimal polynomial $g$ of $s$ over $K=\mathrm{Frac}(R)$ divides a monic $h\in I$, so its coefficients are integral over $R$ and lie in $K$, hence in $R$; division by the monic $g$ shows $I=gR[x]$. (b) $R\hookrightarrow S=R[x]/I$, $I=\{f\mid f(\bar x)=0\}$ and $\bar x$ is integral, so apply (a).

solutions.title: Minimal polynomial has integral coefficients
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $K$ be the fraction field of $R$, contained in the fraction field $F$ of $S$, and work in an algebraic closure $\overline F$. Let $I'=\{f\in K[x]\mid f(s)=0\}$, an ideal of the PID $K[x]$, with $I=I'\cap R[x]$. Since $s$ is integral, $I$ contains a monic $h\in R[x]$, so $I'\ne0$ and $I'=g(x)K[x]$ with $g$ monic (the minimal polynomial of $s$ over $K$). Then $g\mid h$ in $K[x]$, so every root of $g$ in $\overline F$ is a root of $h$, hence integral over $R$. The coefficients of $g$ are $\pm$ elementary symmetric functions of its roots, hence integral over $R$ (integral elements form a ring); they lie in $K$, and $R$ is integrally closed, so $g\in R[x]$. Thus $g\in R[x]\cap I'=I$.

Let $f\in I$. Since $g$ is monic, division in $R[x]$ gives $f=qg+r$ with $q,r\in R[x]$, $\deg r<\deg g$. Then $r=f-qg\in I\subseteq I'$, so $g\mid r$ in $K[x]$, forcing $r=0$. Hence $I=gR[x]$ is principal.

**(b)** $S=R[x]/I$ is an integral domain since $I$ is prime. The composite $R\to R[x]\to S$ has kernel $I\cap R=0$, so we may regard $R\subseteq S$ (same $1$). With $s=x+I\in S$, the quotient map is $f(x)\mapsto f(s)$, so $I=\{f\in R[x]\mid f(s)=0\}$. Since $I$ contains a monic polynomial, $s$ is integral over $R$. By (a), $I$ is principal. ∎

prompt:
Let $K$ be a field of prime characteristic $p$ and let $F = K(t)$ be the rational function field over $K$ in the indeterminate $t$. Write $f(x) = x^{2p} - tx^p + t \in F[x]$.

(a) Show that $f(x)$ is an irreducible polynomial in $F[x]$.

(b) Let $E = F[s]$, where $s$ is a root of the polynomial $x^p - t \in F[x]$. If $L$ is the splitting field of $f(x)$ over $E$, prove that $|L : E| \leq 2$.

(c) Show that $L = F[\alpha]$, where $\alpha$ is a root of $f(x)$.
answer: (a) Eisenstein at the prime $t$ of $K[t]$ (Gauss's lemma). (b) Over $E$, $f=(x^2-sx+s)^p$, and one root of the quadratic gives the other (they sum to $s$). (c) $2p=|F[\alpha]:F|\le|L:F|=|L:E||E:F|\le2p$.

solutions.title: Eisenstein and degree count
solutions.body:
**(a)** $R=K[t]$ is a UFD with fraction field $F$ and $t$ is a prime of $R$. $f\in R[x]$ is monic, $t$ divides the other coefficients $-t$ and $t$, and $t^2\nmid t$. By Eisenstein's criterion (with Gauss's lemma) $f$ is irreducible in $F[x]$.

**(b)** In $E$, $s^p=t$, and in characteristic $p$ the Frobenius map is additive, so
$$(x^2-sx+s)^p=x^{2p}-s^px^p+s^p=x^{2p}-tx^p+t=f(x).$$
Hence the roots of $f$ are the roots of $q(x)=x^2-sx+s\in E[x]$, and $L$ is the splitting field of $q$ over $E$. If $\alpha$ is a root of $q$, the other root is $s-\alpha\in E[\alpha]$, so $L=E[\alpha]$ and $|L:E|\le\deg q=2$.

**(c)** Let $\alpha\in L$ be a root of $f$. Since $f$ is irreducible over $F$, $|F[\alpha]:F|=2p$, and $F[\alpha]\subseteq L$. On the other hand, $|E:F|\le p$ (as $s$ is a root of $x^p-t$) and $|L:E|\le2$, so $|L:F|\le2p$. Therefore $2p\le|L:F|\le2p$, equality holds throughout, and $F[\alpha]=L$. (This holds for every root $\alpha$ of $f$.) ∎

prompt:
Let $V$ be an $n$-dimensional vector space over the field $K$ and let $T\colon V \to V$ be a linear operator. Write $K[T]$ to denote the ring of all linear operators on $V$ that can be expressed as polynomials in $T$, and let $C$ denote the $K$-vector space of all linear operators on $V$ that commute with $T$. Assume that there exists a vector $v_0 \in V$ that is contained in no proper $T$-invariant subspace of $V$.

(a) Show that $v_0K[T] = V$ and deduce that $\dim_K K[T] \geq n$.

(b) If $S \in C$ with $v_0S = 0$, show that $S = 0$. Deduce that $\dim_K C \leq n$.

(c) Show that $K[T] = C$, and deduce that the minimal polynomial of $T$ has degree equal to $n$.
answer: (a) $v_0K[T]$ is $T$-invariant and contains $v_0$; $f(T)\mapsto v_0f(T)$ maps $K[T]$ onto $V$. (b) $\ker S$ is $T$-invariant and contains $v_0$, so $S=0$; $S\mapsto v_0S$ embeds $C$ in $V$. (c) $K[T]\subseteq C$ and $n\le\dim K[T]\le\dim C\le n$; $\deg(\text{min poly})=\dim K[T]=n$.

solutions.title: Cyclic vector
solutions.body:
Operators act on the right.

**(a)** $W=v_0K[T]=\{v_0f(T)\}$ is a subspace with $WT\subseteq W$ and $v_0=v_0I\in W$; by hypothesis $W=V$. The $K$-linear map $\alpha\colon K[T]\to V$, $f(T)\mapsto v_0f(T)$, is therefore onto, so $\dim_KK[T]\ge n$.

**(b)** Let $W=\{v\mid vS=0\}$, a subspace containing $v_0$. Since $ST=TS$, for $w\in W$, $(wT)S=(wS)T=0$, so $W$ is $T$-invariant; hence $W=V$ and $S=0$. Thus the $K$-linear map $\beta\colon C\to V$, $S\mapsto v_0S$, has kernel $0$, so $\dim_KC\le n$.

**(c)** Polynomials in $T$ commute with $T$, so $K[T]\subseteq C$. Then $n\le\dim K[T]\le\dim C\le n$, so $\dim K[T]=\dim C=n$ and $K[T]=C$. The evaluation homomorphism $K[x]\to K[T]$, $f\mapsto f(T)$, is onto with kernel $(g)$, $g$ the minimal polynomial of $T$. So $K[T]\cong K[x]/(g)$, which has $K$-dimension $\deg g$. Hence $\deg g=n$. ∎

prompt:
Let $R$ be a ring with $1$, let $V$ be a right $R$-module with a composition series, and let $E = \mathrm{End}_R(V)$ be the ring of $R$-endomorphisms of $V$.

(a) If $\theta\colon V \to V$ is an element of $E$, prove that $\theta$ is one-to-one if and only if it is onto and hence if and only if it is invertible in $E$.

(b) If $V$ has a unique minimal $R$-submodule $U$, prove that $E$ has a unique maximal ideal $I$ and that every element of $E \setminus I$ is invertible. Be sure to verify that $I$ is indeed an ideal.

(c) Again, let $V$ have unique minimal submodule $U$, and suppose in addition that $U$ has multiplicity $1$ as an $R$-composition factor of $V$. Prove that $E$ is a division ring.
answer: (a) $\mathrm{len}(\ker\theta)+\mathrm{len}(\mathrm{im}\,\theta)=\mathrm{len}(V)$. (b) $I=\{\theta\mid\theta(U)=0\}$ is exactly the set of noninvertible elements and is an ideal, so it is the unique maximal ideal. (c) A nonzero noninvertible $\theta$ would have $U\subseteq\ker\theta$ and $U\subseteq\theta(V)\cong V/\ker\theta$, giving $U$ multiplicity $\ge2$.

solutions.title: Composition length
solutions.body:
Assume $V\neq0$. Let $\mathrm{len}$ be composition length (well defined by Jordan–Hölder); for $W\le V$, $\mathrm{len}(W)+\mathrm{len}(V/W)=\mathrm{len}(V)$, $W=0\iff\mathrm{len}(W)=0$ and $W=V\iff\mathrm{len}(W)=\mathrm{len}(V)$. Every nonzero submodule of $V$ contains a minimal submodule (DCC).

**(a)** Let $K=\ker\theta$, $L=\theta(V)\cong V/K$. Then $\mathrm{len}(K)+\mathrm{len}(L)=\mathrm{len}(V)$. So $\theta$ is injective $\iff\mathrm{len}(K)=0\iff\mathrm{len}(L)=\mathrm{len}(V)\iff L=V\iff\theta$ onto. A bijective $\theta\in E$ has inverse map that is again $R$-linear, so $\theta^{-1}\in E$; hence these conditions are equivalent to invertibility in $E$.

**(b)** $\theta$ fails to be injective iff $\ker\theta\ne0$ iff $\ker\theta\supseteq U$ (a nonzero submodule contains a minimal one, which must be $U$). Let $I=\{\theta\in E\mid\theta(U)=0\}$. By (a), $I$ is exactly the set of noninvertible elements of $E$. It is an ideal: if $\alpha,\beta\in I$ then $(\alpha-\beta)(U)=0$; for $\gamma\in E$, $\gamma\alpha(U)=\gamma(0)=0$; and $\alpha\gamma\in I$, since if $\alpha\gamma$ were invertible then $\alpha$ would be onto, hence invertible by (a), contradicting $\alpha\in I$. Also $1\notin I$. Any proper ideal of $E$ consists of noninvertible elements, so it is contained in $I$; hence $I$ is the unique maximal ideal, and $E\setminus I$ consists of invertible elements.

**(c)** Suppose $0\ne\theta\in E$ is not invertible. By (b), $K=\ker\theta\supseteq U$, so $U$ is a composition factor of $K$. Also $\theta(V)\ne0$, so $\theta(V)\supseteq U$, and $V/K\cong\theta(V)$ has $U$ as a composition factor. Refining $0\subseteq K\subseteq V$ to a composition series, $U$ appears at least twice, contradicting multiplicity $1$. So every nonzero element of $E$ is invertible and $E$ is a division ring. ∎

prompt:
Let $G$ be a finite group of order $504 = 2^3 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 7$.

(a) Show that $G$ cannot be isomorphic to a subgroup of the alternating group $\mathrm{Alt}_7$.

(b) If $G$ is simple, determine the number of Sylow $3$-subgroups of $G$.
answer: (a) $N_{\mathrm{Alt}_7}(P)$ has order $21$ for a Sylow $7$-subgroup $P$, so $n_7(G)\in\{72,24\}$, neither $\equiv1\pmod 7$ (alternatively: a subgroup of index $5$ in the simple group $\mathrm{Alt}_7$ is impossible). (b) $n_3=28$.

solutions.title: Normalizer of a 7-cycle
solutions.body:
**(a)** Suppose $G\le\mathrm{Alt}_7\le\mathrm{Sym}_7$. Let $P\in\mathrm{Syl}_7(G)$; $|P|=7$, and after relabeling $P=\langle\sigma\rangle$ with $\sigma=(1\,2\,3\,4\,5\,6\,7)$. The centralizer of $\sigma$ in $\mathrm{Sym}_7$ has order $7!/|\text{class of }7\text{-cycles}|=7!/6!=7$, so $C_{\mathrm{Sym}_7}(P)=P$. Hence $N=N_{\mathrm{Sym}_7}(P)$ satisfies $N/P\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Aut}(P)\cong C_6$, so $|N|\le42$. The element $x=(1\,7)(2\,6)(3\,5)$ inverts $\sigma$ (it is the reflection $i\mapsto 8-i$ of the $7$-gon), so $x\in N$; $x$ is odd, so $N\not\le\mathrm{Alt}_7$ and $|N_{\mathrm{Alt}_7}(P)|$ divides $21$. Therefore $|N_G(P)|\in\{7,21\}$ and
$$n_7(G)=|G:N_G(P)|\in\{72,\,24\}.$$
But $72\equiv2$ and $24\equiv3\pmod7$, contradicting Sylow's theorem $n_7\equiv1\pmod 7$.

*Alternative:* $|\mathrm{Alt}_7:G|=2520/504=5$. The action of the simple group $\mathrm{Alt}_7$ on the $5$ cosets of $G$ is a nontrivial homomorphism $\mathrm{Alt}_7\to\mathrm{Sym}_5$, hence injective, impossible since $2520>120$.

**(b)** Let $G$ be simple and $n_3=n_3(G)$. Then $n_3\mid 56$, $n_3\equiv1\pmod3$ and $n_3\ne1$, so $n_3\in\{4,7,28\}$. If $Q\in\mathrm{Syl}_3(G)$ and $N=N_G(Q)$, then $|G:N|=n_3$, and the action of $G$ on the cosets of $N$ is a nontrivial homomorphism $G\to\mathrm{Sym}_{n_3}$, injective because $G$ is simple.
- $n_3=4$ is impossible since $504>4!$.
- If $n_3=7$, then $G\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Sym}_7$. $G\cap\mathrm{Alt}_7$ is normal in $G$ of index $\le2$; as $G$ is simple of order $>2$, $G\cap\mathrm{Alt}_7=G$, so $G\le\mathrm{Alt}_7$, contradicting (a).

Hence $n_3=28$. (This occurs: $G=\mathrm{PSL}(2,8)$, where the Sylow $3$-normalizers are dihedral of order $18$ and $504/18=28$.) ∎

prompt:
Let $R$ be a commutative integral domain with $1$.

(a) Let $K$ be the field of fractions of $R$, let $t \in R$ be a nonzero element, and suppose that $K = R[1/t]$. In other words, every element of $K$ can be written as a polynomial in $1/t$ with coefficients in $R$. Show that $t$ is contained in every nonzero prime ideal of $R$.

(b) Now suppose that $R$ is the polynomial ring $R = F[X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n]$ where $F$ is an infinite field. If $f(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n)$ is contained in every nonzero prime ideal of $R$, show first that $f(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n) = 0$ for all $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n \in F$. Then prove that the latter zero-value property implies that $f$ is the zero polynomial.
answer: (a) For $0\ne p\in P$, writing $1/p=\sum_{i\le n} r_i t^{-i}$ gives $t^n\in pR\subseteq P$, so $t\in P$. (b) $f$ lies in each maximal ideal $(X_1-a_1,\dots,X_n-a_n)$, so it vanishes on $F^n$; a nonzero polynomial over an infinite field has a nonvanishing point (induction on $n$).

solutions.title: Clear denominators; induct on variables
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $P$ be a nonzero prime ideal and $0\ne p\in P$. Since $1/p\in K=R[1/t]$, write $1/p=r_0+r_1t^{-1}+\cdots+r_nt^{-n}$ with $r_i\in R$. Multiplying by $pt^n$:
$$t^n=p\,(r_0t^n+r_1t^{n-1}+\cdots+r_n)\in pR\subseteq P.$$
Since $P$ is prime, $t\in P$.

**(b)** Let $a=(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in F^n$. The evaluation map $R\to F$, $g\mapsto g(a)$, is a surjective ring homomorphism onto a field, so its kernel $\mathfrak m_a$ is a maximal (hence prime) ideal; it is nonzero since it contains $X_1-a_1$. By hypothesis $f\in\mathfrak m_a$, i.e. $f(a)=0$.

Now we show by induction on $n$ that a nonzero $f\in F[X_1,\dots,X_n]$ does not vanish at some point of $F^n$. For $n=1$, $f$ has at most $\deg f$ roots and $F$ is infinite. For $n>1$, write $f=\sum_{i=0}^m g_i(X_1,\dots,X_{n-1})X_n^i$ with $g_m\ne0$. By induction there are $a_1,\dots,a_{n-1}$ with $g_m(a_1,\dots,a_{n-1})\neq0$; then $f(a_1,\dots,a_{n-1},X_n)\in F[X_n]$ is a nonzero polynomial (of degree $m$), so by the case $n=1$ some $a_n\in F$ gives $f(a_1,\dots,a_n)\ne0$.

Hence a polynomial vanishing on all of $F^n$ is $0$, so $f=0$. (Together with (a), this shows that the fraction field of $F[X_1,\dots,X_n]$ is never of the form $R[1/t]$.) ∎

prompt:
Let $F \subseteq E$ be fields and suppose $0 \neq \alpha \in E$ with $E = F[\alpha]$. Assume that some power of $\alpha$ lies in $F$ and let $n$ be the smallest positive integer such that $\alpha^n \in F$.

(a) If $\alpha^m \in F$ with $m > 0$, show that $m$ is a multiple of $n$.

(b) If $E$ is a separable extension of $F$, prove that the characteristic of $F$ does not divide $n$.

(c) If every root of unity in $E$ lies in $F$, show that $|E : F| = n$.
answer: (a) Division with remainder: $\alpha^r=\alpha^m/(\alpha^n)^q\in F$ forces $r=0$. (b) If $p=\operatorname{char}F\mid n$, $\beta=\alpha^{n/p}$ is a root of $X^p-\beta^p=(X-\beta)^p$, and separability gives $\beta\in F$. (c) $X^n-\alpha^n$ is irreducible: a monic factor of degree $m$ has constant term $\pm\alpha^m\delta$ with $\delta$ a root of unity in $E$, hence in $F$, so $\alpha^m\in F$ and $m=n$.

solutions.title: Minimality of n
solutions.body:
**(a)** Write $m=nq+r$ with $0\le r<n$. Then $\alpha^r=\alpha^m(\alpha^n)^{-q}\in F$, so minimality of $n$ forces $r=0$, i.e. $n\mid m$.

**(b)** Suppose $\operatorname{char}F=p>0$ and $p\mid n$. Put $\beta=\alpha^{n/p}\in E$ and $b=\beta^p=\alpha^n\in F$. The minimal polynomial $g$ of $\beta$ over $F$ divides $X^p-b$, which equals $(X-\beta)^p$ in $E[X]$. Since $E/F$ is separable, $g$ has distinct roots, so $g=X-\beta$ and $\beta=\alpha^{n/p}\in F$, contradicting the minimality of $n$.

**(c)** Let $a=\alpha^n\in F$; $\alpha$ is a root of $f(X)=X^n-a$. We show $f$ is irreducible over $F$. Let $g\in F[X]$ be a monic factor of $f$ of degree $m\ge1$. In a splitting field, every root $\gamma$ of $g$ satisfies $\gamma^n=a=\alpha^n$, so $\gamma=\alpha\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon^n=1$. Thus the product of the roots of $g$ (with multiplicity) is $\alpha^m\delta$ with $\delta^n=1$, and it equals $\pm g(0)\in F$. Then $\delta=\pm g(0)\alpha^{-m}\in E$ is a root of unity in $E$, hence $\delta\in F$, so $\alpha^m\in F$. By (a) $n\mid m$, and $m\le n$, so $m=n$. Hence $f$ is irreducible, it is the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$, and $|E:F|=|F[\alpha]:F|=\deg f=n$. ∎

prompt:
Let $A$ be a real $n \times n$ matrix. We say that $A$ is a *difference of two squares* if there exist real $n \times n$ matrices $B$ and $C$ with $BC = CB = 0$ and $A = B^2 - C^2$.

(a) If $A$ is a diagonal matrix, show that it is a difference of two squares.

(b) If $A$ is a symmetric matrix that is not necessarily diagonal, again show that it is a difference of two squares.

(c) Suppose $A$ is a difference of two squares, with corresponding matrices $B$ and $C$ as above. If $B$ has a nonzero real eigenvalue, prove that $A$ has a positive real eigenvalue.
answer: (a) Write each $a_i=b_i^2-c_i^2$ with $b_ic_i=0$ ($b_i=\sqrt{a_i}$ or $c_i=\sqrt{-a_i}$). (b) $A=U^{T}A_0U$ with $U$ orthogonal; conjugate the diagonal solution. (c) If $Bv=\lambda v\ne0$, then $\lambda Cv=CBv=0$ so $Cv=0$ and $Av=\lambda^2v$.

solutions.title: Diagonalize
solutions.body:
**(a)** For a real number $a$: if $a\ge0$ put $b=\sqrt a$, $c=0$; if $a<0$ put $b=0$, $c=\sqrt{-a}$. Then $a=b^2-c^2$ and $bc=0$. For $A=\mathrm{diag}(a_1,\dots,a_n)$ choose such $b_i,c_i$ and let $B=\mathrm{diag}(b_i)$, $C=\mathrm{diag}(c_i)$. Diagonal matrices multiply entrywise, so $B^2-C^2=\mathrm{diag}(b_i^2-c_i^2)=A$ and $BC=CB=\mathrm{diag}(b_ic_i)=0$.

**(b)** By the spectral theorem there is a real orthogonal $U$ with $A=U^{-1}A_0U$, $A_0$ real diagonal. By (a), $A_0=B_0^2-C_0^2$ with $B_0C_0=C_0B_0=0$. Put $B=U^{-1}B_0U$, $C=U^{-1}C_0U$ (real). Conjugation is a ring automorphism of $M_n(\mathbb R)$, so $B^2-C^2=U^{-1}(B_0^2-C_0^2)U=A$ and $BC=U^{-1}B_0C_0U=0=CB$.

**(c)** Let $\lambda\ne0$ be a real eigenvalue of $B$ with real eigenvector $v\ne0$ (it exists since $B-\lambda I$ is a singular real matrix). Then $B^2v=\lambda^2v$ and $\lambda\,Cv=C(Bv)=(CB)v=0$, so $Cv=0$ and $C^2v=0$. Hence $Av=B^2v-C^2v=\lambda^2v$, and $\lambda^2>0$ is a positive real eigenvalue of $A$. ∎

prompt:
Let $K$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and view the polynomial ring $V = K[x]$ as a $K$-vector space. Let $M\colon V \to V$ be the linear operator given by multiplication by $x$, so that $M(x^n) = x^{n+1}$ for all integers $n \geq 0$. In addition, let $D\colon V \to V$ be the linear operator given by differentiation with respect to $x$, so that $D(x^n) = nx^{n-1}$ for all $n \geq 0$. Let $\mathcal{L}$ denote the set of all linear operators of the form $M^iD^j$ with $i, j \geq 0$, where $M^0 = D^0 = I$ is the identity operator on $V$.

(a) Prove that $DM - MD = I$.

(b) Show that $\mathcal{L}$ is a $K$-linearly independent set.

(c) For all nonnegative integers $t$, prove that $DM^t$ is in the $K$-linear span of the set $\mathcal{L}$.
answer: (a) $(DM-MD)(x^n)=(n+1)x^n-nx^n=x^n$. (b) In a relation $\sum k_{ij}M^iD^j=0$, apply it to $x^n$ with $n$ the least $j$ occurring: $n!\sum_ik_{in}x^i=0$. (c) Induction: $DM^{t+1}=(I+MD)M^t=M^t+M\cdot DM^t$ (indeed $DM^t=M^tD+tM^{t-1}$).

solutions.title: Weyl algebra relations
solutions.body:
**(a)** $DM(x^n)=D(x^{n+1})=(n+1)x^n$ and $MD(x^n)=M(nx^{n-1})=nx^n$. So $(DM-MD)(x^n)=x^n$ for all $n\ge0$, and by linearity $DM-MD=I$.

**(b)** Suppose $\sum_{i,j}k_{ij}M^iD^j=0$ is a finite relation with not all $k_{ij}=0$. Let $n$ be the smallest $j$ with some $k_{ij}\ne0$. Apply the relation to $x^n$: $D^j(x^n)=0$ for $j>n$, $D^n(x^n)=n!$, and $k_{ij}=0$ for $j<n$. So
$$0=\sum_{i,j}k_{ij}M^iD^j(x^n)=\sum_ik_{in}M^i(n!)=n!\sum_ik_{in}x^i .$$
As $\operatorname{char}K=0$, $n!\ne0$, so $\sum_ik_{in}x^i=0$ in $K[x]$ and all $k_{in}=0$, a contradiction.

**(c)** Induction on $t$. For $t=0$, $DM^0=M^0D\in\mathcal L$. If $DM^t\in K\mathcal L$, then by (a)
$$DM^{t+1}=(DM)M^t=(I+MD)M^t=M^t+M(DM^t).$$
$M^t=M^tD^0\in\mathcal L$, and $M\cdot K\mathcal L\subseteq K\mathcal L$ since $M\cdot M^iD^j=M^{i+1}D^j$. Hence $DM^{t+1}\in K\mathcal L$. (Explicitly, $DM^t=M^tD+tM^{t-1}$ for $t\ge1$.) ∎

prompt:
Let $N$ be a normal subgroup of the finite group $G$ and suppose that $G/N$ is a $p$-group for some prime $p$.

(a) If $N \subseteq \mathbf{Z}(G)$, the center of $G$, show that the commutator subgroup $G'$ of $G$ is a $p$-group.

(b) Now assume that $N$ is cyclic (but not necessarily central in $G$). Prove that $N \cap G' \subseteq \mathbf{Z}(G')$ and deduce that $G''$ is a $p$-group.
answer: (a) $G=NP$ with $P\in\mathrm{Syl}_p(G)$, and central factors drop out of commutators, so $G'=P'\le P$. (b) $G/C_G(N)\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Aut}(N)$ is abelian, so $G'\le C_G(N)$; then apply (a) to $N\cap G'\trianglelefteq G'$, as $G'/(N\cap G')\hookrightarrow G/N$.

solutions.title: Commutators modulo a central subgroup
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $P\in\mathrm{Syl}_p(G)$. Then $NP/N\cong P/(P\cap N)$ is a $p$-subgroup of $G/N$ of index $|G:NP|$, which divides $|G:P|$ and hence is prime to $p$; as $G/N$ is a $p$-group, $NP=G$. For $a,b\in N\subseteq Z(G)$ and $x,y\in P$,
$$[ax,by]=(ax)^{-1}(by)^{-1}(ax)(by)=x^{-1}y^{-1}xy=[x,y],$$
since $a,b$ are central. So the set of commutators of $G$ equals the set of commutators of $P$, and $G'=P'\le P$ is a $p$-group.

**(b)** $G$ acts on $N$ by conjugation, giving an embedding $G/C_G(N)\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Aut}(N)$. Since $N$ is cyclic, $\mathrm{Aut}(N)$ is abelian, hence $G/C_G(N)$ is abelian and $G'\le C_G(N)$. In particular every element of $G'$ commutes with every element of $N\cap G'$, i.e. $N\cap G'\subseteq Z(G')$.

Now apply (a) to the group $G'$ and its normal subgroup $N\cap G'$: it is central in $G'$, and $G'/(N\cap G')\cong G'N/N\le G/N$ is a $p$-group. Hence $(G')'=G''$ is a $p$-group. ∎

prompt:
Let $R$ be a commutative integral domain with $1$. A nonzero, nonunit element $s \in R$ is said to be "special" if, for every element $a \in R$, there exist $q, r \in R$ with $a = qs + r$ and such that $r$ is either $0$ or a unit of $R$.

(a) If $s \in R$ is special, prove that the principal ideal $(s)$ generated by $s$ is maximal in $R$.

(b) Show that every polynomial in $\mathbb{Q}[X]$ of degree $1$ is special in $\mathbb{Q}[X]$.

(c) Prove that there are no special elements in the polynomial ring $\mathbb{Z}[X]$. (Hint. Apply the definition of special with $a = 2$ and with $a = X$.)
answer: (a) If $A\supsetneq(s)$ and $a\in A\setminus(s)$, then $a=qs+r$ with $r=a-qs\in A$ a unit, so $A=R$. (b) Division algorithm: remainders are constants. (c) Units of $\mathbb Z[X]$ are $\pm1$; $s$ divides one of $1,2,3$ (so $s\in\mathbb Z$) and one of $X,X\pm1$, so $s=\pm1$, a contradiction.

solutions.title: Use the definition with good test elements
solutions.body:
**(a)** $(s)\ne R$ as $s$ is not a unit. Let $A$ be an ideal with $(s)\subsetneq A$ and pick $a\in A\setminus(s)$. Write $a=qs+r$ with $r=0$ or $r$ a unit. If $r=0$ then $a\in(s)$, which is false; so $r=a-qs\in A$ is a unit and $A=R$. Hence $(s)$ is maximal.

**(b)** Let $s\in\mathbb Q[X]$ have degree $1$; it is nonzero and not a unit (units are nonzero constants). For $a\in\mathbb Q[X]$ the division algorithm gives $a=qs+r$ with $r=0$ or $\deg r<1$; in the latter case $r$ is a nonzero constant, a unit.

**(c)** Units of $\mathbb Z[X]$ are $\pm1$ (degrees add in a domain, so a unit is a constant unit of $\mathbb Z$). Suppose $s$ is special. For any $a$, $a-r=qs$ with $r\in\{0,1,-1\}$, so $s$ divides one of $a,a-1,a+1$.
- $a=2$: $s$ divides $2$, $1$ or $3$, so $\deg s=0$ and $s\in\mathbb Z$.
- $a=X$: $s$ divides $X$, $X-1$ or $X+1$. An integer constant $s$ dividing such a polynomial divides all its coefficients, in particular the coefficient $1$ of $X$. So $s=\pm1$ is a unit, a contradiction.

Hence $\mathbb Z[X]$ has no special elements. (Consistently with (a): $\mathbb Z[X]$ has no maximal principal ideals.) ∎

prompt:
Let $F$ be a field with $\mathbb{Q} \subseteq F \subseteq \mathbb{C}$, where $F/\mathbb{Q}$ is a finite Galois extension. Let $\alpha \in F$ and let $f(X) \in \mathbb{Q}[X]$ be its minimal monic polynomial. Assume that $1 = |\alpha|$, the absolute value of $\alpha$, and that $\mathrm{Gal}(F/\mathbb{Q})$ is abelian.

(a) Show that $F$ is closed under complex conjugation.

(b) Prove that $|\beta| = 1$ for every complex root $\beta$ of $f(X)$.

(c) Writing $f(X) = X^n + a_{n-1}X^{n-1} + \cdots + a_1X + a_0$, show that $|a_i| \leq 2^n$ for all $i$ with $0 \leq i < n$.

(d) Prove that $F$ contains only finitely many algebraic integers having absolute value $1$ and deduce that each of these is a root of unity.
answer: (a) $F$ is the splitting field in $\mathbb C$ of some $g\in\mathbb Q[X]$, and conjugation permutes the roots of $g$. (b) $\beta=\sigma(\alpha)$ and conjugation $c\in\mathrm{Gal}(F/\mathbb Q)$ commutes with $\sigma$, so $\beta\bar\beta=\sigma(\alpha\bar\alpha)=1$. (c) $|a_i|\le\binom{n}{i}\le2^n$. (d) Such $\alpha$ have minimal polynomials in $\mathbb Z[X]$ of degree $\le m=[F:\mathbb Q]$ with coefficients bounded by $2^m$; finitely many, and the powers of $\alpha$ are among them, so $\alpha^j=\alpha^k$.

solutions.title: Conjugation is central in the Galois group
solutions.body:
**(a)** As $F/\mathbb Q$ is finite Galois, $F$ is the splitting field in $\mathbb C$ of some $g\in\mathbb Q[X]$, i.e. $F=\mathbb Q(\gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_k)$ for the roots $\gamma_i$ of $g$. Complex conjugation fixes $g$, so it permutes the $\gamma_i$; hence $\overline F=\mathbb Q(\bar\gamma_1,\dots,\bar\gamma_k)=F$.

**(b)** By (a), complex conjugation restricts to an element $c\in\mathrm{Gal}(F/\mathbb Q)$. Since $f$ is irreducible and $F/\mathbb Q$ is normal, each root $\beta$ of $f$ lies in $F$ and $\beta=\sigma(\alpha)$ for some $\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(F/\mathbb Q)$. The group is abelian, so $\bar\beta=c\sigma(\alpha)=\sigma c(\alpha)=\sigma(\bar\alpha)$, and
$$|\beta|^2=\beta\bar\beta=\sigma(\alpha)\sigma(\bar\alpha)=\sigma(\alpha\bar\alpha)=\sigma(|\alpha|^2)=\sigma(1)=1 .$$
Hence $|\beta|=1$.

**(c)** With roots $\beta_1,\dots,\beta_n$, $a_i=\pm e_{n-i}(\beta_1,\dots,\beta_n)$, a sum of $\binom{n}{n-i}$ products of roots, each of absolute value $1$ by (b). So $|a_i|\le\binom{n}{i}\le\sum_k\binom nk=2^n$.

**(d)** Let $m=[F:\mathbb Q]$ and let $\alpha\in F$ be an algebraic integer with $|\alpha|=1$, with minimal polynomial $f$ of degree $n\le m$. The roots of $f$ are conjugates of $\alpha$, hence algebraic integers, so the coefficients $a_i$ are algebraic integers in $\mathbb Q$, hence in $\mathbb Z$ ($\mathbb Z$ is integrally closed). By (c), $|a_i|\le2^n\le2^m$. So there are finitely many possible $f$, each with finitely many roots, and thus only finitely many such $\alpha$.

Finally, if $\alpha$ is one of them, then $\alpha,\alpha^2,\alpha^3,\dots$ are again algebraic integers in $F$ of absolute value $1$, so they are not all distinct: $\alpha^j=\alpha^k$ with $j<k$. As $\alpha\neq0$, $\alpha^{k-j}=1$ and $\alpha$ is a root of unity. ∎

prompt:
Let $V$ be vector space over the field $K$ and let $(\ ,\ )\colon V \times V \to K$ be a bilinear form on $V$.

(a) If $V$ is finite dimensional and if $W$ is a proper subspace of $V$, show that there exists a nonzero vector $v \in V$ with $(w, v) = 0$ for all $w \in W$.

(b) Now let $V$ have an infinite basis $\mathcal{B}$ and let $(\ ,\ )$ be the unique bilinear form such that, for all $a, b \in \mathcal{B}$, we have $(a, b) = 0$ if $a \neq b$ and $(a, b) = 1$ if $a = b$. If $W$ is the subspace of $V$ spanned by all vectors of the form $a - b$ with $a, b \in \mathcal{B}$, show that $W$ is a proper subspace of $V$ and that there is no nonzero vector $v \in V$ with $(w, v) = 0$ for all $w \in W$.
answer: (a) For a basis $w_1,\dots,w_m$ of $W$ ($m<n$), the $m$ functionals $v\mapsto(w_i,v)$ have a common nonzero kernel vector. (b) $W\subseteq\ker\mu$ where $\mu(b)=1$ on $\mathcal B$; if $v=\sum k_cc$ is orthogonal to $W$, pick $b$ with $k_b=0$, then $k_a=k_b=0$ for all $a$.

solutions.title: Count linear conditions
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $n=\dim V$ and let $w_1,\dots,w_m$ be a basis of $W$, $m<n$. Each $\lambda_i\colon v\mapsto(w_i,v)$ is a linear functional, so $\ker\lambda_i$ has codimension $\le1$, and $U=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\ker\lambda_i$ has dimension $\ge n-m>0$. Take $0\ne u\in U$. Then $(w_i,u)=0$ for all $i$, and by linearity in the first variable $(w,u)=0$ for all $w\in W$.

**(b)** Let $\mu\colon V\to K$ be the linear functional with $\mu(b)=1$ for all $b\in\mathcal B$. Each $a-b$ lies in $\ker\mu$, so $W\subseteq\ker\mu\neq V$ (as $\mu\ne0$); thus $W$ is proper.

Suppose $(w,v)=0$ for all $w\in W$, and write $v=\sum_{c\in\mathcal B}k_cc$ (finite sum). Since $\mathcal B$ is infinite, some $b\in\mathcal B$ has $k_b=0$. For every $a\in\mathcal B$, $a-b\in W$, so
$$0=(a-b,v)=k_a-k_b=k_a .$$
Hence all $k_a=0$ and $v=0$. So (a) fails in infinite dimensions. ∎

prompt:
Let $R$ be a ring with $1$. We say that a right $R$-module $W$ is "infinitely generated" if it is not finitely generated as an $R$-module.

(a) Let $V$ be a right $R$-module and let $W$ be a submodule of $V$. If $W$ is infinitely generated, prove that there exists a submodule $M$ with $W \subseteq M \subseteq V$ such that $M$ is infinitely generated, but such that all submodules of $V$ properly containing $M$ are finitely generated.

(b) If $R$ is right Noetherian, show that $M = V$ in the above situation.

(c) If $R$ is not right Noetherian, show that it is possible to choose $V$ and $W$ as in part (a) so that $M \neq V$.
answer: (a) Zorn's lemma on infinitely generated submodules containing $W$: a union of a chain cannot be finitely generated (finitely many generators lie in one member). (b) A finitely generated $V$ over a right Noetherian ring is Noetherian, so $V$ itself is infinitely generated and maximality forces $M=V$. (c) $V=R_R$ and $W$ an infinitely generated right ideal; $V=1\cdot R$ is finitely generated, so $M\neq V$.

solutions.title: Zorn's lemma
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $\mathcal X$ be the set of infinitely generated submodules $X$ with $W\subseteq X\subseteq V$, ordered by inclusion; $W\in\mathcal X$. Let $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal X$ be a nonempty chain and $C=\bigcup_{X\in\mathcal C}X$. Since $\mathcal C$ is a chain, $C$ is a submodule (any two elements lie in a common member), and $W\subseteq C$. If $C$ were finitely generated, say by $x_1,\dots,x_n$ with $x_i\in X_i\in\mathcal C$, then some $X_k$ contains all $X_i$, and $C=\sum x_iR\subseteq X_k\subseteq C$, so $X_k=C$ would be finitely generated — a contradiction. So $C\in\mathcal X$ is an upper bound. By Zorn's lemma $\mathcal X$ has a maximal element $M$: it contains $W$, is infinitely generated, and every submodule of $V$ properly containing $M$ is finitely generated (otherwise it would lie in $\mathcal X$).

**(b)** If $V$ were finitely generated, then as $R$ is right Noetherian, $V$ would be a Noetherian module and all its submodules, including $W$, would be finitely generated — a contradiction. So $V$ is infinitely generated. Since $M\subseteq V$ and every submodule properly containing $M$ is finitely generated, $V$ cannot properly contain $M$; thus $M=V$.

**(c)** If $R$ is not right Noetherian, it has a right ideal $W$ that is not finitely generated. Take $V=R_R$. Then $W\subseteq V$ is infinitely generated, while $V=1\cdot R$ is finitely generated. Any $M$ as in (a) is infinitely generated, so $M\ne V$. ∎

prompt:
Let $G$ be a finite group of order $pm$, where $p$ is a prime that does not divide $m$, and let $n$ denote the number of Sylow $p$-subgroups of $G$.

(a) Show that the [sic] exists a homomorphism $\theta$ from $G$ to the symmetric group $\mathrm{Sym}(n)$ such that, for all $x \in G$ of order $p$, the image $\theta(x)$ has exactly one fixed point.

(b) Now suppose that $G$ is simple and contains an element $y$ of order $pq$, for some prime $q \neq p$. If $\theta$ is as in part (a), show that $\theta(y)$ must contain a cycle of length $pq$ in its cycle decomposition.

(c) Now let $p = 5$ and suppose that $G$ is a simple group of order $660$. Show that $G$ has no element of order $15$.
answer: (a) Conjugation on $\mathrm{Syl}_p(G)$: $x$ fixes $P$ iff $x\in P$, and Sylow subgroups of order $p$ meet trivially. (b) $\theta$ is injective; $\theta(y)^q$ has one fixed point, so $\theta(y)$ has one fixed point and no $q$-cycles, while $\theta(y)^p\ne1$ needs a $q$- or $pq$-cycle. (c) $y$ normalizes $P=\langle y^3\rangle$, so $15\mid|N_G(P)|$ and $n_5\mid44$, i.e. $n_5=11$; but by (b) $n_5\ge1+15$.

solutions.title: Action on Sylow subgroups
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $G$ act on $\mathrm{Syl}_p(G)$ (a set of size $n$) by conjugation; this gives $\theta\colon G\to\mathrm{Sym}(n)$. Each Sylow $p$-subgroup has order $p$, so two distinct ones intersect trivially. Let $x$ have order $p$. Then $\langle x\rangle$ is a Sylow $p$-subgroup, so $\theta(x)$ fixes $\langle x\rangle$. If $\theta(x)$ fixes $P$, then $x\in N_G(P)$, and $\langle x\rangle P$ is a $p$-subgroup of $N_G(P)$ containing the Sylow subgroup $P$, so $x\in P$ and $P=\langle x\rangle$. Hence $\theta(x)$ has exactly one fixed point.

**(b)** If $n=1$, the Sylow $p$-subgroup is normal, so by simplicity $G$ has order $p$ and no element of order $pq$. So $n>1$, the action is transitive and nontrivial, $\ker\theta\neq G$, and $\ker\theta=1$ by simplicity. Thus $\pi=\theta(y)$ has order $pq$ and its cycles have lengths in $\{1,p,q,pq\}$.

A cycle of length $\ell$ contributes fixed points to $\pi^q$ iff $\ell\mid q$, and then contributes $\ell$ of them. Since $y^q$ has order $p$, $\pi^q$ has exactly one fixed point by (a); so $\pi$ has exactly one $1$-cycle and no $q$-cycles. On the other hand $\pi^p=\theta(y^p)\ne1$ by injectivity, and $\pi^p$ moves exactly the points in cycles of length $\ell\nmid p$, i.e. $\ell\in\{q,pq\}$. Since there are no $q$-cycles, $\pi$ contains a $pq$-cycle.

**(c)** $|G|=660=2^2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot11$. $n=n_5$ divides $132$ and is $\equiv1\pmod5$, so $n\in\{1,6,11,66\}$, and $n\ne1$ by simplicity. Suppose $y\in G$ has order $15$ and let $P=\langle y^3\rangle\in\mathrm{Syl}_5(G)$. $y$ commutes with $y^3$, so $y\in N_G(P)$ and $15\mid|N_G(P)|=660/n$; hence $n\mid44$, which leaves $n=11$. But by (b) (with $q=3$), $\theta(y)\in\mathrm{Sym}(n)$ has a $15$-cycle and also a fixed point, so $n\ge16$. Contradiction; $G$ has no element of order $15$. (Indeed $\mathrm{PSL}(2,11)$ has element orders $1,2,3,5,6,11$.) ∎

prompt:
Let $R$ be a ring with $1$, let $M$ be a finitely generated right $R$-module, and let $N < M$ be a proper submodule of $M$.

(a) Prove that there exists a maximal submodule $K$ of $M$ with $N \subseteq K < M$.

(b) Show that $N + MJ < M$, where $J = J(R)$ denotes the Jacobson radical of $R$.
answer: (a) Zorn's lemma: a union of a chain of proper submodules containing $N$ is proper, because finitely many generators would lie in one member. (b) $M/K$ is simple, so $(M/K)J=0$, i.e. $MJ\subseteq K$; thus $N+MJ\subseteq K<M$.

solutions.title: Zorn's lemma and annihilators of simple modules
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $M=m_1R+\cdots+m_kR$ and let $\mathcal S$ be the set of proper submodules of $M$ containing $N$, ordered by inclusion; $N\in\mathcal S$. If $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal S$ is a nonempty chain, $U=\bigcup\mathcal C$ is a submodule containing $N$. If $U=M$, then each $m_i$ lies in some $C_i\in\mathcal C$, and the largest $C_j$ among $C_1,\dots,C_k$ contains all $m_i$, so $C_j=M$, a contradiction. Thus $U\in\mathcal S$ is an upper bound. By Zorn's lemma $\mathcal S$ has a maximal element $K$; it is a maximal submodule of $M$ (any submodule strictly between $K$ and $M$ would lie in $\mathcal S$), and $N\subseteq K<M$.

**(b)** Take $K$ as in (a). Then $M/K$ is a simple right $R$-module. $J(R)$ is the intersection of the annihilators of all simple right $R$-modules (the primitive ideals), so $(M/K)J=0$, i.e. $MJ\subseteq K$. Therefore $N+MJ\subseteq K<M$.

*Alternative (Nakayama):* $\bar M=M/N$ is finitely generated and nonzero. If $N+MJ=M$, then $\bar MJ=\bar M$, so $\bar M=0$ by Nakayama's lemma, a contradiction. ∎

prompt:
In the field $\mathbb{C}$ of complex numbers, let $\mathbb{Q}$ be the subfield of rational numbers, let $i = \sqrt{-1}$, and let $\sqrt[4]{2}$ be the positive real fourth root of $2$.

(a) Prove that the polynomial $X^4 - 2$ is irreducible over the field $\mathbb{Q}[i]$.

(b) If $\sqrt[4]{2} + i$ is a root of a polynomial $f(X) \in \mathbb{Q}[X]$, show that $i\sqrt[4]{2} + i$ is also a root of that polynomial.

(c) Compute the degree of the minimal polynomial of $\sqrt[4]{2} + i$ over $\mathbb{Q}$.
answer: (a) $[\mathbb Q(\sqrt[4]2,i):\mathbb Q]=8$, so $[\mathbb Q(i)(\sqrt[4]2):\mathbb Q(i)]=4$. (b) Apply the automorphism $\sqrt[4]2\mapsto i\sqrt[4]2$, $i\mapsto i$. (c) $8$ (minimal polynomial $X^8+4X^6+2X^4+28X^2+1$).

solutions.title: Galois group of X^4-2
solutions.body:
Let $\alpha=\sqrt[4]2$ and $L=\mathbb Q(\alpha,i)$, the splitting field of $X^4-2$ over $\mathbb Q$ (roots $\pm\alpha,\pm i\alpha$).

**(a)** $X^4-2$ is irreducible over $\mathbb Q$ (Eisenstein at $2$), so $[\mathbb Q(\alpha):\mathbb Q]=4$. $\mathbb Q(\alpha)\subseteq\mathbb R$ does not contain $i$, so $[L:\mathbb Q(\alpha)]=2$ and $[L:\mathbb Q]=8$. Hence $[L:\mathbb Q(i)]=4$, i.e. $[\mathbb Q(i)(\alpha):\mathbb Q(i)]=4$, so the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $\mathbb Q(i)$ has degree $4$ and divides $X^4-2$; thus $X^4-2$ is irreducible over $\mathbb Q(i)$.

**(b)** By (a), $\alpha$ and $i\alpha$ are roots of the same irreducible polynomial over $\mathbb Q(i)$, so there is a $\mathbb Q(i)$-isomorphism $\sigma\colon\mathbb Q(i)(\alpha)\to\mathbb Q(i)(i\alpha)=L$ with $\sigma(\alpha)=i\alpha$, $\sigma(i)=i$; so $\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(L/\mathbb Q)$. If $f\in\mathbb Q[X]$ and $f(\alpha+i)=0$, then $0=\sigma(f(\alpha+i))=f(\sigma(\alpha)+\sigma(i))=f(i\alpha+i)$.

**(c)** $G=\mathrm{Gal}(L/\mathbb Q)$ has order $8$; its elements are determined by $\alpha\mapsto i^k\alpha$ ($k=0,1,2,3$) and $i\mapsto\pm i$, so all $8$ such maps occur. The images of $\beta=\alpha+i$ are $i^k\alpha\pm i$:
$$\alpha\pm i,\quad -\alpha\pm i,\quad i(\alpha\pm1),\quad i(-\alpha\pm1).$$
The first four have nonzero real part $\pm\alpha$ and are distinct; the last four are purely imaginary with imaginary parts $\alpha+1,\alpha-1,1-\alpha,-1-\alpha$, distinct because $\alpha\ne0,1$. So $\beta$ has $8$ distinct conjugates, $\mathbb Q(\beta)=L$, and the minimal polynomial of $\beta$ has degree $8$.

*Check:* $\beta$ is a root of $(X-i)^4-2$, so it is a root of the rational polynomial $\big((X-i)^4-2\big)\big((X+i)^4-2\big)=X^8+4X^6+2X^4+28X^2+1$; having degree $8$, this is the minimal polynomial. ∎

prompt: Let $V$ be a vector space of dimension $n$ over a field $K$. Suppose $V$ is spanned by the $n + 1$ vectors $v_0, v_1, \ldots, v_n$ where $v_0 + v_1 + \cdots + v_n = 0$. Now let $W$ be a second $K$-vector space and let $w_0, w_1, \ldots, w_n \in W$. Find necessary and sufficient conditions on the elements $w_0, w_1, \ldots, w_n$ so that there exists a linear transformation $T\colon V \to W$ with $T(v_i) = w_i$ for $i = 0, 1, \ldots, n$.
answer: Such $T$ exists (and is unique) if and only if $w_0+w_1+\cdots+w_n=0$.

solutions.title: v_1,...,v_n is a basis
solutions.body:
**Necessity.** If $T$ exists, $w_0+\cdots+w_n=T(v_0+\cdots+v_n)=T(0)=0$.

**Sufficiency.** Since $v_0=-(v_1+\cdots+v_n)$, the $n$ vectors $v_1,\dots,v_n$ already span $V$; as $\dim V=n$ they form a basis. Hence there is a (unique) linear $T\colon V\to W$ with $T(v_i)=w_i$ for $1\le i\le n$. If $\sum_{i=0}^nw_i=0$, then
$$T(v_0)=-\sum_{i=1}^nT(v_i)=-\sum_{i=1}^nw_i=w_0 .$$
So $T(v_i)=w_i$ for all $i=0,\dots,n$.

*Remark:* equivalently, the space of linear relations $\sum c_iv_i=0$ has dimension $(n+1)-n=1$ and is spanned by $(1,\dots,1)$; a map exists iff the $w_i$ satisfy every relation satisfied by the $v_i$. ∎

prompt: Let $k$ be a field, let $K = k(x, y)$ be the rational function field over $k$ in the indeterminates $x$ and $y$, and let $\overline{K}$ denote the algebraic closure of $K$. Suppose $s$ and $t$ are elements of $\overline{K}$ with $s^2 = x + y$ and $t^3 = xy$, and let $R = k[s, t]$ be the subring of $\overline{K}$ generated by $k$, $s$ and $t$. Show that every element $r \in R$ is the root of some irreducible monic polynomial $f(Z) \in K[Z]$ of degree at most $6$ with all coefficients in the polynomial ring $k[x, y]$.
answer: Take $f$ = the minimal polynomial of $r$ over $K$: $r\in K(s,t)$, which has degree $\le2\cdot3=6$ over $K$; $r$ is integral over $A=k[x,y]$ (as $s,t$ are), and since the UFD $A$ is integrally closed, the minimal polynomial of an integral element has coefficients in $A$.

solutions.title: Degree bound plus integral closure
solutions.body:
Let $A=k[x,y]$, a UFD with fraction field $K$, and $L=K(s,t)$.

**Degree.** $s$ is a root of $Z^2-(x+y)\in K[Z]$, so $[K(s):K]\le2$; $t$ is a root of $Z^3-xy\in K(s)[Z]$, so $[L:K(s)]\le3$. Hence $[L:K]\le6$. Since $R=k[s,t]\subseteq L$, every $r\in R$ is algebraic over $K$ with minimal polynomial $f\in K[Z]$ monic, irreducible, and $\deg f=[K(r):K]\le[L:K]\le6$.

**Integrality.** $s$ and $t$ are roots of the monic polynomials $Z^2-(x+y)$, $Z^3-xy$ with coefficients in $A$, so they are integral over $A$. The elements of $\overline K$ integral over $A$ form a subring containing $k\subseteq A$, $s$ and $t$, hence containing $R$. So each $r\in R$ satisfies some monic $h\in A[Z]$.

**Coefficients.** In $\overline K[Z]$ write $f=\prod_{j}(Z-r_j)$. Since $f\mid h$ in $K[Z]$, each $r_j$ is a root of $h$, hence integral over $A$. The coefficients of $f$ are $\pm$ elementary symmetric polynomials in the $r_j$, hence integral over $A$; they also lie in $K$. A UFD is integrally closed in its fraction field (if $a/b$ in lowest terms is a root of a monic $A$-polynomial of degree $d$, then $b\mid a^d$, so $b$ is a unit). Therefore all coefficients of $f$ lie in $A=k[x,y]$.

Thus $f$ is irreducible and monic in $K[Z]$, has degree $\le6$, has coefficients in $k[x,y]$, and $f(r)=0$. ∎

prompt:
Let $G$ be a finite group and let $H \subseteq G$ be a subgroup of index $|G : H| = n$.

(a) Show that $|H : (H \cap H^g)| \leq n$ for all $g \in G$.

(b) If $H$ is a maximal subgroup of $G$ and $H$ is abelian, show that $(H \cap H^g) \triangleleft G$ for all $g \notin H$.

(c) Now suppose that $G$ is simple. If $H$ is abelian and $n$ is a prime, prove that $H = 1$.
answer: (a) $|H:H\cap K|\le|G:K|$ with $K=H^g$. (b) $C=C_G(H\cap H^g)\supseteq\langle H,H^g\rangle$, so $C=G$ (then $H\cap H^g\le Z(G)$) or $H^g=H$ (then $H\trianglelefteq N_G(H)=G$). (c) $H\cap H^g=1$, so $|H|\le n$ and $|G|<n^2$; the Sylow $n$-subgroup is normal, so $G=C_n$ and $H=1$.

solutions.title: Intersections of conjugates
solutions.body:
**(a)** For subgroups $H,K$, the map $h(H\cap K)\mapsto hK$ from left cosets of $H\cap K$ in $H$ to left cosets of $K$ in $G$ is well defined and injective, so $|H:H\cap K|\le|G:K|$. With $K=H^g$, $|G:H^g|=|G:H|=n$, giving $|H:H\cap H^g|\le n$.

**(b)** Let $g\notin H$ and $D=H\cap H^g$. $H$ and $H^g$ are abelian and contain $D$, so both lie in $C=C_G(D)$. Since $H\le C$ and $H$ is maximal, $C=H$ or $C=G$.
- If $C=G$, then $D\le Z(G)$, so $D\trianglelefteq G$.
- If $C=H$, then $H^g\le H$, so $H^g=H$ and $g\in N_G(H)$. As $g\notin H$, $H<N_G(H)$, so $N_G(H)=G$ by maximality; then $D=H\trianglelefteq G$.

**(c)** Since $n$ is prime, there is no subgroup strictly between $H$ and $G$ (its index would divide $n$), so $H$ is maximal, and $H\ne G$. Pick $g\notin H$. By (b), $H\cap H^g\trianglelefteq G$; it is contained in $H<G$, so simplicity gives $H\cap H^g=1$. By (a), $|H|\le n$, so $|G|=n|H|\le n^2$. A group of order $n^2$ is abelian (a $p$-group of order $p^2$), and an abelian simple group has prime order, so $|G|\neq n^2$ and $|G|=nm$ with $m=|H|<n$. Then the Sylow $n$-subgroups have order $n$ and their number divides $m<n$ and is $\equiv1\pmod n$, so it is $1$. That Sylow subgroup is normal and nontrivial, so it equals $G$; thus $|G|=n$ and $H=1$. ∎

prompt:
Let $K$ be a field and let $R$ be the subring of the polynomial ring $K[X]$ given by all polynomials with $X$-coefficient equal to $0$.

(a) Prove that the elements $X^2$ and $X^3$ are irreducible but not prime in the ring $R$.

(b) Show that $R$ is a Noetherian ring, and that the ideal $I$ of R consisting of all polynomials in $R$ with constant term $0$ is not principal.
answer: (a) A nontrivial factorization in $K[X]$ would need a factor $aX\notin R$; $X^3\mid X^2\cdot X^4$ and $X^2\mid X^3\cdot X^3$ in $R$ but not the factors, since $X\notin R$. (b) $R=K[X^2,X^3]$ is a quotient of $K[Y,Z]$ (Hilbert basis theorem); a generator of $I$ would be an associate of both $X^2$ and $X^3$.

solutions.title: Degree arguments in K[X]
solutions.body:
Units of $R$ are the nonzero constants (units of $K[X]$ lying in $R$).

**(a)** $X^2,X^3\in R$ are nonzero nonunits. Suppose $X^3=fg$ with $f,g\in R$. This holds in the UFD $K[X]$, so if neither is constant then $\{f,g\}=\{aX,bX^2\}$ with $a,b\in K^\times$; but $aX\notin R$. Hence $f$ or $g$ is a nonzero constant, a unit of $R$, and $X^3$ is irreducible. Likewise $X^2=fg$ with both nonconstant forces $f=aX$, $g=bX$, impossible; so $X^2$ is irreducible.

Not prime: in $R$, $X^2\cdot X^4=X^6=X^3\cdot X^3$, so $X^3\mid X^2X^4$; but $X^3\nmid X^2$ (degree) and $X^3\nmid X^4$ (the quotient would be $X\notin R$). Similarly $X^2\mid X^3\cdot X^3=X^2\cdot X^4$, but $X^2\nmid X^3$ since $X\notin R$.

**(b)** $R$ consists of the polynomials $a_0+\sum_{k\ge2}a_kX^k$, and every $X^k$ with $k\ge2$ is a product of $X^2$ and $X^3$; so $R=K[X^2,X^3]$ is the image of $K[Y,Z]$ under $Y\mapsto X^2$, $Z\mapsto X^3$. $K[Y,Z]$ is Noetherian by the Hilbert basis theorem, and quotients of Noetherian rings are Noetherian.

Suppose $I=(f)$. Then $f$ is not a unit ($I\ne R$), and $f\mid X^2$; since $X^2$ is irreducible, $X^2=uf$ with $u$ a unit, i.e. $f=aX^2$, $a\in K^\times$. Likewise $f\mid X^3$ gives $f=bX^3$. But $aX^2\ne bX^3$. So $I$ is not principal (in fact $I=(X^2,X^3)$). ∎

prompt:
Recall that a field $K$ is algebraically closed if every polynomial $f \in K[X]$ splits over $K$ (is a product of linear factors in $K[X]$). Now let $F \subseteq E$ be an algebraic field extension.

(a) If every polynomial $f(X) \in F[X]$ splits over $E$, prove that $E$ is algebraically closed.

(b) If every polynomial $f(X) \in F[X]$ has a root in $E$ and if $F$ has characteristic $0$, prove that $E$ is algebraically closed.
answer: (a) A root $\alpha$ of an irreducible $g\in E[X]$ is algebraic over $F$; its minimal polynomial over $F$ splits in $E$, so $\alpha\in E$ and $g$ is linear. (b) For $f\in F[X]$ with splitting field $L=F[\beta]$ (primitive element), the minimal polynomial of $\beta$ has a root $\gamma\in E$ and $F[\gamma]\cong F[\beta]$, so $f$ splits in $E$; apply (a).

solutions.title: Reduce to polynomials over F
solutions.body:
**(a)** It suffices to show every irreducible $g\in E[X]$ is linear. Let $\alpha$ be a root of $g$ in the extension $E[\alpha]\cong E[X]/(g)$. Then $\alpha$ is algebraic over $E$, which is algebraic over $F$, so $\alpha$ is algebraic over $F$; let $f\in F[X]$ be its minimal polynomial. By hypothesis $f=\prod(X-e_i)$ with $e_i\in E$, and $f(\alpha)=0$ forces $\alpha=e_i$ for some $i$, so $\alpha\in E$. Thus $g$ is irreducible over $E$ with a root in $E$, so $g$ is linear.

**(b)** By (a) it suffices to show each $f\in F[X]$ splits over $E$. Let $L$ be a splitting field of $f$ over $F$. $L/F$ is finite, and separable as $\operatorname{char}F=0$, so by the primitive element theorem $L=F[\beta]$. Let $p\in F[X]$ be the minimal polynomial of $\beta$; by hypothesis $p$ has a root $\gamma\in E$. Since $p$ is irreducible, there is an $F$-isomorphism $\varphi\colon F[\beta]\to F[\gamma]$ with $\beta\mapsto\gamma$. In $F[\beta][X]$, $f=c\prod(X-\beta_i)$; applying $\varphi$ (which fixes $f$'s coefficients) gives $f=c\prod(X-\varphi(\beta_i))$ in $F[\gamma][X]\subseteq E[X]$. So $f$ splits over $E$, and $E$ is algebraically closed. ∎

prompt:
Let $V$ be a finite dimensional vector space over the field $F$. Suppose $T\colon V \to V$ is a linear operator and let $f(X) \in F[X]$ be its minimal polynomial.

(a) If $f(X)$ has a nonconstant polynomial factor of degree $m$, show that $V$ has a nonzero subspace $W$ of dimension $\leq m$ with $T(W) \subseteq W$.

(b) Conversely, if $V$ has a nonzero subspace $W$ of dimension $n$ with $T(W) \subseteq W$, show that $f(X)$ has a nonconstant polynomial factor of degree $\leq n$.
answer: (a) Write $f=gh$, $\deg g=m$; pick $v$ with $w=h(T)v\ne0$; $W=\mathrm{span}(w,Tw,\dots,T^{m-1}w)$ is $T$-invariant since $g(T)w=0$. (b) The minimal polynomial of $T|_W$ has degree $1\le\deg\le n$ and divides $f$.

solutions.title: Cyclic subspaces and restricted minimal polynomials
solutions.body:
**(a)** Write $f=gh$ with $\deg g=m\ge1$. Then $\deg h<\deg f$, so $h(T)
e0$ by minimality of $f$; choose $v$ with $w=h(T)v
eq0$. Let $W=\mathrm{span}\{w,Tw,\dots,T^{m-1}w\}$; then $W
e0$ and $\dim W\le m$. Note $g(T)w=g(T)h(T)v=f(T)v=0$. Divide: $X^m=q(X)g(X)+r(X)$ with $r=0$ or $\deg r<m$. Then $T^mw=q(T)g(T)w+r(T)w=r(T)w\in W$. Hence $T(T^iw)\in W$ for $0\le i\le m-1$, and $T(W)\subseteq W$.

**(b)** Let $g$ be the minimal polynomial of $T|_W$. Since $W
e0$, $\deg g\ge1$, and by Cayley–Hamilton on $W$, $\deg g\le\dim W=n$. Write $f=qg+r$ with $r=0$ or $\deg r<\deg g$. On $W$, $f(T)$ and $g(T)$ vanish, so $r(T)|_W=0$; by minimality of $g$, $r=0$. Thus $g$ is a nonconstant factor of $f$ of degree $\le n$. ∎

prompt:
Let $R$ be a ring with $1$ and let $V$ be a right $R$-module. Suppose that $V = X \dotplus Y$ is the internal direct sum of the two nonzero submodules $X$ and $Y$.

(a) Show that $0$, $X$, $Y$ and $V$ are the only $R$-submodules of $V$ if and only if $X$ and $Y$ are nonisomorphic simple $R$-modules.

(b) If $X$ and $Y$ are nonisomorphic simple $R$-modules, prove that $\mathrm{End}_R(V)$, the ring of $R$-endomorphisms of $V$, is isomorphic to the direct sum of two division rings.
answer: (a) A fifth submodule $U$ would satisfy $V=X\dotplus U=Y\dotplus U$, giving $X\cong U\cong Y$; conversely a proper submodule of $X$ or the graph $\{x+\theta(x)\}$ of an isomorphism $\theta\colon X\to Y$ would be a fifth submodule. (b) Every endomorphism preserves $X$ and $Y$, so $\mathrm{End}_R(V)\cong\mathrm{End}_R(X)\oplus\mathrm{End}_R(Y)$, division rings by Schur.

solutions.title: Submodule lattice of a sum of two simples
solutions.body:
**(a)** ($\Leftarrow$) Let $X,Y$ be simple and nonisomorphic, and suppose $U\le V$ is a submodule other than $0,X,Y,V$. Since $X$ is simple and $U\not\supseteq X$ (otherwise $U/X$ would be $0$ or $V/X\cong Y$ by simplicity of $Y$, giving $U=X$ or $U=V$), $U\cap X=0$. Then $U+X\supsetneq X$, and $V/X\cong Y$ is simple, so $U+X=V$ and $U\cong V/X\cong Y$. By symmetry $U\cong V/Y\cong X$. Hence $X\cong Y$, a contradiction.

($\Rightarrow$) If $X$ had a submodule other than $0,X$, it would be a submodule of $V$ different from $0,X,V$, and from $Y$ (since $X\cap Y=0$ and it is nonzero). So $X$ is simple, and likewise $Y$. If $\theta\colon X\to Y$ were an isomorphism, $S=\{x+\theta(x)\mid x\in X\}$ would be a submodule with $S\cap X=0=S\cap Y$ and $S\ne0$, so $S\notin\{0,X,Y\}$, and $S\neq V$ since $S\cap X=0\neq X$ — a fifth submodule. So $X\not\cong Y$.

**(b)** Let $\alpha\in E=\mathrm{End}_R(V)$. $\alpha(X)$ is a homomorphic image of the simple module $X$, so $\alpha(X)=0$ or $\alpha(X)\cong X$; by (a) the only submodule of $V$ isomorphic to $X$ is $X$ (not $0$, $V$ by length, nor $Y$). So $\alpha(X)\subseteq X$, and similarly $\alpha(Y)\subseteq Y$. Hence
$$\Phi\colon E\to\mathrm{End}_R(X)\oplus\mathrm{End}_R(Y),\qquad \alpha\mapsto(\alpha|_X,\alpha|_Y)$$
is a ring homomorphism. It is injective (an endomorphism vanishing on $X$ and $Y$ vanishes on $V=X+Y$) and surjective (given $\beta,\gamma$, $\alpha(x+y)=\beta(x)+\gamma(y)$ is well defined because the sum is direct). By Schur's lemma $\mathrm{End}_R(X)$ and $\mathrm{End}_R(Y)$ are division rings. ∎

prompt:
Let $G$ be a finite group with $|G| = 660 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 11$ and suppose that $E \subseteq G$ is a subgroup of order $11$. Assume that $C_G(E) = E$.

(a) Prove that $|N_G(E)| = 55$.

(b) If $M \triangleleft G$, show that either $E \subseteq M$ or $|M| \equiv 1 \bmod 11$.

(c) Show that every minimal normal subgroup of $G$ contains $E$.
answer: (a) $N_G(E)/E\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Aut}(E)\cong C_{10}$, so $|N_G(E)|\in\{11,22,55,110\}$, and only $55$ gives $n_{11}=660/|N_G(E)|\equiv1\pmod{11}$. (b) If $E\not\subseteq M$, $E$ acts on $M\setminus\{1\}$ without fixed points ($C_M(E)=M\cap E=1$), so orbits have size $11$. (c) Otherwise $|M|\in\{1,12\}$; a group of order $12$ has a normal, hence characteristic, Sylow subgroup, contradicting minimality.

solutions.title: N/C theorem and fixed points
solutions.body:
**(a)** $N=N_G(E)$ acts on $E$ by conjugation with kernel $C_G(E)=E$, so $N/E\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Aut}(E)\cong C_{10}$. Hence $|N|=11d$ with $d\mid10$, i.e. $|N|\in\{11,22,55,110\}$. $E$ is a Sylow $11$-subgroup, so $n_{11}=|G:N|\equiv1\pmod{11}$. The candidates give $|G:N|=60,30,12,6$, which are $\equiv5,8,1,6\pmod{11}$. So $|N|=55$.

**(b)** Suppose $E\not\subseteq M$. Since $|E|=11$ is prime, $E\cap M=1$. $E$ acts on the normal subgroup $M$ by conjugation, fixing $1$. An element $m\in M$ is fixed by all of $E$ iff $m\in C_G(E)\cap M=E\cap M=1$. So $E$ acts on $M\setminus\{1\}$ with no fixed points, and every orbit has size dividing $11$ but not $1$, i.e. size $11$. Hence $|M|\equiv1\pmod{11}$.

**(c)** Let $M$ be a minimal normal subgroup and suppose $E\not\subseteq M$. Then $11\nmid|M|$ (else a Sylow $11$-subgroup of $M$, being Sylow in $G$, would be conjugate to $E$, and $M\trianglelefteq G$ would contain $E$). So $|M|$ divides $60$ and by (b) $|M|\equiv1\pmod{11}$; the divisors of $60$ are $1,2,3,4,5,6,10,12,15,20,30,60$, and only $1$ and $12$ are $\equiv1\pmod{11}$. As $M\ne1$, $|M|=12$.

Every group of order $12$ has a normal Sylow $2$- or Sylow $3$-subgroup: if $n_3=4$, the four Sylow $3$-subgroups contain $8$ elements of order $3$, leaving only $4$ elements, which must form the unique Sylow $2$-subgroup. A normal Sylow subgroup $Q$ of $M$ is characteristic in $M$, hence normal in $G$, and $1<Q<M$, contradicting minimality of $M$. Therefore $E\subseteq M$. ∎

prompt:
All rings in this problem are commutative with $1$. A ring $S$ is said to be *finitely generated* if there exist finitely many elements $s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n \in S$ such that every element of $S$ can be written as a sum of products of these generators. Now let $R$ be a ring, let $G$ be a finite group of automorphisms of $R$, and let $R^G = \{r \in R \mid r^g = r \text{ for all } g \in G\}$ be the fixed subring.

(a) If $r \in R$, prove that $R^G$ contains a finitely generated subring $T$ such that $r$ is integral over $T$.

(b) If $R$ is finitely generated, show that $R^G$ contains a finitely generated subring $S$ such that $R$ is integral over $S$.

(c) Let $R$ and $S$ be as in (b). Deduce that $R$ is a finitely generated $S$-module and hence that $R^G$ is a finitely generated $S$-module. Conclude that $R^G$ is a finitely generated ring. (Hint. You can use the fact that any finitely generated ring is a homomorphic image of a polynomial ring in finitely many variables over the integers and hence is a Noetherian ring.)
answer: (a) $p_r(X)=\prod_{g\in G}(X-r^g)$ is monic with $G$-invariant coefficients; let $T$ be the subring they generate. (b) Let $S$ be generated by the coefficients of all $p_{s_i}$; integral elements form a ring. (c) $R=S[s_1,\dots,s_n]$ is spanned by monomials of bounded degree; $S$ is Noetherian, so the submodule $R^G$ is finitely generated over $S$, and generators of $S$ plus module generators generate $R^G$ as a ring.

solutions.title: Characteristic polynomial of the orbit
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $p_r(X)=\prod_{g\in G}(X-r^g)\in R[X]$. It is monic of degree $|G|$, and each $h\in G$ permutes the factors ($g\mapsto gh$), so $h$ fixes every coefficient: $p_r\in R^G[X]$. Let $T\subseteq R^G$ be the subring generated by the (finitely many) coefficients. Since $p_r(r)=0$ (factor $g=1$), $r$ is integral over $T$.

**(b)** Let $s_1,\dots,s_n$ generate $R$ and let $S\subseteq R^G$ be the subring generated by all coefficients of $p_{s_1},\dots,p_{s_n}$; it is finitely generated. Each $s_i$ is integral over $S$, and the elements of $R$ integral over $S$ form a subring, which contains $S$ and all $s_i$, hence equals $R$.

**(c)** $R=S[s_1,\dots,s_n]$ and $s_i$ satisfies a monic equation of degree $d=|G|$ over $S$, so $s_i^{d}$ is an $S$-combination of $1,s_i,\dots,s_i^{d-1}$. By induction, every monomial $s_1^{a_1}\cdots s_n^{a_n}$ is an $S$-combination of the finitely many monomials with all $a_i<d$. So $R$ is a finitely generated $S$-module.

$S$ is a finitely generated ring, hence a quotient of $\mathbb Z[X_1,\dots,X_m]$, which is Noetherian (Hilbert basis theorem); so $S$ is Noetherian. A finitely generated module over a Noetherian ring is Noetherian, so its $S$-submodule $R^G$ (note $S\subseteq R^G$, so $R^G$ is closed under multiplication by $S$) is finitely generated, say $R^G=Sm_1+\cdots+Sm_k$. Then $R^G$ is generated as a ring by the generators of $S$ together with $m_1,\dots,m_k$. ∎

prompt: Let $F$ be a field and let $f(X) \in F[X]$ be an irreducible polynomial. Suppose $E \supseteq F$ is an extension field of $F$ containing a root $\alpha$ of $f(X)$ satisfying $f(\alpha^2) = 0$. Show that $f(X)$ splits over $E$.
answer: The $F$-embedding $\sigma\colon F[\alpha]\to F[\alpha]$, $\alpha\mapsto\alpha^2$, shows all $\alpha^{2^k}$ are roots of $f$; finitely many roots force $\alpha^{2^k-2^j}=1$, so $\alpha$ is a root of unity of some order $N$, and $f\mid X^N-1=\prod_{j<N}(X-\alpha^j)$ splits in $F[\alpha]\subseteq E$.

solutions.title: α must be a root of unity
solutions.body:
If $\alpha=0$ then $f$ is a constant multiple of $X$ and splits. Assume $\alpha\ne0$; we may take $f$ monic, so $f$ is the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $F$.

Since $\alpha$ and $\alpha^2$ are roots of the same irreducible $f$, there is an $F$-isomorphism $F[\alpha]\to F[\alpha^2]$ with $\alpha\mapsto\alpha^2$; as $F[\alpha^2]\subseteq F[\alpha]$, this is an $F$-embedding $\sigma\colon F[\alpha]\to F[\alpha]$. Iterating, $\sigma^k(\alpha)=\alpha^{2^k}$, and $\sigma^k$ maps roots of $f$ to roots of $f$. So $\alpha,\alpha^2,\alpha^4,\dots$ are all roots of $f$ in $E$.

$f$ has finitely many roots, so $\alpha^{2^j}=\alpha^{2^k}$ for some $j<k$, and since $\alpha\neq0$, $\alpha^{2^k-2^j}=1$. Thus $\alpha$ has finite multiplicative order $N\ge1$. The elements $1,\alpha,\dots,\alpha^{N-1}$ are distinct roots of $X^N-1$, which has degree $N$, so
$$X^N-1=\prod_{j=0}^{N-1}(X-\alpha^j)\quad\text{in }F[\alpha][X].$$
Since $\alpha^N=1$, the minimal polynomial $f$ divides $X^N-1$ in $F[X]$, and by unique factorization in $F[\alpha][X]$, $f$ is a product of some of the factors $X-\alpha^j$. Hence $f$ splits over $F[\alpha]\subseteq E$. ∎

prompt: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field and let $M_n(F)$ be the ring of $n \times n$ matrices over $F$. Describe those matrices $X \in M_n(F)$ with the property that all matrices that commute with $X$ are diagonalizable.
answer: Exactly the matrices with $n$ distinct eigenvalues.

solutions.title: Centralizers of diagonal matrices
solutions.body:
**If $X$ has $n$ distinct eigenvalues**, write $X=PDP^{-1}$ with $D=\mathrm{diag}(d_1,\dots,d_n)$, $d_i$ distinct. If $YX=XY$, put $Z=P^{-1}YP$; then $ZD=DZ$, so $z_{ij}d_j=d_iz_{ij}$ and $z_{ij}=0$ for $i\ne j$. Thus $Z$ is diagonal and $Y=PZP^{-1}$ is diagonalizable.

**Conversely**, suppose $X$ does not have $n$ distinct eigenvalues ($F$ algebraically closed, so the characteristic polynomial has a repeated root).
- If $X$ is not diagonalizable, then $X$ itself commutes with $X$ and is not diagonalizable.
- If $X$ is diagonalizable, $X=PDP^{-1}$ with $D$ diagonal and, after reordering, $d_1=d_2$. Let $E_{12}$ be the matrix unit. Then $DE_{12}=d_1E_{12}=d_2E_{12}=E_{12}D$, so $Y=PE_{12}P^{-1}$ commutes with $X$. But $Y\ne0$ and $Y^2=0$, so $Y$ is not diagonalizable (a diagonalizable nilpotent matrix is $0$).

Hence the required matrices are exactly those whose characteristic polynomial has $n$ distinct roots (for $n=1$, every matrix). ∎

prompt:
Let $M$ be a minimal normal subgroup of the finite group $G$ and let $N/M$ be a nontrivial normal subgroup of $G/M$. Assume that $M$ is a $p$-group and that $N/M$ is a $q$-group for some primes $p$ and $q$, not necessarily distinct.

(a) Show that $G = MH$ where $H$ is a subgroup of $G$ having a nontrivial normal $q$-subgroup.

(b) If $M$ is self-centralizing in $G$, prove that $p \neq q$.

(c) If $M$ is self-centralizing and if $H$ is as in part (a), prove that $M \cap H = 1$.
answer: (a) Frattini: with $Q\in\mathrm{Syl}_q(N)$, $N=MQ$ and $G=NN_G(Q)=M\,N_G(Q)$; take $H=N_G(Q)\trianglerighteq Q\ne1$. (b) If $p=q$, $1\ne Z(N)\le C_G(M)=M$ forces $Z(N)=M$ and then $N\le C_G(M)=M$. (c) $M$ is abelian, so $M\cap H\trianglelefteq MH=G$; if $M\le H$ then $G=H$, $Q\trianglelefteq G$ centralizes $M$, so $Q\le M$, impossible.
